source_title: Pat Summitt Leadership Group Definite Dozen
source_description:
Great teams start with a great leader.

Pat Summitt Leadership Group empowers leaders on and off the court to create winning teams using the wisdom and principles of legendary basketball coach, Pat Summitt.

This program harnesses The Definite Dozen principles that were the foundation of Pat Summitt’s winning teams and applies them to leading in the workplace and achieving personal success.

In this series of 14 lessons, you will walk through Pat’s Definite Dozen and gain insights on how you can apply these principles to achieve your goals in life and develop strong relationships along the way.

video.transcript_text:
Meet Pat Summitt: Introduction Featuring Peyton Manning 
 
Peyton Manning, 2021 Pro Football Hall of Fame Inductee & Super Bowl Champion 
Hi, everyone. Peyton Manning, here. I’m thrilled that all of you are here today to hear the 
words of wisdom put forth by my dear friend, Pat Summitt. Pat was not just an iconic basketball 
coach. She was a trailblazer for women, a champion for gender equality, and an amazing 
educator who graduated 100 percent of her student-athletes at the University of Tennessee.  
Pat was clearly an American treasure. She used to say, ‘Nobody cares how much you know until 
they know how much you care.’ Pat’s caring attitude motivated her to create a formula for 
success and leadership in life called the Definite Dozen. These principles were the foundation 
of her programs for decades. 
 
Narrator 
Pat Summitt was a leadership and coaching superstar. Her stats alone are the stuff of legend. 
1,098 wins, 16 SEC titles, eight national championships, eight-time SEC coach of the year, 
seven-time NCAA coach of the year, Naismith coach of the century in 2000, and one of The 
Sporting News’ 50 greatest coaches of all time.  
Pat Summitt’s career was nothing short of spectacular, but her stats, as extraordinary as they 
are, only tell part of the story. Pat Summitt’s influence extends beyond the court to the lives 
she impacted and the lessons she left behind for achieving greatness.  
This is the story of a farm girl who fell in love with basketball and grew up to change the world 
of sports forever. Pat’s coaching tree continues to make an impact on the game today. Her 
influence has left an indelible impression on the entire sporting world.  
Pat Summitt always demanded the best from others and held herself to the same standard. 
When she was diagnosed with early onset dementia Alzheimer’s type in 2011, Pat faced it head 
on and decided to keep coaching. She stayed in the public eye while dealing with a crippling 
disease and displayed the sort of courage and resilience that mark a true leader.  
Those who tuned in for what many assumed would be Pat’s last season saw a woman bolstered 
by the tremendous support from the community she had cultivated at Tennessee. True to form, 
Coach Summitt kept on fighting and led her team to their 16th SEC championship. It would be 
the last time she performed the champion’s ritual of cutting down the basketball after the 
game.  
A few weeks later, Pat Summitt decided it was time to move on from the great passion of her 
life. In 2012, she retired from her position as head coach of the Lady Vols and was named head 

coach emeritus. That same year, she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom and the 
Arthur Ashe Courage Award.  
Even as she stepped away from the spotlight Pat never admitted defeat. Instead, she shifted 
her focus to the fight against Alzheimer’s. Shortly after her diagnosis, Pat and her son Tyler 
created the Pat Summitt Foundation, an organization for awarding grants to nonprofits 
dedicated to advancing research into treatment and a cure for Alzheimer’s. Pat Summitt was in 
attendance when in January 2015 the University of Tennessee Medical Center and the Pat 
Summitt Foundation announced a partnership to build the Pat Summitt Clinic for furthering 
treatment capabilities, research initiatives, and family support for Alzheimer’s and other 
dementias. Sadly, Pat would not live to see the clinic’s opening in 2017. She passed away at the 
age of 64 on June 28, 2016.  
Shortly after her death, the Pat Summitt Leadership Group was formed to spread the words and 
teachings of Pat Summitt, using film, educational programs, and publishing, the Pat Summitt 
Leadership Group uses the core principles of Pat’s Definite Dozen to help leaders of all ages 
find personal and professional success.  
Pat’s influence lives on with every life that continues to be impacted by the enduring wisdom of 
her leadership philosophy and practice. Pat Summitt was more than a coach. She was a role 
model, a lifelong teacher, and a sterling example of courage and leadership.  
Her legacy is that of being the most successful coach in the history of women’s basketball, but 
she lived a life that goes beyond stellar statistics. It’s a life filled with lessons for what it looks 
like to win with people and leave the world a better place because of it.

steps.source_title: Pat Summitt’s Gift for Leaders Who Follow
steps.exact_visible_copy:
Pat Summitt’s Gift for Leaders Who Follow

Great leaders can be studied, and their principles and approaches emulated. In Pat Summitt’s case, decades of anecdotes from players and assistant coaches could give us at least a working understanding of what she did as a leader to become the most effective and successful college basketball coach of all time. However, Coach Summitt went one step further. She came up with a formula for outstanding leadership and peak performance. 

This formula, explored and applied in this learning experience, provides a very direct pathway to success that leaders and ascending performers can follow to more consistently and predictably achieve their goals. She called it The Definite Dozen, and it represents 12 critical habits and commitments that form the foundation of success for any leader or ascending performer who wants to improve and put themselves and those they lead in a much better position to win!

The Workbook for Reflection Activities

We have provided you a Definite Dozen Workbook in Microsoft Word format to accompany this online experience. It is not intended to be shared with the course instructors or participants. You can use this document as your personal learning journal and for note-taking as you work through the materials.  At many points along the way, we will ask you an open-ended reflection question where we'd really like you to think about the concept being introduced and how it might play out in your current or future leadership. To make the most of this experience, please respond to these open-ended questions honestly and consider also responding in your workbook. We have intentionally included questions that will help you apply the Definite Dozen principles, and your responses will serve as valuable guidance as you put the principles into practice. 

When you receive one of these questions, think about it, submit your response, and consider saving your response in your workbook for future reference and reflection. You can download a PDF and/or Word version of the workbook below.

Welcome to the Pat Summitt Definite Dozen Leadership Program!

If you aspire to be an effective leader, you may have pondered the question, "Are we born to be leaders, or can we develop the capacities we need in our life experience to lead effectively?" Pat in Her Own Words

There is no such thing as self-respect without respect for others.

Pat Summitt

Respect Yourself and Others: Pat in Her Own Words

m1v1_transcript.pdf
115.2 KB

Defining leadership self-respect

Leadership self-respect includes both the level of respect leaders have for themselves, and the level of respect teammates observe the leader has for themselves.  

For example, a leader who shows up looking professional, in a good state of health, rested and ready, sends the message to the team that they care enough about themselves to bring the best version of who they are to the team. Then, the team will often respond well to the leader, and they become more likely to respect themselves in the same way.  

This creates a success cycle that builds momentum and begins to improve results.

video.transcript_text:
Respect Yourself and Others: Pat in Her Own Words 
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
My mom taught me a lot about respect. She only went through the ninth grade … loving, caring, 
respectful of everyone. The only person in my life I’ve never heard anyone say a bad word 
about was my mom. But she taught me about respect.  
If you want to have a great team, everyone on your team has to feel important. Do they not? 
My secretary has been with me (for) 23 years. Now that’s a long time to be with anyone. My 
husband hasn’t even lived with me that long.  
But Katie is the person that I talk to every morning when I get up. And when I started out 
working with Katie, I didn’t know Katie. I might call her and say, ‘Katie, look. Tell me the four 
things I have to do this morning.’ I quickly learned to say, ‘Katie’ … on a Monday morning … 
‘how was your weekend? How are you doing? How’s your family doing?’ And start to develop 
(the) relationship.  
My student managers … when you do what we do, we just recruit a lot of people to come help 
us. And our student managers are really, really key. We got ready this year to go to the Final 
Four. I turned in my list of who on our staff would be going to the Final Four.  
And Joan Cronan, our AD (athletic director), called me up and she said, ‘Pat, is it really 
necessary to take all eight student managers to the Final Four?’ And I said, ‘How many of your 
administrators are going?’ She said, ‘It’ll be fine if you take all eight of your student managers.’ 
You know, they’re the people behind the scenes. They’re not the up-front people.  
But everyone in your organization has to feel that they will bring something to the table and 
something to the team to allow you to be successful.

In this section, we will share Pat Summitt’s simple truths of respect and self-respect. As you reflect on these truths, think about their application in your work.

Be the boss you would want for yourself

Earn and cultivate respect by demonstrating competence, staying strong in difficult situations, and thoughtfully advocating for the team

Scenario Complete!
START OVER

Pat Summit and her team

You can't demand it or whack it out of them!

Pat Summitt was a notoriously demanding coach. Creating a demanding environment with respect, high standards, and rigor brings good outcomes.  

However, imposing hard work or punitive measures on others to gain respect is futile. She used the example of forcing her players to run suicides and push themselves physically as a mechanism for earning respect. That demand, she went on to realize, would never build the kind of respect she needed to build a championship team. She learned that respect must be cultivated and earned.

The stack of cards below contains some actions that either can be considered great ways to earn respect or ways to destroy or harm it. Sort the cards into the appropriate category based on what we've discussed so far.

6/6 Cards Correct
REPLAY
Great ways to earn respect
Ways to destroy or harm respect

Conversely, the leader must communicate to the team that they too must work hard to earn the respect of each other and of the leaders. This expectation helps teams to pull together to create the reciprocal support needed to establish mutual respect all around.

Respect Yourself and Others: Introduction Featuring Teela Jackson 
  
Coach Pat Summitt 
Sometimes I ask myself, ‘Could I play for me?’ The answer is not always yes. 
Back in 1974, I was a 22-year-old head coach, and I had four players who were 21. I was hard on 
them and myself and everyone around me. I thought I had to be. I thought that’s how you 
commanded respect. My first day on the job I stood in front of a packed room of Tennessee 
undergrads who came to open tryouts for the team. I decided I was going to set the tone right 
then and there. I was going to let everyone know how in charge I was.  
I gave a long speech about how demanding it would be to play for the Lady Volunteers. Well, 
after that meeting at least 30 kids never came back. The opening day of practice was pretty 
funny, too. I worked those prospects up and down the court at full speed for two solid hours.  
At the end of that, I ordered them to run a bunch of conditioning drills. I ran them in ‘suicide 
drill’ after ‘suicide drill.’ A group of four young ladies were running together. When they got to 
the end of the line they just kept on running. They ran out the door and up the steps and I 
never saw them again. 
My ideas about how to command respect have changed since then. I’ve learned you can’t 
demand it or whack it out of people with a two-by-four. You have to cultivate it, in yourself and 
those around you. 
  
Teela Jackson, Vice President, HR 
Over the years, Pat Summitt recognized that she could not simply demand respect from her 
players. She had to earn it, just as they had to earn her respect and the respect of their peers.  
As we dive into Pat’s Definite Dozen principle, Respect Yourself and Others, you will see how 
Pat’s philosophy about respect evolved over time, and how Pat emphasized trust and respect to 
build championship-winning teams.  
In addition, we will examine how to use peer-to-peer accountability for achieving results as well 
as ways in which we can demonstrate respect for ourselves and behaviors that might 
undermine the respect we hope to gain from our teammates. So, buckle up, and enjoy the ride 
while you respect yourself and others.

Pat Summit and her team
You can't demand it or whack it out of them!
Pat Summitt was a notoriously demanding coach. Creating a demanding environment with respect, high standards, and rigor brings good outcomes.

However, imposing hard work or punitive measures on others to gain respect is futile. She used the example of forcing her players to run suicides and push themselves physically as a mechanism for earning respect. That demand, she went on to realize, would never build the kind of respect she needed to build a championship team. She learned that respect must be cultivated and earned.

video.transcript_text:
Respect Yourself and Others: It Starts with You, Featuring Doug Buce 
 
Doug Buce, President, CLO, Boing Dynamics, Inc. 
There are three dimensions of energy you need to foster to be a healthy teammate. And when 
you intentionally foster these areas, respect for yourself will grow. 
The most obvious dimension is physical. Here are some tips to foster this dimension.  
Get up and move. Have stand-up meetings. Take a break every hour or so to walk around your 
floor. If you have a gym at work or nearby, use it. Stay committed to your own personal 
wellness and well-being. A heathy you is a productive you. 
Eat better. Don’t skip meals. Eat healthy snacks like fruit, nuts, and yogurt. Stay hydrated, 
because even mild dehydration zaps cognitive ability. 
Get more sleep. Go to bed an hour earlier, and turn off all technology an hour earlier before 
you get into bed, to clear your mind. 
The next dimension is mental. You can increase your mental activity in the following ways.  
Quit multitasking. It drains mental energy and actually reduces efficiency by up to 40 percent. 
Although Pat was a master multitasker, it does take a mental toll and lowers overall 
productivity. Leverage your mornings for success throughout the day. You are more focused in 
the morning. By the way, 10:26 a.m. is the most focused minute of your day. 
Use your vacation days or personal time off. Oh, and leave your computer at home. Use this 
time to rest and reenergize. You will come back a stronger, more focused leader with new ideas 
and inspiration.  
And turn off your smartphone notifications. Digital distractions are driving our society to a 
counter-productive state.  
Dedicate specific times of the day to respond to email and other communications. 
The third dimension is emotion. 
Most of us feel best when we’re positive, so, at the beginning of each week, write down a list of 
things you’re thankful for. Share this list with others as appropriate and reflect on all the good 
things in your life.  
Laugh a little. Pat believed in the power of laughter and was able to laugh at herself. When Pat 
was 29 years old, she got braces and one night she and (assistant coach) Mickie DeMoss were 
scouting at a high school game, and while watching the game, Pat and Mickie chatted and ate 
popcorn.  

Finally, Mickie said, ‘You know, you have popcorn stuck in your braces.’ Mickie razzed her about 
it until she started giggling. Pat laughed at herself and said, ‘It was a good feeling, too.’ That’s 
when you know you have a real self-respect. 
And finally, tell others how much you appreciate them. They will feel more bonded to you, and 
it makes you feel good. 
There you have it. Physical, mental, and emotional dimensions that you should focus on to 
create a healthier you worthy of respect. Pat embodied these dimensions and it showed in both 
her life and in her leadership. 
Are you respecting yourself enough so that others, in turn, will respect you?

Physical Habits for Building Self-Respect from Within
Physical Habits for Building Self-Respect from Within

Coach Summitt found that several physical habits help build and sustain self-respect from within:

Keep moving
Meet standing up
Have a brain break each hour
Go exercise
Eat well
Hydrate
Sleep
Remove technology from where you sleep

Select the Start button to learn more about each habit and practical ways to put them into action.


Physical Habit 1

Keep moving

In a world where you can run a business from a computer or mobile device, it’s easy to begin to become sedentary. The world is a better place when we are healthy, so resisting remaining sedentary is good for your long-term physical health.

The habit of Keeping Moving does even more! 

Moving on a consistent basis:

changes your emotional and mental states
enhances blood-flow, and in some cases, moves blood away from your legs and feet and toward the most important destination: your brain

Physical Habit 2

Meet standing up

This may seem a bit awkward at first but give it a try! Many business leaders today begin the morning with a standing, huddle meeting where team members quickly review their priorities for the day and aspirations for outstanding performance.

So why is it helpful to stand up for these meetings? Slouching in your chair, scooting down and getting too comfortable, and perhaps to some degree, relaxing too much, keeps us from feeling active and engaged.

A quick standing meeting that allows you to touch base and review major talking points is both healthy for the body and dynamic for the brain.

Physical Habit 3

Have a brain break each hour

Have you ever found yourself checking social media during your workday? Most of us have. Have you ever found yourself thinking about a movie or music at a time when you’re supposed to be working? Our brains are full of distractions that we must learn to ignore to some degree. 

But part of the reason why we get distracted is because our brains need a bit of a break. In learning, the younger you are, the more breaks you need. In preschool, for example, lessons are made up of very small chunks, giving children playtime in between. The fact is, we aren’t that different than children. 

Although there may be times when this isn’t possible, there are some definite neurological, energy, and creative advantages to taking a break every 60 minutes. Some companies today, for example, actually build in social media update moments throughout the day so that team members can reconnect with their outside world or their social networks. 

Whatever you do with your break, giving yourself five minutes every 60 minutes or so to break your concentration from your work and check in on something you enjoy, setting a timer, and bringing yourself back to your work quickly, can represent a habit that will renew your spirit and ultimately help you to concentrate much better after your break is over.

Physical Habit 4

Go exercise

The best leaders and top performers almost always follow an established exercise routine. They might be training for a marathon, getting a little bit more in shape for an upcoming social event or vacation, or they may have decided that they are going to go for a walk at least four days a week in nature as an expression of gentle exercise. Whatever your workout routine may be, it builds incredible self-confidence and self-respect to consistently follow that routine.  

When you make a commitment to yourself to exercise, and then remain faithful to the commitment to yourself, you not only feel physically better from the exercise, but you also feel emotionally and mentally better about the person you are becoming by staying healthy and keeping your promises.  Also, the time you give up exercising is worth it because invariably the version of you that comes back after exercise will be much more creative and effective.  

When your teammates observe you setting a habit and routine for yourself and living with it, they are far more likely to do the same for themselves and for the work they bring each day.

Physical Habit 5

Eat well

There is no shortage of information on healthy eating today. Although there is a wide variety of purported, healthy diets, what’s important for our purposes is that you do your own research and select eating habits that give you energy and allow you to be your absolute best.  

Most research-based, healthy diets include:

a healthy observation of portion sizes
careful restrictions on fast food
the avoidance of an overindulgence of fat and sugar, and 
the habit of enjoying food that provides nutrients and vitamins to help us stay healthy and replenished.  

Physically, we’ve all seen people that begin to either embrace or depart from the habit of eating well. Leaders who have teams that follow successfully and eagerly recognize that their leader has self-respect, as demonstrated by how they choose to feed themselves.

Physical Habit 6

Hydrate

Doctors will tell you that many of their patients are dehydrated.  Transcendent, high-achieving athletes like NFL quarterback Tom Brady drink more water than most of us can imagine. Water is the ultimate system-cleansing agent and helps with cell rejuvenation. After all, our brains and bodies are made up mostly of water, so consuming our very essence helps keep us energized and rejuvenated.

Physical Habit 7

Sleep

Did you ever hear someone say, “You’d better sleep on it?”  There’s wisdom in letting ideas percolate, giving time for reflection, overnight or otherwise. But there are also numerous other advantages to the habit of sleep.  The great Kobe Bryant was famous for sleeping just a few hours a night, committing even more hours of the day to honing his craft.  Keep in mind, there are individuals who obviously can get by with less sleep, but it’s actually very rare. Most of us can find a way to “get by” with less sleep, but generally speaking, we aren’t at our physical and mental peak when we deny ourselves sleep.  

What would it be like if you were actually rested? How much better could you be?

Physical Habit 8

Remove technology from where you sleep

You may have heard about this old trick for doing well on exams in school. For decades, instructors have suggested that students study for their exam in the place where the exam is going to take place. The reason this is said to work is because when you learn something new, your surroundings and the context of your surroundings make a difference. Learning to hit a tennis ball on a golf driving range wouldn’t create the familiarity in your brain that learning it on a tennis court would.

This idea of familiarity makes a difference to learning something new, and the same is true with technology. If your handheld tools are used on a consistent basis to help you work as hard as you can with the utmost concentration and engagement at work, it’s a bad idea to curl up with that same piece of technology and try to go to sleep. Many people struggle mightily with their sleep habits, due in part to the habit of taking technology to bed with us and our eyes being exposed to the stimulating screen light. Thoughtful leaders once again respect themselves enough to remove these distractions when it benefits them, which in this case results in the restorative advantage of sleep.

Summary

To summarize, there are several important physical habits that can help you establish and build self-respect from within:

Keep moving
Meet standing up
Have a brain break each hour
Go exercise
Eat well
Hydrate
Sleep
Remove technology from where you sleep

Most of us can find a way to “get by” with less sleep, but generally speaking, we aren’t at our physical and mental peak when we deny ourselves sleep.  

What would it be like if you were actually rested? How much better could you be?

Remove technology from where you sleep

You may have heard about this old trick for doing well on exams in school. For decades, instructors have suggested that students study for their exam in the place where the exam is going to take place. The reason this is said to work is because when you learn something new, your surroundings and the context of your surroundings make a difference. Learning to hit a tennis ball on a golf driving range wouldn’t create the familiarity in your brain that learning it on a tennis court would.

This idea of familiarity makes a difference to learning something new, and the same is true with technology. If your handheld tools are used on a consistent basis to help you work as hard as you can with the utmost concentration and engagement at work, it’s a bad idea to curl up with that same piece of technology and try to go to sleep. Many people struggle mightily with their sleep habits, due in part to the habit of taking technology to bed with us and our eyes being exposed to the stimulating screen light. Thoughtful leaders once again respect themselves enough to remove these distractions when it benefits them, which in this case results in the restorative advantage of sleep.

Summary

Keep moving
Meet standing up
Have a brain break each hour
Go exercise
Eat well
Hydrate
Sleep
Remove technology from where you sleep

changes your emotional and mental states

steps.source_title: Mental Habits for Building Self-Respect from Within
steps.exact_visible_copy:
Four Mental Habits for Building Self-Respect from Within

In addition to physical approaches to building self-respect, four key mental habits can help establish self-respect from within:

Minimize multitasking
Leverage mornings
Take distraction-free vacations
Turn off notifications

Select the Start button to learn more about each habit and practical ways to put them into action.


Mental Habit 1

Minimize multitasking

Teenagers are famous for telling their parents that they are much better at multitasking than their older teachers or family members. The fact is, multitasking represents a division of your attention, no matter your age. And with every division of your attention, you are less focused and less able to bring the best of yourself to whatever you’re doing. So, to demonstrate self-respect, adopt the habit of minimizing multitasking.  

As a general rule, try to limit multitasking to activities that don’t require a generous amount of brainpower. For example, if you are doing a load of laundry while boiling some eggs and waiting for the dishes in the dishwasher to run a cycle, you may be working in a very efficient manner. 

However, balance that against really important tasks or obligations, such as writing a key report or creating a multimedia presentation for an upcoming meeting. In those instances, the best leaders and peak performers understand that minimizing distractions in those moments and putting full mental power towards the task at hand is a far more powerful strategy for achieving better results. It also helps to demonstrate self-respect and represents an excellent habit for others to follow.

Mental Habit 2

Leverage mornings

There’s no doubt that many of the most successful leaders are "morning people."  They get up, get going, and get more done before work than many get done all day long. Competitive leaders will start making progress on their goals before others even start their day.  

Now, being a morning person sometimes has to do with your body’s natural rhythms, suggesting that if you are not a morning person, you may never be at your best in the early morning hours. The degree to which you can become a morning person is perhaps debatable. 

However, even if you cannot bring it to yourself to get up earlier than others and get a lot of work done before anybody else does, the notion of leveraging mornings has a secondary application.  To leverage mornings can also mean that you follow the old Stephen Covey adage of putting "first things first."  This simple adage suggests that prioritizing the things that matter the most and getting them done before anything else helps foolproof your success and make it more likely that progress towards a goal will happen.  

Whether it’s at 5 a.m. or simply a commitment to schedule the top priorities as early in the day as possible, you’re far more likely to make progress if you put what matters most at times of the day that won’t be interrupted.  Why do so many successful leaders exercise so early in the morning? Often times they will suggest to you that this is a time when interruptions are less likely to occur, allowing them to tackle their health before turning themselves over to their work.

Mental Habit 3

Take distraction-free vacations

The video specifically recommends that you take your vacation time and refrain from taking your work with you. It’s often a sign of honor in hyper-competitive work environments to check in on work during vacation, responding to copious emails and checking in on key performance indicators.  This is not necessarily a sign of strength or self-respect.   

By always checking in, there is an implied suggestion that the system can’t work for a while without you, and that’s not a good sign if you’re a leader.  Checking in during vacations also deviates from your commitment to taking care of yourself and giving yourself the gift of rest.

Great leaders and top performers often take vacations that are more engaging and rigorous than their work. They may trek a challenging landscape or engage in some interesting and rigorous retreat. While a few emails may take longer to respond to, there is a recognition of self-care and the expansion of personal interests that only serve to make a leader or top performer more valuable to the system and the team.  Refraining from staying attached to laptops and other devices goes back to our recommendation about technology as well. Taking a sabbatical from technology for a week definitely has physical, emotional, and spiritual advantages.

Mental Habit 4

Turn off notifications

Notifications are good for business—the app business, that is.  Remember, as wonderful as our phones and mobile devices have become in helping us execute our daily functions, there is embedded functionality within them designed primarily to advance the business interests within the applications on our phones. It is in the best interest of our most popular social media destinations to keep our eyes glued to the screen and to continue scrolling. The same is true for all of our embedded news channels or personal interest apps. Think of each of them like baby birds in the nest, screeching for the mother’s attention. Every time one of these baby bird applications chirps and your phone causes you to move away from whatever you’re doing and towards the content, you are submitting to their business intention instead of your own.  

To be clear, there’s nothing wrong with a good product trying to entice us and capture our attention. However, what we would suggest is that you at least turn off your notifications and refrain from responding like Pavlov’s dog every time one of your favorite app destinations pushes out an update. Simply put, our brain can’t withstand that many interruptions a day. We’re more likely to be successful if we can schedule our own time to catch up on our favorite social media. We get to limit the exposure and choose to spend time in these spaces at a point where it makes sense in our day - not when the app company decides to focus and get our attention.

Summary

To summarize, there are four important mental habits that can help you establish and build self-respect from within:

Minimize multitasking
Leverage mornings
Take distraction-free vacations
Turn off notifications
1234
START AGAIN

steps.source_title: Emotional Habits for Building Self-Respect from Within
steps.exact_visible_copy:
Three Emotional Habits for Building Self-Respect from Within

We've gone over both physical and mental habits for building self-respect. There's yet another dimension: emotional habits. There are three important emotional habits that can help you establish and build self-respect from within:

Establish weekly and daily gratitude practice
Unleash laughter
Declare appreciation

Select the Start button to learn more about each habit and practical ways to put them into action.


Emotional Habit 1

Establish weekly and daily gratitude practice

We all can visualize a life and levels of performance that are better than our current situation. More importantly, there are others out there who could only dream of having what you have. To that end, one of the most empowering emotional habits you can establish is to specifically and directly recognize the people, things, achievements, situations, etc. for which you should be grateful.

Writing down what you should be grateful for each week or even daily can give you a deep sense of fulfillment and happiness. It also helps you in striving to achieve more so that our brains begin to see that pleasant things come from hard work and discipline. There’s nothing worse than, for example, working hard towards a goal, achieving that goal, and then not taking the time to be grateful for your achievement!

Emotional Habit 2

Unleash laughter

Throughout history, jesters and comedians have been in high demand.  Funny people tend to remain surrounded by friends and find themselves included in a variety of social situations, often with more invitations than time to fulfill them. This is true because laughter is an amazingly euphoric emotional state. When we laugh, we breathe, we are distracted from our troubles or our daily grind, and we land in a lighter, happier place, even for just a moment. 

This is so important for leaders and high performers, especially in high-stress situations. Leaders who are incredibly competitive can, and arguably should, remain very demanding of themselves and others around them. While this culture of demand may be necessary overall, it can create an ongoing level of stress that requires a break, and that break can come from laughter. Therefore, as a leader or top performer, be willing to laugh at yourself, your circumstance, a situation, or just a crazy moment in the day. Be willing to laugh uproariously, sharing joy with others.  

Psychologists and sociologists have suggested that sharing a laugh helps bring groups closer, which is why you see humor, even in small doses, being used all the time by successful teams. This use of humor does not suggest that everything is a laughing matter, or that your system needs a steady diet of slapstick jokes. Instead, make room for laughter that can break the tension, give yourself an opportunity to connect, and then get right back to the work at hand with renewed focus and joy.

Emotional Habit 3

Declare appreciation

When the people you work with feel good, it’s palpable to others. The leader who genuinely and authentically declares appreciation for coworkers creates an amazing feeling of goodwill on the team or individual. Think about the last time you looked into someone’s eyes and thanked them and told them how much you appreciated them for who they were or what they were doing.

How did you feel the last time someone said that to you? When that appreciation is declared, it’s impossible to ignore, and we share a mutually good feeling. When you declare appreciation for somebody in a group, everyone feels that good grace, and the team invariably grows closer and improves their bond to one another.

Summary

To summarize, there are three important emotional habits that can help you establish and build self-respect from within:

Establish weekly and daily gratitude practice
Unleash laughter
Declare appreciation

Instead, make room for laughter that can break the tension, give yourself an opportunity to connect, and then get right back to the work at hand with renewed focus and joy.

Emotional Habit 3

Declare appreciation

When the people you work with feel good, it’s palpable to others. The leader who genuinely and authentically declares appreciation for coworkers creates an amazing feeling of goodwill on the team or individual. Think about the last time you looked into someone’s eyes and thanked them and told them how much you appreciated them for who they were or what they were doing.

How did you feel the last time someone said that to you? When that appreciation is declared, it’s impossible to ignore, and we share a mutually good feeling. When you declare appreciation for somebody in a group, everyone feels that good grace, and the team invariably grows closer and improves their bond to one another.

Summary

To summarize, there are three important emotional habits that can help you establish and build self-respect from within:

Establish weekly and daily gratitude practice
Unleash laughter
Declare appreciation

Emotional Habit 1
Establish weekly and daily gratitude practice

We all can visualize a life and levels of performance that are better than our current situation. More importantly, there are others out there who could only dream of having what you have. To that end, one of the most empowering emotional habits you can establish is to specifically and directly recognize the people, things, achievements, situations, etc. for which you should be grateful.

Writing down what you should be grateful for each week or even daily can give you a deep sense of fulfillment and happiness. It also helps you in striving to achieve more so that our brains begin to see that pleasant things come from hard work and discipline. There’s nothing worse than, for example, working hard towards a goal, achieving that goal, and then not taking the time to be grateful for your achievement!
Emotional Habit 2
Unleash laughter

Throughout history, jesters and comedians have been in high demand.  Funny people tend to remain surrounded by friends and find themselves included in a variety of social situations, often with more invitations than time to fulfill them. This is true because laughter is an amazingly euphoric emotional state. When we laugh, we breathe, we are distracted from our troubles or our daily grind, and we land in a lighter, happier place, even for just a moment.

This is so important for leaders and high performers, especially in high-stress situations. Leaders who are incredibly competitive can, and arguably should, remain very demanding of themselves and others around them. While this culture of demand may be necessary overall, it can create an ongoing level of stress that requires a break, and that break can come from laughter. Therefore, as a leader or top performer, be willing to laugh at yourself, your circumstance, a situation, or just a crazy moment in the day. Be willing to laugh uproariously, sharing joy with others.

Psychologists and sociologists have suggested that sharing a laugh helps bring groups closer, which is why you see humor, even in small doses, being used all the time by successful teams. This use of humor does not suggest that everything is a laughing matter, or that your system needs a steady diet of slapstick jokes. Page 11 of 18
Respect & Accountability
Play Video

Respect Yourself and Others: Respect and Accountability, featuring Doug Buce

m1v4_transcript.pdf
122.1 KB

One of the most powerful elements of being a team is the possibility of supporting each other to improve individual and collective performance and outcomes. This improvement is generated by respect and accountability, thoughtfully established by both leaders and committed team members who work together for excellence.

Two Truths about Team Respect and Accountability

Here are two important truths to keep in mind:

TRUTH #1: 
"We go is more important than ego." 

                                                   Pat Summitt




How many times have you been on a team when one or more members of the team began working toward their own advantage vs. what’s good for the team? This is the chasm between we go (the team) and ego (the individual). 

When teams are fully formed, they realize that the team is better when all members consistently focus on what’s good for their collective purpose instead of focusing on individual opportunities. In most cases, individual performance can be dramatically enhanced when the team is there to provide support. 

In other words, when teams are fully formed and working effectively, the individual or ego doesn’t have to suffer unnecessarily for the sake of the team because the team, while working together, improves the team outcome and sets the best environment for individual performance.

TRUTH #2: 
Team (peer-to-peer) accountability has more impact than power-based accountability.







With power-based accountability, individuals might be motivated to perform or react due to the expectations of a particular person in some level of authority. This level of influence isn’t an earned area. It is assigned. It means you pay attention or respond because of the authority that exists. A certain amount of authority will always exist. However, the best organizations and the most successful teams respond to leadership because they genuinely respect the leader. 

When the leader creates an expectation of accountability, there’s a desire to reach the expectation out of respect for the leader. To take it one step further, the very best teams don’t wait for the leader’s accountability to kick in. They create their own by supporting and holding each other accountable on the team. This is always the most powerful form of accountability because it’s immediate and ever present. 

Work cultures that are creative, positive, and engaging can’t remain that way if one leader alone carries that expectation. There are frankly too many moments when the boss isn’t there. This has to be an accountability where everybody engages without being forced. 

"Teamwork allows common people to obtain uncommon results."

                                                    Pat Summitt

Pat Summitt's 3 Keys to Team Accountability

Team, or peer-to-peer accountability, is the most powerful form of accountability that helps teams dramatically improve their production and output. Let's look at Pat Summitt’s keys to developing this accountability with teams or groups:

bullet

Authentic trust

bullet

Healthy debate

bullet

Commitment

Which of these 3 approaches do you already use in your team?

Do you trust your team?
+
Do you encourage healthy debates?
+
Do you build team commitment?
+

video.transcript_text:
Respect Yourself and Others: Respect and Accountability, Featuring Doug Buce 
 
Doug Buce, President, CLO, Boing Dynamics, Inc. 
You know a team is great when all the players respect each other, have good chemistry, and 
everyone pulls their own weight. Under these conditions, collaboration is healthy and 
productive, everyone is positive, everyone is fully dedicated, and team success is measured 
more by “we go” versus ego. 
Let’s face it. There will be times when certain people that are respected don’t make great team 
members. They make mistakes. They aren’t fully dedicated. They undermine the work of 
others. How do you handle that? Well, most team members expect the team leader to step in 
and fix the problem. And that is understandable because that’s the default approach. That 
approach is called power-based accountability where the leader forces accountability. 
In Patrick Lencioni’s book, The Five Dysfunctions of a Team, he talks about the best form of 
accountability—peer -to-peer accountability, where individuals hold each other accountable for 
results. If you see me doing something that is detrimental to the team goal, you talk with me 
about it. You see the best sports teams do this all the time. Somebody misses an assignment 
and a team member immediately gets in their face. Now, it may be a bit awkward and 
unprofessional to get into each other’s faces in the workplace, but there is a right way to do it—
and a need to do it. 
Three things have to be in place for peer-to-peer accountability to work. The first is trust. We 
need to have honest trust for the team, not artificial harmony where the team pretends that 
things are good. We need to be able to trust each other and know that what we share will not 
be used against us at a later time.  
The second is our ability to engage in healthy debate. We can, in a healthy way, debate 
conflicting views on how to approach work challenges.  
And the third thing is commitment. If all of us on the team have a clear vision of the goals and 
we buy in to the approach because we’ve had a chance to weigh in on the decision, we can 
commit. 
Those three things—authentic trust, healthy debate, and commitment —provide the foundation 
to have peer-to-peer accountability discussions. 
Pat created trust of her staff and players by being consistent, always keeping her word, and 
getting to know her players and staff on a personal level. Pat also had no problem engaging in 
healthy debate. Her assistant coaches were never “yes” people. They were always empowered 
to disagree with Pat and offer an alternative viewpoint. And there is no doubt Pat was 100 
percent committed to her teams and their goals.  

Pat’s mastery of peer-to-peer accountability was one reason for her extraordinary success.  
Do you create an environment of trust, healthy debate, and commitment? Are you leveraging 
peer-to-peer accountability on your team?

states_text.text:
If yes, that's great! Teams work at their creative best when there is trust within the team and organization. With trust, the team's ability to dream, work creatively, take chances, and innovate flourish.




Can you imagine an industry-leading technology company today suddenly firing an engineer for trying to develop a creative app that happens to fall short? How much innovation would exist within that company when others see their colleague get fired for trying something new? The trust would be broken and innovation would fade.

If so, then kudos to you as a leader! The best leaders indeed value the diversity of multiple perspectives. They can help the team consider numerous options when making decisions.




What’s essential to make this work are two things:




Distinguish the difference between disagreement and being disagreeable. Disagreeable people always seek negative or contrarian perspectives, which is not good for the system or the people within it. In thoughtful debates, team members debate ideas, not each other.
Encourage healthy disagreement with, and even debate in, the face of the leader. Having a line of “yes” people only serves to reinforce the current direction. If individuals feel the need to speak up and offer a different perspective, they should be given the authority to do so.

If you do, then way to go! Commitment is a simple act of coming together, acknowledging the pursuit of a particular goal or outcome, and agreeing that aiming at that outcome will be an ongoing, often-reviewed, emotionally-based exercise.

steps.source_title: Respect-Busting Behaviors You Must Avoid and Eliminate
steps.exact_visible_copy:
Page 14 of 18
Respect-Busting Behaviors You Must Avoid and Eliminate

It’s difficult to build an environment with a profound level of respect without recognizing those variables that can have a significant capacity to diminish or degrade a culture of respect. 

Play Video

Respect Yourself and Others: Respect-Busting Behaviors, featuring Doug Buce

m1v5_transcript.pdf
165.1 KB
Behaviors to Avoid

The following are elements that Pat Summitt understood were respect-busting behaviors that had to be recognized and consistently dealt with in order to create a respectful, high-performing environment.

START 

Behavior 1

Gossiping

If you have to look over your shoulder when telling someone on your team something, maybe you shouldn’t say it. Gossip almost always serves to diminish someone in the organization or on the team and ultimately hurts the team as a whole.

Establishing the expectation that honest sharing is welcome, but gossip isn’t will go a long way in building an honest and authentic team atmosphere. 

12345

Behavior 2

Hoarding Information

Information is power, in almost every professional setting, on every team. Individuals who engage in respect-busting behaviors will often hoard key pieces of information, either for political purposes or for personal, situational advantage. Once again, this needs to be addressed and directly discouraged.

12345

Behavior 3

Being a Blame-Thrower

Blame-throwers refuse any level of accountability and are always looking for opportunities to throw other people under the bus for lack of progress or failure. Rather than honestly acknowledging what’s going on with the situation, energy is spent literally finding blame and taking previous time away from finding solutions.

Creating an environment where the team owns and learns from its mistakes, and where teammates cheer on each other's victories, creates a far better environment.

12345

Behavior 4

Being Late

Individuals who fail to be on time consistently send a very powerful message. They may believe that they are special and that the system should wait for them. Maybe they are sloppy or can't manage their time. None of these are good for building a strong and interconnected team.

12345

Behavior 5

Being Negative

"What’s wrong" is usually easier to discover than "what’s right." Furthermore, if the leader is unusually negative, the team will get the message, and they will begin to pursue and present negativity on a more consistent basis, simply following the expectations of the leader.

Negativity can operate like a magnet, pulling in more negativity every day. Therefore, negative individuals cannot be allowed to flourish without confrontation. An environment where negativity is allowed loses respect and momentum.

12345
Think about it

Do you recognize any of these behaviors in your team? Within you? Can you think of any strategies to end them?

Gossiping
Hoarding information
Being a blame-thrower
Being late
Being negative

Respect Yourself and Others: Respect-Busting Behaviors, Featuring Doug Buce 
 
Doug Buce, President, CLO, Boing Dynamics, Inc. 
It takes a lot of intentionality, and sometimes a lot of time, to gain the respect of others. But 
respect-busting behaviors occur daily, and they are committed by everyone at every level. Not 
intentionally, but out of a lack of awareness. Don’t destroy the respect capital you have built for 
yourself by engaging in these behaviors.  
So, what are they? Good question. Here are some of the top respect-busting behaviors. 
Gossip. You know when that other team member comes to you and says, ‘I shouldn’t be telling 
you, but …?” Well, we kinda feel good, we’re in the know. But there’s also that part of you that 
thinks, “What are you saying about me behind my back?” Gossip is team poison. 
Hoarding information. Doesn’t it drive you crazy when someone has information that can help 
the entire team, but they keep it to themselves? People may do that because it gives them a 
sense of power. They want to be relevant. I’ve got something you don’t. Do you want to be 
relevant? Share the information. Help the team succeed. 
Throwing others under the bus. You know, some people walk around the office with a blame-
thrower on their back. They’re not accountable for anything and they will gleefully pull the 
trigger and torch everybody and everything else. Not my fault, but yours. Sometimes, things are 
your fault. Own it. It may not feel good at the time but it’s the professional thing to do. And you 
will gain respect. 
Not being on time. Doesn’t it drive you crazy when other people believe their time is more 
valuable than yours? 
 
Sound bite of Pat Summitt 
That word respect can be so powerful. I want you to think about that. Being on time is respect, 
isn’t it? 
 
Video resumes with Doug Buce 
Lateness sends a message that you’re either too sloppy, too careless, or too special to be on 
time. 
Negativity. We know people commiserate and talk about how bad things are at times but, if 
you are that person who always starts those conversations, stop it. Negativity kills team morale. 

And negativity is like a magnet. After a while, all of those negative people get stuck to each 
other. They’re like a toxic blob that poisons the team. Don’t be that toxic person. 
And finally, taking credit for others’ work. If you’ve ever been on the receiving end of this, you 
know how it feels. (If) in front of the boss at a committee meeting that team member says, “I 
did this, or I found that.” It’s infuriating because the team did this or found that. A team that 
respects each other operates as one.  
Don’t let these respect-busting behaviors creep into your life. If respecting yourself and others 
is a priority, become dedicated to modeling appropriate behaviors for your team as well as for 
others for whom you may be an unknowing role model.

activity.instructions_text: The following are elements that Pat Summitt understood were respect-busting behaviors that had to be recognized and consistently dealt with in order to create a respectful, high-performing environment.

states_text.text:
Behavior 1

Gossiping

If you have to look over your shoulder when telling someone on your team something, maybe you shouldn’t say it. Gossip almost always serves to diminish someone in the organization or on the team and ultimately hurts the team as a whole.

Establishing the expectation that honest sharing is welcome, but gossip isn’t will go a long way in building an honest and authentic team atmosphere.

Behavior 2

Hoarding Information

Information is power, in almost every professional setting, on every team. Individuals who engage in respect-busting behaviors will often hoard key pieces of information, either for political purposes or for personal, situational advantage. Once again, this needs to be addressed and directly discouraged.

Behavior 3

Being a Blame-Thrower

Blame-throwers refuse any level of accountability and are always looking for opportunities to throw other people under the bus for lack of progress or failure. Rather than honestly acknowledging what’s going on with the situation, energy is spent literally finding blame and taking previous time away from finding solutions.

Creating an environment where the team owns and learns from its mistakes, and where teammates cheer on each other's victories, creates a far better environment.

Behavior 4

Being Late

Individuals who fail to be on time consistently send a very powerful message. They may believe that they are special and that the system should wait for them. Maybe they are sloppy or can't manage their time. None of these are good for building a strong and interconnected team.

Behavior 5

Being Negative

"What’s wrong" is usually easier to discover than "what’s right." Furthermore, if the leader is unusually negative, the team will get the message, and they will begin to pursue and present negativity on a more consistent basis, simply following the expectations of the leader.

Negativity can operate like a magnet, pulling in more negativity every day. Therefore, negative individuals cannot be allowed to flourish without confrontation. An environment where negativity is allowed loses respect and momentum.

Think about it

Do you recognize any of these behaviors in your team? Within you? Can you think of any strategies to end them?

Hoarding information
Being a blame-thrower
Being late
Being negative

m1v6_transcript.pdf

Remember, there are two very important types of respect you need to be a good leader:

Self-respect, which you must reflect on and pursue on your own. That self-respect doesn’t have to be advertised. It will be obvious to other people as you carry yourself in front of others.

Earned respect, which creates a condition where you earn the respect of the team or your followers and team members earn each other’s respect by similarly setting high standards and remembering the importance of respect in their lives.

We learned in this section that individual success most often emerges thanks to thoughtful, reflective, teams who learn to engage in certain attitudes and behaviors that contribute to trust and success, and avoid elements that can degrade or destroy trust and success. Sort the stack of cards below into these two categories to summarize what we've covered.

8/8 Cards Correct
REPLAY
Contributes to trust & success
Degrades trust & success

Finally, one of the most important points Pat Summitt makes about the principle of Respect Yourself & Others revolves around the importance of remembering that everyone at one point or another can lose confidence, feel insecure, and generally be uncertain about what to do next. This is what it means to be human and the best leaders remain engaged in behaviors that generate respect and drive outcomes that will improve the team.

video.transcript_text:
Respect Yourself and Others: Wrap-Up, Featuring Teela Jackson 
 
Teela Jackson, Vice President, HR 
Pat Summitt said that ambition can transform you. The starting point of ambition is self-
respect. Pat also reminds us that there is no such thing as self-respect without respect for 
others. Individual success is a myth. No one succeeds all by herself. 
In this module, we learned that peer-to-peer accountability can be an effective tool where we 
hold each other accountable for results. But for peer-to-peer accountability to work, three 
things must already be in place—trust, healthy debate, and commitment. Without these 
principles, our team will not be ready for peer-to-peer accountability to work within our 
system. 
Second, respect starts with you and the respect you have for yourself. Your team needs a 
healthy you, and taking care of yourself reflects your level of self-respect. After all, if you don’t 
respect yourself, you aren’t giving your team the respect they deserve because you aren’t going 
to be able to give it your all. 
Finally, we were reminded of some detrimental respect-busting behaviors like gossip, 
negativity, not being on time, and taking credit for other people’s work. Become aware of these 
behaviors that diminish your respect capital, and be intentional to not engage in them.  
Pat said, “Self-respect can be hard won. I know. It’s an ongoing process.” But once you attain it, 
it will bear you up through almost anything, whether you’re dealing with a difficult parent, 
teasing from others, self-doubt, or ordinary work tensions. In critical situations, we all ask 
ourselves the same silent question, “Do I deserve to succeed?”  
Under pressure, uncertainty can creep into the subconscious of even the most outwardly 
confident person, including me.  
If you haven’t developed self-respect and mutual respect with those around you, the whisper is 
deep down … you know you don’t deserve it.  
The next time you ask yourself—“Do I deserve to succeed?”—make sure the answer is yes.

RESUME

Pat Summitt made it clear. Leadership is exhibited when the team is willing to follow. Furthermore, teams won’t follow a leader they don’t respect. So, how do leaders get followers on the team to respect them? It starts with observing leadership self-respect and respecting others.

video.transcript_text:
Take Full Responsibility: Pat in Her Own Words 
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
You know, I always tell the story about when I came home and he (my son Tyler) was 9 years 
old and I go in and he’s upset and I walk in the room and I said, ‘Tyler, what’s wrong with you?’ 
And he goes, ‘I got cut.’  
Well, my first thought is—What coach in East Tennessee would cut my son? I mean, think about 
it. You know, put him at the end of the bench but give him a uniform.  
And then I guess the coach came out in me and I looked at Tyler and I said (voice trails off) …  
He had a basketball under each arm and he was crying so hard and I said, ‘Tyler, if you wear out 
both of those basketballs I promise you, I guarantee, you will make the team next year. Do you 
hear me?’  
And he goes, ‘Yes, ma’am.’  
And I said, ‘Well, then let’s get it done.’  
And he goes, ‘Mom, will you help me?’  
I said, ‘Son, I will help you but I will not start your engine. You must start your engine every day. 
Do you understand that?’  
And he goes, ‘Yes, ma’am.’  
(It was) a defining moment in his life. It changed him. It changed his focus, it changed his work 
ethic, his drive, and I haven’t had to motivate him since then. Not at all. It’s a pretty incredible 
story.  
But, you know, as I look back and I tell people about it they’re like, ‘Well, it’s not that easy, is 
it?’ And I said, ‘It is, if you’re driven to be successful.’  
And I’ve always been driven to be successful. I hate to lose.

activity.instructions_text:
Tyler Had Been Cut from the Basketball Team
Pat got to watch her son Tyler come home from basketball practice and share with her that he had been cut from the team. What would you do and how does it relate to responsibility?

states_text.text:
Tyler Had Been Cut from the Basketball Team
Pat got to watch her son Tyler come home from basketball practice and share with her that he had been cut from the team. What would you do and how does it relate to responsibility?

How Did Tyler Feel?
The pressure and potential impact of getting cut for Tyler emotionally was tremendous. A young kid trying to make the team happened to be the son of the most successful developer of basketball talent.

Was It Fair?

Pat and Tyler didn't feel that it was fair. Justified or not, the feelings of frustration in those moments when you don't feel that you are being treated fairly can be overwhelming.

CONTINUE

You could see anger in Pat's eyes. Seeing her son treated unfairly was frustrating. Why couldn't Tyler's coach simply give him a jersey and keep him on the bench? So what would you do if you were Pat?
1 Talk to Tyler
2 Talk to Tyler's coach
That's exactly what Pat did, she talked to Tyler. The only way for Tyler to earn his coach's, and others', respect was to put in the hard work and earn that respect.

states_text.state_name: "Not fair" Is Part of the Job
states_text.text:
"Not fair" Is Part of the Job

No matter what your leadership position is, you won't always be treated fairly. The first step is to acknowledge that unfair treatment is both possible and indeed part of the job.

CONTINUE

states_text.state_name: "It’s Not Fair. So Go to Work, and Make It Right."
states_text.text:
"It’s Not Fair. So Go to Work, and Make It Right."

The only way to gain respect and self-respect when you feel you are being treated unfairly is to find the opportunity to work hard and make the difference.

CONTINUE

states_text.state_name: "I Will Help, But I Won’t Start Your Engine."
states_text.text:
"I Will Help, But I Won’t Start Your Engine."

Pat offered her son exactly what he needed — help improving his basketball skills. However, igniting motivation was Tyler's own job. This realization enabled him to stay focused on his goals in life.

CONTINUE

states_text.state_name: “You Have to Start Your Engine Every Day.”
states_text.text:
“You Have to Start Your Engine Every Day.”

Motivation, inspiration, and passion can only come from within a person. Your role as a leader is to create conditions to help people around you grow and find the best versions of themselves.

START OVER
Pat could've talked to Tyler's coach, demanding respect for her legendary status and pressuring Tyler back to the team. Instead, Pat chose to talk to her son and teach him how to build self-respect.

Successful Leaders Commit to Learning and Growth

In this video, we addressed the startling statistic that over half of the executives assigned to a new position are unsuccessful in that position and either move on or are removed from their post in just a couple of years. This would suggest a couple of things. First, leadership positions are very difficult. Second, perhaps not everyone is cut out to be a leader. That would seem pretty obvious. Third, and perhaps most importantly, the job of being a leader requires a lot of what you're engaged in right in this moment - learning, reflection, practice, and growth.

If there's one thing you will see that is consistent through the Definite Dozen made famous by Coach Pat Summitt, it's that commitment to growth is non-negotiable. Even highly successful leaders will eventually fail if they don't commit to growth, so keep this leadership statistic in mind. Failure is remarkably consistent in the positions you strive for. Own the fact that the job is going to be tough, believe in yourself, and commit to growth. You definitely want to be on the right side of that 50% statistic!

Having a Title Isn't Enough

One of the mistakes leaders make is assuming that once the title is ascribed to them, the world around them changes. Granted, if suddenly you earn a huge promotion and much more responsibility is put upon you, the people around you may look at you a bit differently. However, the overall effectiveness of a leader or the power and influence they are able to wield has a lot more to do with their influence and authority than their title. In other words, your ability to adopt the right practices and to treat people in a way that gives you the best opportunity to be successful as a leader will have a greater impact than any change in job title that you are given.

Take Full Responsibility: Introduction Featuring Katy Kvalvik 
 
Video clip of Coach Pat Summitt 
You don’t have to be necessarily the captain of a team. You can impact people and lead by 
example and how you handle the role you’re in and the responsibility that you have. 
 
Katy Kvalvik, Founder of Southwestern Empowerment, Executive Coach, Corporate Training & 
Speaker 
Ask anyone who has been leading for a while and they’ll tell you leading required a lot more of 
them than they understood when they took the job.  
A recent Harvard Business Review article revealed that 50 to 60 percent of executives fail within 
the first 18 months of being promoted or hired. That startling revelation leaves us wondering 
what can be done to increase the success rate for those of us who are leading, who aspire to 
lead, and for those of us who want to expand our skills. Sixty out of 100 executives miss the 
mark. And one thing we know that they all share in common is that they’re in charge … of 
something.  
So, what do the other 40 possess that pushes them into the category of success? Is it raw 
talent? Functional competence? Do they have the right internal connections or is it just dumb 
luck? Leading isn’t easy, and being responsible means you’ll have to make tough decisions that 
may not be very popular with everyone on your team.  
The truth is, being in charge or having a title, isn’t enough. And, as we’re going to learn in the 
module, Coach Pat Summitt’s approach to leadership can teach us some powerful and relevant 
lessons about what it means not just to be in charge but to take full responsibility as a leader.  
Leadership requires sacrifice, commitment, and action. Those descriptions sound like 
something out of a superhero movie. But, what about when leadership requires us to make 
hard, unpopular decisions?  
Who can think about basking in the glory of sitting in the big chair when there is a seemingly 
constant stream of complaints and problems? It’s no wonder that taking full responsibility 
crushes nearly 60 percent of newly promoted or hired leaders.  
When you complete this module, you’ll have some practical examples and actionable strategies 
for being the kind of leader that takes full responsibility.  
As Coach Summitt believed, there are no shortcuts to success and you can’t assume larger 
responsibility without taking responsibility for the small things, too.

Responsibility and Modeling: Or Born Knowing?

Sometimes when thoughts or skills are so ingrained within us, or are such an integral part of a specific team or group, they can almost be taken for granted. Take riding a bike as an example. You weren't born with the knowledge of riding a bike. However, after some trial and error, you began to get the hang of it and eventually you rode a bike effortlessly. This is the aspiration of skill development on a team or with a group: developing skills that may be foreign in the beginning, but altogether commonplace and easily accessible at the end.

Watching someone else riding a bike shows a future rider how it should be done. It also provides a sense of engagement and motivation.

One of the most powerful ways of developing skills like this is through modeling. We can't assume, for example, that a child who wants to learn to ride a bike would have any idea what to do if they hadn't seen their older brother and sister or parent riding a bike before them.

Watching someone else ride a bike gives the would-be rider a model to follow and maybe even an incentive to get up on that bike seat. Modeling not only shows us the skills and dispositions needed to demonstrate the behavior, but it also provides, in some cases, a sense of engagement and motivation, driving us to work even harder to get to where we want to go.

Four Elements of Full Responsibility

Element #1: Own Everything
+
Element #2: See the Big Picture
+
Element #3: Embrace the Mundane
+
Element #4: Get Others to Embrace Responsibility

Organizational culture isn’t built with a slogan or a speech. It’s built by individual actions, repeated and observed. Put another way, if others working in your organization see the leader taking responsibility, they are far more likely to likewise take full responsibility. We’ve all known leaders who fail to take responsibility. They are quick to lash out, blame others, and look for excuses. This can create an environment where the leader can quickly feel burned out in their job. This may seem a bit counterintuitive. Wouldn’t it be more exhausting to take full responsibility? Wouldn’t rejecting responsibility be more relaxing? Actually, the answer is no. In leadership positions, arguably the most stressful part of the job revolves around aspects of the work that are beyond your control. If the leader is in control of the surroundings and can make changes, they at least have a fighting chance to be competitive. The problem with individual performers or leaders who fail to take full responsibility is that without knowing it, they are creating a lot of stress for themselves.

Think about your own life. Are you happier when you sit back and blame others for your personal circumstance, or do you feel better and perhaps less stressed when you take responsibility for your life and take action to resolve whatever personal goals or objectives you might have? This same dynamic exists in organizations or on teams.

If you want to see less turnover, support those you work with by taking full responsibility.

Toni, a very energetic, middle manager in a manufacturing company in the Midwest, found that her division was facing a logistical nightmare as suppliers had failed to fulfill an order, and their warehouse was completely backlogged. She observed her line workers working as fast as they could to meet the demand. With only four members on her shift team, there was real concern that their backlog was going to affect the delivery of the goods to the client. So, in that moment, she rolled up her sleeves and jumped in and helped. Her presence increased productivity, and there was real hope that they could get caught up.

By jumping in and getting involved, the message was sent that there was no job too mundane for anyone in the organization. Furthermore, everyone understood that the leaders in the organization saw themselves as responsible — for everything. This creates a deep sense of ownership about the work and makes it more likely for everyone to embrace responsibility in the future.

To that end, organizations who don’t show support for their employees and are led by leaders who don’t take responsibility are more likely to see a great amount of employee turnover. If you want to minimize the amount of "Help Wanted" signs you hang as a leader, support those you work with by taking full responsibility and showing them that this is indeed the type of culture that you’re trying to create.

Take Full Responsibility: Introduction to Modeling, Featuring Karen Hilton 
 
Karen Hilton, Founder and President, Executive Coaching 
Being a leader, while deeply rewarding, is ultimately a pursuit that you have to want. As Coach 
Summitt said, ‘If you don’t want responsibility, don’t sit in the big chair.’ Your long-term 
effectiveness as a leader depends on your ability to take full responsibility.  
Fail to model the behaviors of leadership that your organization values and people will follow 
you only because they have to, not because they want to. Miss the mark on replicating the 
leadership that can make your company great and you’ll lose your best leaders and burn out 
yourself.  
Modeling is doing the work, both the mundane and the significant, that you require others to 
do in a way that sets a standard that produces positive results people can see and feel. So, it 
begs the question, ‘Why do we model?’  
In a 21st century environment where change happens at blazing speed, isn’t it just easier for 
busy leaders to tell people what to do? Leaders who rely on telling their teams what to do and 
how to act on a regular basis have sunk to a level of micromanaging.  
Modeling, at its best, does two things that inspires teams both individually and collectively to 
become wholly committed to helping your team win.  
First, modeling creates a roadmap for others to follow. It’s the how behind the what.  
Second, modeling reinforces credibility and trust in the eyes of those you lead. You’re doing 
what you’ve asked others to do. Pat Summitt modeled the behavior she wanted to see from her 
staff and her players for her entire career.  
In the early days, Pat had no choice but to set the example as she drove the team bus, taped 
ankles, and washed jerseys. But even after the Lady Vols experienced tremendous success and 
Pat had access to many more resources, she still modeled the behavior she wanted to see.  
Now (that) we know what we mean by modeling full responsibility and why we do it, let’s shift 
and talk about how to model full responsibility.

Responsibility and Modeling: Or Born Knowing?

Sometimes when thoughts or skills are so ingrained within us, or are such an integral part of a specific team or group, they can almost be taken for granted. Take riding a bike as an example. You weren't born with the knowledge of riding a bike. However, after some trial and error, you began to get the hang of it and eventually you rode a bike effortlessly. This is the aspiration of skill development on a team or with a group: developing skills that may be foreign in the beginning, but altogether commonplace and easily accessible at the end.
Watching someone else riding a bike shows a future rider how it should be done. It also provides a sense of engagement and motivation.

One of the most powerful ways of developing skills like this is through modeling. We can't assume, for example, that a child who wants to learn to ride a bike would have any idea what to do if they hadn't seen their older brother and sister or parent riding a bike before them.
