states_text.text:
To fully understand this concept, maybe the best illustration might come from a non-example. Several years ago, the commercial airways were bombarded with a rather famous retired athlete spokesman selling home repair insurance. This insurance covered water-heater repair, dishwasher and refrigerator malfunction, and other expensive home repairs. To encourage the viewer to buy the insurance, the video snippet in the commercial would show the celebrity spokesman hovering over a broken dishwasher, a failed heater, or a melting freezer, each time repeating a phrase over and over again. “Not my problem! Not my problem! Not my problem!”

 

While this pitch might have provided comfort to those who are seeking insurance coverage, it’s the exact opposite perspective that leaders who take full responsibility embrace on a daily basis. When you’re a leader who takes full responsibility, everything is your problem. The system breaks down in your company? Yes, it’s your problem. The person that you hire fails to execute at their job? Yes, it’s your problem. The person that you hire hires someone else, and that person struggles? Yes, that’s your problem. Finally, your boss does something that makes it tough for you to do your job as a leader and you still have to perform at a great level with a good attitude? You guessed it. Yes, it’s your problem.

 

As a leader, to take full responsibility means that you have to own everything. You have to own the problems, the solutions, the history —even if you weren’t part of it —the challenges, and the opportunities. You also have to own the truth that the success of the organization can be driven by a number of factors such as opportunity and even some luck. But, historically speaking, the most consistent element of success within an organization revolves around leadership behaviors and dispositions. Without ownership of the full responsibility of what it means to lead, the positive momentum and success aren't as likely to be achieved.

The best leaders have blue-sky horizons. They see amazing results in front of them and visualize people in their organization performing at outstanding levels. They see the big picture and recognize that in order to achieve something new and better, the leader must first visualize it, and then work diligently on these big-picture perspectives that will deliver better outcomes.

How many times have you seen leaders who have forgotten or ignored the mundane, only to their peril? During his run for re-election, President George H. W. Bush wanted to increase his relatability with the public, so he went shopping in a grocery store with Secret Service in tow. When he went to check out at the cashier station, he had no idea how to scan his groceries because for quite some time, he had avoided that responsibility. His lack of understanding of the mundane — in this case, shopping for groceries — didn’t help his goal in creating political relatability with the general public.

 

In leadership positions, failure to embrace the mundane can also hurt leadership progress. When Pat Summitt began her coaching career, she had to do everything from driving the team bus to washing the team jerseys. There was no task associated with her program that she didn’t embrace. Indeed, she owned everything, including the boring and mundane, and the big picture. As success emerged, she never forgot the mundane, and neither should you as a leader. Even though as a CEO or major division leader you may not necessarily understand some of the technical elements of the mundane work going on in different parts of the organization, you must embrace the importance of the mundane details, and be willing to roll up your sleeves and do them if needed.

We Adopt What We See

Model the behaviors that you want others to exhibit.

Once leaders begin to display certain behaviors, it's highly likely that others will follow suit. We tend to follow the leader and observe the modeling that's going on. Therefore, if you're a leader in an organization and you don't like how things are going, one of the very first, and perhaps the most powerful steps you can take, is to model the kinds of behaviors that you want to see others exhibit. It's a formula that works with coaching, parenting, and indeed in the leadership realm.

This also is an important dynamic to consider when you think about the fact that unchecked behaviors are also modeled. If you are a leader and you have a very important person underneath you (perhaps another leader who reports to you), operating in a way that is unbecoming of the organization, their impact will have a cascading influence on others and potentially have a much more negative result than you could have ever imagined.

Careful Modeling Requires Clarity 

Define behaviors to set clear expectations for the performance.

If the goal is to provide modeling that shapes behavior, then that behavior has to be clearly defined. In the case of coaching basketball, if you want a strong team captain, what specific behaviors do you expect from any team captain? If you can't define those behaviors, then it's hard to make expectations for anybody that does the job! So, one of the more important steps that a leader can take to reach expectation with this request is to get really clear about the kinds of performance they expect, so that the expectation of modeling can emerge.

Comfort and Aspiration Don’t Go Together 

"If comfort is what you are seeking, don't aspire. Ambition is uncomfortable by definition." - Pat Summitt

Ambition is uncomfortable.

If you aspire to something that isn't easy to obtain, it's going to require something special. It might require that you develop a special set of skills that others don't have or are unwilling to commit themselves to develop.

How many coaches over the years attempted to create schemes, recruit players, and probably take on a number of additional strategies designed to disrupt the team success of Pat Summitt? In addition to any internal pressure, Pat had to deal with entire programs from all over the country built around arguably strong leaders wholly committed to defeating her and her team. That kind of pressure undoubtedly made even Pat Summitt uncomfortable. 

Are you willing to aspire to something difficult and deal with the discomfort that comes with both the pursuit and realization of peak performance?

Great Leaders Understand They Don’t Have All the Answers 

The more elevated the leader or the expert, the more likely it is that they ask others for advice, or admit to not having all the answers. Socrates, arguably one of the wisest human beings in history, is famous for saying, “The more I know, the more I realize I know nothing.” Without question, great leaders ask others for opinions, continue to grow, and recognize that even in the execution of their main function or position, they don't have all the answers.

Socrates came to his conclusion because he learned so much and realized there was so much more to consume. It's almost like going on a hike and reaching the top of a clearing only to see even greater heights on the mountain just ahead. This is what great leaders understand...and they never stop climbing towards that next peak, recognizing the need to continue to learn and grow.

CONTINUE

video.transcript_text:
Take Full Responsibility: How to Model, Featuring Karen Hilton 
 
Karen Hilton, Founder and President, Executive Coaching 
Famous psychologist Albert Bandura studied modeling behaviors and found that we adopt the 
same types of actions that we observe and see modeled in others. So it becomes critical that 
the behaviors we’re modeling are actually behaviors we want our team members to replicate.  
One key component of modeling is assessment. Leaders must identify and define the measures 
of success for ourselves, our team, and our customers. Be clear on the definition of a successful 
outcome.  
Then, ask, ‘How is that outcome measured? Is it the right measurement?’ If not, what do we 
need to start, stop, or continue doing to ensure we’re successful in assessing the right things.  
Coach Summitt said, ‘You can’t pick and choose the days you feel like being responsible.’  
Coach Summitt would follow with this powerful insight, ‘If comfort is what you’re seeking, then 
don’t aspire. Ambition is uncomfortable by definition.’  
I can’t state it enough. The best leaders you and I know don’t have all the answers. But, they do 
model the behaviors they want to see in others. In fact, great leaders are quick to acknowledge 
that they don’t have all the answers. They get good at repeating the behavior of trusting and 
relying on the collective contribution of the team.  
Next, a leader who is taking full responsibility must consistently calibrate. That is, measure and 
gather honest feedback on how they’re performing and adjust accordingly. Responsibility 
evolves.  
So as leaders, if we refuse to evolve, we might as well wear a T-shirt that says, ‘I’m stuck.’ 
Ultimately, our success as a leader, a team, or an organization is only as certain as our ability to 
seek input against what we think or know.  
In order to grow, you must accept new responsibilities, no matter how uncertain you may feel 
or how unprepared you are to deal with them. Unless, of course, you want to do the same thing 
day after day for the rest of your life.  
As you consider your own performance as a leader, ask this, ‘Who can serve as a strong source 
of feedback and accountability? Is your model of success accurate? Does your performance 
metric stretch you?’  
Or are you in a comfort zone?

Replication: Let’s Not Make Success an Accident

In business today, one of the most important questions asked is whether the task at hand, or the strategy and skill being implemented, is replicable. Put another way, will the success being experienced in this moment be an episodic accident? Will we experience the success and then be unsure as to how to make that success happen again? Or, can we be strategic and find ways of purposefully replicating the steps necessary to make sure that we are in fact engaged and performing at the highest levels?

This is why leaders today must have an eye on modeling and replication. We have to model the behaviors or skills we know lead to success, and we need to make sure that whatever systems we put in place give us a fighting chance to make replication a predictable, systematic set of behaviors.

The most successful leaders or peak performers understand that the more they can replicate in terms of the specific practices that lead to success, the greater chance there is that deeper levels of innovation and profound and lasting levels of success can and will emerge.

Practice the Art of Taking Full Responsibility

Taking responsibility isn't necessarily a natural thing. In many cases, before becoming a leader, your responsibilities may revolve around making sure that your own performance is up to speed without necessarily owning the results of others. However, once you become a leader, the shift happens. You suddenly have your own set of responsibilities to be executed consistently, as well as purview over the work and ultimately the outcomes of others.

This obviously is challenging because leaders aren't afforded the opportunity in most cases to stand idly by with your arms crossed, watching the work of others, and owning every element of process and product. Instead, in the midst of executing your own numerous tasks and responsibilities, you have to make sure that the performance, and performance products of others, meets the standards and expectations of the organization. You are ultimately responsible for their work.

This can be frustrating for a new leader, and there may even be a quiet voice within that wants to resist it. There is obviously always a chance of a colossal failure. Let's say that this new leader is chugging along and suddenly, one of the members of the team has a rather significant failure, the leader's supervisor observes the failure, and confronts the leader. While the leader may provide the details about what happened, identifying the individual at the center of the conflict, it's essential that the leader own both the process and the product in relationship to the shortcoming happening at the moment.

It would be a mistake of the leader to speak to his or her superior and absolve themselves of the responsibility, simply blaming the person in their unit. This does not breed confidence in anyone and sends the message that responsibility is something that can shift depending on the circumstance.

Good leaders own the responsibility and share the credit.

Wear the Responsibility, Share and Give Away the Credit

With this idea of responsibility comes a very interesting juxtaposition. As a leader you must wear the responsibility, owning the problems or missteps of your team. You also must be willing to share and preferably give away the credit when the team or group or unit does exceptionally well. 

This means, if a significant mistake is made on a team, the team leader ultimately needs to own the mistake and address those issues with the individual(s) at hand.

Second, this also means that if there is a significant victory, it's very important that the leader give credit where credit is due and ensure that warm assurance of praise and compliments shines down on those who are on the frontline executing a majority of the work. Again, to a novice leader, this may seem unfair. There may be a quiet voice inside of you who wishes you could get the credit and avoid the blame. In fact, however, it just doesn't work that way.

Leaders who own their mistakes and give credit for the victories tend to be on the winning side time and time again, and respect and adulation will indeed follow.

Responsibility and Holding People Accountable

One of the most powerful things a leader can do to improve the performance of an organization or a team is to give away responsibility. If you give away both power and responsibility, you will develop significant skills in others.

Most of the work we do today requires a greater degree of technical acumen, and the old system of waiting for the boss to identify problems and recommend innovations no longer works. Most jobs today are such that the boss might have a general idea about what needs to be done, but in many cases the person in the layman’s position has to establish priorities, create schedules, and identify how they can be most efficient and effective.

It’s pretty clear: leaders need to give away power and let their people innovate, experiment, and grow. Furthermore, leaders need to measure results and hold accountable those who are asking for change and improvement.

video.transcript_text:
Take Full Responsibility: Replicating, Featuring Karen Hilton 
 
Karen Hilton, Founder and President, Executive Coaching 
We’ve covered why modeling is so essential to taking full responsibility as a leader. The second 
key is replicating. Replicating involves actively coaching, mentoring, and sponsoring others 
within your organization to exhibit the behaviors that will lead to success. Replicating inspires 
curiosity and encourages commitment from others to practice the art of taking full 
responsibility.  
So, as a leader, how do you initiate the practice of replicating? First, make sure responsibilities 
are clearly delineated and that everyone understands their role. The best way to handle 
responsibility is to break it down into smaller parts. Take care of one small thing at a time. 
Second, empower your team. Equip people to make their own decisions and to own their piece 
of the equation. 
Finally, a leader must create accountability. The leader must hold people accountable through 
self-reporting. Performance management systems that only engage people at scheduled times 
create kind of an obligatory performance that stifles creativity, innovation, ownership, and 
passion. It neutralizes the kind of responsibility that we know transforms individuals, teams, 
and organizations.  
Pat (Summitt) was nothing if not a genius at holding people accountable, including herself. The 
more responsibility they’re (your team members) given, the more committed they will be to a 
project, and the more they will make it their project. When it’s theirs, they feel more 
accountable for its success or failure and they do whatever it takes to help it succeed. It 
becomes our team instead of my team. 
What behaviors do you want your team members to replicate? Are you modeling those 
behaviors every day in ways both small and large? A culture of modeling and replicating 
success-oriented behaviors will help lead your team to the next level.

Taking Full Responsibility: Wrap-Up, featuring Katy Kvalvik

m2v6_transcript.pdf
124.2 KB
Continued

The world is a dynamic place where expectations continue to change, and in most cases, are on the rise. This means that, in order to be competitive, we can't simply stay the same. We have to get better and improve. This improvement is most likely achieved with a commitment to focusing on the future, building a better way, and practice. Practice allows us, even as leaders, to continue to develop new skills that will serve us and help us remain competitive.

Leadership: Exhausting and Isolating

When we visualize what it means to be a leader, we rarely see ourselves successfully charging towards our destination with our teams, mired by exhaustion. In fact, stress and fatigue represent some of the more challenging aspects of what it means to be a leader. Leadership positions make enormous demands on our time, emotional energy, and spirit. The number of hours you must spend in many cases to successfully lead an organization is beyond what a normal work output would demand. Similarly, the job of reacting emotionally to other people, judging other's emotions, and attempting to read the psychological subtext of what's going on in the situation is altogether mentally taxing work!

Leadership can also be very isolating. You may be the only leader at your level in your organization. This is why it's so important for leaders to have strong social networks outside of work to allow them to connect, debrief, and maintain personal connections. Professional organizations also serve in this role and can't be forgotten.

Let’s Not Work Overtime at Finding Fault!

Evidence of the inability to take responsibility will show up on teams who become experts at finding fault. Put another way, organizations who are weak in creating a culture of responsibility will consistently find a scapegoat for whoever is going to take the blame for the latest rounds of failure. This becomes an extremely toxic environment, because with every new initiative, employees look around and prepare themselves for a default person to blame if things go south. This is the opposite of what great leaders promote. If you have a culture of responsibility at your work, everyone "owns" every issue. They are willing to jump in and help to make sure no one fails. Furthermore, when there is an overall failure, they all work together to try to fix the issue.

Culture of Full Responsibility

Work cultures that are willing to embrace responsibility feel very different than those that are finding fault. There's a degree of safety in groups who find solutions and work together to solve problems rather than finding fault. Furthermore, in those situations, there's probably a greater likelihood that fewer mistakes will be made. If you are trying to perform in front of a group, don't you usually perform a little bit better if you aren't surrounded by people who are praying that either you fail, or if you fail that they're not going to be in any way involved? That kind of thinking makes you feel very alone. A culture of responsibility creates conditions where everyone feels "in it" together, allowing for momentum to build and teams to work together in new and solidified ways.

video.transcript_text:
Take Full Responsibility: Wrap-Up, Featuring Katy Kvalvik 
 
Katy Kvalvik, Founder of Southwestern Empowerment, Executive Coach, Corporate Training & 
Speaker 
Leaders must practice, just like Coach Summitt and her teams practiced. Practice becomes even 
more important when you’re exhausted, isolated, and feeling less confident. It’s about 
consistently doing the things that point you back to measurable and meaningful outcomes.  
Even when you don’t feel like it, or you don’t have all the answers, consistently putting these 
principles into practice will create and reinforce a culture of full responsibility. If you study 
success long enough and closely enough, when mediocrity starts to creep in, you can identify 
and address it early. In the assessment phase, if you set specific goals, boundaries, and 
standards of behavior that facilitate the outcomes you want for yourself and others, you and 
your team will begin to develop an appetite for full responsibility.  
Accountability is essential to personal growth, as well as team growth. How can you improve if 
you’re never wrong? If you don’t admit a mistake and take responsibility for it, you’re bound to 
make the same one again. You learn as much from getting it wrong as you do from getting it 
right. But you must be willing to take responsibility for failure and be willing to examine it 
closely no matter how excruciating or embarrassing.  
Ask this question: What does success look and feel like on my team, in my company, in my life? 
What’s the customer experience like? What’s the product cycle like? How do the teams 
behave? What are my performance review scores like?” 
Maybe at this point you are silently saying, “But, Katy, you don’t understand. I don’t have a 
team that I can trust.” I understand. Taking full responsibility means that everyone on the team 
has to be committed to doing the work, upholding the standards, or whatever else it is that 
you’ve identified as the driver of success. 
As a leader, ask yourself this question: Do I have the right team? If not, what criteria would 
make up the right team? What courageous steps do I need to take to get the right team in 
place? When am I going to start taking those steps? 
As a team member, ask yourself if you’re contributing to the mission of your organization. Are 
you part of a high-functioning team that delivers results and contributes to the overall success 
of the organization? If not, what steps could you take to make a greater contribution? 
Whether you’re a leader of a large unit or a team member on a very small team, it is up to each 
of us to take full responsibility.

Practice allows us, even as leaders, to continue to develop new skills that will serve us and help us remain competitive.
Leadership: Exhausting and Isolating

When we visualize what it means to be a leader, we rarely see ourselves successfully charging towards our destination with our teams, mired by exhaustion. In fact, stress and fatigue represent some of the more challenging aspects of what it means to be a leader. Leadership positions make enormous demands on our time, emotional energy, and spirit. The number of hours you must spend in many cases to successfully lead an organization is beyond what a normal work output would demand. Similarly, the job of reacting emotionally to other people, judging other's emotions, and attempting to read the psychological subtext of what's going on in the situation is altogether mentally taxing work!

Leadership can also be very isolating. You may be the only leader at your level in your organization. This is why it's so important for leaders to have strong social networks outside of work to allow them to connect, debrief, and maintain personal connections. Professional organizations also serve in this role and can't be forgotten.
Let’s Not Work Overtime at Finding Fault!

Evidence of the inability to take responsibility will show up on teams who become experts at finding fault. Put another way, organizations who are weak in creating a culture of responsibility will consistently find a scapegoat for whoever is going to take the blame for the latest rounds of failure. This becomes an extremely toxic environment, because with every new initiative, employees look around and prepare themselves for a default person to blame if things go south. This is the opposite of what great leaders promote. If you have a culture of responsibility at your work, everyone "owns" every issue. They are willing to jump in and help to make sure no one fails. Furthermore, when there is an overall failure, they all work together to try to fix the issue.
Culture of Full Responsibility

Work cultures that are willing to embrace responsibility feel very different than those that are finding fault. There's a degree of safety in groups who find solutions and work together to solve problems rather than finding fault. Furthermore, in those situations, there's probably a greater likelihood that fewer mistakes will be made. If you are trying to perform in front of a group, don't you usually perform a little bit better if you aren't surrounded by people who are praying that either you fail, or if you fail that they're not going to be in any way involved? That kind of thinking makes you feel very alone. A culture of responsibility creates conditions where everyone feels "in it" together, allowing for momentum to build and teams to work together in new and solidified ways.

Leadership Reflections: Foiling the Fault-Finder

Let's discuss fault-finding. Have you ever known an expert fault-finder? An expert fault-finder makes it his or her mission to consistently look out for maladies or mistakes in others. They are quick to point out a weakness or a struggle. When the team fails to perform, they look for somebody to blame rather than looking collectively for a way to improve.

For this reflection, let's imagine that you are a leader who is seeking growth, and your team struggles to meet expectation on an important project. You notice that one of your senior team members once again demonstrates a consistent habit of finding fault in others and reflecting on the failure.

What would you do about this fault-finder who consistently brings these grievances to the team in a very public way?
How would you address this issue while teaching the importance of taking full responsibility?

Reflect on these questions in your workbook.

I tell our players right off that loyalty is so big. Loyalty. I would not hire anyone I couldn't trust. I would struggle with any player that wasn't loyal to our system.

Pat Summitt

Develop & Demonstrate Loyalty: Pat in Her Own Words

m3v1_transcript.pdf
100.1 KB

Until we become a leader with a certain level of responsibility, it’s essential within the organization to remain loyal. It would be very easy for somebody to observe some dynamic within an organization, or on a team, and quietly whisper to those around them that they have better ideas than the leader. This only serves to diminish the overall momentum and fluidity of the team.

Scenario

Paul, one of your employees, has just come to you with an idea for a change he'd like to see made in the organization.

You think about it. While you agree it's a good idea, the timing just doesn't seem right for making such a change. And you're not even sure that senior leadership will buy into it at this point.

You thank Paul for sharing his idea, but you respectfully let him know this is not a change the organization will be able to implement any time soon. You give him some rationale for your reasoning.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

If Paul is a disloyal employee, what are some ways you think he might respond in this situation?

Let’s assume that you, as the leader, are right, and better outcomes emerge by ignoring Paul's advised changes. Let's also assume that Paul is a loyal employee. From that experience, what could both the leader and follower learn?

Now let’s assume yet another outcome. What if Paul, as the follower, was right about his suggestion? What if Paul’s prediction was correct and your team or group falters because the leader made the wrong choice?

Thank you!
You might also save this response in your workbook.

video.transcript_text:
Develop and Demonstrate Loyalty: Introduction, Featuring Greg Hiebert 
 
Greg Hiebert, Leadership Coach & Managing Partner 
By far the greatest influence and source of purpose in Pat Summitt’s life was family. As much as 
she loved basketball, competition, and, of course, winning, family always came first. So it is not 
surprising that she created and nurtured the family model within Tennessee basketball. Her 
assistant coaches stayed with her for decades, through triumphs and travails, through every up 
and every down, because she treated them as so much more than just paid employees. To Pat 
Summitt, they were family, and her loyalty to family was absolute ... a non-negotiable. 
In fact, today, years after the untimely passing of Coach Summitt, hundreds of former players, 
assistant coaches, and colleagues consider themselves all part of Coach Pat Summitt’s family. 
Coach Summitt said, “To build a sound organization, you must surround yourself with people 
who share the same basic values. People who are constant and who will be true to your 
organization. In pressure situations, you don’t wonder how the person next to you will react. 
You know.” 
Isn’t it better to work with someone you have a regard for … in a relationship with … someone 
you have shared good and bad with … and have developed some trust in and loyalty to? 
The single most common reason organizations self-destruct is disloyalty, especially when they 
are made up of young people who have a tendency to talk behind each other’s back. When 
Coach Summitt talked about loyalty, it is powerfully revealing to notice that the conversation 
always started with her focus of being loyal, not on receiving loyalty, as well as expressing her 
appreciation for those who were deeply loyal to her.  
Coach Summitt was asked how she kept her core staff intact for so long. She replied, “How do 
you keep your family? I’ll tell you. You take care of your family, and you protect your family.” 
And the next obvious question is: How do you do that? Paying people well is a start, but you 
must find a way to show that you appreciate them, even with a simple gesture like buying them 
lunch. The joy that comes from giving without worrying about what you’ll receive in return is 
the unsolicited bonus that comes when you demonstrate genuine loyalty, for only when you 
give it away will it come back to you.

states_text.text: Hiring people who don't share the organization's values and ethics

Simply put, if you hire people who are unethical, no amount of kindness or training can turn an unethical person into something better. Of course, there are always exceptions, but as a rule for leaders, finding talented, hard-working, and ethical people to join your organization is an essential point. They don’t have to be perfect, but their ethical alignment is essential.
Failing to start with demonstrating loyalty themselves

The second important ingredient a leader must consider in developing loyalty is to start with themselves, or with things they can control. In other words, instead of operating as a leader, waiting for others to demonstrate their loyalty, a great way to build that family environment is for the leader to demonstrate that loyalty themselves through how they interact with others.

A Family Model

Develop & Demonstrate Loyalty: A Family Model, featuring Joan Cronan

m3v3_transcript.pdf
119 KB

If you want to develop loyalty, the first thing you have to do is demonstrate it. My staff and my family are one and the same. My staff is my family.

Pat Summitt

In most families, it is the aspiration of the elders that younger members of the family will learn what they need to someday create and lead their own family. For that to happen, the family needs to give younger members a chance to learn what it means to establish and maintain a family. The notion of building knowledge within the family to allow for more families is at the heart of why the world continues to grow and prosper. This concept of living like a family and gradually giving responsibilities that allow others to lead is true for teams and businesses as well. A successful family is one that is closely knit and loyal. The same should be true of teams and your organization. Loyalty and respect are both a two-way street and have to be given consistently if anyone in the family or in the organization expects reciprocation.

Knowledge Check: Multiple Response

In Pat’s example, she described some important steps she took to ensure members of her "professional family" were ready to lead, both in the moment and the future. Which of the following do you think were some of her suggestions?

Absolutely! Pat suggested all of these steps to ensure her "professional family" was ready to lead.

The Loyalty List

Finally, one very practical way that loyalty can be rehearsed and promoted on the team or within an organization is to establish what Pat Summitt called loyalty lists. Here’s how it works:

1. Identify three people who are important to you.
2. Identify what you think would happen to your relationship if you were disloyal to them.
3. Identify what you think would happen to your relationship if you show consistently how loyal you could be.
4. Identify three things you can do right away to demonstrate your loyalty to these very important people in your life.
5. Take action and monitor what happens when you live out loyalty, in both your personal and professional life.

Remember, "It’s all a family."

video.transcript_text:
Develop and Demonstrate Loyalty: Loyalty – A Family Model, Featuring Joan 
Cronan 
 
Joan Cronan, Women’s Athletic Director Emeritus, University of Tennessee 
Pat’s philosophy was ... “If you want to develop loyalty, the first thing you have to do is 
demonstrate it. My staff and my family are one and the same. My staff is my family.” 
What would it take to be considered one of the most loyal leaders in your company, where 
your team is always willing to go the extra mile for you and you are a leader the entire team 
looks to for guidance and direction?  
What would that mean to you? Is that even possible? 
Pat (Summitt) was fiercely loyal. Pat was also very clear about what loyalty was and what it 
wasn’t. Loyalty was not a one-way street where people blindly followed others. It was very 
much a give-and-take where loyalty has to be given in order to be received.  
Pat never wanted to be surrounded by “yes people” who appeared loyal and would never 
challenge her when needed or push her to get better. The best way to acknowledge talent is to 
let people do the job you hired them to do and trust them to do it. 
This is often difficult for leaders – letting go and trusting.  
Pat’s humility allowed her to see that if she surrounded herself with “yes people” who simply 
pandered to her every decision, Tennessee basketball would not go very far.  
She wanted coaches who she believed were better in areas which she knew were not her 
greatest strengths. She wanted coaches who would challenge her and call her out when they 
felt her actions or emotions were becoming counterproductive.  
When she found those coaches, she created an environment where her coaches were free to 
tell her what she needed to hear, not just want she wanted to hear. She gave them both 
responsibility and authority and created loyalty by treating them with trust, gratitude, and 
ultimate respect. 
Remember, you build loyalty first by being loyal. So write out a loyalty list today. 
List three important people in your life and then define three ways you commit to demonstrate 
your loyalty to them. 
Post this list on your mirror or another prominent place where you will see it each day and 
condition your focus on being loyal.

video.transcript_text:
Develop and Demonstrate Loyalty: The EQ Wacky Stack, Featuring Joan Cronan 
 
Joan Cronan, Women’s Athletic Director Emeritus, University of Tennessee 
There is no doubt you have a high IQ. If you didn’t, you wouldn’t be watching these videos. But 
IQ doesn’t equal EQ – your emotional quotient, or emotional intelligence. 
Emotional intelligence plays an enormous role in these dynamics, and simply put, emotional 
intelligence is being aware of how you come across to others and your willingness and ability to 
adjust. 
Now, there is a right way to build emotional intelligence and there is a wrong way.  
Let’s start with the right way. There are four building blocks to emotional intelligence, and they 
need to be stacked in a particular order.  
It starts with you understanding yourself. Pat (Summitt) started by taking a personality profile 
and analyzing its insight. She took it a step further and insisted that all members of the team – 
her coaches, her players, her assistants, and staff – took that personality profile test as well. I 
even took one. 
Secondly, use that knowledge to better manage yourself. Having the information about yourself 
doesn’t matter if you aren’t using it to manage yourself better. Right? 
Thirdly, focus on understanding others. You know your strengths, your tendencies, and now 
you (can) become a student of others’ strengths and tendencies. 
Then fourthly, a final block is to manage the relationships.  
Pat always individualized her approach with players based on how they best responded to her 
feedback. Some players needed to be yelled at, while others needed to be quietly pulled to the 
side for a calm chat. 
But here is how many of us have stacked the blocks in the past. We start off correctly with self-
awareness but then we jump right in to relationship management.  
Whoops! That’s not working. 
There’s often negative friction and misunderstanding. So we backtrack and then try to 
understand the other person. 
If you want to grow your emotional intelligence, better manage your relationships, and come 
across in the right way, focus on understanding and managing yourself first.

The EQ Wacky Stack
Develop & Demonstrate Loyalty: The EQ Wacky Stack, featuring Joan Cronan

m3v4_transcript.pdf
123.2 KB

IQ, or Intelligence Quotient, allows us to assess a person's mental or intellectual capacity. A person with a high IQ has the ability to understand complex issues and apply what they are learning at a higher level due to their intelligence. Certainly, IQ testing is an imperfect science, but generally speaking, the scientific community is pretty good in the modern era at identifying human potential by measuring intelligence with an IQ test and other measures.
However, like Joan Cronan suggested in the video, it isn’t all about our IQ, is it? Our heads and our hearts work together in ways that can’t always be easily predicted.

In fact, there was a rather famous mistake in the scientific community many decades ago where a handful of students were accidentally told that they had a much higher IQ than they were able to demonstrate. With this knowledge, these students performed at a much higher level than their IQ would have predicted. After this rather famous discovery, it became clear that human potential was more than intellectual potential alone. We’ve come to realize that it is more about the heart and head connection when it comes to making a difference. In other words, human performance is both an emotional and intellectual proposition. As a result, we have become fascinated with the concept of both: IQ (Intelligence Quotient), and EQ (Emotional Quotient, or "emotional intelligence").

What is Emotion? Simply put, your emotions are your feelings, and they are key to survival. Let’s start with the obvious. Human beings are always ebbing and flowing from one emotional state to the next.

Emotions play a critical role in our very existence. As you work your way through this learning material, we hope you are energized and curious. Those are emotional states. If, while you're reading this, the roof of your house starts caving in, it would be very logical for you to shift from curiosity to fear and terror! In fact, your ancestors responded emotionally to life-threatening situations, shifted their state, and made choices that enabled them to live another day. Had they not done so, you wouldn't be here today, going through this lesson! That's right — emotions aren’t merely ‘mushy’ things reserved for romance, birthdays, or rare poignant moments, as some believe. Emotions are lived each day, and the best leaders understand that they are shared experiences, and that people all around you are constantly experiencing emotional states that will make them more or less effective.

The two sides of that card describe two very different types of organization, don't they? One of the quickest ways to differentiate between them is by really reflecting on how it feels to be there. Feelings are just the signal. But being aware of the feelings is the first step in addressing the concerns behind them. Because of the importance of emotions, the term emotional intelligence has emerged. Emotional intelligence refers to an individual’s ability to recognize their own emotional state and likewise to recognize the emotional states of others.

If you missed the announcement and had at least some small degree of emotional intelligence, you would walk into the room and immediately recognize that something was different. You could tell by people’s facial expressions or by the tone of their voice that something had happened. If you had poor emotional intelligence, you might miss the emotional signals being put out by all of the sad people in the room and begin to be boisterous or act in a way that's completely out of touch with what’s going on. We’ve all been imperfect in understanding the emotional mood others are experiencing at one point or another, but really trying to be emotionally intelligent is helpful because it allows you to be more aware of exactly how people are feeling and, as a result, more responsive. Therefore, the term "EQ" is simply another way of discussing emotional intelligence or awareness. If you have high levels of emotional intelligence, you have the ability to sense emotions in others, and you know your own emotions.

Emotional Intelligence Is Knowing the Difference. When you have advanced levels of emotional intelligence, you have the ability to understand the difference between one emotional state and another. For example, most people understand the difference between being happy and being deeply satisfied. You could eat a piece of chocolate when you’re hungry before dinner and enjoy the impact of the cocoa on your taste buds. You can appreciate the sugar and carbohydrate surge in your bloodstream and feel good, even for just a second. That might give you a ‘happy’ feeling. You could also cross the finish line after training for a year to run in the Boston Marathon, collapsing in the arms of your partner, weeping in exhaustion. The happiness you feel after eating a piece of chocolate versus the deep sense of satisfaction after training and running a marathon represent two very different emotional experiences. It's also understanding the difference between being angry versus being disappointed in an outcome that didn't quite turn out the way it should. The better you're able to understand these emotional reactions and channel them, the more successful you will be as a leader.

How EQ Shows Up. Leaders with high levels of EQ can sense what their team is feeling and can reflect on the appropriateness of that feeling. What if the team failed to achieve expectations and the team members didn’t seem very frustrated? Might the leader worry more about that? Indeed, the best leaders understand that emotions are a signal, and what to do with that signal might be different depending on the circumstances. Leaders must be able to sense these emotions if they are going to make the right choices for the team.
Developing Emotional Intelligence. Yes, emotional intelligence can be developed! The keys are four building blocks: Understand Yourself; Manage Yourself; Understand Others; Manage Relationships.

The Accident: It's a Tuesday morning. Collette, a coworker, is spending the day—perhaps the next week or more—at the hospital. Her partner was in a terrible car accident last night and is in critical condition. The Meeting: As the workday begins, Alejandra, the manager, shares the news with the team. They're deeply moved and feeling empathy for Collette and her partner. Devastated by the news, everyone in the room has a collective sense of palpable sadness and concern. Your Morning: On that same Tuesday, you oversleep and get stuck in traffic. Your Response: You missed your manager's announcement and you're a little late for the meeting.

You notice Collette is missing and you ask if something is wrong. | You say, ‘You all seem upset. What's going on? Is everything okay?’ | You recognize the team is upset. Clearly something bad has happened.

You wonder why the team is so upset that you are running a bit late. | You say, ‘Sorry I'm late, but I see we're also waiting for Collette anyway!’ | You run into the meeting, fuming about the freeway congestion this morning.
6/6 Cards Correct

Suppose your team just had a major failure. It fell short of expectations by a mile! Team members feel frustrated and anxious. Is their collective response a good thing or a bad thing? Why? Think about it and respond below.
Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

To understand yourself, recognize that you experience a variety of emotions throughout each day. Understanding your recurring states helps identify contributing habits or unresolved issues. Personality assessments can also reveal your emotional tendencies and how you address problems.
Once you understand yourself better, manage your work life accordingly. If many choices, voices, and stress overwhelm you, moving somewhere quiet to reflect may help you stay productive.

Recognize that other people also move among emotional states. By understanding the mood of the room and distinctions such as happiness versus deep satisfaction, leaders can make better decisions and encourage productive direction.

Good leaders provide personalized support. Some people need verbal praise and motivation; others prefer one-on-one contact and quiet observation. Emotional intelligence in action requires listening, flexibility, and practice.
The keys to developing emotional intelligence are: 1. Understand Yourself; 2. Manage Yourself; 3. Understand Others; 4. Manage Relationships.

video.transcript_text:
Develop and Demonstrate Loyalty: Being Loyal While Managing Conflict, 
Featuring Joan Cronan 
 
Joan Cronan, Women’s Athletic Director Emeritus, University of Tennessee 
Most of us don’t like conflict. It’s uncomfortable.  
Emotions get involved. People get defensive. Some people get angry.  
(It’s) better to avoid the hard conversations … right? Wrong! Wrong! 
So how do you get into one of those uncomfortable conversations? There is a six-step 
framework for navigating those tough encounters. 
First, own the conversation.  
Start the conversation with -- “I have a problem,” or “I have a concern that I want to discuss.” 
Never start with -- “You’ve got a problem we need to discuss” because you immediately put the 
other person on the defense. Own the conversation. 
Second, position the conversation to disarm the tension. Say something like, “I’m concerned 
that this conversation will hurt our relationship, and I don’t want to do that.” 
When people sense a hard conversation is coming, tensions build. So disarm it. 
Third, describe the situation factually. Say something like, “I observed, I heard, or I noticed.” 
But keep it factual. 
Fourth, describe the impact. “When that happened, or when you said that, I felt, or I thought, 
or I believed, or I was confused because ….” But describe the impact on you. 
Fifth, ask for any response or perspective from the other person. You’ll ask something like, 
“How do you see what happened?” Amazingly, the perspective we have going into one of these 
conversations is not always right. 
Finally, state your request.  
Oh, yeah. You need something out of this conversation, so you may something like, “It would 
really help me if …,” or “I would appreciate if you would ….” You need to communicate your 
desired outcome and obtain their buy-in. 
Coach Summitt believed passionately that human beings will do more for others than they’ll do 
for themselves. It was perhaps the most important truth to her about the human spirit and the 
power of a team. 
By developing and demonstrating loyalty, difficult conversations become more productive.

Develop & Demonstrate Loyalty: Being Loyal While Managing Conflict, featuring Joan Cronan

m3v5_transcript.pdf
123.9 KB

In the previous section, we discussed the importance of emotions. Throughout this learning experience, we’ve discussed the advantage of positive emotions and the simple truth that the best organizations are consistently experiencing a collective set of emotions that lead to better outcomes. The best teams experience emotions like pride, curiosity, joy, and excitement more than less successful organizations. This being said, it’s a mistake for a leader to assume that other types of emotions aren't going to emerge constantly. This is part of what it means to be human. A great place to start reflecting on this comes in the inevitable moment when a leader must deal with conflict.

Are You in Denial? Some leaders see it as a strength to avoid conflict. In reality, the avoidance of conflict can actually create even deeper chasms and do more to hurt an organizational culture than help it. While none of us likes the discomfort of dealing with a difficult circumstance, the ultimate opportunity for growth makes it worthwhile. Don’t deny the opportunity to grow by being afraid to deal with conflict! Indeed, in many cases after dealing with the conflict, better feelings will emerge, and in some cases, warring factions will actually become loyal allies!

The 6-Step Process for Dealing with Conflict. Dealing with conflict isn't easy. Emotions can get amped up, and you may not think as clearly as you normally would in a given situation. To that end, having a plan or a process to effectively deal with conflict can help.

media_refs.note: Docebo-provided transcript for the Being Loyal While Managing Conflict video.

activity.instructions_text: Visit all six steps in The 6-Step Process for Dealing with Conflict and its summary.

states_text.text: When you own the conversation when dealing with conflict, you don’t begin the discussion by saying, ‘Do you know what your problem is?’ It’s important to enter a conflict conversation without the burden of initial blame. The leader should immediately own, without accusation or assumption, their desire to address the issue and their desire first and foremost to understand, to listen, and to learn. It’s important when doing this, however, to be honest about the situation. For example, if a leader is addressing a circumstance where someone they work with didn’t take responsibility for a mistake they made, they would start by benignly communicating what they heard, and describing how it made them feel, while once again clarifying the desire to learn about the other person’s perspective or experience.

Even if a leader assumes that they have a reputation for being a good listener and giving people a chance, it’s important in a situation like this to reiterate these facts. Remind those involved that they are important to the organization; their feelings matter; and even if this conversation is challenging, the goal is to learn and for everyone (including the leader) to continue to grow and get better. This type of disarming will free the participants from being defensive, preparing them instead for personal and career growth.

As a leader, when you bring the situation to the attention of those involved, it’s important to describe that situation as benignly as possible. This isn’t always easy, but it also is important to discuss these issues without accusation. For example, if the leader had observed a team member acting in a cruel and thoughtless way towards another, it would be important in that discussion to describe what was observed in careful detail without qualifying statements (‘And then, you RUDELY said...’). Notice, with that statement, you’ve already judged the action and intention. This can be difficult, because in some cases, maybe the rude behavior is obvious to everyone. Remember that the goal of dealing with conflict isn’t to assert the leader's observation. The goal is to bring behaviors to light and learn what those behaviors mean. A much better outcome is when those involved recognize on their own that they were being rude rather than a supervisor declaring the obvious. If leaders want excellence in others, they have to be consistently engaged in showing them how to grow. In this case, pointing out an opportunity to grow and letting them absorb it and declare it will result in more growth.

After a factual recitation of what was observed, the leader then needs to once again benignly describe the impact, without accusation. In the previous example, let’s assume the team member was rude in a public way to another team member. It would be a mistake to say, ‘And after you said that awful thing, you got your wish. Your team member was humiliated.’ The mistake here is that you’ve already assumed intention. After all, maybe the person was trying to be funny or was just clueless and truly missed the mark. To make that person feel like they would intentionally hurt another person could be enormously hurtful to them, even after an egregious mistake. Though you don’t want to assume intent, it is important to describe the impact as thoroughly as possible. If feelings were hurt, or people were discouraged, it’s important to share the absolute truth about that impact. Remember, you can be truthful without being accusatory.

Early in the conversation, it’s helpful to remind the individual being addressed that they will be given a chance to share their version of the facts and to respond. After sharing the facts and the impact above, it’s important to allow the person to gather their thoughts and respond. Remember, if you are initiating a difficult conversation, you have had the advantage of preparing in advance for the discussion. The person at the center of the conversation may not have had that luxury, so slow down and give them time to reflect. This might keep them from overreacting or acting out further.

Making sure things are clear at the end is important. The leader may decide to provide a summarized overview of what they just heard, in terms of what was presented, what other perspectives were shared, and what the next steps are. If the leader is forced to make some recommendations at this point, factually and thoughtfully lay them out. Put these requests in gentle terms such as, ‘It would really help me if...,’ allowing the conversation to conclude in a less confrontational way.

While dealing with conflict isn't easy, having a plan or process to effectively deal with it can be very helpful: 1. Own the conversation. 2. Disarm the tension. 3. Describe the situation factually, without emotion. 4. Describe the impact. 5. Ask for a response. 6. Conclude and state your request.

video.transcript_text:
Develop and Demonstrate Loyalty: Wrap-Up, Featuring Greg Hiebert 
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
You’ve got to have an unbelievable desire to compete at this point in time. An attitude. OK? I go 
back and say, “We’re not going to lunch tomorrow night. We’re going to war.” 
 
Greg Hiebert, Leadership Coach & Managing Partner 
Pat Summitt is remembered by all who knew her as a great motivator. Her greatest gift was to 
help everyone around her instill that foundational understanding within their own spirits.  
In other words, she ignited everyone she touched, and with the determination to be loyal to 
their deepest values. Her great power as a coach was not that she made her players fear her 
and answer to her.  
Instead, she made them fear and answer first to themselves. She told every single Lady Vol 
team, “If you take a shortcut or cheat, you’ll know it. And you’ll keep cheating and taking 
shortcuts for the rest of your life.” 
The reason her look, also called the Pat Summitt Stare, was so powerful was because it cut 
through you like an X-ray to say, “You just let yourself down. I know it, but more importantly, 
you know it.” 
Loyalty, like character, starts on the inside and eventually reveals itself to the outside. 
Pat said, “Value those colleagues who tell you the truth, not just what you want to hear.” 
When your focus is first and foremost on giving loyalty, receiving it in return is simply the 
natural result. You can’t demand loyalty, but you can choose to be loyal and to support that 
decision by being 100 percent consistent in the way you speak about others. 
When Mickey DeMoss and Nancy Darsh moved on from Tennessee pursuing other career 
opportunities after many years as assistant coaches, Pat did not waiver in the glowing, positive, 
deeply appreciative way she spoke about them. She stayed in constant contact when they left. 
She wasn’t loyal when they were just there and disloyal when they weren’t.  
This consistency and constant loyalty spoke volumes to everyone around Pat Summitt. They 
knew her loyalty was not conditional. Nor was it temporary. It was unconditional and 
permanent.  
When Pat Summitt was loyal to you, it was for life. The confidence and inspiration that result 
from such loyalty cannot be measured. And what a great lesson for all of us to learn and apply 
in our lives. 

Do you value your team and treat them like family? 
What areas might you need to improve so that you can develop and demonstrate loyalty every 
day?

Pat Summitt believed that high levels of success would never come without a strong desire to compete. She believed that the desire to compete came from a deep sense of motivation, and that motivation was internal. Put another way, she didn't want to motivate people to perform as much as she wanted to help them to develop their own internal ability to motivate themselves.

The simplicity of this statement can't be underestimated. You can give a person a fish, or teach them to fish. You can try to motivate them in the moment, or teach them to find the pride that lies within and to spark that internal motivation whenever they need it.

It's no wonder so many of Pat’s players went on to have very successful careers, coaching or otherwise. She gave them the gift of that internal fire that taught them to stay motivated and bring the best of themselves to work every day. She also believed that loyalty was paramount, and the best way to receive loyalty was to give it without hesitation and with great enthusiasm. Pat believed in unconditional loyalty, for life.

The best leaders or peak performers have a unique ability to manage conflict. In other words, they learn to not only minimize or eliminate the debilitating aspects of dealing with conflict, but they actually learn to use conflict to identify areas of growth, clarify potential misunderstandings, and build better relationships. This takes a unique level of commitment, and this learning experience offers a six-step process for dealing with conflict.

video.transcript_text:
Learn to Be a Great Communicator: Pat in Her Own Words 
 
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
Communication is key. Communication on the floor. You know, we have a “rebound two 
points” philosophy. We make a mistake, they are to verbalize, “Rebound. Rebound from your 
mistake. Move on.” The mental training aspect of this game now is much needed. 
You know, we’re not driving a car. If we’re driving a car, and if we don’t stop at the stop sign, 
we usually get pulled over if anybody catches us, right? Because we did something wrong. If we 
do stop at the stop sign, nobody ever says, “Good job.” When they do things on the court, they 
need to hear, “Good job.”  
 
So, I’ve really tried to become a better communicator by becoming a better listener. 
  
You communicate with your body language. You know, you see assistant coaches and you see 
them in the huddle -- and I have a wonderful staff. I would not have enjoyed the success that 
I’ve enjoyed without the people around me. And I just know that no matter what we talk about, 
they’re going to be right there with me. When you go into a huddle, coaches, you ever think 
about being a great leader and communicating what they need? It’s not about what you need.  
 
I remember for the Vanderbilt game here, my outlet is, I have to exercise. I don’t like it. I just 
have to do it because I need an outlet. And that day, when I was working out, I thought, 
“Tonight, you’ve got to be in a really tough ballgame.” I communicated with myself and I said, 
“It’s going to be real important that you stay calm for the team.” And to get back to that 
afternoon, I just wanted to come to the gym and do everything within my power to help our 
team.  
 
It’s not about you, it’s about them. I wanted them to be prepared. I wanted them to come to 
the huddle and even after a bad play, say, “That’s all right. We’re OK.” Because they watch you. 
You can be the barometer for that team. You can be the inspiration, or you can pull them down. 
This is bigger than any offense you’re going to run, in my opinion, is how you communicate with 
your players and how they perform and respond as a result.

A Journey in Leadership: Becoming a Better Listener. The best leaders are always trying to improve their ability to communicate. Pat Summitt strongly advocated the importance of listening. By listening, a leader does a number of things.

items: Leaders invest their time in the most important place of all -- with their people.
By listening, leaders better understand the specific needs of the individual and how to make the most of their working experience together.

Finally, by listening carefully, leaders can get a better impression of exactly how their message is being received. When leaders remain quiet long enough, they will hear what message is being received...and that can be a great indicator of a leader’s success. In a careful moment of listening, leaders may discover that their message hasn’t been communicated as accurately as they thought.

body_blocks.text: Keep listening, and listen intently! Communication Analogies: Based on the images, try to guess the meaning of the analogies before flipping the cards.
Qualities and Practices of an Effective Communicator. Below, we introduce you to several qualities and practices of a leader who is an effective communicator.

Give Praise: It Could Be the Needed Nourishment. In this section, Coach Summitt discussed her experience in discovering and ultimately rediscovering the merits of praise. As discussed earlier, it’s important not to praise just anything. Instead, leaders should reinforce, congratulate, and recognize efforts that are part of what it means to succeed within the organization. Leaders who are successful discover that the longer they are on the job, the more praise is undeniably valuable and important. The longer you lead, the more certain you become of yourself, and the more your team needs to hear from you when they are doing things right. And when they do, you may find they are far more likely to do right more often.

You’re the Leader, and It’s Not About You. As leaders mature, they become increasingly aware that leadership is ultimately a transformation that becomes increasingly less about you, the leader. In fact, research shows that leaders who talk about only themselves, their own efforts, and consistently talk about the organization in terms of their presence within it are doomed to failure. This is likely due to a couple of obvious reasons. First, if a leader communicates that the primary mission of the organization is to recognize the leader, then that’s where efforts will go. Second, when leaders make the mission about them -- even in the best of circumstances -- the mission becomes far too dependent on the leader. The best leaders attempt to share power and create conditions where everyone is successful and everyone contributes to success within the program.

You’re the Leader...It’s About Them, and Your Results. When a leader ascends to a new position, it’s easy for them to get convinced that they have superpowers. Without question, a leader who gets a great promotion should be proud of their accomplishments. However, as soon as the job gets started, as mentioned above, it shouldn’t be about the leader. It needs to be about who the leader is there to serve. In Coach Pat Summitt’s case, the people she served included her players, her assistant coaches, and other members of the administrative team. She knew that she needed to keep the emphasis on them, because after all, they were the ones on the court each year. They were also the ones supporting her efforts, making sure that everything she was trying to do could be executed successfully. Your people and your results are what your job as a leader is all about.

You Are the Barometer. As we have learned more about how teams respond to the power of a leader, it’s clear that leaders are the unmistakable barometer of success. While this unit uses the ‘barometer analogy’ as being predictive of the success of the team, it’s probably even more illustrative to think about the leader as the ‘spark’ and the ‘fire.’ Without question, leaders have the ability to spark things on a team.

A very combative coach who has the reputation for swearing or fighting will often times lead teams that will do the same. Coaches who are caring, communicative, and culture-building are famous for having players who lock arms and never give up on one another. It has been said that whatever strengths or weaknesses that reside within a leader will likewise reside on a team within an organization. This is why good leaders always surround themselves with people who are better than they are at their blind spots. All that said, it can be an enormous pressure to be that spark or flame for the team! But it is also the key for being successful. Highly successful tech companies are often led by leaders who are enormously gifted at creating environments where mind-blowing innovations emerge and working together toward new solutions is commonplace. It’s not an accident. It’s about a commitment to the kind of thinking that drives the behaviors and results that lead to success. And leaders are the key. So in your leadership journey, it’s incredibly important to think about the institutions that you are leading and their needs. You need to be the barometer, the spark, and the flame -- factors that inspire creativity, level out uneven performance, and inspire new levels of engagement.

How to Prepare to Be the Barometer. If an organization is going to watch the leader closely, it’s very important that the leader is prepared to lead. Coach Summitt famously exercised on a consistent basis, even on game days. She wanted to be able to work off any unnecessary stress and bring the most relaxed, healthy, and happy version of herself to her game. This is why so many high-performing leaders regularly exercise, meditate, practice yoga, and work out to be their best so they can bring positive energy to their role as the barometer.

steps.exact_visible_copy:

Learn to Be a Great Communicator: Introduction

By communicating effectively, what I mean is, how can you best command the attention of those you are speaking to. Decide what you are trying to accomplish, whether you are trying to motivate, elicit a confession, ask for a raise, or instill confidence. Be clear on what you want to say, and say it in a way that is appropriate to your surroundings.

Pat Summitt

Learn to Be a Great Communicator: Introduction, featuring Virginia Means

m4v2_transcript.pdf
148.9 KB
Complete the content above before moving on.

Continued

Why Communication Is So Important for Leaders

Becoming adept at good communication is at the heart of what good leaders must do to be effective.

One could argue that the skill to communicate is perhaps the most important skill any leader can develop. Day in and day out, leaders spend their time communicating. They communicate with customers, clients, colleagues, direct reports, and outside partners who can have a huge impact on their success. With every artery of communication emerges an opportunity to influence and improve the trajectory of your organization. If a leader is a good communicator, literally every moment of their day is spent infusing good energy and possibility in the organization or team. If they are a bad communicator, things can spiral in the wrong direction very quickly.

While Talkers Talk, Communicators Listen and Empathize

The best leaders understand that good verbal skills are helpful. But they are only part of the puzzle. Good communication involves the ability to be a good listener. While listening, it’s also important to be able to absorb the feelings attached to those providing the message. Listening to an irate colleague may be a signal that the system is broken, the individual is struggling with their job, or there was a significant (or maybe only episodic) breakdown leading to this outburst. This understanding can't happen without carefully observing the surroundings, listening to the message, feeling the intention, and being able to use discernment to reflect on next best steps.

There’s NO Small Stuff!

When attempting to communicate, the little things matter! If a leader has a difficult conversation to execute, it’s helpful for them to consider the location of the meeting, the leader’s body language, the facial expressions, and any other potential contextual factors that could impact of the message is received. The more careful the delivery of the message, the more likely the successful receipt of that message.

Timing, and Other Factors, Are Everything

It is said that "timing is everything." Communicating to a person or a group at a point in which they’re ready to hear it makes for a much more dynamic message. As a coach, speaking to a team after losing in triple overtime versus a speech after winning by 30 points represents very different timing. And it isn’t just about timing – it’s about wanting to pick the right message, at the right time, delivered to the right people, at a moment that will provide the greatest opportunity for growth.

Three Keys to Great Communication

In reflecting on the keys to great communication, three essentials stand out.

KEY 1 — Authenticity

There is currently a lot of talk in business and politics about the importance of "transparency." One of the key elements to transparency and believability is whether the leader communicates with authenticity. Is the leader believable? If a leader is seen as suspicious or insincere, they aren’t seen as authentic. One notorious example of how important authenticity is came during the infamous presidential election between Richard Nixon and John F. Kennedy. This was the first nationally televised debate, and Nixon was observed to be sweating and fidgety. Those who watched the debate on TV indicated that they didn’t think Nixon was authentic or trustworthy. Conversely, of those listening to the debate on the radio, some actually favored Nixon in the discussion because they only heard the words and weren’t privy to the nervous behavior in front of the TV audience.

KEY 2 — Relationships

When you have strong relationships, there are greater opportunities to communicate quickly and with precision. As a leader, if you have established a strong relationship with your team, in a moment of stress you can be somewhat demanding without worrying whether or not you have a good enough relationship with them to withstand it.

KEY 3 — Nonverbal Communication

How can you tell that the two persons in the image are having a positive, engaging conversation?

The nonverbal element of communication can sometimes have a greater impact than the exact words used. The debate between Kennedy and Nixon is a great example. Another example might include a leader who needs to call in an employee and remind them to report to work on time. If the leader calls in the employee and stands up during the meeting with arms crossed, scowling, it’s likely that the employee will get the message that there is displeasure in that moment. Or, a leader who might physically stand close to somebody could create an intimidating environment that changes what the meeting feels like. Imagine if you were in a meeting and you had a boss that was 6’8”, and he chose to confront you about a topic, while leaning into your personal space! That could be intimidating.

The problem with these non-verbal miscues is that they can send a message that isn’t exactly intended. The well-intended, tall boss may not like the idea of intimidating those around them, but that could be the perception if he doesn’t use his nonverbal communications correctly. It’s true of every leader, and being conscious of it is half the battle.

Summary

We will review these three communication strategies more closely further in this module.

video.source_visible_title: Learn to Be a Great Communicator: Introduction
video.transcript_text:
Learn to Be a Great Communicator: Introduction, featuring Virginia Means 
 
 
Virginia Means, Chief People Officer, United Distributors, Inc. 
 
Coach Summitt said, “By communicate effectively, what I mean is how can you best command 
the attention of those you are speaking to? Decide what you’re trying to accomplish, whether 
you’re trying to motivate, elicit a confession, ask for a raise, or instill confidence. Be clear on 
what you want to say and say it in a way that’s appropriate to your surroundings.” 
  
To better understand the challenge and opportunity of leadership communication, consider this 
reality. First, most leaders spend the majority of their time each day in some type of 
interpersonal behavior, communicating with team or staff, other managers, customers, or other 
stakeholders. Second, a substantial number of organizational difficulties occur as a result of 
ineffective communication or no communication at all. This is why effective communication is 
an essential element of leadership success, whether it’s interpersonal, group, organizational, or 
external in nature. 
  
Great communicators are great listeners – you’re going to hear that again -- perceptive in their 
observations and skilled at discerning the feelings, concerns, and priorities of others. The 
message isn’t about who delivers the message. It is, however, about delivering the right 
message to the right person in the right way. There’s a difference between merely talking and 
communicating. Words with no meaning will not provide communication, understanding, and a 
response. There needs to be a purpose behind every word, sentence, and expression. 
  
Talking is the least of it. If you really want to get something across, body language, facial 
expression, eye contact, and listening are all necessary parts of communication.  
 
In this series, we’ll invest our time in three key areas that dramatically impact our ability to 
effectively communicate. We’ll examine why authenticity, relationships, and nonverbal 
communication are all critically important on our quest to be effective communicators.

As a coach, speaking to a team after losing in triple overtime versus a speech after winning by 30 points represents very different timing. And it isn’t just about timing – it’s about wanting to pick the right message, at the right time, delivered to the right people, at a moment that will provide the greatest opportunity for growth.
Three Keys to Great Communication
In reflecting on the keys to great communication, three essentials stand out.
KEY 1 — Authenticity

There is currently a lot of talk in business and politics about the importance of "transparency." One of the key elements to transparency and believability is whether the leader communicates with authenticity. Is the leader believable? If a leader is seen as suspicious or insincere, they aren’t seen as authentic. One notorious example of how important authenticity is came during the infamous presidential election between Richard Nixon and John F. Kennedy. This was the first nationally televised debate, and Nixon was observed to be sweating and fidgety. Those who watched the debate on TV indicated that they didn’t think Nixon was authentic or trustworthy. Conversely, of those listening to the debate on the radio, some actually favored Nixon in the discussion because they only heard the words and weren’t privy to the nervous behavior in front of the TV audience.
KEY 2 — Relationships

When you have strong relationships, there are greater opportunities to communicate quickly and with precision. As a leader, if you have established a strong relationship with your team, in a moment of stress you can be somewhat demanding without worrying whether or not you have a good enough relationship with them to withstand it.
KEY 3 — Nonverbal Communication
How can you tell that the two persons in the image are having a positive, engaging conversation?

The nonverbal element of communication can sometimes have a greater impact than the exact words used. The debate between Kennedy and Nixon is a great example. Another example might include a leader who needs to call in an employee and remind them to report to work on time. If the leader calls in the employee and stands up during the meeting with arms crossed, scowling, it’s likely that the employee will get the message that there is displeasure in that moment. Or, a leader who might physically stand close to somebody could create an intimidating environment that changes what the meeting feels like. Imagine if you were in a meeting and you had a boss that was 6’8”, and he chose to confront you about a topic, while leaning into your personal space! That could be intimidating.

The problem with these non-verbal miscues is that they can send a message that isn’t exactly intended. The well-intended, tall boss may not like the idea of intimidating those around them, but that could be the perception if he doesn’t use his nonverbal communications correctly. It’s true of every leader, and being conscious of it is half the battle.
Summary
We will review these three communication strategies more closely further in this module.
