6 of 15
Authenticity Matters

Learn to Be a Great Communicator: Authenticity Matters, featuring John Horton

m4v3_transcript.pdf
114 KB
Complete the content above before moving on.

Continued

Good leaders remain acutely aware that every interaction they have with other people affords an opportunity to enhance or diminish their message. No matter how much or how little a leader pays attention to their ability to communicate, they continue to send out a myriad of messages every day. This is why it is incredibly helpful for leaders to invest energy in learning how to communicate and deliver a message that hits the intended target. Whether a leader likes it or not, their ability to communicate is the wellspring of their effectiveness.

What does it mean to be authentic in communication?

1. Be honest and transparent.
2. Be the true you. Don't pretend to be something you are not.
3. Speak with candor.
4. Move aside your ego and be open to have your ideas challenged.
5. Strategically balance the amount of compliments and criticism.
6. Don't compromise your principles. Stay true to your principles, values, and ethics.

Now let's delve deeper into each of these qualities.

1. Be Honest and Transparent

When a leader is seen as honest, there’s greater trust. With greater trust comes the ability to grow as a team and take chances. Be honest when you become a leader!

2. Be Authentic: Be You!

Have you ever seen a politician, in an attempt to find favor with local voters, find themselves in situations that don’t at all seem authentic? Maybe they are trying to act comfortable on the back of a horse, or in a factory, or bowling, when in reality, this isn’t who they are. Although some may give them points for trying, in most cases these attempts go awry because leaders were seen as inauthentic. This goes back to the idea of honesty and transparency. Leaders should, by-and-large, be themselves. If they are going to put themselves in the position where they are trying something they haven’t tried before, they should admit it! Don’t be afraid to claim to be an outsider. Former President Barack Obama had a long history of being comfortable around the game of basketball. However, when he went into a bowling alley he openly admitted he had no game! In that situation, he didn’t pretend to be anything he wasn’t, and the bowlers in the alley had fun showing him the ropes.

3. Speak with Candor, Even When It’s Uncomfortable

This can be difficult, because it can’t always be premeditated. Individuals within an organization may suddenly spring a question on a leader that requires uncomfortable candor. For example, if a leader is asked by an employee about a promotion they just aren't ready for, telling someone the truth can be hurtful, but that’s part of what being a leader is all about. A leader is better off sticking with the truth and trying to deliver the message with kindness than to be inauthentic and insincere. In general, speaking with candor always improves the organization and enhances everyone's opportunity to grow.

4. Move Aside Your Ego

Once again, ego can stand in the way of thoughtful communication. If a leader isn’t honest, open, willing, or interested in listening, the ability to communicate successfully disappears. In many cases, a leader will fail in this area because they lack the confidence in themselves to take the risk of being open. In order to be open to communication, you have to be open to having your ideas challenged...and in some cases even replaced.

You can simply stick to whatever script you’ve imagined, but leaders like this are rarely successful. In a world that requires flexibility, creativity, and spontaneous pivots in the face of challenges of competition, it’s impossible to maintain a large ego and communicate well.

5. Don’t Overuse Compliments or Criticisms

Pat Summitt always believed you need to be strategic with compliments and criticisms, and refrain from overusing either one. If Coach Summitt were effusive in her compliments for the team after a hard-fought victory, the words probably would mean something and stick with the players for quite some time. On the other hand, if she praised her players on how quickly they got back on the court after taking a water break in practice, the compliments would begin to seem meaningless and ultimately become less impactful.

6. Don’t Compromise Your Principles

Don’t go there if your heart, head, and gut tell you not to go. As a leader, you’re going to hear a lot of feedback from a lot of people. Through it all, you must stay true to your principles, values, and ethics. Take in the information you receive in stride, but don’t let anyone talk you into compromising those principles, values, and ethics. If someone tries to get you to go against your beliefs and it won’t work for you and your organization's core values, you must have the courage to just say "No."

Let's practice our understanding of authenticity in communication. Sort the stack of cards into 2 piles: Authenticity (for behaviors that show authenticity and improve communication) and Lack of Authenticity (for behaviors that hinder communication).

Situational Leadership and Authenticity

Throughout this course, we’ve discussed situational leadership. It suggests that the particular situation a leader finds themselves in should dictate the strategy and approach they take. The audience and the situation do make a difference when communicating! Is it possible to be authentic in situational leadership? Pat Summitt discussed this in the video, Authenticity Matters. No matter how she adjusted her communication based on the context, she was always true to herself and never compromised her principles.

video.transcript_text:
Learn to Be a Great Communicator: Authenticity Matters, Featuring John Horton 
 
 
John Horton, Executive Coach 
 
Authenticity matters a lot. Pat Summitt was one of the most authentic individuals to ever step 
on a basketball court. Pat was authentic in her interactions and her communication. As a 
leader, you must, of course, be honest and sincere. More important than that, you must be 
open and transparent; and even more important than that, you must find your own authentic 
voice. Bring who you are, where you come from, and what you value to your communication. 
  
Pat Summitt: “Hey, Daddy! Can I have my old job back?” Pat’s Dad: “Yeah. I can’t pay what they 
pay, though.” Pat Summitt: [laughing]. That makes you real, sincere, and authentic. 
  
So how do you do this? First, you speak with respectful candor and make sure you are acutely 
aware of both your audience and the situation. As Pat said, “Circumstances dictate how you 
need to speak or whether you need to just shut up and listen. You don’t holler at a golf 
tournament and you don’t whisper at a forest fire.” 
  
Second, replace ego with empathy. Honesty plus empathy and caring create an environment for 
high performance to grow. Authenticity and transparency-based communication builds trust, 
relationships, and performance; while an overly crafted persona, supported by an inflated ego, 
will produce just the opposite. Authenticity leads to credibility, and Pat said the best way to 
maintain the credibility of compliments and criticisms is to use them meaningfully. Don’t 
overuse them. 
  
And finally, stay in your lane. A prerequisite for being an authentic leader is knowing your own 
strengths, values, and limitations. Staying in your lane comes down to if and how you can add 
value to a conversation.  
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
“Always be true to myself. Never, never compromise my principles. That came from my mom 
and dad, and it has stuck with me. When people want to lead you down the wrong path, have 
the courage to say, ‘I’m not going there.’”

8 of 15
Relationships Matter

I know my reputation. I'm that lady who's so mean to those poor young women.

Pat Summitt

Learn to Be a Great Communicator: Relationships Matter, featuring John Horton

m4v4_transcript.pdf
123.8 KB

Continued

Why invest in developing good relationships?

Did you ever have a friend who could say tough things to you? “Hey! You need to try harder," "Eat healthier," or "Spend more time with your family.” People who care about you can say tough things.

We are willing to accept the tough love advice from people with whom we have trusting relationships. But what if you hear the same words from a stranger? You would likely be angered and insulted.

To the outside observer, Pat Summitt probably appeared to be someone who was tough on her players. But to her team, she had a way of being that friend who could say things that needed to be said.

This is why investing in relationships is such an important part of being a leader!

What’s Private? What’s Public?

For a leader, arguably what's most important is the communication dynamic in private spaces. In one-on-one opportunities to communicate, a leader must create a space for authentic and healthy communication with those they lead. In Coach Summitt’s case, she served as a confidant, a mother figure, and a friend to so many of her players. And while so many observers of her program saw her scowling visage roaming the sidelines, they weren't necessarily there to see her kind engagement in those private, one-on-one moments.

Coach Pat Summitt served as a confidant, a mother figure, and a friend to her players, including two-time Naismith player of the year recipient Chamique Holdsclaw.

Coach Pat Summitt in a Huddle

This is not to say that what is said publicly isn't important. It certainly is. A good leader understands that a kind word said in front of the entire work group or team can send a powerful message that the effort it took to receive that compliment is to be duplicated. Furthermore, the decision to admonish or embarrass somebody in public can be one that leads to long-term pain and even resentment. The decision to call out a player or a colleague in a public space where others are able to observe is a decision that can have multiple ramifications. Leaders who make these decisions do so knowing that may be the case. If a leader, for example, recognizes that an individual's behavior is so abhorrent that they can't avoid it in that moment, the public admonishment might be totally appropriate. It is, as we've said along the way, entirely situational.

Maintaining awareness of situational variables in effective communication is a skill that good leaders must continue to work on throughout their careers.

Do They Know Who You Are?

While leaders need a personal life away from the scrutiny of the workplace, it's clear that one of the fastest ways to build relationships with others is to let them into your life. Leaders who are willing to share stories about their childhood struggles, continued imperfections, and other examples that reveal they are just like everyone else, arguably help a leader get closer to their colleagues. A wise strategy to this end is to identify parts of your life that you're willing to share.

Consider What to Share

Sharing family anecdotes and certain hobbies and pursuits represent safe and identifiable reveals within a larger work group.

Sharing your continued attempts to disrupt the efforts of an opposing political party, or a deep dive into a faith journey that others may not share perhaps should be saved for a closer set of friends.

Great Ways to Create Connections

Connect with High Touch! — Manage by Walking Around

Leaders must get connected with their teams and peers. Many times, leaders who start new jobs spend a huge chunk of their day simply walking around the organization and talking to people, getting to know who they are, and learning about their tasks. It would be very easy for a new leader to get caught up in the myriad of office-bound meetings that are arguably necessary. But, there's a great likelihood that the leader’s overall effectiveness and chance of success within the organization will be greater by making those initial connections and allowing those perceptions to drive understanding. Successful leaders understand the importance of establishing and maintaining high-touch. Some of the best leaders on the planet establish within their calendar time to simply walk around, observing the work environment and looking to connect with those who are on the front lines of doing the work, looking for clues to success and are seeking understanding, solving problems on the spot, and resolving conflicts before they emerge.

Connect with High Tech — Manage by Effectively Using Technology

So, can you manage by walking around online? Can you do high touch as a leader with high tech? The answer is yes. However, you shouldn't use technology to the exclusion of opportunities to connect with face-to-face. To put it in perspective, probably the best thing that a leader can do today with all the access points of technology is to simply see these tools as another mechanism for making connection.

For example, if a leader recognizes that there is an individual in the organization with whom they haven't spoken in a while and for whatever reason they still haven't been able to see them face-to-face, a warm text message indicating that they were thinking about them and checking in can mean the world to the person receiving the message.

Another advantage of these high-tech tools is that they are very scalable. Certainly a leader could send a group text and literally connect with everybody in the organization in a heartbeat. However, deeper levels of personalization emerge when the messages themselves are more personalized. So, as a point of practice, technology can be used to enhance a steady diet of face-to-face, heartfelt connection.

Put It in Writing! It’s Permanent! — Manage Using Written Notes

In an era of technology that can ebb and flow in the blink of an eye, the permanence of a handwritten card or note makes a big difference to those who receive them. Some of the best leaders have maintained a habit of writing a personal note every day to different people within the organization, expressing gratitude or the observance of something positive within the organization. For example, some leaders will maintain a stack of these notes. After they manage by walking around, observing noteworthy attitudes, behaviors, and accomplishments, they will follow up with the permanence of a written note. The good news and the good feelings within are hard to deny.

Learn to Be a Great Communicator: Relationships Matter, Featuring John Horton 
 
 
John Horton, Executive Coach 
 
Pat said ...  
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
“I know my reputation. I’m that lady who’s so mean to those poor young women.” 
 
John Horton, Executive Coach 
 
However, if you really knew Pat and her players, you would realize that perception is not always 
reality. Pat said, “Off the court is an entirely different matter. You have to see the inside of our 
team structure and understand our relationships to understand why I speak to them the way I 
do and how they transfer it. Off the court, I’m a confidant and a substitute mother. In that 
situation, my chief role is to listen, advise, and comfort.”  
 
The bottom line is relationships matter. People need to see and feel who you are to feel 
connected to the work you want them to do. Don’t be known only by your emails and official 
messages. Show up in person as often as possible. Balance high tech with high touch. Show 
your human side! 
  
In 1978, management guru Tom Peters was a consultant for McKinsey and Company, working 
on a project with a relatively small and largely unknown electronics company, Hewlett Packard. 
There, he discovered a powerful leadership and communication practice they called 
“management by walking around.” This may not seem like managing at all. Yet, at its heart, it’s 
about being there in person, conversing face to face.  
 
Pat said, “Listening has allowed me to be a better coach. You have to listen to develop effective, 
meaningful relationships with people. The more I’ve listened to our players, the better I have 
known them and understood them.” 
  
Good leaders are good communicators and good communicators are good listeners. When you 
listen well, you gain a clear understanding of another’s perspective and knowledge. Listening 
fosters trust, respect, and openness. 
  
Finally, never underestimate the power of the written word. Pat was a master at writing notes, 
not email, but old-school, handwritten notes. Pat said, “Words on paper, it struck me, have 
more meaning than something spoken aloud. They have permanence. I could say something 25 
times, but when they read it once, it seemed to make a difference.”  
 

So, how will you build relationships with your team so that they are loyal to you, committed to 
what you’re trying to accomplish, and willingly follow your lead?

Relationships Matter
I know my reputation. I'm that lady who's so mean to those poor young women.
Pat Summitt
Learn to Be a Great Communicator: Relationships Matter, featuring John Horton

123.8 KB
Continued
Why invest in developing good relationships?
Did you ever have a friend who could say tough things to you? “Hey! You need to try harder," "Eat healthier," or "Spend more time with your family.” People who care about you can say tough things.
We are willing to accept the tough love advice from people with whom we have trusting relationships. But what if you hear the same words from a stranger? You would likely be angered and insulted.
To the outside observer, Pat Summitt probably appeared to be someone who was tough on her players. But to her team, she had a way of being that friend who could say things that needed to be said.
This is why investing in relationships is such an important part of being a leader!
What’s Private? What’s Public?

For a leader, arguably what's most important is the communication dynamic in private spaces. In one-on-one opportunities to communicate, a leader must create a space for authentic and healthy communication with those they lead. In Coach Summitt’s case, she served as a confidant, a mother figure, and a friend to so many of her players. And while so many observers of her program saw her scowling visage roaming the sidelines, they weren't necessarily there to see her kind engagement in those private, one-on-one moments.
Coach Pat Summitt served as a confidant, a mother figure, and a friend to her players, including two-time Naismith player of the year recipient Chamique Holdsclaw.
Coach Pat Summitt in a Huddle

This is not to say that what is said publicly isn't important. It certainly is. A good leader understands that a kind word said in front of the entire work group or team can send a powerful message that the effort it took to receive that compliment is to be duplicated. Furthermore, the decision to admonish or embarrass somebody in public can be one that leads to long-term pain and even resentment. The decision to call out a player or a colleague in a public space where others are able to observe is a decision that can have multiple ramifications. Leaders who make these decisions do so knowing that may be the case. If a leader, for example, recognizes that an individual's behavior is so abhorrent that they can't avoid it in that moment, the public admonishment might be totally appropriate. It is, as we've said along the way, entirely situational.
Maintaining awareness of situational variables in effective communication is a skill that good leaders must continue to work on throughout their careers.
Do They Know Who You Are?

While leaders need a personal life away from the scrutiny of the workplace, it's clear that one of the fastest ways to build relationships with others is to let them into your life. Leaders who are willing to share stories about their childhood struggles, continued imperfections, and other examples that reveal they are just like everyone else, arguably help a leader get closer to their colleagues. A wise strategy to this end is to identify parts of your life that you're willing to share.
Consider What to Share
Sharing family anecdotes and certain hobbies and pursuits represent safe and identifiable reveals within a larger work group.

Sharing your continued attempts to disrupt the efforts of an opposing political party, or a deep dive into a faith journey that others may not share perhaps should be saved for a closer set of friends.
Great Ways to Create Connections
Connect with High Touch! — Manage by Walking Around

Leaders must get connected with their teams and peers. Many times, leaders who start new jobs spend a huge chunk of their day simply walking around the organization and talking to people, getting to know who they are, and learning about their tasks. It would be very easy for a new leader to get caught up in the myriad of office-bound meetings that are arguably necessary. But, there's a great likelihood that the leader’s overall effectiveness and chance of success within the organization will be greater by making those initial connections and allowing those perceptions to drive understanding. Successful leaders understand the importance of establishing and maintaining high-touch. Some of the best leaders on the planet establish within their calendar time to simply walk around, observing the work environment and looking to connect with those who are on the front lines of doing the work, looking for clues to success and are seeking understanding, solving problems on the spot, and resolving conflicts before they emerge.
Connect with High Tech — Manage by Effectively Using Technology

So, can you manage by walking around online? Can you do high touch as a leader with high tech? The answer is yes. However, you shouldn't use technology to the exclusion of opportunities to connect with face-to-face. To put it in perspective, probably the best thing that a leader can do today with all the access points of technology is to simply see these tools as another mechanism for making connection.

For example, if a leader recognizes that there is an individual in the organization with whom they haven't spoken in a while and for whatever reason they still haven't been able to see them face-to-face, a warm text message indicating that they were thinking about them and checking in can mean the world to the person receiving the message.

Another advantage of these high-tech tools is that they are very scalable. Certainly a leader could send a group text and literally connect with everybody in the organization in a heartbeat. However, deeper levels of personalization emerge when the messages themselves are more personalized. So, as a point of practice, technology can be used to enhance a steady diet of face-to-face, heartfelt connection.
Put It in Writing! It’s Permanent! — Manage Using Written Notes

In an era of technology that can ebb and flow in the blink of an eye, the permanence of a handwritten card or note makes a big difference to those who receive them. Some of the best leaders have maintained a habit of writing a personal note every day to different people within the organization, expressing gratitude or the observance of something positive within the organization. For example, some leaders will maintain a stack of these notes. After they manage by walking around, observing noteworthy attitudes, behaviors, and accomplishments, they will follow up with the permanence of a written note. The good news and the good feelings within are hard to deny.

Leadership Reflections: The Keys to Great Communication

We learned in these past two units that great communication doesn't happen by accident. In fact, we found out that authenticity, relationships, and carefully considered nonverbal communication can have a huge impact on those with whom you communicate. For this reflection, let's think about the first two, since this is a lot to reflect upon. Authenticity and relationships may seem abstract or amorphous, but in reality, they are attributes in communication that we can sense or feel right away.

Have you ever met somebody who is completely inauthentic? Maybe they were trying to sell you something or convince you to do something for them. Their inauthenticity made your communication with them more difficult. Furthermore, we usually don't create a relationship with inauthentic people.

So, for this reflection, what steps could you take to create a deeper sense of authenticity and improved relationships in your organization?

Reflect on these questions in your workbook.

Continued

What things could you do as a leader to demonstrate that you are authentic and committed to those that you are in relationship with?

Get specific and reflect on things that you can do right away.

11 of 15
Nonverbals Matter

While you’re listening to someone, don’t just take in their words -- study the speaker. Be aware of the speaker’s voice and mannerisms. Notice his effect on you. Become aware of your own voice and body language, too.

Pat Summitt

Learn to Be a Great Communicator: Nonverbals Really Matter, featuring John Horton

m4v5_transcript.pdf
117.9 KB

Continued

The Stare

Much has been written over the years about the famous Pat Summit stare. Her very expressive eyes and face had a stirring emotional impact on her players, the fans, the referees, and all levels of her opponents. None of this was by accident. She understood at a very high level the power of nonverbal communications. She understood that how she carried herself could have a significant impact on her message. She understood that words alone weren’t enough. In order to have a significant impact on other people (the true goal of leadership), a leader must take advantage of all the tools at their disposal. In this case, nonverbal tools, when used thoughtfully, can become an expert leverage point in reinforcing your message.

A Deeper Understanding of Nonverbal Communication

The goal of communication is to create impact or understanding. If you were delivering a college commencement speech, you may want to send the message of hope or inspiration to those in attendance. Or, if you were trying to mend a broken relationship, you may convey the right words of apology to move the relationship forward. In both examples, we search for tools to help carry our message, hoping that what’s in our hearts and in our heads can be transferred to our audience. When you think about it, it’s a painfully difficult translation. Our brains are enormously complicated, and we still have a lot to learn about mental processing. If you are trying to share a feeling with someone who hasn’t lived your life experience, hasn’t grown up in your world, or may be a very different age, all those differentiating factors can make communicating even basic ideas more difficult.

The Impact of Three Communication Elements on Messages of Feelings and Attitudes

Pie chart: Words: 7; How words are said: 38; Facial expression/nonverbal: 55.

Albert Mehrabian. 1981. Silent Messages: Implicit Communication of Emotions and Attitudes

To help better break this down, we need to reflect on how we currently take in the signals during communication and which signals we tend to pay the most attention to. Although scientific research doesn’t represent a comprehensive understanding of the art of communication, it does give us a starting point. When communicating with someone face-to-face, extensive research concluded that 7% of the impact came from the words being used, while 38% was conveyed by the way the words were said. This means somebody could use the words "I love you" in a sentence. But if this is said sarcastically or with laughter, the message is significantly altered. Perhaps, more importantly, the same research revealed that the message received was 55% impacted by the use of a person's facial expressions and body language.

Why Read a Face Over Listening to Words?

So, why would our brains work this way? It likely comes down to a basic survival instinct. There are hundreds of muscles in our face, and the evidence of joy, frustration, and fatigue all show up in our bodies — arguably a lot more authentically than in our words. How many times, for example, has a friend told you “I’m fine,” when you knew they weren’t? How about when someone you love says, “I’m not tired,” when you can see they are exhausted? Our brains have learned to study others and know the signs of what’s really going on with them. It’s an instinct that has helped us protect each other and survive.

So How Can I Apply This?

Study yourself on video

If facial expressions and body language mean so much, you need to spend some time in the mirror or on video. Without taking the time to really study ourselves, we can't begin to observe how others are likely perceiving our behaviors. How many times have you seen yourself on video and disliked what you saw? Does this person look strong and confident? Would you believe what they were saying if you didn't know them? It is important to be really honest with yourself and look at your facial expressions.

Do you need to slow down or pick up the pace?
Do you need to speak with more confidence?
Do you need more humor?
Do you appear in control?

Take a good look at your nonverbal communication and think about how others may be receiving the messages you are sending.

video.transcript_text:
Learn to Be a Great Communicator: Nonverbals Really Matter, Featuring John 
Horton 
 
 
John Horton, Executive Coach 
 
“While you’re listening to someone, don’t just take in the words. Study the speaker. Be aware 
of the speaker’s voice and mannerisms. Notice his effect on you. Become aware of your own 
voice and body language, too.” If you need an example of the power of nonverbal 
communication, simply look no further than Coach Summitt’s own famous stare. The stare was 
legendary and accompanied by stories from almost every player who played for her and surely 
every referee who ever blew a whistle against Coach Summitt’s Lady Vols. 
  
In fact, former Lady Vols player Kara Lawson said, “Here’s the thing about the stare, about how 
powerful it was. You knew when it was on you, when you couldn’t even see it. There were 
times we would be in the huddle, and I would feel that she was staring at me. And I would say 
to one of my teammates, ‘She’s looking at me right now, isn’t she?’ And they’d say, ‘Yes, she is.’ 
You felt it. You felt like wherever you were.” 
  
Albert Mehrabian is professor emeritus of psychology at UCLA. In his foundational work, Dr. 
Mehrabian and his colleagues studied nonverbal communication in an effort to understand the 
relative impact of facial expressions and spoken words. Mehrabian’s research provided the 
basis for a widely quoted and unfortunately, often much oversimplified statistic on the 
effectiveness of spoken communications. Mehrabian found that 7 percent of a message 
pertaining to feelings and attitudes is in the words that are spoken. Thirty-eight percent of a 
message pertaining to feelings and attitudes is paralinguistic, or the way the words are said. 
And 55 percent of a message pertaining to feelings and attitudes is in facial expression. 
  
The important points of Mehrabian’s work are these: it’s not just the words.  
 
A lot of communication comes through nonverbal communication. Without seeing and hearing 
nonverbal communication, it’s easier to misunderstand the words. When we’re unsure about 
what the words mean, we pay more attention to the nonverbal communication.  
 
Pat Summitt found that listening and being aware of her own nonverbal communication made 
her a better coach. Are you effectively using nonverbal cues and expressions in your own daily 
communication? As you go about your day for the next few days, be cognizant of how your 
nonverbal cues help or hurt your communication as a leader.

Wrap-Up

Learn to Be a Great Communicator: Wrap-Up, featuring Virginia Means

m4v6_transcript.pdf
126.1 KB

Continued

It’s Not About Your Great Speech, It’s About Their Great Performance

Once again, it’s important for leaders to recognize that their success will not be driven by their ability to give speeches. While strong verbal skills are always an advantage, leaders are measured by the degree to which they empower and ultimately super-empower other people to perform at high levels. The very best leaders create conditions where their teams blossom and contribute in a way that’s rarely observed in other similar organizations. These leaders are able to get other people to give more and try harder when others are exhausted.

Let's review the keys to effective communication: Authenticity; Relationships; Nonverbal communication.

Key 1 — Authenticity

You can only play a role for so long. What you are, who you are, what you value, and where you invest your emotional energy will become obvious to everyone around you in time. This is why it’s so important to know yourself and to be authentic with others about who you are. When you meet highly successful leaders they are often acutely aware of the values and beliefs that drive their behaviors. They can describe them with certainty because they know that living these values and beliefs is inherent to the journey of successful leader.

Key 2 — Relationships

Relationships are always under construction. If you are just getting to know someone new to your organization or social circle, your investment in getting to know them will pay big dividends in enhancing the relationship. Additionally, the strength and quality of your relationships will influence the quality of your outcomes. By investing in relationships, you are investing in the very fabric of success of every organization or team.

Key 3 — Nonverbal Communication

Many people think they have a good poker face. But, in reality, many of us give away our feelings through our body language. When people go through periods of depression, their posture is rarely in peak form. When people fall in love, their eyes are bright and their steps are light. What’s important to remember here is that it’s very difficult to fake body language. Being your authentic self and investing in your health and well-being make good nonverbals less of a chore. Video technology makes it easy to see ourselves, and when you do, ask yourself whether you would follow the person that you see. Remember, one of the most compelling elements of a leader is the expression of confidence. Confidence is almost impossible to ignore, and in many cases, it is the invisible, quiet, determining factor of success.

Nonverbal Communication (cont.)

As an exercise, you may want to consider visualizing something you’re confident about and examine your face and body when you’re thinking about that element. How do you look when you are feeling confident? Remember that look and hold onto it! As often as you possibly can, try to express that look on your face, or hold your body in that place of confidence. Finally, what is really exciting about this exercise is that it actually becomes predictive of your emotional state. In other words, even if you aren’t feeling particularly confident or calm, successful facial expressions or body language can take you there. Try it!

Practical Thoughts on Communication

In ending this section, it’s helpful to reflect on and revisit some very simple yet profound truths about communication:

1. Shorter messages make a deeper impact

Have you ever opened your phone to a really long text or email? Unless you are in love with the sender, you may feel a sense of dread at having to wade through it all. Don’t feel guilty — it's not about your unwillingness to read a long message. The amount of brainpower it takes to understand a long message, and then reflect on its meaning and intention, represents one of the more complex brain function activities in processing communication. The best leaders today edit themselves to make sure they aren’t using too many words.

2. Simple is better than complex

The most popular website on the planet is Google. Have you ever noticed the simplicity of the homepage? Think of how many gadgets could be attached to the Google homepage. Instead, the aspiration is to make it look simple and accessible. The same is true when it comes to learning. Simplify the game plan and make it accessible to everyone. Boil it down to simple and easily digested steps. When we do this, we increase the opportunity for those learning the ropes to master the fundamentals...and ultimately become masters of what they do.

3. The truth is better than anything

Sticking with the truth makes life so much easier as a leader. When you tell the truth, you don’t have to keep track of your story or manage perception. You can tell the truth and do the best you can to support those around you in dealing with that truth.

video.transcript_text:
Learn to Be a Great Communicator: Wrap-Up, Featuring Virginia Means 
 
 
Virginia Means, Chief People Officer, United Distributors, Inc. 
 
Coach Summitt said, “Communication is not just about giving great speeches. It’s about 
allowing others to express themselves.” Effective communication is about more than just 
exchanging information. Let’s take a look back at several characteristics highlighted by John 
Horton that can apply to increasing understanding and communication. 
  
Great communicators are authentic, place high value on relationships, and are also aware of 
the impact of their nonverbal communication, body language, eye contact, etc.  
 
Authenticity matters a lot. Leaders must be open and transparent and find their own authentic 
voice. Bring who you are, where you come from, and what you value into your communication. 
  
Consider this: 161 players played for Coach Summitt. Of those, 74 became coaches themselves. 
Forty-six percent of Coach Summitt’s student athletes followed in her footsteps. Relationships 
and authenticity are the only way to explain such a staggering number of individuals following 
Pat into the coaching ranks. 
  
But remember, it’s not just your words that matter. A great deal of communication comes 
through nonverbal communication. If we’re not aware of the nonverbal communication, it can 
be easy to misunderstand the message. As humans, when we’re unsure about what the words 
mean, we pay more attention to the non-verbal signs, cues, and expressions. So, be aware of 
the message you may be sending with your nonverbal communication. Pat’s famous stare is 
one of the clearest nonverbal examples ever sent. 
  
In the end, always remember John (Horton’s) communication maxim: short is better than long. 
Simple is better than complex. Truth and authenticity are more important than everything else.

It’s Not About Your Great Speech, It’s About Their Great Performance

Once again, it’s important for leaders to recognize that their success will not be driven by their ability to give speeches. While strong verbal skills are always an advantage, leaders are measured by the degree to which they empower and ultimately super-empower other people to perform at high levels. The very best leaders create conditions where their teams blossom and contribute in a way that’s rarely observed in other similar organizations. These leaders are able to get other people to give more and try harder when others are exhausted.
Let's review the keys to effective communication: Authenticity; Relationships; Nonverbal communication.
Key 1 — Authenticity

You can only play a role for so long. What you are, who you are, what you value, and where you invest your emotional energy will become obvious to everyone around you in time. This is why it’s so important to know yourself and to be authentic with others about who you are. When you meet highly successful leaders they are often acutely aware of the values and beliefs that drive their behaviors. They can describe them with certainty because they know that living these values and beliefs is inherent to the journey of successful leader.

Relationships are always under construction. If you are just getting to know someone new to your organization or social circle, your investment in getting to know them will pay big dividends in enhancing the relationship. Additionally, the strength and quality of your relationships will influence the quality of your outcomes. By investing in relationships, you are investing in the very fabric of success of every organization or team.
Key 3 — Nonverbal Communication

Many people think they have a good poker face. But, in reality, many of us give away our feelings through our body language. When people go through periods of depression, their posture is rarely in peak form. When people fall in love, their eyes are bright and their steps are light. What’s important to remember here is that it’s very difficult to fake body language. Being your authentic self and investing in your health and well-being make good nonverbals less of a chore. Video technology makes it easy to see ourselves, and when you do, ask yourself whether you would follow the person that you see. Remember, one of the most compelling elements of a leader is the expression of confidence. Confidence is almost impossible to ignore, and in many cases, it is the invisible, quiet, determining factor of success.
Nonverbal Communication (cont.)

As an exercise, you may want to consider visualizing something you’re confident about and examine your face and body when you’re thinking about that element. How do you look when you are feeling confident? Remember that look and hold onto it! As often as you possibly can, try to express that look on your face, or hold your body in that place of confidence. Finally, what is really exciting about this exercise is that it actually becomes predictive of your emotional state. In other words, even if you aren’t feeling particularly confident or calm, successful facial expressions or body language can take you there. Try it!
Practical Thoughts on Communication
In ending this section, it’s helpful to reflect on and revisit some very simple yet profound truths about communication:
1. Shorter messages make a deeper impact

Have you ever opened your phone to a really long text or email? Unless you are in love with the sender, you may feel a sense of dread at having to wade through it all. Don’t feel guilty — it's not about your unwillingness to read a long message. The amount of brainpower it takes to understand a long message, and then reflect on its meaning and intention, represents one of the more complex brain function activities in processing communication. The best leaders today edit themselves to make sure they aren’t using too many words.
2. Simple is better than complex

The most popular website on the planet is Google. Have you ever noticed the simplicity of the homepage? Think of how many gadgets could be attached to the Google homepage. Instead, the aspiration is to make it look simple and accessible. The same is true when it comes to learning. Simplify the game plan and make it accessible to everyone. Boil it down to simple and easily digested steps. When we do this, we increase the opportunity for those learning the ropes to master the fundamentals...and ultimately become masters of what they do.
3. The truth is better than anything

Sticking with the truth makes life so much easier as a leader. When you tell the truth, you don’t have to keep track of your story or manage perception. You can tell the truth and do the best you can to support those around you in dealing with that truth.

Leadership Reflections: Let’s Talk…About Nonverbals

Why is a picture worth 1,000 words? Because in many cases, words can be imprecise. You can describe in a beautifully written essay the majesty of the Swiss Alps, but it doesn't compare to actually standing there and taking it all in. To that end, your nonverbals work the same way. You can tell somebody you love them, but if your facial expression looks like you just chomped on a lemon, they may be less likely to believe your message!

While this may sound like overly simple advice, let's get a little more technical and practical. First, have you ever seen yourself in a video or in a picture and been able to think about what others might see in your face when you look at them?

Think about the facial expressions that you have when you're sitting in a meeting, issuing a directive, or encouraging somebody. If at all possible, take a picture of yourself looking in the mirror and imagining yourself in those positions. While it may not be perfect, it can at least give you some perspective on the facial expressions that you make when you are in these moments. If you can take a picture of these images, it can give you something to reflect on.

As you think about these images, what do you have to say about your own facial expressions?

Do you look interested?
Do you look engaged?

Some people give off facial expressions that don't exactly inspire confidence, or even trust. Good facial expressions sometimes need to be practiced. Take the time to actually reflect on the expressions you see and what you think others may be perceiving of your nonverbal communications.

Reflect on these questions in your workbook.

Continued

Page 1 of 15
Pat in Her Own Words

It's very important...that we have great work ethic. Some of the most talented players are not always the ones who work the hardest. Why? Because they don't have it right here. You've got to have it in your heart. You've got to be invested.

Pat Summitt

Discipline Yourself So No One Else Has To: Pat in Her Own Words

m5v1_transcript.pdf
107.4 KB

Continued

Outstanding Work Ethic

It’s difficult to argue the importance of an outstanding work ethic — a consistent commitment around working with energy and focus towards things that matter. People with an outstanding work ethic usually have outrageous levels of success in life, both personally and professionally. The reason is fairly simple — with hard work comes the ability to learn new things along the way, try things and fail, and then rebuild strategies. Individuals and teams with less talent, but with a strong work ethic, will often prevail over more talented teams that lack an outstanding work ethic.

Within Your Control

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

When it comes to work ethic in your team or organization, what aspects do you think are within your control and which are not?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Continued

As a leader, you can't necessarily control your and your team's innate gifts or talents. However, what is within your control is the development and cultivation of an outstanding work ethic. With a great work ethic, almost anyone can at least reach some level of competence and success. When talented people come together and demonstrate stellar work ethic, the sky is truly the limit. No matter what the context, strategy, technology, or time, work ethic will always be a key factor in determining success.

When talented people come together and demonstrate stellar work ethic, the sky is truly the limit.

People with Talent

Sometimes you'll find people with outstanding talent who don't seem to work as hard as the rest of the group. If you've ever found yourself on a team observing a person with great talent, but a poor work ethic, it may have been tempting to feel a little jealous of their raw talent. However, in business and in life, work ethic makes a huge difference in your overall success. Simply put, you can't be successful in life without consistently developing your work ethic. Period. So don't be jealous of people with outstanding talent. Just commit to working as hard as you can, and if you're on a team with these talented people, encourage them to do the same!

Work Ethic Is a Daily Investment That Pays

Compounding interest is arguably a pretty good analogy for a work ethic. If you find a simple investment calculator and evaluate the power of compound interest each month over a period of years or decades, the accumulation of wealth is surprising — $100 a month for 30 years becomes $100,000. An investment of $1,000 a month for 30 years becomes a million. What starts off as a modest sum, with a modest effort, becomes a formidable financial force! It's the same with work ethic! You might barely notice the commitment you make in putting in that extra effort each day, similar to setting aside a few dollars each month. Over time, with that extra effort or funding, you'll end up with a fortune.

Work Hard Every Day

To that end, leaders should demonstrate a commitment to themselves and with others to work hard every day. By making that investment, teams or groups can overcome even more talented adversaries or competitors.

Everyone Needs to Work Hard

If everyone on a team isn’t working hard, a lack of synergy emerges. For example, if a leader permits a more talented team member to stop working hard, the other members of the team will become demotivated. On the other hand, there is nothing more motivating to a team than to look around and realize that everyone, including the leader, is working absolutely as hard as they can. Therefore, it's important for a leader to build the expectation within a group that hard work is a consistent expectation within the organization. Once that's established, it's very difficult to do anything but continuously progress.

video.transcript_text:
Discipline Yourself So No One Else Has To: Pat in Her Own Words 
 
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
It’s very important in athletics and particularly with our teams here at the University of 
Tennessee is that we have great work ethic. And the amazing thing is, some of the most 
talented players are not always the ones that work the hardest. Go figure that out. Why? 
Because they don’t have it right here. You’ve got to have it in your heart. You’ve got to be 
invested. And it’s not just in what you do as you work hard, but when you’re building a big team 
concept, I mean, you’ve got to go get other people and you’ve got to bring them in and say, 
“You’re not working as hard as you can work. And what does that do to our team?”  
 
But it starts with the individual -- just knowing that if they invest every day, when it’s game 
time, things are going to fall in place; because you’re going to make them happen because of 
the habits that you have. And then for me, as a coach, I’m going to bring the whole team 
together and I’m going to say, “If you don’t work hard, you don’t need to be at the University of 
Tennessee; because what you’re doing is taking away from the team concept and you’ve got to 
be invested in our team concept and everyone has to work hard every day.”

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Page 3 of 15
Discipline Yourself So No One Else Has To

Discipline Yourself So No One Else Has To: Introduction, featuring Joan Cronan

m5v2_transcript.pdf
124.2 KB

Continued

I don’t like this subject. It makes me bite my lip. I warn you right now that my warmest, friendliest side doesn’t show up in these pages. By the time you’re done, you’ll think I’m one tough lady, and you may even like me a little less. That’s okay, as long as you respect me and believe in what I tell you — because that’s what discipline is all about. It’s about belief. — Pat Summitt

The Importance of Discipline

At the most basic level, discipline is a term that relates to the ability to strictly adhere to a set of standards or obligations. If you have a health challenge and your doctor indicates you must avoid certain foods, the gift of discipline is what gives you the psychological certainty to purposefully and predictably avoid those foods that would make you unhealthy. So, in this context, to be a good leader, you need to be used to practicing and applying the benefits of discipline. Without question, in order to understand and embrace the benefits of discipline, you also have to have the maturity to realize that discipline isn’t about taking things away. It’s about growing and improving by eliminating, saying "no," or simply making different choices. If you are under doctor’s orders to eat different things, you’re not saying "no" to food. You are, however, making different choices at breakfast, lunch, and dinner — and you have the mental ability, or the discipline, to navigate that choice.

External and Internal Discipline Forces

You can think of discipline as coming from two primary forces: external and internal. Think for a moment about what this might mean. Then, sort the stack of cards below into either external or internal forces of discipline.

Continued

For the patient whose doctor says they need to make some changes; for the child whose parents insist on good behavior; and yes, for Coach Summitt demanding discipline and alignment with her players — these are all examples of external forces building discipline. For the patient making lifestyle changes as an investment in their future; for the team member knowing the expectations and committing to hard work and dedication to meet or exceed them; and for Coach Summitt's players who committed to excellence even without her immediate oversight — these all reflect internal forces building discipline. Coach Summitt didn’t make "suggestions" about certain essential behaviors or conduct. She doggedly demanded them and held her players accountable rigorously and continuously. Her force within the program made it impossible for the players to make any other choices if they wanted to be on her team. Her external reinforcement, carefully established and clearly articulated, helped her players live and work with the level of discipline required to be champions.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

Pat rather famously (and loudly) confronted behaviors not aligned with her high performance standards and disciplined approach. Do you think these external forces of discipline were enough to produce her highly successful teams over the years? Why or why not?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Continued

High performance and discipline are not all she asked of her players, right? Indeed, like any great leader, Pat was interested in building her players' discipline, but eventually without her oversight. Once they understood the expectations, she wanted her players to begin to operate with a certain level of discipline and conduct without her having to observe or correct them.

To that end, which of the following would you say are important truths about discipline? Select all that apply.

Exactly! All of these are true about discipline. When individuals take on the leader's expectations as their own internal, individualized, personal expectations, this becomes a huge differentiator in helping the organization go "from good to great" or "from great to exceptional."

Continued

Well-led organizations understand and embrace this required discipline to the point where those expectations become the internal guardrails that govern every decision.

Self-Discipline: Who Needs Drive?

Ultimately, self-discipline is the primary destination. Organizations are far more effective when they are teaming with individuals who don’t need to be driven, but instead drive themselves. This is a powerful differentiator. Like our earlier example, without question, well-behaved children aren't born that way. Similarly, in organizational settings, even the most creative and innovative companies have expectations of behavior and effort. Yet even with those expectations, the most powerful companies employ people that don’t just comply with the requested behaviors out of a sense of duty. They behave that way because those expectations are in alignment with who they are as people. This is why it is so important to go to work for organizations that have a climate, culture, and expectations aligned with your own. Furthermore, it’s essential to be in charge of your own internal discipline and drive. So who needs drive? We all do, and leadership should be looking for individuals in their organization who are willing to hold the standard of discipline without having to be monitored every minute by the leader.

What Do You Get from Self-Discipline?

You will have far greater effectiveness as a leader if you can demonstrate self-discipline yourself. As leaders, we need to perform! In fact, many extremely successful leaders will actually hold themselves to a much higher standard than even the standards they might hold for others. This sends the message to others that meeting and exceeding expectations is the gold standard.

Exactly! In all these situations, the leaders are living out their own high standards in front of their teams or followers, helping those individuals internalize and build their own self-discipline.

Continued

Most of us would rather be moved by internal voices than be externally driven. The message is clear: in the best organizations with the best leaders, we see evidence that leaders set high standards, and then those standards become the cultural expectation. Each individual in the organization begins to adopt and internalize those expectations, allowing performance to be pushed to ever-higher levels!

Discipline fosters achievement and self-confidence. Discipline is the only sure way I know to convince people to believe in themselves. Discipline gets you out of bed in the morning. It gets you to work on time, and it tells you when you need to work late. It drives you. It is essential to success, whether individually or in a group. — Pat Summitt

Firm, Fair, and Consistent

We've established that leaders need to lead with expectations of a highly disciplined environment, starting with themselves. Pat Summitt believed in setting some specific parameters around discipline practices for leaders — that they are firm, fair, and consistent.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

Before we give you our thoughts on these three areas, how would you describe what it means to be firm, fair, and consistent with discipline?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Continued

Firm

To be firm means to be certain. If, for example, as a leader you expect everyone to arrive on time and to deliver their work to a certain standard, to be firm means to meet the expectation, take it seriously, and maintain it. If an unmet expectation is not addressed by the leader, it sends the message that the expectation really wasn't that firm. It moves from being an "expectation" to a casual recommendation or desire.

Fair

To be fair means that the expectation is reasonable. To have a fair expectation of someone means that even if the expectation is rigorous it’s not impossible or unattainable for them. It might require growth or stretching on the team member's part, but it is achievable.

Consistent

The expectation of consistency goes back to keeping your word. Favoring an individual or group over another and allowing them to slack off violates the consistency clause. The best coaches and leaders understand that a consistent standard for all creates a culture or climate where everyone sees discipline as something that is equally shared and expected.

Discipline Yourself So No One Else Has To: Introduction, Featuring Joan Cronan 
 
 
Joan Cronan, Women’s Athletic Director Emeritus, University of Tennessee 
 
Pat wrote in her book, “I don't like this subject. It makes me bite my lip. I warn you right now 
that my warmest, friendliest side doesn’t show up in these pages. By the time you’re done, 
you’ll think I’m one tough lady and you may even like me a little less. That’s OK as long as you 
respect me and believe in what I tell you, because that’s what discipline is about. It’s about 
belief.”  
 
Coach Summitt was a master at self-discipline. From a hard upbringing on a dairy farm, 
discipline was a way of life for Pat. She couldn’t escape it if she tried. But that early work ethic 
made an incredible mark on Pat’s life and her willingness to discipline in everything she did, 
including following her dreams. Pat’s passion and genius was in learning all she could about 
each of her players. What inspired them? What built them and brought out the best in them?  
 
But when it came to discipline, Coach Summitt was steadfast. Discipline needed to be the same 
for everyone. She was an equal opportunity disciplinarian. In this module, we will dive into the 
topic of self-discipline. After all, as Pat said often, you “discipline yourself before someone else 
has to.” We will learn from Pat’s leadership wisdom that discipline must be fair, firm, and 
consistent. 
  
Pat often said ... 
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
“Discipline fosters achievement and self-confidence. Discipline is the only sure way I know to 
convince people to believe in themselves. Discipline gets you out of bed in the morning. It gets 
you to work on time and it tells you when you need to work late. It drives you. It’s essential to 
success, whether individually or in a group.”  
 
Joan Cronan, Women’s Athletic Director Emeritus, University of Tennessee 
 
“Discipline is the only sure way I know to convince people to believe in themselves.” 
  
Discipline is the internal mechanism that self-motivates you. Are you your own self-
disciplinarian? Although it is difficult and not fun, when we discipline ourselves, we clear the 
path for realizing our goal.  
 
Let’s learn from Pat how to discipline ourselves where no one else has to.

The Importance of Discipline

At the most basic level, discipline is a term that relates to the ability to strictly adhere to a set of standards or obligations. If you have a health challenge and your doctor indicates you must avoid certain foods, the gift of discipline is what gives you the psychological certainty to purposefully and predictably avoid those foods that would make you unhealthy. So, in this context, to be a good leader, you need to be used to practicing and applying the benefits of discipline. Without question, in order to understand and embrace the benefits of discipline, you also have to have the maturity to realize that discipline isn’t about taking things away. It’s about growing and improving by eliminating, saying "no," or simply making different choices. If you are under doctor’s orders to eat different things, you’re not saying "no" to food. You are, however, making different choices at breakfast, lunch, and dinner — and you have the mental ability, or the discipline, to navigate that choice.
External and Internal Discipline Forces

You can think of discipline as coming from two primary forces: external and internal. Think for a moment about what this might mean. Then, sort the stack of cards below into either external or internal forces of discipline.
Continued

For the patient whose doctor says they need to make some changes; for the child whose parents insist on good behavior; and yes, for Coach Summitt demanding discipline and alignment with her players — these are all examples of external forces building discipline. For the patient making lifestyle changes as an investment in their future; for the team member knowing the expectations and committing to hard work and dedication to meet or exceed them; and for Coach Summitt's players who committed to excellence even without her immediate oversight — these all reflect internal forces building discipline. Coach Summitt didn’t make "suggestions" about certain essential behaviors or conduct. She doggedly demanded them and held her players accountable rigorously and continuously. Her force within the program made it impossible for the players to make any other choices if they wanted to be on her team. Her external reinforcement, carefully established and clearly articulated, helped her players live and work with the level of discipline required to be champions.
Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

Pat rather famously (and loudly) confronted behaviors not aligned with her high performance standards and disciplined approach. Do you think these external forces of discipline were enough to produce her highly successful teams over the years? Why or why not?
Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.
Continued

High performance and discipline are not all she asked of her players, right? Indeed, like any great leader, Pat was interested in building her players' discipline, but eventually without her oversight. Once they understood the expectations, she wanted her players to begin to operate with a certain level of discipline and conduct without her having to observe or correct them.
To that end, which of the following would you say are important truths about discipline? Select all that apply.

Exactly! All of these are true about discipline. When individuals take on the leader's expectations as their own internal, individualized, personal expectations, this becomes a huge differentiator in helping the organization go "from good to great" or "from great to exceptional."
Continued

Furthermore, it’s essential to be in charge of your own internal discipline and drive. So who needs drive? We all do, and leadership should be looking for individuals in their organization who are willing to hold the standard of discipline without having to be monitored every minute by the leader.
What Do You Get from Self-Discipline?

You will have far greater effectiveness as a leader if you can demonstrate self-discipline yourself. As leaders, we need to perform! In fact, many extremely successful leaders will actually hold themselves to a much higher standard than even the standards they might hold for others. This sends the message to others that meeting and exceeding expectations is the gold standard.
Exactly! In all these situations, the leaders are living out their own high standards in front of their teams or followers, helping those individuals internalize and build their own self-discipline.
Continued

Most of us would rather be moved by internal voices than be externally driven. The message is clear: in the best organizations with the best leaders, we see evidence that leaders set high standards, and then those standards become the cultural expectation. Each individual in the organization begins to adopt and internalize those expectations, allowing performance to be pushed to ever-higher levels!

Discipline fosters achievement and self-confidence. Discipline is the only sure way I know to convince people to believe in themselves. Discipline gets you out of bed in the morning. It gets you to work on time, and it tells you when you need to work late. It drives you. It is essential to success, whether individually or in a group. — Pat Summitt
Firm, Fair, and Consistent

We've established that leaders need to lead with expectations of a highly disciplined environment, starting with themselves. Pat Summitt believed in setting some specific parameters around discipline practices for leaders — that they are firm, fair, and consistent.
Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.
Before we give you our thoughts on these three areas, how would you describe what it means to be firm, fair, and consistent with discipline?
Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.
Continued
Firm

To be firm means to be certain. If, for example, as a leader you expect everyone to arrive on time and to deliver their work to a certain standard, to be firm means to meet the expectation, take it seriously, and maintain it. If an unmet expectation is not addressed by the leader, it sends the message that the expectation really wasn't that firm. It moves from being an "expectation" to a casual recommendation or desire.
Fair

To be fair means that the expectation is reasonable. To have a fair expectation of someone means that even if the expectation is rigorous it’s not impossible or unattainable for them. It might require growth or stretching on the team member's part, but it is achievable.
Consistent

The expectation of consistency goes back to keeping your word. Favoring an individual or group over another and allowing them to slack off violates the consistency clause. steps.exact_visible_copy:
Page 6 of 15
Discipline Should Be Fair

As a leader, you cannot develop discipline in others if you don't have self-discipline. It starts at the top. You have to demonstrate that no staff member, no employee, no star player, is above the rules. I don't ask anything of our players that I haven't asked of myself. — Pat Summitt

Discipline Yourself So No One Else Has To: Discipline Should Be Fair, featuring Teela Jackson

m5v3_transcript.pdf
120 KB

Continued

Walking the Talk

As a leader, it's difficult to demand discipline and work ethic in others if you don't demonstrate that same level of discipline and work ethic for yourself. This is why we hold leaders to such a high standard. We watch how they carry themselves, how they dress, how they prepare, and how they execute their role. We notice what time a leader arrives at work, what time they leave, and we have a tendency to carefully observe the intensity a leader brings to their work each and every day.

Leaders Hold the Standard

Outstanding leaders hold an incredibly high standard for themselves and are always looking for opportunities to demonstrate the level of discipline required. By holding the standard and remaining consistent, the team understands that this standard of work, discipline, and performance is the common expectation. Everyone understands that this level of effort is what the team is committed to providing for the team and, ultimately, themselves.

Team Synergy Is Destroyed by the Lack of Discipline

A team's energy erodes significantly when there is a collective lack of discipline. Consider this example:

Suppose your team has an important commitment to keep. The leader has clearly set the expectations for the team.

One team member is particularly talented to the extent one would expect them to consistently exceed those expectations.

It turns out, though, that this individual, while talented in their work, is cutting corners in some areas. Perhaps they feel their attendance or meeting participation can slide because they’re so valuable to the team that they deserve some slack.

The leader seems to have this same philosophy and doesn’t hold this talented individual to the same standards as others on the team.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

How would other, less-talented and less-skilled team members likely feel about this situation?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Continued

Those teammates who didn’t have that same talent or skill would observe the other person getting a break, being relieved in the moment of discipline.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

If you were on a team where a talented member was allowed to slack, would you put in the extra effort? Would you continue to extend yourself?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Continued

Maybe you would put in the extra effort. But in many cases, teams are quickly diminished and the level of effort compromised when exceptions are made and discipline is sacrificed.

There's a Difference Between Personalization and Consistency

Situational leadership is very popular in business today and it applies to both coaching and leadership. With situational leadership, the leader recognizes that it's important to recognize the individual person or psychological makeup of a team and try to support or lead within that context. The leader would support and engage them differently depending on the style they prefer in terms of motivation or engagement. Now, there is nothing perfect about this approach, and a leader can't expect that every interaction has to be perfectly tailored to every individual person. This would be impossible. It is, however, a good rule of thumb. Take team feedback, for example. Consider both sides of the following card:

Some team members may be highly social. They might find themselves needing a lot of feedback from the leader.

Other team members may prefer less interaction. They might only need occasional encouragement or redirection.

Continued

With situational leadership, the leader would support and engage these team members differently depending on the style they prefer in terms of motivation or engagement. This can be an effective, yet imperfect, approach. A leader can't possibly tailor every interaction to every individual person. But it's a good rule of thumb.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

How might a leader mistakenly apply situational leadership in a way that negatively impacts the team or organization? In other words, how do you think situational leadership might be misapplied?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Continued

It’s critical that you not mistake situational leadership for inconsistency or overly personalized group expectations. To that end, sort the following stack of cards into either situational leadership or inconsistency/over-personalization.

Continued

To summarize, two of the following behaviors combine to represent the very essence of situational leadership. All the other behaviors are quite the opposite. Select the two behaviors that, together, model situational leadership.

You got it! Situational leadership is not: being inconsistent or overly personalized with group expectations; compromising a team goal or expectation; or personalizing the standard or "bar" and letting people slide. Instead, situational leadership is: maintaining the expectations for everyone on the team, including the leader; and helping members of a team individually with as much stealth and grace as possible.

Continued

Rules Few in Number

Have you ever read case law? It’s very complicated. Overly-complicated laws or rules take far too much effort to understand or execute. We hire tax attorneys because tax law is very hard to understand. As a leader, if you want fluid, unfettered compliance with the rules, while maintaining high levels of momentum, you simply can't make the rules so complex that it requires a specialist to interpret them.

Coach Pat Summitt believed one way you can do this is to make sure your rules are few in number, yet important and impactful. Rather than 15 complex rules, you're better off with three to five very impactful rules that cover the majority of the conditions that would make a difference on the team or in the group. As a leader, spending time creating rules for every outlier example is arguably a waste of time and energy. Ultimately, teams don't work as quickly or with as much fluidity if they're thinking about the rules every moment. However, if the rules are clear and understandable, they can get momentum going by just keeping a few basic and essential elements in mind.

Rules That Solve Problems

When you think about it, rules on a team or group are really aimed at solving problems on the way to success. The more mature the group or team, the more time that should be spent explaining the rule and clarifying its intent.

For example, suppose a preschool teacher makes a rule about hand washing to help keep her students from getting sick. That's the goal she wants to reach or problem she wants to tackle. She might explain to the children the basics of hand washing and germs. She then might create conditions where hand washing becomes a fun ritual. When these same kids get to grade school, that teacher may also have a hand washing rule. Several years have passed and the children are more mature, so this teacher might include a deeper explanation of germs, how they mature, and their impact on human health. When you're working with a more advanced group, give them the opportunity to understand that the rules should give the group an opportunity to work together in a more fluid way for peak performance. High-performing teams today will often establish team protocols within their group. For example, consider a team that wants to ensure they make better use of their time, while making everyone feel respected as a commitment to being part of the group. That's the problem they want to solve. As a group, they might collectively: 1. establish a rule together that timeliness in meetings is important; 2. decide that during team meetings, everyone must report in and provide feedback; and 3. establish a rule for minimizing distractions during the meeting in order to keep momentum.

These three simple rules would help solve the team's problems with meeting attendance, participation, and distractions. Rather than mechanisms for controlling behavior, the rules would create levels of freedom and improve the experience of everyone on the team — while deeply improving team performance.

Cracking Down Means Finding Balance

Finally, it’s very important to set a high standard. The very best teams are willing to create highly disciplined conditions and aren't afraid to crack down on individuals who aren't meeting the expectations. It's also important that these high-expectation environments be encouraging and nurturing, or you will lose members of the team. If all you do is spend your time cracking down, eventually people will burn out and break out and no longer be part of the team.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

What potential challenges do you see for a leader who wants to both crack down on those not meeting expectations, while also being encouraging and nurturing? What are some ways you might overcome these challenges as a leader?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Continued

Part of what it takes to be a leader is finding the balance between cracking down, nurturing, pulling back, and pushing forward. Leadership is an art, and being able to feel the energy of the group is important.

Leaders can push a team too hard, where team members feel exhausted.

Leaders can fail to push a team hard enough, leaving team members short of expectations.

The very best leaders aren’t always perfect, and even the great ones will miss out on opportunities either way. Remaining aware of this dynamic is important. Set that high expectation, and then be willing to observe the need to pull back the pressure and to make sure that the experience is rewarding.
