video.source_visible_title: Discipline Yourself So No One Else Has To: Discipline Should Be Fair
video.transcript_text:
Discipline Yourself So No One Else Has To: Discipline Should Be Fair, Featuring 
Teela Jackson 
 
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
“As a leader, you cannot develop discipline in others if you don’t have self-discipline. It starts at 
the top. You have to demonstrate that no staff member, no employee, no star player, is above 
the rules. I don’t ask anything of our players that I haven’t asked of myself.” 
 
Teela Jackson, Vice President, HR 
  
Like all great coaches, business managers, and leaders, Pat Summitt did not believe you should 
treat everyone exactly the same. Some of her players needed to be pushed and challenged. 
Some thrived on more praise. Others just needed an occasional pat on the back or for someone 
to simply just give them the ball and get out of their way. Still others required a very pointed 
stare -- you know, Pat’s famous stare.  
 
Whether you are a coach or a business leader, discipline, according to Pat, must be consistent, 
firm, and fair. To her mind, there is no faster way to destroy synergy and respect on a team or 
in an organization than to administer discipline unequally. There can be no playing favorites. 
She was clearly an equal opportunity disciplinarian. The rules must be fair and aimed at solving 
problems or potential problems before they materialize, and the consequences for breaking 
those rules must be clear, consistent, and firm. 
  
Disciplinary measures should not be compromised. 
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
“Be fair. The fewer rules you have, the fewer rules will be broken.”  
 
Teela Jackson, Vice President, HR 
 
Establishing discipline will be a lot easier if you don’t burden people with a lot of silly, minor 
regulations. All you need is a handful of fair ones that you are prepared to enforce, and when 
people participate in setting their own goals, standards, and regulations, they tend to be more 
cooperative. 
  
Pat continued this thought with, “If all you ever do is crack down on people, they won’t stay in 
your program or your business. They’ll leave. Why would you stay someplace if all it offered 
was punishment? You wouldn’t. Similarly, if all you do is punish yourself, chances are you won’t 
maintain your training regimen or work regimen. You’ll quit on it. If you are fair with yourself, 
you stand a better chance of maintaining your self-discipline.”

Page 6 of 15
Discipline Should Be Fair

As a leader, you cannot develop discipline in others if you don't have self-discipline. It starts at the top. You have to demonstrate that no staff member, no employee, no star player, is above the rules. I don't ask anything of our players that I haven't asked of myself. — Pat Summitt
Discipline Yourself So No One Else Has To: Discipline Should Be Fair, featuring Teela Jackson

m5v3_transcript.pdf
120 KB
Continued
Walking the Talk

As a leader, it's difficult to demand discipline and work ethic in others if you don't demonstrate that same level of discipline and work ethic for yourself. This is why we hold leaders to such a high standard. We watch how they carry themselves, how they dress, how they prepare, and how they execute their role. We notice what time a leader arrives at work, what time they leave, and we have a tendency to carefully observe the intensity a leader brings to their work each and every day.
Leaders Hold the Standard

Outstanding leaders hold an incredibly high standard for themselves and are always looking for opportunities to demonstrate the level of discipline required. By holding the standard and remaining consistent, the team understands that this standard of work, discipline, and performance is the common expectation. Everyone understands that this level of effort is what the team is committed to providing for the team and, ultimately, themselves.
Team Synergy Is Destroyed by the Lack of Discipline
A team's energy erodes significantly when there is a collective lack of discipline. Consider this example:
Suppose your team has an important commitment to keep. The leader has clearly set the expectations for the team.
One team member is particularly talented to the extent one would expect them to consistently exceed those expectations.

It turns out, though, that this individual, while talented in their work, is cutting corners in some areas. Perhaps they feel their attendance or meeting participation can slide because they’re so valuable to the team that they deserve some slack.
The leader seems to have this same philosophy and doesn’t hold this talented individual to the same standards as others on the team.
Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.
How would other, less-talented and less-skilled team members likely feel about this situation?
Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.
Continued
Those teammates who didn’t have that same talent or skill would observe the other person getting a break, being relieved in the moment of discipline.
Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.
If you were on a team where a talented member was allowed to slack, would you put in the extra effort? Would you continue to extend yourself?
Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.
Continued
Maybe you would put in the extra effort. But in many cases, teams are quickly diminished and the level of effort compromised when exceptions are made and discipline is sacrificed.
There's a Difference Between Personalization and Consistency

Situational leadership is very popular in business today and it applies to both coaching and leadership. With situational leadership, the leader recognizes that it's important to recognize the individual person or psychological makeup of a team and try to support or lead within that context. The leader would support and engage them differently depending on the style they prefer in terms of motivation or engagement. Now, there is nothing perfect about this approach, and a leader can't expect that every interaction has to be perfectly tailored to every individual person. This would be impossible. It is, however, a good rule of thumb. Take team feedback, for example. Consider both sides of the following card:
Some team members may be highly social. They might find themselves needing a lot of feedback from the leader.
Other team members may prefer less interaction. They might only need occasional encouragement or redirection.
Continued

With situational leadership, the leader would support and engage these team members differently depending on the style they prefer in terms of motivation or engagement. This can be an effective, yet imperfect, approach. A leader can't possibly tailor every interaction to every individual person. But it's a good rule of thumb.
Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.
How might a leader mistakenly apply situational leadership in a way that negatively impacts the team or organization? In other words, how do you think situational leadership might be misapplied?
Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.
Continued

It’s critical that you not mistake situational leadership for inconsistency or overly personalized group expectations. To that end, sort the following stack of cards into either situational leadership or inconsistency/over-personalization.
Continued

To summarize, two of the following behaviors combine to represent the very essence of situational leadership. All the other behaviors are quite the opposite. Select the two behaviors that, together, model situational leadership.

You got it! Situational leadership is not: being inconsistent or overly personalized with group expectations; compromising a team goal or expectation; or personalizing the standard or "bar" and letting people slide. Instead, situational leadership is: maintaining the expectations for everyone on the team, including the leader; and helping members of a team individually with as much stealth and grace as possible.
Continued
Rules Few in Number

Have you ever read case law? It’s very complicated. Overly-complicated laws or rules take far too much effort to understand or execute. We hire tax attorneys because tax law is very hard to understand. As a leader, if you want fluid, unfettered compliance with the rules, while maintaining high levels of momentum, you simply can't make the rules so complex that it requires a specialist to interpret them.

Coach Pat Summitt believed one way you can do this is to make sure your rules are few in number, yet important and impactful. Rather than 15 complex rules, you're better off with three to five very impactful rules that cover the majority of the conditions that would make a difference on the team or in the group. As a leader, spending time creating rules for every outlier example is arguably a waste of time and energy. Ultimately, teams don't work as quickly or with as much fluidity if they're thinking about the rules every moment. However, if the rules are clear and understandable, they can get momentum going by just keeping a few basic and essential elements in mind.
Rules That Solve Problems

When you think about it, rules on a team or group are really aimed at solving problems on the way to success. The more mature the group or team, the more time that should be spent explaining the rule and clarifying its intent.

For example, suppose a preschool teacher makes a rule about hand washing to help keep her students from getting sick. That's the goal she wants to reach or problem she wants to tackle. She might explain to the children the basics of hand washing and germs. She then might create conditions where hand washing becomes a fun ritual. When these same kids get to grade school, that teacher may also have a hand washing rule. Several years have passed and the children are more mature, so this teacher might include a deeper explanation of germs, how they mature, and their impact on human health. When you're working with a more advanced group, give them the opportunity to understand that the rules should give the group an opportunity to work together in a more fluid way for peak performance. High-performing teams today will often establish team protocols within their group. For example, consider a team that wants to ensure they make better use of their time, while making everyone feel respected as a commitment to being part of the group. That's the problem they want to solve. As a group, they might collectively: 1. establish a rule together that timeliness in meetings is important; 2. decide that during team meetings, everyone must report in and provide feedback; and 3. establish a rule for minimizing distractions during the meeting in order to keep momentum.

These three simple rules would help solve the team's problems with meeting attendance, participation, and distractions. Rather than mechanisms for controlling behavior, the rules would create levels of freedom and improve the experience of everyone on the team — while deeply improving team performance.
Cracking Down Means Finding Balance

Finally, it’s very important to set a high standard. The very best teams are willing to create highly disciplined conditions and aren't afraid to crack down on individuals who aren't meeting the expectations. It's also important that these high-expectation environments be encouraging and nurturing, or you will lose members of the team. If all you do is spend your time cracking down, eventually people will burn out and break out and no longer be part of the team.
Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

What potential challenges do you see for a leader who wants to both crack down on those not meeting expectations, while also being encouraging and nurturing? What are some ways you might overcome these challenges as a leader?
Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.
Continued

Part of what it takes to be a leader is finding the balance between cracking down, nurturing, pulling back, and pushing forward. Leadership is an art, and being able to feel the energy of the group is important.
Leaders can push a team too hard, where team members feel exhausted.
Leaders can fail to push a team hard enough, leaving team members short of expectations.

The very best leaders aren’t always perfect, and even the great ones will miss out on opportunities either way. Remaining aware of this dynamic is important. Set that high expectation, and then be willing to observe the need to pull back the pressure and to make sure that the experience is rewarding.

Page 8 of 15
Discipline Should Be Firm

Discipline Yourself So No One Else Has To: Discipline Should Be Firm, featuring Teela Jackson

m5v4_transcript.pdf
117.5 KB

Continued

Eat Your Vegetables...They’re Good for You

Parents often struggle getting their children to eat healthy foods. Obviously, foods like raw vegetables aren’t as appealing as other food choices. New parents may try to negotiate with their children. In an effort to get them to consume the healthy options, they will remind them that eating vegetables is good for them. Depending on the age of the child, this may not necessarily be a successful strategy. After all, promising a 3-year-old a longer, healthier life by eating more broccoli may be a tough sell!

Similarly, leaders are often put in positions where they need to convince those around them that discipline isn’t just something they have to endure to be on the team or part of the group. Instead, discipline becomes a common denominator that leads to good things personally for the individual. By convincing the group that discipline is a great thing for them as individuals (not just the team), success is more likely to happen. Clearly, Coach Summitt was successful at this. She was able to get her players to commit to success through discipline, and they remained dedicated to that commitment throughout the rest of their lives. Many of her former players went on to become coaches and successful in a variety of other business endeavors. Though they would graduate from the program, they realized the discipline they had learned was not only the undergirding element for their success in college, but for the success they would enjoy the rest of their lives.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

As a leader, what are some ways you could help your team members see discipline as a benefit and a pathway to success, rather than a set of requirements and restrictions to endure?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Continued

Pain in the Moment, Pleasure in the Mission

Without question, discipline brings pain. The pain in the moment can be physical pain, such as committing to a rigorous exercise program, a diet, or even staying up late to concentrate on finishing a report or putting together a project plan when sleep is calling. We have to push ourselves at times to meet our own expectations when we have a dedicated, strong, and ascending work ethic. If a team member loses focus on the future or the mission, the sacrifice seems senseless and irrelevant. Suppose you have an upcoming event or experience that makes you want to get in better shape:

Maybe it’s a vacation and you want to get in shape to have more fun.

Maybe it’s a wedding and you know pictures are going to be taken, so you want to lose a few inches.

With those goals in mind, you’re willing to tolerate the low-carb diet.

You push yourself through your workouts because you know what you’re working for.

That motivation or mission in front of you makes the pain associated with disciplining yourself tolerable. The best leaders are excellent at painting that picture for what’s possible and getting the team to work with energetic enthusiasm towards the goal. This enthusiasm makes any pain of the moment tolerable.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

What are the potential risks of establishing discipline and high standards without a clear, motivating mission?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Continued

Without the Mission, It Becomes Drudgery

The opposite of what we just described is also possible. Leaders who don’t build a clear mission don’t make the pursuit of discipline seem worthwhile. Without a clear goal and the understanding of the commitment it will take to achieve that goal, the discipline in the moment can seem unnecessary and wearisome. Individuals might set aside cash and perhaps deprive themselves of certain things so they can appreciate accumulated wealth in the future. But if they didn’t have that vision for the future, the sacrifice they’d make to put that money aside would seem unnecessary. This is why, in some cases, people don’t save the money, don’t lose the weight, or fail to achieve any number of goals in front of them. They simply don’t relate the momentary sacrifice to the eventual success that comes with it. Fundamentally, getting individuals to see the endgame and understand the merits of pain in the moment for pleasure in the long run represents one of the most important elements of what it means to be a good leader. Once that vision is created, it becomes much easier to commit to the disciplined actions needed to achieve it. Without selling that vision and getting the team or group to commit, submitting to discipline simply becomes an act of drudgery that individuals execute out of a sense of obligation or compliance.

Have you ever seen someone go through a workout without much enthusiasm? You can almost see it in their eyes. They don’t believe in what they’re doing, they’re not excited about it, and they appear to be going through the motions.

On the other hand, have you ever seen someone who gets really excited about their exercise program? Maybe they have some vision in their mind about what they’re trying to accomplish, and suddenly they hit those workouts with a deep level of enthusiasm! When they have that enthusiasm, they are hard to beat.

Leadership Is Getting Others to Discipline Themselves

At the end of the day, even highly engaged leaders can’t be everywhere, creating expectations for every decision for every minute of the day. The best leaders create a rigorous environment where expectation is very clear. However, the very best leaders with the very best outcomes on the best teams create conditions within that team where self-discipline becomes an expectation. The motivation to achieve the group goals is in the hearts and minds of everyone there. Everyone holds one another accountable as together they pursue the goals that they have clearly articulated.

video.transcript_text:
Discipline Yourself So No One Else Has To: Discipline Should Be Firm, Featuring 
Teela Jackson 
 
 
Teela Jackson, Vice President, HR 
 
Pat said, “You have to have a daily goal and you have to make a daily commitment to the goal. 
Once you have set that reachable goal for the day, set up a reward and penalty system. Take 
something away from yourself if you don’t reach the goal. In my own case, when I was training, 
I would set a distance I needed to run. If I should have run five miles, but only ran three, I 
forced myself to make it up the very next morning. I’d run two extra miles. I did the same thing 
with eating. If I ate too much, I’d make myself do a second workout; or if I did a great job all 
week with eating healthy foods, I’d give myself a milkshake. I’d go to Baskin-Robbins and get a 
chocolate shake made with French vanilla ice cream. That was important.”  
 
Pat loved fostering the myth, though it wasn’t all that far from the truth, that she was ever-
present and omniscient -- because although she was known as a strict disciplinarian, her hope 
was to never have to discipline her players. Instead, by being firm, fair, and consistent, she 
wanted to instill self-discipline because she knew that was the most enduring, effective, and 
positive form of discipline. She demanded nothing less from herself.  
 
Coach Summitt said ... 
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
“Be firm. You need to be willing to set a precedent. It’s no good just announcing a set of rules. 
Trust me, whether you’re dealing with colleagues or your own child or yourself, the best way to 
discourage anarchy is to be uncompromising in enforcing the regulations. A stiff, non-
negotiable penalty, the first time out, will prevent a repeat offense.”

The motivation to achieve the group goals is in the hearts and minds of everyone there. Everyone holds one another accountable as together they pursue the goals that they have clearly articulated.

Leadership Reflections: Strength in Numbers

In these sections, we've discussed that one of the best ways to build a disciplined environment is to limit the number of rules you are trying to implement. You will create a much more disciplined environment if you consistently focus on a small handful of priorities that you remain disciplined about.

What would be an example of a handful of rules in your organization that could make for a more disciplined environment? Remember, this doesn't have to be an articulation of sins at work you're not supposed to commit. Innovative tech companies, for example, often set a rule that every employee will spend a certain amount of time innovating towards some unique and perhaps unplanned outcome as a way of creating a discipline around creativity. This priority wouldn't work if there were 50 other priorities.

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Page 11 of 15
Discipline Should Be Consistent

Discipline Yourself So No One Else Has To: Discipline Should Be Consistent, featuring Teela Jackson

m5v5_transcript.pdf
117 KB

Continued

Discipline Is About Structure, Not Words

Failed leaders will make the mistake of attempting to infuse discipline with well-crafted speeches. They will extol the virtues of discipline in one form or another and hope that their oratory skills will get the message across. Verbally reminding people what to do and when is valuable. But structure, systems, and guided practice will create conditions where discipline and structure are lived rather than simply talked about. Let’s use the tech industry as an example. Many companies today expect team members to consistently innovate on the job by trying new things and creating new ways of doing business. Suppose a senior leader at one of these companies gives a keynote speech stressing the importance of innovation.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

What impact — both positive and negative — might this leader's speech have on the organization? Do you think this approach is enough to create a disciplined culture of innovation at his company?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Continued

Sure, talking about the importance of innovation routinely may motivate some people to change some behaviors. Now, suppose that instead of the keynote about innovation, or perhaps in addition to it, that leader establishes the expectation that a certain number of hours each week are to be devoted to innovation. Those innovations are to be tracked so that the company continues moving forward.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

How might the leader’s new approach play out in his company? What specifically is different about this approach?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Continued

This time, the leader creates structure around innovation that makes it much more likely to happen. The structure, indeed, really matters.

Leadership Is Architecture

This is where leadership becomes a process of engineering, design, and architecture. If creating an environment where structure creates the opportunity to pursue what's important, leadership has to be adept enough to create the structure that makes it more likely to flourish. With Coach Summitt, for example, if a team's physical readiness was important, building in strength practice on a consistent basis would provide the necessary structure to make that happen.

Original lesson photograph accompanying Leadership Is Architecture.

Earlier in the course, we discussed how remarkably common that high-achieving leaders, coaches, and peak performers will get up and exercise in the morning before their day because they view self-care and peak physical conditioning as keys to their success. They recognize that in order for them to bring the most to their jobs, they have to prepare themselves physically. Your challenge as a leader will be creating structures in the organization where discipline becomes a lived component of the team or organization. Everyone will recognize the importance of discipline by operating in a structure that prioritizes it, features it, and makes it a non-negotiable element of what it means to work there or be there.

Integrity Talk vs. Integrity Structure

Suppose an organization has a goal of building integrity — certainly a critical value. As we've established, the best leaders would approach this goal by creating discipline around activities that reinforce this outcome. If an individual fails to meet the expectation, a failure in integrity emerges.

Imagine you're a leader taking over an organization or team that hasn't been very successful.
You and your team collaborate to come up with some expectations for things that the team can do to begin to demonstrate greater levels of success.
Together, you make a commitment to certain activities, and everyone is accountable to those disciplines or practices that will lead to a better outcome.
As everyone looks at one another while doing this, an undeniable sense of integrity will develop within the team.

In this example, integrity has become a lived attribute. It wouldn't be something that a CEO or top leader just talks about. Integrity would become a lived property. Earned integrity is undeniable. And without question, teams who create those critical integrity-building moments almost always begin to have higher levels of success.

But what if discipline and integrity drive people away from your team or organization? Which of these do you think would be the best response?

Exactly! Leaders often face this difficult question. However, if you drive away those who lack discipline and integrity, you're much better off than had you sacrificed either of these values to keep talented people around.

Continued

A team will lose momentum if there isn't a collective sense of discipline. Furthermore, a team collectively and unanimously disciplined will be more successful than a team that allows certain members to cut corners. So, as Pat Summitt showed us in her tenure as the most successful basketball coach of all time, you're better off losing even supremely talented team members who are unwilling to be disciplined than to sacrifice the team for people that are unwilling to make the commitment. If you drive them away, they probably weren't going to contribute to your success anyway.

If you have the commitment to enforce the philosophy that we just covered, which of the following do you think could be improved as a result? Select all that apply.

Absolutely! All of these will be improved if you have the commitment to adopt this philosophy.

Continued

Discipline Is All About Setting Standards, for Performance and Practice

These standards of discipline become the guideposts for performance. When mistakes are made or opportunities to grow present themselves, standards of discipline create the conditions to work on growth in these areas. The highest performing teams set high standards for their practice and are very disciplined about the steps they take to get themselves to the next level. Leaders in these organizations set high standards, speak to these high standards, and lead to these high standards. They have high standards for the outcomes they hope to achieve, and for the standards of practice that must be executed on a consistent level to achieve these outcomes. However, these standards have little value unless they meet four criteria:

Standards must be collectively established

Once again, depending on the level of sophistication within the team or group, one of the best things a leader can do is to work collectively with the team to establish the standards for performance on the team. When team members or group members are involved in the process, there is an even greater likelihood that they will be energized and engaged in making sure that these standards are met.

Standards must be understood

One of the most basic mistakes some leaders make in establishing discipline standards revolves around the failure to make clear what the standards actually mean. This can cause frustration both for the leader and within the team. It's hard to get a team or individual to comply with a set of expectations that they truly don't understand. So, a highly functional leader spends the time to make sure that the standards for performance are thoroughly explained. Ideally, team members or members of the group are given a chance to ask questions and clarify any misunderstandings they may have. Once again, with greater levels of understanding comes greater fluidity and execution.

Standards must be automatic

In families who have a very consistent standard, there are certain habits and rituals that don't ever need to be discussed. There is a standard set of expectations and habits that are undeniable and completely automated.

EXAMPLE: If a family has already established they consistently go to religious services each weekend, they won't find themselves wondering what they'll be doing at 8am on Sunday. It has become automatic.

With high functioning teams or groups, this level of automation also revolves around punishments or consequences for the lack of compliance to the standard.

EXAMPLE: Football coaches may develop consequences in practice for mistakes made during the game, especially mistakes within the players' control.

The fact that they are automated is what's extraordinarily important in this section. Automated consequences take the debate off the table.

EXAMPLE: If the family with four children preparing for church on Sunday had to individually negotiate with each child, each Sunday, about each church service, it would take a while to engage in any faith-based activities. However, if there is a common set of expectations and an understanding about what happens when results aren't achieved, the automation becomes the formative element to once again build momentum.

Therefore, the message here is that, as a leader, we must build standards and create automated responses that are non-negotiable, without regard to the circumstances or the people involved. This keeps everyone honest and moving forward and allows them to more consistently know what to expect on their team and for themselves.

Standards must be non-negotiable

If a family of four has established a standard of attending weekly religious services, time spent negotiating with each family member on a Sunday morning would result in a rather chaotic exchange. When standards become non-negotiable, they become bigger than the individual and even bigger than the leader. It becomes an overall dynamic that exists in the organization. It becomes all about the individual’s awareness of what they need to do to get to where they need to go collectively to enjoy everyone's desired outcomes.

EXAMPLE: If a family or team practices certain behaviors (hand washing, faith, exercise, or other health practices), these behaviors become a standard they collectively work toward. They aren't the nagging expectations of Mom, Dad, or a leader. Instead, each individual is aware of where the family or team is going collectively and what they must do, as individuals, to help them get there. This is truly an example of what happens when leaders elevate the conversation. In the case of the family of four, the weekly standard has already been established, so there's no need for wasting time negotiating with each family member on Sunday mornings.

video.source_visible_title: Discipline Yourself So No One Else Has To: Discipline Should Be Consistent
video.transcript_text:
Discipline Yourself So No One Else Has To: Discipline Should Be Consistent, 
Featuring Teela Jackson 
 
 
Teela Jackson, Vice President, HR 
 
Pat said, “Discipline is all about structure. It is the bare-bones architect of your organization -- 
the beams and joists that hold everything together. Maintaining the integrity of your interior 
philosophy is crucial, even if it costs you a valued member of the team. Otherwise, your 
structure will collapse.” 
  
It’s important to remember that discipline is not something you wield on others for your own 
personal empowerment. It’s not something that should be inflicted capriciously, either.  
 
In the right hands, discipline is simply a tool for fostering organizational success. 
It provides conviction to a philosophy. Really, discipline is just a way of getting people to 
cooperate with each other. You agree to obey a set of predetermined regulations so that you 
can all work together toward success. When you are self-disciplined, you hold yourself to high 
standards. Self-discipline is respect-based, while punishment is fear-based.  
 
When discipline is administered fairly, firmly, and consistently, you bring structure and clarity to 
the team and the organizational environment. Pat would jokingly say, “You kill the monster 
before it grows.” Coach Summitt wanted her players to know the rules and the consequences 
right up front, so they knew what was coming if they tried to sneak around a rule or consciously 
break one.  
 
Pat also wanted her players to believe that if they did try to hide an infraction -- if they broke 
curfew or missed class -- she would know. She believed that great coaches, as well as great 
managers, worked diligently to see all and know all. By making it blatantly clear that actions 
have consequences, and though you have a choice about your actions, the consequences are 
automatic, non-negotiable, and mandatory. No exceptions.  
 
Self-discipline is enduring and habitual. It removes the need for external discipline. Self-
discipline, simply put, means you exemplify genuine integrity, which is doing the right thing 
when no one else is watching.  
 
Pat said, “People who exercise self-discipline have an effect on everyone around them. They 
are tremendously influential in motivating their coworkers and colleagues. Conversely, 
undisciplined people can have a lousy influence.”

m5v6_transcript.pdf
119.3 KB

Continued

The Discipline Formula

Creating a disciplined environment isn’t easy. One of the keys to making discipline happen regularly and with quality is a very simple formula:

1. Setting a goal
2. Creating a reward
3. Leveraging that reward against the potential penalty, and
4. Remaining consistent to that choice on a daily basis.

Let’s break each of these down and reflect on how they can have an impact on individual and team or group success.

Step 1
Setting a goal

Goals are very important. The best leaders understand that chasing a goal gives direction to both individuals and a group. The goal of getting in shape for a vacation puts a long-range aspiration in mind and impacts how an individual might respond in making daily food choices. Therefore, "long-term" goals are really good at helping to establish daily or "short-term" goals.

The great thing about a daily goal is that it can sit right in front of you and require immediate action. Daily goals are simple that way. Long-term goals are harder because they're bigger and can be overwhelming. This is why having a daily goal is so important. A daily goal allows you to look at that one solitary day and make decisions on what’s important for that day in alignment to these long-term aspirations.

EXAMPLE: If an individual wants to hike the Grand Canyon from rim to rim and that person is 50 pounds overweight, they won't be ready to do that in a day. It will take days, weeks, even months to achieve that long-term goal. The prospect of being lean and fit enough to enjoy this experience may seem nearly unimaginable given where this person is in their journey.

This aspirational hiker can only control the next 24 hours, a short-term goal. Making good decisions over a 24-hour period brings them one day closer to their bigger goal.

Step 2
Setting a reward

Rewards matter! The very best teams, organizations, and Fortune 100 companies rigorously celebrate the accomplishment of big goals. When annual, quarterly, or even monthly benchmarks are met, the best companies don’t miss out on the celebration! Celebrations provide a psychological reinforcement for the behaviors that made that achievement possible. This is important, because sometimes highly disciplined, high-achieving people will set high standards for themselves...and fail to celebrate benchmark progress. This is a mistake. Even though these highly motivated achievers might make their mark, there is tremendous advantage psychologically in celebrating milestones.

Smartwatches and fitness trackers are incredibly popular today. They offer advanced feedback opportunities on your sleep quality, how many steps you've taken each day, and how long it's been since you moved around. They reward the wearer for achieving daily or weekly fitness goals. These simple digital celebrations are popular because they work! We respond well to even simple rewards, and they make us more likely to repeat the behavior.

So, whether you are used to having rewards in your life or not, you need to include them if you’re going to be an effective leader. Reward yourself and others when goals are achieved. The quality of the reward is less important than the recognition itself in making the greatest difference. How many of us have saved little notes along a journey or other seemingly insignificant recognitions of progress toward a goal, only because these small recognitions meant a lot to us?

By giving ourselves a little reward, our hearts and minds feel good and that will give us the discipline to continue doing what was expected to get the reward. Small rewards, day by day, lead to accomplishment of the overall goal.

EXAMPLE: If the aspirational hiker wants to tackle their short- and long-term goals, perhaps they'll invest in and take advantage of a smartwatch for daily fitness tracking. Those simple daily rewards from the fitness tracker help motivate this individual to do it again tomorrow!

Perhaps they'll go on some short, basic local hikes at first, gradually increasing the distance and challenge. Building strength and endurance through these increasingly challenging workouts help further feed the individual's drive and reward their progress. All the while, they're getting better equipped to tackle that upcoming challenge of hiking the Grand Canyon rim to rim.

Just think, though — if this person failed to celebrate the wins along the way, would they ever feel ready to go for their long-term goal? Rewards matter!

Step 3
Leveraging the reward against the potential penalty

Okay, so you didn’t meet expectations today! Ugh! It doesn't feel good to fail to meet expectations. This is why a simple structure established on a daily basis can reinforce the power of self-discipline. Decide up front what penalty may apply to missing the mark on your short-term goals along the way to your longer-term goals. The penalty should consist of some form of discomfort that serves to remind you in small and simple ways of the expectations you've held for yourself and that failing to meet your daily disciplined objective is not an option. The penalty reinforces how important it is to be vigilant each day if you're going to achieve your bigger goals!

EXAMPLE: Remember our aspirational hiker? If they start slacking on their daily or weekly workouts and fail to make short-term progress, what will get them back on track? This individual might decide they have to execute an even more rigorous diet and exercise schedule the day after a miss to make up for the mistake. Or they might decide to temporarily lose a privilege for a day or two to help regain their focus. Or perhaps they revisit some self-portraits from when they began their weight loss journey to remind them where they came from and where they could return if they don't get back on track.

Step 4
Remaining consistent to that choice on a daily basis

You've set the goal, determined how you'll reward progress, and decided how you'll prevent the penalty for not successfully moving toward the goal. Now, it comes down to consistently making those choices every day and taking those steps that bring you closer to your goal.

EXAMPLE: Our Grand Canyon hiker has to get out there daily and do the work. It's as simple as that, right? We know it may not necessarily be easy. We also know that working toward our short-term goals is the only way we'll move toward the longer-term goals. So, now this individual has to continue getting into better shape to be ready to tackle that amazing and challenging canyon!

Summary

Creating a disciplined environment isn’t easy. One of the keys to making discipline happen regularly and with quality is a very simple formula:

1. Setting a goal
2. Creating a reward
3. Leveraging that reward against the potential penalty, and
4. Remaining consistent to that choice on a daily basis.

Continued

Ever-Present, but Unnecessary

Pat Summitt’s goal for her players was to be "ever-present," meaning her players knew that she was always there to maintain the standard—daily, weekly, and so on. However, she also believed that she was doing her job as a leader if eventually her presence became unnecessary at times. In other words, her players would respond when she wasn't looking by maintaining the standard as if she was. This is the true mark of excellent, successful leadership.

You Get to Keep What You Do for Yourself

Many of Pat Summitt’s players went on to become highly successful coaches. Many went on to become successful at business and other endeavors. Great leaders create conditions through discipline where high levels of individual performance occur daily. Self-discipline becomes a permanent internal feature for those who embrace it. So, as a leader, you have an opportunity to touch the future by helping other people find an even better version of themselves through discipline.

Be firm. You need to be willing to set a precedent. It’s not good just announcing a set of rules. Trust me, whether you are dealing with colleagues, or your own child, or yourself, the best way to discourage anarchy is the uncompromising enforcing the regulations... The first timeout will prevent a repeat offense. — Pat Summitt

video.transcript_text:
Discipline Yourself So No One Else Has To: Wrap-up, Featuring Joan Cronan 
 
 
Joan Cronan, Women’s Athletic Director Emeritus, University of Tennessee 
 
I heard Pat say many, many times, “The most difficult part of self-discipline is convincing 
yourself that it’s in your own best interest. Being disciplined doesn’t always feel good. In fact, it 
can feel awful.”  
 
She also wrote, “It makes your knees hurt and your ego suffer. It’s easy to say to yourself, ‘I 
really should take a break, give myself a rest.’ Self-discipline is not the path to instant 
gratification. The reward is much further down the road and not always obvious. But in the end, 
it is a much deeper form of gratification. The real reward is self-respect and long-term success.” 
  
Pat’s key takeaways from this module are discipline must be fair, firm, and consistent. Being fair 
means there is no playing favorites, and the rules are in place to avoid problems before they 
start.  
 
Consequences for breaking rules must also be delivered in a consistent manner. Nothing will 
break the spirit and morale of a team quite like applying rules differently for different team 
members. Consistency matters.  
 
Being firm is necessary with both yourself and your team members, but above all, being 
consistent is the most important aspect of disciplining yourself. Consistency in how you deal 
with people is the hallmark of a great leader.  
 
Pat’s mindset was, “Discipline is the only sure way I know to convince people to believe in 
themselves.”

Pat in Her Own Words

I grew up on a dairy farm. Cows don't take a day off. We worked, and we worked hard. — Pat Summitt

Make Hard Work Your Passion: Pat in Her Own Words

m6v1_transcript.pdf

Continued

Who would have anticipated that life on a dairy farm would have prepared Pat Summitt to be the winningest basketball coach of all time at the point of her retirement? Clearly her father had a great impact on her, and all of us lucky enough to enjoy elements of her legacy are grateful for his efforts. Several of the lessons her father taught her represented foundational elements of her approach to being a leader and can be of assistance to us as we think about outstanding leadership. • I work only because I need a source of income.
• I bring mental focus and dedication to what I do.
• I bring passion and enthusiasm to my work.
• I have high expectations for my performance.

How Do You Define Hard Work?

Reflect on your choices. Do you work, or do you work hard? It’s important to see the difference.

Defining hard work is at the heart of differentiating between being willing to work and be willing to work hard. A commitment to work at some level is a given. Even if you are retired, it’s likely that you have to work to keep your body moving, get ready for your day, and to continue to keep your life together. Work is part of your life. I set expectations that meet job requirements

I set rigorous goals and objectives
I bring mental focus and enthusiasm to everything I do
I show up on time or earlier
I leave when I am supposed to leave or later

How High Are Your Expectations?

Of the two examples above, which best represents you? How high are your expectations for hard work each week? After all, most of us aren't doing physical work that wears us out. It's the psychological fatigue at the end of the week that usually makes us tired. Would you rather have psychological fatigue after giving it your all, or would you rather have fatigue associated with boredom just for doing what's expected?

If you want to excel as a leader and as a peak performer, make it your commitment to simply bring more effort, enthusiasm, and engagement to the pursuit of your goals.

steps.source_title: Make Hard Work Your Passion: Introduction
steps.exact_visible_copy:
3 of 15
Make Hard Work Your Passion: Introduction

Here’s how I’m going to beat you. I’m going to outwork you. That’s it. That’s all there is to it. — Pat Summitt

Make Hard Work Your Passion: Introduction, featuring Phillip Fulmer

m6v2_transcript.pdf
127.4 KB

Continued

Any outstanding achievement includes some degree of hard work. Of course, we've heard the old adage, it's better to "work smarter" than to "work harder." However, to work smart, you have to work hard to get either the perspective or the overall level of preparation necessary to achieve success. Remember, hard work doesn't have to mean working hard for a long period of time. Sometimes, working with very little effort will take you forever to get a job done, while working hard can cut the time in half. The purpose of this unit is to bring the concept of hard work into light, reflect on its elements, and establish the things that leaders can do to make hard work an endless component of personal and organizational development.

Hard Work is Practical

One of the merits of hard work is that it's entirely practical. If you are new on the job and you don't have experience, hard work helps mitigate that. If you have a deficit that you or your team is trying to overcome, hard work is the most accessible tool available to you.

You could start to work harder right now, and everything you do in your life would be better — your fitness, your finances, your career, and your relationships. Hard work is, without question, a very practical equalizer in giving everyone access to at least some level of success.

Coach Pat Summitt instructs Semeka Randall on the sideline.

Does Hard Work Tire or Inspire You?

Hard work isn't easy. Coach Summitt worked hard every day of the year. She wanted everyone to know the merits of hard work and to emulate that ethic. If you can achieve something without working at it very hard, maybe you should ask yourself, "Did I choose a difficult enough goal?" If the goal is too easy, that level of inspiration just doesn't show up. You need to pick a goal that is rigorous enough to inspire you. The "hard work" part, however, is non-negotiable. You will be tired at the end no matter what you do.

Challenge yourself with goals that are difficult to reach and rigorous enough to inspire you, and make the hard work non-negotiable.

Coach crouching in front of bench, 1984.

The Advantage of Loving What You Do

When you love what you do, your life is spent in pursuit of things that make you happy. The trick in life — and in successful leadership — is to find those aspirational outcomes that mean a lot to you. Our brains work at their best when we feel those amazing impulses chasing what we really, really care about. When aspiration and enthusiasm are evident, there is almost unlimited opportunity to get creative.

Revealing, Unleashing, and Continuously Elevating the Purpose and Passion

The very best leaders make a habit of continuously reminding everyone of the purpose and passion for their organization. If the team has the aspiration to win a national title, the coach must continuously remind the team that daily efforts will lead to this outcome. And if this outcome is something that everyone is interested in pursuing, it will indeed unleash the collective power of everyone involved. The leader then must become excellent at continuously presenting this mission and reminding the team every day.

When the Leader Loves the Work

When the leader of an organization or a team consistently demonstrates their heartfelt love for the mission or the goal, there's a far greater likelihood that this passion will be shared by others in the organization. And as that feeling spreads, momentum tends to build. In many cases, these individuals who will go on to other places and continue to share this same aspirational message and energy. Conversely, toxic leaders or people who work in organizations with a negative attitude will many times share that negativity, anger, and stress...and indeed create more of it. Therefore, the very best leaders must understand that it is critical for them to consistently demonstrate the love that they have for their work and for their mission.

Preparation, Effort, and Energy Are All Within Your Control

The best leaders understand they can't wait for the ideal situation in order to be a prepared, energetic, and highly influential leader. They may be so busy with day-to-day efforts that they're exhausted, which makes them less impactful than they would like. A leader who makes excuses could throw their hands in the air and say that they simply can't lead with excellence within those conditions. However, the best leaders don't rely on this type of excuse. Instead, they recognize that tools like preparation, effort, and energy are indeed within their control, and that with strategy, time, and energy, they can put themselves in a position to create better outcomes.

How to Make Hard Work Your Passion

Let's summarize what you can do to make hard work your passion, rather than an exhausting chore.

1. Set challenging goals, and the hard work in pursuit of these goals will inspire you.
2. Set aspirational goals that you and your team care about, and the hard work will turn into the labor of love.
3. Persistently remind the team of the final outcomes of the team's efforts to unleash the collective power.
4. Consistently demonstrate the love for your work and for the organization's mission.
5. Do things that are within your control: your daily preparation, best effort, energy, and focus. You'll be better equipped for the day when things will get out of control.

Make Hard Work Your Passion: Introduction, eaturing Phillip Fulmer 
 
 
Phillip Fulmer, Head Coach for the 1998 National Championship Football Team, University of 
Tennessee 
 
One of Pat’s greatest quotes was this ... 
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
“Here’s how I’m going to beat you. I’m going to outwork you. That’s it. That’s all there is to it.”  
 
Phillip Fulmer, Head Coach for the 1998 National Championship Football Team, University of 
Tennessee 
 
Does the thought of working hard toward your goals inspire you or tire you? The answer likely 
depends on how much you love what you do. Pat Summitt firmly believed that her players 
wanted to achieve success, so she daily put in the work to help her teams find and walk the 
path to greatness. Pat showed up every day with her best effort, ready to go, and she expected 
everyone else to do the same. 
  
Her players understood this. Pat said, “They know I’ll work as hard at it as they do, and they 
know that I love my work.” A talented superstar may have a lot of natural ability, but ability 
without commitment is wasted. Real winners strive daily to improve upon their natural talent 
and expand their potential. They make hard work their passion.  
 
In this module, you’ll learn what goes into applying yourself every day to do the work. There 
will always be certain factors beyond your control that influence your journey toward meeting 
your goals. What is in your control, however, is the preparation, effort, energy, and focus you 
nurture along the way. We would often hear Coach Summitt say, “Hard work is about 
controlling those things that you are capable of controlling.” 
 
As we dig into the Definite Dozen principle, Make Hard Work Your Passion, think about the 
factors you can control on your path to success. Are you leveraging each of those factors to the 
fullest? Let’s get started.

steps.exact_visible_copy:
5 of 15
Leadership Reflections: The Hard Work You Love

If winners, effective leaders, and peak performers fall in love with hard work, they must go through a process to make this happen. It's rare when people are born with this sensibility. As Coach Pat Summitt indicated, this is generally accomplished by consistently committing to hard work and consistently associating that hard work with the pleasure of meeting work aspirations that are important to you. To that end, what are work efforts you consistently engage with that helped to lead to your success? For example, maybe you have found that getting to work early and responding to your email and setting up your day is a hard work example that truly makes you feel prepared each day. Think about the routines that you have that would be good demonstrations of hard work, and reflect on the positive things that dedication to hard work brings. In this case, taking the time to reflect really does serve to reinforce the link between hard work and passion. That's necessary for you to continue to grow as a leader!

Take some time and reflect on these questions in your workbook.

steps.exact_visible_copy:
6 of 15
Commitment

How can you make work fun? You can't, at least not entirely. Fun is the wrong word for something that makes your back hurt, your hands stiff, and your head ache. Work is drudgery, grind, toil. But you can make your work more satisfying. The first step is to commit to it. Decide to do it well. — Pat Summitt

Make Hard Work Your Passion: Commitment, featuring Marie Mouchet

m6v3_transcript.pdf
114.1 KB

Continued

As discussed, one of the keys to outstanding levels of performance is practice and preparation. When it comes to hard work, be a leader who loves the practice, preparation, and anticipation. Success won't happen by accident.

A player has socks with hand-written “It’s in me” and “Focus.”

High Performance Requires High-Level Practice

When peak performers do amazing things, there's a tendency to assume those amazing things happened for the first time when all eyes were on them. The truth is, outstanding leaders and peak performers practice at the level they hope to perform. Top sales professionals have practiced their pitch, have a plan for rejections, and have gone over their script so many times that it's second nature. Think about how much more confident a leader can be when they put this level of effort into their preparation.

The harder you work, the harder it is to surrender. Tennessee wins because, in the end, our players feel they have worked too hard not to. — Pat Summitt

Wins, Losses, Potential, and Hard Work

Wins and losses are easier to calculate when you reflect on games like basketball. Coach John Wooden from UCLA was famous for declaring that wins and losses in team sports weren't as important as the degree to which a team matched their potential. He was famously proud of some less-talented teams he coached who lost hard-fought games, but met and exceeded expectations. In business, things can sometimes get a bit cloudy. Amazing efforts can sometimes result in very little immediate return on investment, while in other cases, an unexpected win can emerge in the face of a rather indifferent or lucky effort. High-achieving leaders refrain from taking either of these anomalies too seriously, consistently reminding the team that it is important to work hard.

It’s Harder to Give Up When You Have Put in the Work

Another advantage of hard work is that it sets the expectation that winning or achievement is the expectation. A sports team who practices every imaginable game scenario is less surprised when those game scenarios show up in primetime. Businesses who anticipate the actions of their competitors and work rigorously to prepare for them are less surprised when these challenges appear. If they've never practiced or prepared for these scenarios, giving up becomes an easier option. If they have put more time into practice, they simply take the next steps in responding to whatever challenges they face.

You Are Surrounded, with What?

Coaches Holly Warlick, Pat Summitt, and Mickie DeMoss.

Think about the people who are around you each day. When it comes to your work, or even in your social spaces, are you surrounding yourself with people who share your work ethic and celebrate your drive? Think about all the outstanding performers over the years who have given credit to people around them. They may talk about a loving spouse, a faithful father or mother, or supportive son or daughter giving them the energy and grace to continue. That level of support is real. Can you achieve without it? Yes. But it's just a lot harder. The most successful leaders today understand this dynamic and take great steps to surround themselves with people who inspire them, drive them, and help them become even more. This is especially easy today in a world of technology. Surround yourself with people who not only understand your dream, but will push you to reach even farther. Surround yourself with high achievers who may say, "That's not enough." Keep reaching and striving!

There is an unspoken understanding that develops between like-minded people who share a goal. The understanding is, 'Only you know and I know how hard we are willing to work on each other's behalf.' — Pat Summitt

Think of the people on your team. Do they share your work ethic, desire for success, and commitment to improvement and hard work? How do they encourage you to work harder?

grind, toil, but you can make your work more satisfying. The first step is to commit to it. Decide 
to do it well.”  
 
Marie Mouchet, VP & CIO Colonial Pipeline Company 
 
Coach Summitt loved daily practices even more than the games. Practices provided Pat and her 
assistants the opportunity to engage in what they enjoyed most -- teaching. Pat believed her 
players deeply desired success and that her primary role was to guide them in how to achieve 
it. She knew success wasn’t a switch to turn on in game time. It had to be developed. Speaking 
on her program’s high standards for work ethic, Pat said ...  
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
“The harder you work, the harder it is to surrender. Tennessee wins because in the end, our 
players feel they’ve worked too hard not to.” 
 
Marie Mouchet, VP & CIO Colonial Pipeline Company 
  
To foster a high level of commitment, surround yourself with a community that shares your 
work ethic and respects your drive. Pat Summitt never disguised the commitment level she 
required from her players. She openly communicated Tennessee’s high standards and values, 
knowing that those who were not deterred by the promise of hard work were exactly the ones 
who would fit in her program. She said, “There is an unspoken understanding that develops 
between like-minded people who share a goal. The understanding is, ‘Only you know, and I 
know how hard we are willing to work on each other’s behalf.’” 
  
Who’s on your team? Do they share your desire for success? Teams that share a similar 
understanding of the value of work will pursue similar standards of excellence. Shared passion 
for success fuels the commitment to keep improving and working hard, no matter the cost.

body_blocks.text: How can you make work fun? You can't, at least not entirely. Fun is the wrong word for something that makes your back hurt, your hands stiff, and your head ache. Work is drudgery, grind, toil. But you can make your work more satisfying. The first step is to commit to it. Decide to do it well. — Pat Summitt

As discussed, one of the keys to outstanding levels of performance is practice and preparation. When it comes to hard work, be a leader who loves the practice, preparation, and anticipation. Success won't happen by accident.
A player has socks with hand-written “It’s in me” and “Focus.”
High Performance Requires High-Level Practice

When peak performers do amazing things, there's a tendency to assume those amazing things happened for the first time when all eyes were on them. The truth is, outstanding leaders and peak performers practice at the level they hope to perform. Top sales professionals have practiced their pitch, have a plan for rejections, and have gone over their script so many times that it's second nature. Think about how much more confident a leader can be when they put this level of effort into their preparation.
The harder you work, the harder it is to surrender. Tennessee wins because, in the end, our players feel they have worked too hard not to. — Pat Summitt
Wins, Losses, Potential, and Hard Work

Wins and losses are easier to calculate when you reflect on games like basketball. Coach John Wooden from UCLA was famous for declaring that wins and losses in team sports weren't as important as the degree to which a team matched their potential. He was famously proud of some less-talented teams he coached who lost hard-fought games, but met and exceeded expectations. In business, things can sometimes get a bit cloudy. Amazing efforts can sometimes result in very little immediate return on investment, while in other cases, an unexpected win can emerge in the face of a rather indifferent or lucky effort. High-achieving leaders refrain from taking either of these anomalies too seriously, consistently reminding the team that it is important to work hard.
It’s Harder to Give Up When You Have Put in the Work

Another advantage of hard work is that it sets the expectation that winning or achievement is the expectation. A sports team who practices every imaginable game scenario is less surprised when those game scenarios show up in primetime. Businesses who anticipate the actions of their competitors and work rigorously to prepare for them are less surprised when these challenges appear. If they've never practiced or prepared for these scenarios, giving up becomes an easier option. If they have put more time into practice, they simply take the next steps in responding to whatever challenges they face.
You Are Surrounded, with What?
Coaches Holly Warlick, Pat Summitt, and Mickie DeMoss.

Think about the people who are around you each day. When it comes to your work, or even in your social spaces, are you surrounding yourself with people who share your work ethic and celebrate your drive? Think about all the outstanding performers over the years who have given credit to people around them. They may talk about a loving spouse, a faithful father or mother, or supportive son or daughter giving them the energy and grace to continue. That level of support is real. Can you achieve without it? Yes. But it's just a lot harder. The most successful leaders today understand this dynamic and take great steps to surround themselves with people who inspire them, drive them, and help them become even more. This is especially easy today in a world of technology. Surround yourself with people who not only understand your dream, but will push you to reach even farther. Surround yourself with high achievers who may say, "That's not enough." Keep reaching and striving!

There is an unspoken understanding that develops between like-minded people who share a goal. The understanding is, 'Only you know and I know how hard we are willing to work on each other's behalf.' — Pat Summitt

Planning

Make Hard Work Your Passion: Planning, featuring Marie Mouchet

m6v4_transcript.pdf
113 KB

Continued

Are They Really "Winging It"?

Let's consider the following scenario. A seasoned CEO is confronted with a novel challenge in the company, and everyone is pushing the panic button. The leader calmly finds an attainable solution. The solution, to the outside world, looks entirely novel. The leader appears to be "winging it," as the saying goes.

The message here is simple. Everyone at some point is going to have to "wing it" and deal with situations that are new and novel. When those times come, those with a rich set of experiences — practicing along the way, always improving, tackling difficulties, navigating novel territory — will be most successful.

Plan Your Work, and Work Your Plan

This adage is a key element in success as a leader. With goals on the horizon, a competent leader will recognize that they will only be achieved by establishing and executing a plan. We've all seen those leaders or peak performers who put together a plan only to leave it on their desk and fail to take action. Clearly, having a good plan is important, because working hard at a plan that won't work will never allow for the proper results to be achieved. But actually executing the plan is equally important. And within that formula, it's also important to analyze results and make adjustments as needed — potentially changing both the plan and its execution.

You have to work towards a goal in an organized fashion. You don't just show up in March and win a championship. You work every day in a systematic fashion. You have a long-range plan. But you also have a short-range plan. More importantly, you have to plan your daily activity and know what your goal is. — Pat Summitt

Types of Goals

Career/Lifetime Goals

Pat Summitt with graduates Semeka Randall and Tamika Catchings.

Having goals for a career or lifetime are equally helpful. As is the case with any goal-setting, being specific matters. For example, if someone came to you and said they had a lifetime goal of being rich, you would need more information to provide counsel. If, to that person, "being rich" means "being a millionaire," working a modest job and saving $1,000 a month for three decades with a modest return on investment might make them "rich." If it's their desire to be a billionaire, however, and if that's the definition of "rich," that strategy won't be enough. The same is true with almost any goal. The desire to own your own business versus the desire to be the CEO of a major company represent very different goals and very different steps along the way.

Annual/Quarterly Goals

Business leader image for annual and quarterly goals.

You can't reach lifetime goals without creating annual goals. The best leaders establish annual goals and commit to achieving them en route to their overall career or life goals. Sometimes quarterly goals are even needed to enhance motivation and momentum in smaller chunks.

Monthly/Weekly Goals

Weekly planner image for monthly and weekly goals.

By establishing monthly and weekly goals, effective leaders and peak performers can then drill down even further and make plans for every day, built around these expectations. With these goals in mind, it's helpful to create a list of potential tasks for the day. Group these activities in terms of their priority and their relationship to other tasks of the day. As discussed earlier, the most important and intense tasks of the day should be put towards the front of the day so they will be attended to with high levels of energy and commitment.

The three types of goals you reviewed are:
Career/Lifetime Goals
Annual/Quarterly Goals
Monthly/Weekly Goals

Here is a summarized list of planning ideas and tips to help you review your own planning habits.
Have clear career and lifetime goals.
Have annual and quarterly goals to make your career and organizational goals more manageable.
Set and keep track of your monthly and weekly goals.
Create a prioritized list of daily tasks, while grouping similar tasks.
Focus on what's doable and concentrate on small things that can be done to avoid being overwhelmed.
Analyze what's been accomplished and adjust your planning accordingly.

video.transcript_text:
Make Hard Work Your Passion: Planning, Featuring Marie Mouchet 
 
 
Marie Mouchet, VP & CIO Colonial Pipeline Company 
 
Pat Summitt was not one for winging it. Yes, she worked hard, but more than that, she also 
made it her business to know where she was going and what she was doing on a daily basis. Pat 
always had a plan.  
 
She said, “Plan your work and work your plan. You have to work toward a goal in an organized 
fashion. You don’t just show up in March and win a championship. You work every day in a 
systematic fashion. You have a long-range plan, but you also have a short-range plan. More 
important, you have to plan your daily activity and know what your goal is.” 
 
Pat kept a calendar that tracked her yearly, monthly, and weekly goals. Knowing where she was 
going helped her zero in on what she needed to focus on in the day-to-day. Every night she 
would review the plan for the following day. She had to do this because Pat was a master of 
multi-tasking. She regularly juggled multiple responsibilities from running practices, attending 
games, and delivering presentations to filling out paperwork, making dinner, and taking care of 
her family. 
 
Here are two simple practices to help you focus small in your day-to-day progress towards your 
goal.  
 
First, make a list. Plan your workday by pinpointing your task and prioritizing the order in which 
to complete them. The more specific you can be, the better. Try to group similar tasks together. 
That way you can maintain focus and keep your mental energy up throughout the day. 
 
Second, focus on what is doable. Sometimes a job can feel overwhelming when you look at how 
far you have to go to get to the finish line. In these moments, concentrate on the small things 
that can be done first. Ask yourself, “What is something I can do in this moment to make 
progress toward my goal?”  
 
Big wins are born out of devotion to daily improvement. Many times, all you need to see to get 
ahead is just the next step. When hard work is your passion, keep the big picture in mind and 
devote yourself to making it come to life one frame at a time.

113.8 KB

Why Do We Avoid Hard Work?

There is a consistent tendency within human beings to avoid hard work. Before we get too hard on ourselves, let's reflect on why that might be. In nature, there is no advantage for "survival" when running in circles, sweating, and aching, for no material benefit. From a "survival" standpoint, there is great advantage, however, to sweating and potentially running in circles to get something to eat, create shelter, or otherwise protect yourself and your family. With this example in mind, we are hardwired for likely hundreds of generations to work hard at things that matter. We shouldn't have to only reserve hard work for matters of life or death. But it is important for us to understand a biological predisposition to avoid hard work that doesn't directly help the body survive.

Do I Have to Work Hard All the Time?

At the root of charlatan-powered "get rich quick" schemes is the notion that you can have all you want in an instant. What lies beneath this assumption is the notion that maybe we don't have to work hard all the time. Without question, the best leaders and peak performers absolutely reject this kind of thinking. For them, hard work is a way of life. When we are born, we work hard to learn to walk, grow, evolve, and learn. When we become adults, we have to work hard to find our place in society and to maintain it. We have to work hard to find a mate and to raise a family. And when we get older, even if we have found a place of comfort in retirement, we likely will have to work hard to stay healthy and to maintain our quality of life.

The best leaders understand that life doesn't have to be hard. But hard work must be part of life when you embrace hard work as a necessary element of being alive and having a quality standard of living.

Make Hard Work Your Passion

So, given the importance of hard work, the best leaders and peak performers understand that they must make hard work their passion. They must love hard work and see it as a critical element for who and what they are, every day of their lives. Those who are still struggling to achieve what an elite leader achieves often find themselves marveling that a top leader is sometimes also wildly successful in hobbies like running, triathlons, or CrossFit competitions, in addition to their leadership success. If you're wondering how successful leaders can achieve success at work and still find time for elite levels of success in their pastime, you are observing the very essence of the learning in this unit. These leaders and peak performers are successful in nearly everything they do because they've learned that hard work needs to follow them wherever they go. They often work hard to understand what it means to be a good partner, a good parent, a good friend. They might invest in reading, training, listening, and understanding that goes above and beyond, because they know that the harder they work in anything they do, the more success that they have.

One of the reasons winning leaders and peak performers value hard work is because it provides a destination for all their energy and ambition. Peak performers have steadily built their capabilities, and even when they achieve their goals, it's hard for them to turn off the switch that pushes them to work hard. It's almost like a discovery that people make, and once they realize that hard work is going to be a common denominator of everything they do, there is no mountain too difficult to climb and no aspiration too bold to conquer.

Hard Work and Confidence

Another advantage of hard work is that it creates conditions where confidence is more likely to show up. If several team members are tasked with preparing for a major sales presentation, they will feel more confident about the presentation if they've worked really hard to understand the pitch and be well-versed in all the potential objections and questions. By preparing for the work, there's a far greater likelihood that confidence will arise in the presentation itself. Therefore, even if someone isn't a naturally confident person, hard work can give them the confidence they need in otherwise challenging situations.

Hard Work and Hurdles

Once again, with hard work, leaders are more prepared for the eventual hurdles that every team or group faces. High-performing football teams are famous for running two-minute drills, getting players to run their offense in the face of a deficit, in an effort to gain a comeback victory. Practicing "being behind" is an example of practicing for potential hurdles. When you practice for potential hurdles, you put yourself in a much better position to be successful...and to never endure the hurdles in the first place.

Hard Work Is Harder Than It Looks

All of this probably sounds good and may make sense intellectually. The fact is, hard work is actually harder than it looks. There's a million reasons why looking for an easier way out becomes appealing in the moment, and leaders must be aware of these tendencies and try hard to keep the focus on quality and consistent hard work. That said, there are certain strategies that can help make hard work show up more consistently.

Three Hard Work Hacks

1. Lean on your commitment.

If you have an opportunity to compete in the next Olympic Games, hard work may come a little easier in the face of a countdown to an Olympic event. A rigorous Monday morning workout may seem less daunting in the face of an aggressive commitment you've made to yourself to get to the Olympics. The degree to which we can keep that commitment front and center will help drive our success.

Individually, we should always keep our goals in front of us. By reminding ourselves of our annual, quarterly, monthly, and weekly goals, we put ourselves in a position where our daily hard work seems like a practical reaction in the face of a commitment that means a lot to our head and heart. To help this show up with your team, find creative ways of keeping the ascending goal in front of them and keep them excited about the steps they're taking towards the goal. When doing so, the hard work will seem smaller and obvious on the way to the goal.

2. Tackle the least desirable goal first.

In many cases, there are forms of procrastination that keep us from jumping straight into the grind, putting work into the most demanding elements of our goal. As a result, one of the steps you can take is to pursue the least desirable goal first. In other words, if there is a particularly difficult element that must be executed, front-load the most rigorous endeavor first, to put yourself in a position where you guarantee that it's being tackled with the greatest amount of physical, emotional, and mental energy.

3. Emphasize the positive aspects of an unfavorable situation.

This may sound like simple, positive thinking. However, it goes deeper than that.
