Make Hard Work Your Passion: Execution, Featuring Marie Mouchet 
 
 
Marie Mouchet, VP & CIO Colonial Pipeline Company 
 
There is a difference between working hard and making hard work your passion. When you are 
passionate about the work you do, you approach every endeavor with concentration and 
perspective. Pat said, “You have 40 minutes to win, but you have to do it one possession at a 
time.”  
 
Pat Summitt’s 40-minute concept is useful in multiple professional settings. In sales, for 
example, when it comes time to make a big presentation, the preparation should already be 
done. Now it’s time to execute your plan, and the most important thing to have in that moment 
is confidence. Practiced presenters won’t scramble for words, sweat the time, or be distracted 
by the competition.  
 
Pat Summitt made sure her players were focused on winning and executing the game plan 
under pressure. Pressure tests the integrity of your preparation. As obstacles arise, maintain 
your perspective by practicing these simple methods. Start by tackling the undesirable task first. 
When you’re facing something you don’t want to do, start with the difficult task. The task you 
dislike tend to drain your energy the most. So completing them while you’re still alert will give 
you more opportunity to make sure the task is done well. 
  
Next, emphasize the positive aspects in an unfavorable situation. If you’re in a moment or 
season where you’re working on something that’s merely a steppingstone to where you 
ultimately want to end up, take time to focus on what is meaningful in the present. Oftentimes, 
in the rush to get ahead, we can miss opportunities for development that are right in front of 
us. 
  
And finally, live life self-employed. When you invest in your dreams, you invest in yourself. The 
unexpected may threaten to set you back on your path to victory, but you can control how you 
respond to whatever comes your way. Lean on your commitment, trust your preparation, and 
continue working hard toward executing your vision of success.

Why Do We Avoid Hard Work?

There is a consistent tendency within human beings to avoid hard work. Before we get too hard on ourselves, let's reflect on why that might be. In nature, there is no advantage for "survival" when running in circles, sweating, and aching, for no material benefit. From a "survival" standpoint, there is great advantage, however, to sweating and potentially running in circles to get something to eat, create shelter, or otherwise protect yourself and your family. With this example in mind, we are hardwired for likely hundreds of generations to work hard at things that matter. We shouldn't have to only reserve hard work for matters of life or death. But it is important for us to understand a biological predisposition to avoid hard work that doesn't directly help the body survive.
Do I Have to Work Hard All the Time?

At the root of charlatan-powered "get rich quick" schemes is the notion that you can have all you want in an instant. What lies beneath this assumption is the notion that maybe we don't have to work hard all the time. Without question, the best leaders and peak performers absolutely reject this kind of thinking. For them, hard work is a way of life. When we are born, we work hard to learn to walk, grow, evolve, and learn. When we become adults, we have to work hard to find our place in society and to maintain it. We have to work hard to find a mate and to raise a family. And when we get older, even if we have found a place of comfort in retirement, we likely will have to work hard to stay healthy and to maintain our quality of life.

The best leaders understand that life doesn't have to be hard. But hard work must be part of life when you embrace hard work as a necessary element of being alive and having a quality standard of living.
Make Hard Work Your Passion

So, given the importance of hard work, the best leaders and peak performers understand that they must make hard work their passion. They must love hard work and see it as a critical element for who and what they are, every day of their lives. Those who are still struggling to achieve what an elite leader achieves often find themselves marveling that a top leader is sometimes also wildly successful in hobbies like running, triathlons, or CrossFit competitions, in addition to their leadership success. If you're wondering how successful leaders can achieve success at work and still find time for elite levels of success in their pastime, you are observing the very essence of the learning in this unit. These leaders and peak performers are successful in nearly everything they do because they've learned that hard work needs to follow them wherever they go. They often work hard to understand what it means to be a good partner, a good parent, a good friend. They might invest in reading, training, listening, and understanding that goes above and beyond, because they know that the harder they work in anything they do, the more success that they have.

One of the reasons winning leaders and peak performers value hard work is because it provides a destination for all their energy and ambition. Peak performers have steadily built their capabilities, and even when they achieve their goals, it's hard for them to turn off the switch that pushes them to work hard. It's almost like a discovery that people make, and once they realize that hard work is going to be a common denominator of everything they do, there is no mountain too difficult to climb and no aspiration too bold to conquer.
Hard Work and Confidence

Another advantage of hard work is that it creates conditions where confidence is more likely to show up. If several team members are tasked with preparing for a major sales presentation, they will feel more confident about the presentation if they've worked really hard to understand the pitch and be well-versed in all the potential objections and questions. By preparing for the work, there's a far greater likelihood that confidence will arise in the presentation itself. Therefore, even if someone isn't a naturally confident person, hard work can give them the confidence they need in otherwise challenging situations.
Hard Work and Hurdles

Once again, with hard work, leaders are more prepared for the eventual hurdles that every team or group faces. High-performing football teams are famous for running two-minute drills, getting players to run their offense in the face of a deficit, in an effort to gain a comeback victory. Practicing "being behind" is an example of practicing for potential hurdles. When you practice for potential hurdles, you put yourself in a much better position to be successful...and to never endure the hurdles in the first place.
Hard Work Is Harder Than It Looks

All of this probably sounds good and may make sense intellectually. The fact is, hard work is actually harder than it looks. There's a million reasons why looking for an easier way out becomes appealing in the moment, and leaders must be aware of these tendencies and try hard to keep the focus on quality and consistent hard work. That said, there are certain strategies that can help make hard work show up more consistently.
Three Hard Work Hacks
1. Lean on your commitment.

If you have an opportunity to compete in the next Olympic Games, hard work may come a little easier in the face of a countdown to an Olympic event. A rigorous Monday morning workout may seem less daunting in the face of an aggressive commitment you've made to yourself to get to the Olympics. The degree to which we can keep that commitment front and center will help drive our success.

Individually, we should always keep our goals in front of us. By reminding ourselves of our annual, quarterly, monthly, and weekly goals, we put ourselves in a position where our daily hard work seems like a practical reaction in the face of a commitment that means a lot to our head and heart. To help this show up with your team, find creative ways of keeping the ascending goal in front of them and keep them excited about the steps they're taking towards the goal. When doing so, the hard work will seem smaller and obvious on the way to the goal.
2. Tackle the least desirable goal first.

In many cases, there are forms of procrastination that keep us from jumping straight into the grind, putting work into the most demanding elements of our goal. As a result, one of the steps you can take is to pursue the least desirable goal first. In other words, if there is a particularly difficult element that must be executed, front-load the most rigorous endeavor first, to put yourself in a position where you guarantee that it's being tackled with the greatest amount of physical, emotional, and mental energy.
3. Emphasize the positive aspects of an unfavorable situation.

This may sound like simple, positive thinking. However, it goes deeper than that. Successful leaders and peak performers notice and ultimately emphasize the positive aspects that can be found in otherwise unfavorable situations. In other words, in the face of a setback or something negative, they try to find something positive, affirming, or growth-oriented.

For example, many tech companies run into problems when they try a new innovation and it fails. One of the spiraling downfalls is that a team of engineers or inventors can get discouraged after several failures. Pretty soon they go on a "losing streak" and are unable to create. Instead, what some leaders have done to combat this is to actually take the time to celebrate the failure when they have experienced it. This may sound illogical, but it all comes down to how the issue is framed. Rather than "celebrating the failure" in its plainest sense, innovators learn to celebrate the fact that they have strategically identified a new way that won't work. In other words, they have eliminated one possibility, and are now one step closer to the solution. This is exciting, because rather than being discouraged by the failure, they can then get encouraged that they are getting closer to a solution.

13 of 15
Wrap-Up

We simulate, prepare, and train so that the task of winning does not seem so daunting. It's what we are supposed to do, because we have worked hard all year. We expect to win because we practice it. I believe you get what you expect. — Pat Summitt

Make Hard Work Your Passion: Wrap-Up, featuring Phillip Fulmer

m6v6_transcript.pdf
122.2 KB

Continued

Winners Win the Day

It’s been said that we can't do anything about the past, nor can we predict or dictate the future. The only thing we have control of is the present. In the present, we have control of ourselves and our efforts, and our present means putting forth the best effort possible in this moment, on this day. This is why the most successful leaders and peak performers become so obsessed with making meaningful plans for each day, and executing their plans with high focus, concentration, and passion.

High achievers and successful leaders recognize that today is what we have, and we need to make the most of each of our days.

Get Out of Your Comfort Zone

By getting out of our comfort zone and trying something that's more difficult or perhaps a bit out of reach, we put ourselves in the best position to grow. It can sometimes be difficult because we typically need to find something simple enough to understand, yet challenging enough to create new knowledge or skill. Have you ever tried to learn something and it's far too complicated for your level of learning? It's frustrating! Finding that learning zone of "challenging, yet reachable" isn't easy. But it's exactly what leaders target. They try to get their teams out of their comfort zones and reaching for a level of performance that's just beyond their current ability to perform, yet within reach with enough effort.

Put Your Commitment on Display

This is especially true for leaders. In the music industry, some performers try to appear to the outside world like their art is simply a manifestation of their gifts, and that they have only a casual interest in their performance and recordings — but, in reality, they are hyper-competitive and obsessed with progress. Leaders, on the other hand, have no excuse for refusing to continually extol the virtues of hard work. If a leader intends to lead an organization that's deeply committed to growth, they need to show the world that this is their commitment as well.

The best work should have an alive quality. It should be performed with some feeling — even with passion. You may not think your intention is visible, but it is. The intent is obvious in your every action — more than you would ever know. — Pat Summitt

What You Focus on Is What You Create

This sounds like a great motivational phrase, yet it has incredibly practical "Monday morning" application. The human brain tends to pursue what you tell it to. If you wake up every morning and ask yourself "What's wrong with me?," you're likely to find answers. And in doing this, you will spend a lifetime inspecting your flaws. Similarly, if you wake up each day and focus on growth and keep your periodic goals in mind, you'll make the most of each day and be more focused on progress.

Establish a Commitment to the Daily Habit of Making Your Future a Reality

Sadly, some people give up on their dreams and the art of possibility. They see dreams and aspirations as something meant for somebody else. This is incredibly sad, because in reality, the people who continue to succeed in life maintain an unshakable ritual of seeing their future as their reality. It is said that no great dream is ever created without that dream first being built in the hearts and minds of the leaders who hope to see it happen. Keep focusing on that construction and planning for the best use of each day so that you can get there sooner than later.

video.transcript_text:
Make Hard Work Your Passion: Wrap-Up, Featuring Phillip Fulmer 
 
 
Phillip Fulmer, Head Coach for the 1998 National Championship Football Team, University of 
Tennessee 
 
Pat had many sayings, but one of my favorites was, “We simulate, prepare and train so that the 
task of winning does not seem daunting. It’s what we are supposed to do because we have 
worked hard all year. We expect to win because we practice it. I believe you get what you 
expect.” 
  
In this module, we learned that hard work is applying yourself fully to achieving the things that 
are within your control. Winning is about daily improvement, and those who put in effort every 
single day train themselves to expect victory. Showing up to give your best every day isn’t easy, 
but it helps if you truly believe in what you’re doing. 
  
As we covered earlier, hard work requires commitment and great rewards demand sacrifice. Be 
willing to push yourself and get out of your comfort zone. You want people who will encourage 
you and inspire you toward a goal, not hold you back. 
  
Next, have a plan for your work. Planning helps you tackle multiple things in a systematic 
fashion and keeps you from getting overwhelmed. Make a prioritized list of tasks and 
continually focus on what is doable to keep yourself moving forward on that path. 
  
Finally, put your commitment and preparation on display by following through with the 
execution of your vision for success. Hard work generates the confidence you need to secure 
victory. Even when it’s hard, put in the necessary work and remember that you’re working for 
your best interest by investing in your dreams. 
  
Pat said, “The best work should have an alive quality. It should be performed with some feeling, 
even with passion. You may not think your intention is visible, but it is. The intent is obvious in 
your every action, more so than you would ever know.” What you focus on is what you create. 
If you envision a successful future for yourself, then make hard work your passion and form 
daily habits that will set you on the path to making that future a reality.

Leadership Reflections: Your Hard Work on Display

When you put your hard work out there, it does two things. First, it forces you to commit, and second, it makes public a commitment to hard work in the organization, thus pushing everyone to work harder.

What would be an example in your work environment of a commitment to hard work that you could make that would be public enough to get you to commit? What would be public enough to get the attention of the organization you are a part of?

What would committing to 100 calls or 100 contacts do for you? Make this example your own and reflect on what it would mean to put your hard work on display and commit to it.

Reflect on these questions in your workbook.

mini_programs.source_overview: Coach Pat Summitt said, “I'm going to outwork you. That's it. That's all there is to it." But what does it really mean – work harder? Work more? Work overtime? In this module, we’ll discuss what constitutes hard work, as defined by Pat Summitt, and how your hard work may affect you and your organization. As we delve into the sixth principle of the Definite Dozen, Make Hard Work Your Passion, you will reflect on the factors you can leverage on your path to success as a leader.

Coach Summitt discovered the hard way the importance for leaders to know their people. Her program used a yearly Predictive Index — a personality profile — to better understand her players. The best leaders today have a solid understanding of themselves and their teams. There a few ways this can be done:

Personality Assessments and Insights

Leaders today have learned about the advantages of personality assessments and using those assessments to make critical decisions about team interaction. There is a wide variety of assessments available to choose from. Successful leaders use them all the time and use the information gathered to shape their strategies, understandings, and engagement with their team.

Self-Assessments — Leaders Go First

One of the best first steps a leader can do is to take the assessment themselves. Coming away with an analysis such as the Predictive Index used by Coach Summitt creates an increased sense of knowledge and understanding of your own communication and personality styles. Forward-thinking leaders are usually willing to take these assessments and share them with their team so that they can have a better idea about how to work with the leader or CEO.

Testing Others and Sharing

Of course, taking these same assessments with others in your organization is helpful. Many forward-thinking organizations today maintain databases or files of the personality and assessment profiles of everyone who works for the organization. Sometimes they will even use this information to help coordinate and build different types of teams.

Continued

Avoid “Arrival”

One of the most important elements of developing a comprehensive awareness of personality types is to "avoid arrival." The best leaders understand that the only way to remain competitive is to ensure that no one in the organization ever feels they have learned all they need to know in a particular area. It's quite the opposite, in fact. The best organizations understand that situations and personalities evolve, and they are on a never-ending journey of growth and discovery.

video.transcript_text:
Don’t Just Work Hard, Work Smart: Pat in Her Own Words 
 
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
I congratulated and said, “Good job. But let me tell you one thing, Pat Hatmaker.” I said, “I 
cannot believe you didn’t want the ball. We practice that every day.” And I said, “We’re getting 
ready to play for a championship. You know, folks?” And I’m just reaming her out. And then the 
crafty little sucker – we've all got one – the crafty little sucker said, “Hang on, Coach. Hang on, 
Coach. You play for a title tomorrow. You’ve never won one.”  
 
Ah! Immediately, I flipped the switch. You have to do that sometimes, don’t you? When things 
aren’t going the way they need to be going, you better flip the switch. I flipped that switch and I 
said, “You know what, Pat? I bet you learned today and you’re going to be even better 
tomorrow.” And I just started building her up because the crafty little sucker scared me. Scared 
me! I thought, “We’ll get blown out if she doesn’t play.” So, the only point guard you’ve got -- 
how smart are you? So, I tried to build her up. 
  
We went out the next day and she played a pretty good game, but we didn’t win a 
championship. We were in seven title games before we ever won one. Seven times we went to 
the big dance and played for the title before we won one. 
  
So, you’ve got to be persistent, don’t you? You’ve got to keep building people up. And that’s 
what I did that day. And while it didn’t work, it made a difference, thanks to the crafty little 
sucker. 
  
But what I went back, and I realized I did not know my personnel. You better know them. You 
better know your personnel. I didn’t know she didn’t want the ball.  
 
Every year we do what we call Predictive Index. It’s a personality profile. And I know who wants 
the ball. I know who likes pressure and who doesn’t. I know who pays attention to detail. I 
know who can be really persistent; and the players that are very, very short-fused and short-
minded. I use that as a tool to help me when I get in that situation. It has been a powerful tool. I 
know who the most competitive people are on the team. I know who really doesn’t care if we 
keep score, and that’s not good in my business. But there’s a way you can dial those people up, 
too. 
  
So, I took that situation and tried to make something really good out of it. And as a result, I 
continue to learn and grow. I bet you do too, don’t you? Don’t ever believe that you’ve 
“arrived.” You never, ever “arrive.”  
 
If you get to the top, it can be very temporary if you think you just belong there. You’ve got to 
remember how you got there. Don’t ever forget how you got there. And that’s what can inspire 
you to strive to be on top all the time.

steps.source_title: Don't Just Work Hard, Work Smart
steps.exact_visible_copy:
Page 3 of 15
Don't Just Work Hard, Work Smart

Don't Just Work Hard, Work Smart: Introduction, featuring Marie Mouchet

m7v2_transcript.pdf
115.5 KB

Continued

Working Smart Is Just as Important as Working Hard

You won't get anywhere as a leader or a peak performer without working hard. Conversely, you can work really hard at the wrong things and never make progress. This is why, after a leader conceptualizes the merits of hard work, they need to learn to work smart. Let's consider the following example to reflect on the concept of working smarter, not harder.

Maria is the VP of Strategy at her corporation.
The company has been losing ground to its competition.
Maria's expertise is in strategy, certainly. And she knows her company's existing products and services pretty well.
However, she hasn't kept up with the latest emerging technologies — while the competition has. It turns out that their losses to the competition are due to a technological deficit.
Still, Maria is working hard to revamp their strategies and figure out how to make a strong comeback.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

What could Maria have done differently to be better-positioned to help resolve this issue?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Continued

Maria's knowledge of technology and emerging possibilities would need to be substantial enough to help her make the right decisions. If she is hard at work to resolve the technology deficit without any knowledge of the technology options available, Maria would be working hard, but not necessarily smart. The best leaders understand that they must continuously learn, grow, and make decisions on a consistent basis with new, emerging knowledge flowing through them continuously. So what is ‘working smart?’

To Work Smart, Commit to Learning and Growth

Leaders and top performers understand that leaders must have the ability to make a number of critical decisions on the growth trajectory. In order to make those decisions, the leader has to be knowledgeable and prepared. There are numerous ways to build that knowledge base, but simply the conscious act of remaining committed to expanding your knowledge in the first place allows you to be in a better position than most.

Reading and Professional Development

CEOs and peak performers are voracious readers. They are well aware of the trends in their industry and are constantly mining thought leadership and new technological opportunities for new insights. It would be very rare to find highly successful, competitive leaders and performers who didn’t read the news each day and carefully monitor essential trends that specifically relate to their goal. Highly impactful leaders always prioritize such professional development activities. They take classes, even if they have elevated degrees and experiences. They go to webinars or seminars and are always honing their craft by acting as a student.

Learning from Mentors

Great leaders almost always have a network of mentors at their disposal. In many cases, they are more experienced and give advice that helps in the moment. Sometimes having a variety of mentors is helpful as well. But some mentors don’t have to be older than you. You might have a mentor who simply knows more than you do about a topic and is willing to share. You also are probably somebody’s mentor right now, even if you don’t know it yet. What’s important about having a mentor is being open to behaving like a student. Strong leaders and peak performers desire to be taught and to learn from the masters.

Learning from Peers and Competitors

Your competition can tell you a lot. Studying the trends, tendencies, strengths, and weaknesses of your competitors will also help you to grow as a leader. This might involve studying a team or an entire organization; examining the peak performance skills of individuals you know. For example, if you are a CEO of a company that competes with another company thousands of miles away, you may try to study the moves of that competitor’s CEO. This could be to help anticipate their next step or better understand what they are doing to be successful. Does your competitor’s CEO have some skills that you’re not able to demonstrate? Are they skills that you could develop? Or, are they skills that you could bring in through a valued vice president or specialist? The message here is pretty simple. The strongest leaders and peak performers are not self-absorbed. They look around and try to figure out what they can learn from other people, even from those they compete against. Even those who are at the absolute top of their game must remain doggedly committed to learning from others and elevating what they bring to the table.

Learning from Strong Assistants, VPs, or Team Members

Another great place to learn is from those you work with. In corporate America, it’s common to perform a series of confidential, 360-degree assessments. An outside agent comes into the organization and interviews individuals who work with various leaders or top performers. These interviews are designed to establish perception checks throughout the organization to give leaders or peak performers feedback on how their engagement with others is affecting morale and performance. These exercises are incredibly helpful because they give leaders unfettered feedback and allow them to make adjustments that can make an impact. Leaders can also gain formal and/or informal feedback from other members of the organization. Administrative assistants who feel secure in their positions might provide valuable input. A CEO’s vice president or a coach’s assistant can provide helpful feedback. In other words, the best leaders understand that surrounding themselves with strong people only makes them better, and listening to their advice will only make them wiser. Finding people around you who are good at things that you’re not good at will not only grow your competency in those areas, but may also serve the team. We all have our strengths. Part of being a great leader is letting the people around you show theirs.

The best leaders and top performers are knowledgeable, prepared, and always learning and growing. Some powerful sources of learning include: Reading and Professional Development; Learning from Mentors; Learning from Peers and Competitors; Learning from Strong Assistants, VPs, or Team Members.

Continued

Remain Open to Growth, Forever

Receiving a degree from a university is a wonderful blessing. It indicates the conclusion of a learning journey. However, we live in a world today where the commitment to learning is continuous. With so much changing so fast, it's clear that the commitment to continuous learning is a non-negotiable, not just to be excellent, but to even remain competitive. The most competitive systems and teams understand that they must remain open to the opportunity to learn and grow, and grow and learn continuously both on their own and through the hearts and efforts of others around them if they're going to be at their best, and help the organization to perform at its best.

video.transcript_text:
Don’t Just Work Hard, Work Smart: Introduction, Featuring Marie Mouchet 
 
 
Marie Mouchet, VP & CIO, Colonial Pipeline Company 
 
Pat Summitt was as hard a worker as anyone, but her legendary success and legacy as a coach 
are as much a result of working smart as they are of working hard. We’ve all heard the famous 
definition of insanity: doing the same thing over and over again, but expecting different results. 
When you work hard, but lack strategy, you may well find yourself exemplifying that definition.  
 
Coach Summitt always grew from her challenges. She surrounded herself with assistant coaches 
(and) she deeply respected and listened to them when they provided feedback on her 
decisions, methods, or strategies. She stayed open to improvement and constantly looked for 
mentors, teachers, and other coaches from whom she could learn new methods. 
  
When Pat’s rival, Geno Auriemma from the University of Connecticut changed women’s 
basketball using the dominant triple-post offense, Coach Summitt became a student of the 
triple-post in order to learn how to defend against it. Rather than stew in resentment over 
UConn’s success or doggedly pursue the same methods for trying to beat her opponent, Pat 
made the conscious decision to evolve as a leader. 
  
She visited the Chicago Bulls and learned from the masters of the triple-post offense, Tex 
Winter and Phil Jackson. The following year, the Lady Vols integrated triple-post concepts into 
their game play. The shift in strategy proved successful as the team went on to win the 
championship three years in a row. 
  
Pat Summitt never stopped working hard, but she learned how to maximize the impact of her 
hard work by continually finding ways to work smarter. As her leadership maturity increased, so 
did her abilities in strategizing, team building, and finding balance between her strengths and 
weaknesses. 
  
In this module, you’ll hear from visionary strategist Sue Nokes, an experienced senior executive 
who currently serves as the advisory board vice chairman at the leading tech company Asurion. 
She previously worked as the chief customer and operations officer for T-Mobile. Sue was a 
close friend of Pat Summitt’s and sat in many locker rooms with Pat’s championship teams, so 
she has first-hand experience with Pat’s methods for outworking and outsmarting her 
opponents.

In corporate America, it’s common to perform a series of confidential, 360-degree assessments. An outside agent comes into the organization and interviews individuals who work with various leaders or top performers. These interviews are designed to establish perception checks throughout the organization to give leaders or peak performers feedback on how their engagement with others is affecting morale and performance. These exercises are incredibly helpful because they give leaders unfettered feedback and allow them to make adjustments that can make an impact. Leaders can also gain formal and/or informal feedback from other members of the organization. Administrative assistants who feel secure in their positions might provide valuable input. A CEO’s vice president or a coach’s assistant can provide helpful feedback. In other words, the best leaders understand that surrounding themselves with strong people only makes them better, and listening to their advice will only make them wiser. Finding people around you who are good at things that you’re not good at will not only grow your competency in those areas, but may also serve the team. We all have our strengths. Part of being a great leader is letting the people around you show theirs.

The best leaders and top performers are knowledgeable, prepared, and always learning and growing. Some powerful sources of learning include: Reading and Professional Development; Learning from Mentors; Learning from Peers and Competitors; Learning from Strong Assistants, VPs, or Team Members.

Page 6 of 15
Strategize Smart

Don't Just Work Hard, Work Smart: Strategize Smart, featuring Sue Nokes

While I preach hard work, I also preach smart work. What do I mean by smart work? I mean the combination of efficiency and effectiveness that will help me succeed without wasted motion, and with perspective. Smart work is a matter of sizing up the job that has to be done and deciding on the best way of doing it. Pat Summitt

Creating Focused Energy
When team members are clear about the direction they are headed, have trust for one another, and are free to innovate, a synergistic energy is built. These types of teams are more likely to take risks, solve problems, reveal blind spots before those blind spots can hurt them, and focus their energies on growth. By creating this focused energy, the team has a greater chance at reaching its objective.

Be Sure to Define "Success"
Articulating a goal is not the same as defining success. Although they can be aligned, it's important to define both topics within a team or an organization. Consider a common sports example by reviewing both sides of the following card:

Front of card
Team A lacks talent, but has unbelievable passion. They go out and lose in triple overtime to a much more successful team.

Back of card
Team B is extraordinarily talented but riddled with discipline issues and challenges. They go out and win a game by seven points — a game they should have won by more than 20.

In this sports example, would it be appropriate for these two teams to define success based on the number of wins and losses? Why or why not? What other success measures might be possible?

Defining success for Team A and Team B simply by "wins" and "losses" may not be appropriate. In many cases, success can be defined at a more specific level by focusing on progress and growth. In some cases, as momentum is being built, organizations carefully track the critical factors that drive their success. For example, suppose:
1. You take over a leadership position within an organization.
2. You observe that customer deliveries are not being made in a timely manner, and upon researching it, you determine it has been a historical problem.
2. You begin strategizing and working toward fixing this problem to increase customer satisfaction. This might qualify as a small success to the business.

Try to Make Success a Familiar Face
Consider a team or organization that hasn't seen much success in a while. A leader is then faced with the tough challenge of trying to make success common in an organization that may struggle with the very concept.

What might a strong leader do in this situation?

In that example, a good leader would once again begin to introduce small levels of success and work diligently to reward it. This can sometimes be difficult because a leader doesn't want to be seen as rewarding the obvious. However, it's arguably better to celebrate and build on even small victories than for the organization to remain unfamiliar with "success."

Muscle Memory
Coach Summitt talked about the importance of muscle memory within an organization. For example, if she were coaching her team and practicing what to do if the team were down by three points with seven seconds left and no timeouts, she would rehearse the expectation enough times so that when faced with the actual situation, their brains would be free to work from muscle memory. The players would be so well-schooled that they simply go into action and execute as they have been taught. With muscle memory, you can avoid spinning your wheels, thinking about what comes next — and simply go into action. Muscle memory doesn't necessarily guarantee you'll get exactly where you want to go. However, a long history of preparation and a focus on execution powered by muscle memory brings a much better chance at getting the most out of everyone on the team or in the organization.

video.transcript_text:
Don’t Just Work Hard, Work Smart: Strategize Smart, Featuring Sue Nokes 
 
 
Sue Nokes, Advisory Board Vice Chairman, Asurion; Former Chief Customer & Operations 
Officer, T-Mobile 
 
Hard work is fundamental to success; but without a game plan, it’s useless. No one could work 
harder than my friend, Pat Summitt. But what really gave Pat the winning edge was her ability 
to combine smart habits with a clear strategy. 
  
Pat said, “While I preach hard work, I also preach smart work. What do I mean by smart work? I 
mean the combination of efficiency and effectiveness that will help you succeed without 
wasted motion and with perspective. Smart work is a matter of sizing up the job that has to be 
done and deciding on the best way of doing it.” 
  
Pat had a vision, clear strategy, and goals, and she worked hard to get everybody’s buy-in. 
When you work smart, you put yourself in a position to get the most out of your time and 
energy. Before throwing yourself at a project or a task, establish clear goals. By pinpointing 
what you want to achieve together, you create focused energy.  
 
Gather your team and ask, “What are we trying to achieve together? What does success look 
like?” Be clear about what success is and, almost as important, what it isn’t. 
  
Once you have a goal, outline a detailed plan which includes measures of success; make sure 
everyone knows next steps; understand the path forward from the outset. Otherwise, you’ll run 
in circles and waste valuable energy in the process. Pat learned how to prioritize what needed 
to be done by asking, “What are the foundational things we need to get done and get right 
first?” 
  
Peak performance doesn’t just happen. It needs to be built and cultivated along the way. When 
you get to the championship game or that key meeting with a client, it’s not the time to worry 
about preparation. It’s the time to use your muscle memory and focus on execution.  
 
To fully utilize your team’s capabilities, assign clear roles to each team member. Over time, Pat 
learned that it was better to break down responsibilities among the coaching staff by assigning 
them each to a specific area to focus their attention on during the game so that she could focus 
on making executive decisions.  
 
If you’re looking for a game plan to help your team to deliver peak performance, employ a 
smart strategy with a coherent plan that has clear goals and defined roles. If you’ve done the 
right preparation, when it’s game time in sports, business, or in life, rely on muscle memory, 
your preparation, and focus on execution to deliver the win.

Build Smart

Don't Just Work Hard, Work Smart: Build Smart, featuring Sue Nokes

Shared Values Allow for Personal Investment
Leaders must establish shared values within the organization. While every individual in the organization may have their own learning style and learning preference, it is important that organizations establish the values that they will live by collectively.

What values does your organization collectively share? How do they impact your approach to your work?

If, say, your organization values timeliness, honesty, lifelong learning, and gratitude, those values will have a deep and significant impact on everything you do. Even though each individual may express those values differently, maintaining shared, collective values is extremely important.

When presented and shared, values create guardrails for behaviors and may ultimately shape strategy. For example, if honesty is one of the more important shared values, and a company can advance its interests by lying to their clients, it's a non-starter. Even if a short-term benefit can be observed by violating a set of values, the long-term implications are drastic because without alignment to a set of values, then values have no place in the organization. Everyone's values then become only situationally applied. Worse yet, the lack of shared values almost always results in a gradual lowering of the bar. Think of it this way. You have values in your life that guide you and (hopefully) allow you the pleasure of a good, honest life. If you begin ignoring those values when making decisions, you will undermine your long-term progress and, ultimately, diminish who you are as a human being.

What If the Values in the Organization Don't Align With My Own?
This is the question every leader should ask before they take a new job. Consider two potential sources of value misalignment:

The organization hasn't articulated the values, or they haven't been challenged in quite some time. A new leader may come in and create value alignment, helping things improve.
The organization has values in place, but an individual team member disagrees with them. A leader may establish values and articulate them, but if an individual team member doesn't believe in those values, a misalignment has occurred. Usually, that means the team member will have to either operate within this value system or find a new job.

Obviously, not every organization is the same. But in general, leaders shouldn't sacrifice their values. They should clearly articulate values, and seek to build an organization that meets and exceeds those values.

Personal Investment Is Enhanced Through Values
When we have aspirational value statements guiding us, we become aspirational people capable of doing and becoming more. And with that aspirational growth comes the opportunity to become more enhanced, personally invested, and aligned together. Organizations that do deep dives on values and consideration of collective value statements are far more likely to develop deep and sustaining commitments to one another.

Values and Personal Investment Create Ownership
One of the most powerful ways to determine whether or not an organization will be successful is to evaluate the degree to which ownership exists.

What comes to mind when you think about ownership within a team or organization? What does ownership look like in an organization?

To expand your thinking about what ownership is and is not, each card in the following stack contains a behavior exhibited by individuals within an organization or on a team. Sort the cards into the categories of either shows ownership or lacks ownership.

Views both the results and the driving processes as theirs — Shows Ownership
Reflects on weak points in the organization as if they can do nothing about them — Lacks Ownership
Reflects on collective success even when they were not directly involved — Shows Ownership
Uses "we" language when describing results and processes — Shows Ownership
Embraces both the victories and opportunities for growth — Shows Ownership
Talks about the system as if they are detached from it — Lacks Ownership
Views improvement as largely impossible due to political or structural factors — Lacks Ownership

7/7 Cards Correct

Continued

Let's start with what ownership is not. In organizations that are largely disconnected, individuals within the group likely:
• talk about the system as if they are detached from it;
• reflect on weak points in the organization as if they have absolutely no influence on doing something about them; and
• reflect on their own performance and think of change as largely impossible due to political or structural factors they believe are in the way.

In this instance, there is very little ownership in either the results or the vehicle designed to deliver the results. And this is regrettable. On the other hand, great leaders and top performers in high-functioning organizations:
• own both their results and the processes that drive them;
• own every part of the process and system, even if they aren't directly involved in delivering the results;
• embrace both the victories and the areas for growth; and
• speak in terms of "we" when describing the results — things like, "We have struggled lately with accounting, but we are doing really well with logistics and customer satisfaction."

These are clear indicators of organizations that are strong in the area of ownership.

Which of the following do you think has the greatest impact on corporate success and profitability?
Technological advances
Historic performance data
A strong mission statement
Innovation of the human spirit

Incorrect. Correct answer: Innovation of the human spirit. Your answer: Technological advances. Not quite. All of these can play a role in corporate success and profitability, but in a world today that has been flattened and made ultimately more competitive with technology, the value of people has never been so great. One of the many reasons CEOs are paid more today as a percentage of profit than ever before is because arguably, in a world where technology makes anything possible, the innovation of the human spirit has the greatest impact on corporate success and profitability.

Correct. Correct answer: Innovation of the human spirit. Your answer: Innovation of the human spirit. That's right! In a world today that has been flattened and made ultimately more competitive with technology, the value of people has never been so great. One of the many reasons CEOs are paid more today as a percentage of profit than ever before is because arguably, in a world where technology makes anything possible, the innovation of the human spirit has the greatest impact on corporate success and profitability.

You Win in Life with People
If innovation of the human spirit is such a key driving factor for organizational success, then recruiting, retaining, encouraging, training, and improving upon people is indeed the lifeblood of every organization today. Centuries ago, the success of a business might rest almost entirely on access to water systems and wood. Today, access to creative hearts and minds and the establishment of nurturing environments that makes the most of their expertise is the lifeblood of so many businesses. We've always won with people. Today more than ever, businesses can't win without a focus on developing, supporting, and improving the people they recruit and maintain in their organization.

Know Your Team
Because people are so important to the health and vitality of an organization, it's important to know them. Creating systems where teams are interactive helps you both know and engage your team. This is why leaders sometimes invest in retreats or team outings to have shared experiences together. By getting to know one another, there's a greater likelihood of developing trust and understanding.

The Lady Vols team and staff enjoy time together at the Parthenon.

Coach Summitt and her team gather for some casual fun at a local hangout.

Regardless of the type of work a team does, the better the leader and team members know each other, the more they trust, engage, and learn and grow together. This helps develop personal relationships that make learning fun and creates that human touch that can bring people together for a lifetime. Often, these relationships sustain us and become some of the most important bonds in our entire life. By taking the time as a leader to create situations where those bonds can be built, you create generational influence.

Views improvement as largely impossible due to political or structural factors — Lacks Ownership

body_blocks.text: Ownership: What It Is Not and What It Is
Let's start with what ownership is not. In organizations that are largely disconnected, individuals within the group likely:

items: talk about the system as if they are detached from it;
reflect on weak points in the organization as if they have absolutely no influence on doing something about them; and
reflect on their own performance and think of change as largely impossible due to political or structural factors they believe are in the way.

body_blocks.text: In this instance, there is very little ownership in either the results or the vehicle designed to deliver the results. And this is regrettable. On the other hand, great leaders and top performers in high-functioning organizations:

items: own both their results and the processes that drive them;
own every part of the process and system, even if they aren't directly involved in delivering the results;
embrace both the victories and the areas for growth; and
speak in terms of "we" when describing the results — things like, "We have struggled lately with accounting, but we are doing really well with logistics and customer satisfaction."

body_blocks.text: These are clear indicators of organizations that are strong in the area of ownership.
Which of the following do you think has the greatest impact on corporate success and profitability?
items: Technological advances
Historic performance data
A strong mission statement
Innovation of the human spirit

body_blocks.text: You Win in Life with People

If innovation of the human spirit is such a key driving factor for organizational success, then recruiting, retaining, encouraging, training, and improving upon people is indeed the lifeblood of every organization today. Centuries ago, the success of a business might rest almost entirely on access to water systems and wood. Today, access to creative hearts and minds and the establishment of nurturing environments that makes the most of their expertise is the lifeblood of so many businesses. We've always won with people. Today more than ever, businesses can't win without a focus on developing, supporting, and improving the people they recruit and maintain in their organization.
Know Your Team

Because people are so important to the health and vitality of an organization, it's important to know them. Creating systems where teams are interactive helps you both know and engage your team. This is why leaders sometimes invest in retreats or team outings to have shared experiences together. By getting to know one another, there's a greater likelihood of developing trust and understanding.
The Lady Vols team and staff enjoy time together at the Parthenon.
Coach Summitt and her team gather for some casual fun at a local hangout.

Regardless of the type of work a team does, the better the leader and team members know each other, the more they trust, engage, and learn and grow together. This helps develop personal relationships that make learning fun and creates that human touch that can bring people together for a lifetime. Often, these relationships sustain us and become some of the most important bonds in our entire life. By taking the time as a leader to create situations where those bonds can be built, you create generational influence.

video.transcript_text:
Don’t Just Work Hard, Work Smart: Build Smart, Featuring Sue Nokes 
 
 
Sue Nokes, Advisory Board Vice Chairman, Asurion; Former Chief Customer & Operations 
Officer, T-Mobile 
 
In any profession, when a team truly works together towards the same goals, with a shared 
value system, individuals feel personally invested in the task at hand. Pat Summitt was a good 
friend of mine, and I was privileged to sit in Pat’s locker room before the game and at halftime. 
And over the years, I observed one obvious difference between the championship teams and 
the non-championship teams. It’s called ownership.  
 
The culture of ownership can only be built with intention. This happens when the right people 
are put in the right position that best suits their talent. And that’s exactly what Pat did. Pat 
always said that you win in life with people. 
  
Let’s analyze her example. First, know your team. Even if you have clear goals and a coherent 
plan, you won’t get anywhere if you have the wrong people filling the roles. Working smart 
requires building smart teams. The best way to build a strong team is to size up your present 
resources, identify any weaknesses, and identify the resources needed. Knowing your team and 
knowing yourself will illuminate the areas that you can build up through professional 
development and the type of person you should recruit to fill the vacant role. 
  
Second, utilize personality profiles. Pat Summitt used an assessment called the Predictive Index 
to categorize personality traits. She also brought in sports psychologists to help her staff 
understand individual players on her teams. More importantly, Pat involved her players in the 
discussions about their personality profiles. Pat talked with her players about how they saw 
themselves and what they thought about their results. Pat even provided her coaches and the 
players with her profile so they could better understand her own motivations and techniques.  
 
When you take the same evaluations you request from your team, it helps identify what 
motivates you, what you love to do, and what zaps your mental energy. Learn how to delegate 
the tasks that drain you the most so you can focus on what you do the best and what you bring 
to your team. 
  
And third, learn your team’s pressure points. Everyone handles pressure differently, and it’s the 
job of the leader to know how your people respond to pressure before high-pressure moments 
arrive.  
 
Pat used to say, “It’s your chief responsibility as a leader or a manager or CEO to know who you 
can delegate to and when.” When you know your team, their personalities, and how they 
respond to pressure, you will be able to draw out their talents and put them in situations where 
they can be most successful.

steps.source_title: Leadership Reflections: Defining Success for You
steps.exact_visible_copy:
Page 10 of 15
Leadership Reflections: Defining Success for You

As discussed, defining success can be harder than it looks. As humans, we often think in very linear terms about next steps, such as promotion opportunities. However, getting really clear about what "success" actually means to you is altogether different than goals or even promotions. Put another way, getting a promotion doesn't automatically mean you are "successful." If, however, a certain job or position is your dream job, then it's your definition of success. This distinction makes all the difference. For example, you have likely known someone who became angry, toxic, and despondent because they didn't get a particular job they wanted. It might have been at a particular company and they began to believe that success was limited to that position at that moment.

For this reflection, we want you to get clear about what success means to you. Set aside a career path you might have read about, or a lifestyle that you are imagining, and define what success looks like. What will you look back on someday and be proud of in terms of accomplishment and priorities? What does "success" mean to you?

Reflect on this question in your workbook.

Continued

Leaders and peak performers who understand this factor usually become far more successful. This is because people are usually far more accomplished when they are pursuing their own success rather than being locked in to a moment-by-moment perspective on what's next. For this reflection, allow yourself the flexibility to pause and get in touch with what makes you satisfied.

Balance Smart

Don't Just Work Hard, Work Smart: Balance Smart, featuring Sue Nokes

The greatest strength any human being can have is to recognize his or her own weaknesses. Pat Summitt

Solicit (a.k.a. Demand) Feedback and the Declaration of Blind Spots

avoid feedback that fails to glorify the leader's performance;
seek out individuals in the organization who will find a way to directly or indirectly complement them; and
avoid any scenario that might bring some sort of growth-generating criticism.

Formal, such as a "360-degree" assessment, discussed earlier. These can be very valuable forms of feedback as to how others perceive a leader's behavior.
Informal, through conversations with team members, colleagues, other leaders, customers, etc.

Amparo is a relatively new CEO who is trying to turn around her organization.
She has several high-achieving vice presidents on her team. She's come to rely on them while working through her first year.
In that time, the vice presidents have gotten to know Amparo and have begun building relationships with her. They know her well enough to observe her strengths, as well as some weak spots.

What would likely benefit Amparo most in this situation?

Continue operating as she has been, since it seems to be working well
Collect feedback from her team on weak spots and blind spots
Lead a team workshop on identifying and fixing blind spots

Incorrect. Correct answer: Collect feedback from her team on weak spots and blind spots. Your answer: Continue operating as she has been, since it seems to be working well. Not quite! If Amparo has developed enough of a relationship with the vice presidents, the goal would be to collect feedback on weak spots and blind spots.

Correct. Correct answer: Collect feedback from her team on weak spots and blind spots. Your answer: Collect feedback from her team on weak spots and blind spots. Yes, that's correct! If Amparo has developed enough of a relationship with the vice presidents, the goal would be to collect feedback on weak spots and blind spots.

It shows a desire to have an intimate conversation with executives on a similar level.
By letting them know that you are deeply committed to growth and are willing to listen to their feedback, you're sending a clear message to everybody that growth is not negotiable and everyone is fallible.
If handled with integrity, the relationship between the CEO and vice presidents could likely improve, as honest feedback was shared.

Prioritize Problems
In an organization with very little communication, where the leader is largely disconnected from the group, the leader may be unaware of problems in the organization. As a leader, this is not working under some sort of happy, blissful ignorance. It's like floating on a ship without awareness of the iceberg ahead. Keeping lines of communication open and desiring growth will help ensure problems are more readily revealed. Blind spots, skill deficits, and other problems are going to emerge eventually. Teams need to learn to resolve these problems once they've been identified through problem prioritization. By prioritizing the problems in front of us, we have a much better chance of potentially resolving them. The priority helps us determine the order in which we will attend to certain problems. This allows the organization to understand where to put its energy, the problems to address, and in which order. There are several possible approaches to prioritizing problems:

Pick a Strategic Priority
Pick an objective that is entirely strategic. Think of playing a game of Jenga — pull out the wrong block and the entire column will fall. When you are strategic in making changes, you may have limited time and resources, but picking the right change can sometimes have a huge impact in the organization. In some cases, a simple realignment in work process or the elimination of a key obstacle, or in some cases, a toxic individual, can create momentum.

Pick an Easily-Executed Priority
Establish a priority that is perhaps simpler, shorter, and more easily achieved. In other words, a leader may be facing a dilemma and observe a number of problems that need to be solved. When a team is relatively new in working together, or its members are stuck and haven't made progress in a while, sometimes a leader is wise to pick a more easily-resolved priority for the team to tackle first. The advantages here are obvious. Choosing smaller commitments helps the team build confidence and momentum, leading to even more confidence before taking on bigger and more challenging objectives.

Decide If the Problem Is Short-Term or Long-Term
Another question strong leaders ask is whether or not this particular problem is of a long-term nature. For a long-term problem, you can either: Prioritize the long-term problem. If the long-term problem is likely game-changing, consider prioritizing it; or break the long-term problem into smaller, shorter-term problems that should be addressed first. For a short-term problem, consider the potential return on solving the problem. You can: plan how to resolve it and execute the plan, especially if it is a stepping stone toward a larger problem; quickly fix a small problem that could build momentum; limit time and energy on a short-term problem with little return; or allow it to resolve itself due to market conditions or other situations.

Example: An Auto Manufacturer
Suppose the auto maker has been in business for more than 100 years. They've been dealing with a particular problem for several decades. Leaders expect it will take at least five years to address the problem, but the outcome would be game-changing for the company. Strong leaders in this company would have to decide if this long-term problem should be a priority. Since it will take at least five years, these leaders may need to break the problem down into shorter-term challenges that will lead to progress toward solving that longer-term problem. This is the stuff of leadership — reflecting on these different possibilities to better understand how to strategically solve problems and help their organization win.

What are some strategies you use for prioritizing problems in your organization? Do you plan to optimize your approach in any way based on what we've covered so far?

As we near the end of this section on "balancing smart," which of the following would you say is most accurate about strong leaders?

They show strength and confidence by will and absolute rigidity.
They are flexible when it comes to their values, ethics, and commitments.
They are steadfast when it comes to business strategies and approaches.
They show strength and confidence through learning, growth, and compromise.

Incorrect. Correct answer: They show strength and confidence through learning, growth, and compromise. Your answer: They show strength and confidence by will and absolute rigidity.

Correct. Correct answer: They show strength and confidence through learning, growth, and compromise. Your answer: They show strength and confidence through learning, growth, and compromise.

Leaders Know When to Compromise
One of the mistakes that leaders make is assuming that strength is shown by will and absolute rigidity. In fact, one of the greatest signs of strength and confidence is a leader's ability to learn, grow, and compromise. Leaders should remain steadfast when it comes to values, ethics, and commitments. However, they should remain flexible when it comes to business strategies and approaches. The ability to compromise as a leader demonstrates your ability to grow. It's also a wonderful way to demonstrate the expectations of compromise throughout the organization. Organizations are worse off when warring factions within won't compromise. The healthiest organizations have significant debates at times about the best pathway forward. Well-intended and completely loyal team members may have diametrically opposed positions, but this does not mean that they can't still be valued teammates, friends, and valued confidants. These diametrically opposed individuals must also learn to compromise.

How many times have peak performers on a basketball team had to sacrifice points per game in order to keep their teammates involved in the game plan? These sacrifices make everyone stronger and more evolved.

You Can’t Fix Everything at Once
Especially with new leaders, there's a tendency sometimes try to fix everything at once. This is a mistake. Recall our automobile example. If the manufacturer has faced many decades of challenges in a certain area of product development, that problem likely won't be resolved overnight. This doesn't mean that heroic steps can't be taken — but trying to fix everything at once can sometimes cause a great deal of confusion and leave the organization feeling overwhelmed.

Trust Is the Key
When leaders build trust, they once again create increased levels of momentum. As discussed earlier, momentum can be created when expectations are clear. When trust is developed, there is less hesitation and fear. When team members are operating from a position of fear, they are less courageous and innovative.

Working smart is about understanding what you are best at, what you are worst at, and what you will settle for in the interest of progress. It's about arriving at a balance. — Pat Summitt

First, solicit feedback from your peers. It’s hard for employees to be completely honest with the 
boss. The best and oftentimes most critical feedback will come from leaders in your 
organization or on your team, namely your peers. They can be your greatest asset for checking 
emotional blind spots and gaining self-knowledge. Why? Your peers see a different side of you 
than most people. Pat regularly solicited feedback from other coaching leaders such as John 
Wooden, Bruce Pearl, Coach K (Mike Krzyzewski), and Phillip Fulmer, to name a few, for her 
personal growth and development. 
  
Second, prioritize problems. All problems are not created equal. Learn to prioritize both long-
term and short-term opportunities and which one will be accomplished over time. Choose your 
battles. Know when to compromise and save your energy for those problems that most 
threaten your values and goals. You can’t fix everything at once. Over the course of her career, 
Pat persistently chipped away the obstacles and seized each opportunity to achieve the long-
term goal of advancing women’s basketball. She also made short-term adjustments at halftime 
to win a game. 
  
Third, lead through influence and example -- and there was no better example of integrity and 
hard work than my friend, Pat Summitt. A great leader wants their team to follow them, but out 
of commitment to the goals and what you’re trying to achieve together, not out of compliance 
and fear. Leadership is an art, not a science. To gain commitment, good leaders identify and 
communicate a foundational system of values that runs through everything they do. When the 
values and goals are transparent, your team is more likely to trust your leadership and take the 
risks you ask of them.  
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
“Working smart is about understanding what you are best at and what you are worst at and 
what you will settle for in the interest of progress. It’s about arriving at a balance.”

Wrap-Up

The blueprint is this: knowledge, confidence, relaxation, results. Knowledge builds confidence, which causes you to be relaxed, which gives you good results. Pat Summitt

Don't Just Work Hard, Work Smart: Wrap-Up, featuring Marie Mouchet

Strategy and Clear Communication
Working frantically doesn't take you anywhere. Working hard on the right things makes all the difference. This is why it is so essential for leaders to develop clear and actionable strategies. These strategies must be easily communicated throughout the organization. This clarity has two important benefits:

With Clarity Comes Momentum
As discussed earlier, one of the most significant hindrances to building momentum is the lack of clarity. If your team members are uncertain about the strategy, expectation, goals, and aspirations, they are left with the difficult dilemma of trying to look like they're working hard towards a destination that they're just not sure about. Unfortunately, this dynamic is more common than any of us would like to admit. Confusion over the goal creates disconnects, and, under the worst of circumstances, can create situations where the strategy is hijacked and individuals begin to insert their own agendas.

Team Clarity Creates Team Culture
Another advantage of momentum-building clarity is that it can serve as a force to help build and develop culture within an organization. Simply put, organizational culture is built through a series of collective experiences that result in an understanding of expected behaviors and values. When a team has clarity about the strategy ahead and the strategy is built on organizational values, the execution not only moves the organization closer to their goals, but it also serves to build team culture. Teams get stronger and the culture is reinforced. This level of alignment may sound difficult to achieve, but it shows up when leaders consistently adopt strategies with clarity.

Happy Cultures, Predictability, and Progress

What comes to mind when you think of the phrase happy culture? Does your organization or team have a happy culture? How so?

A happy culture is not solely dedicated to having fun. A happy culture is a content culture, and that contentment can come from the predictability of working under conditions that everyone knows. For example, Coach Summitt expected nothing less than rigorous engagement from everyone who ever played basketball at the University of Tennessee. Because everyone knew and shared in those ideas and expectations, the culture was established and excellence emerged as a result.

Players celebrate Coach Summitt's 500th career victory.

Invest in Deep, Collaborative Planning
Another element of working hard and smart is the investment in deep and collaborative planning. This effort involves the establishment of goals and collaborative development of the step-by-step process required to make those goals come to fruition. It puts participants in the position of owning the journey and owning the plan. By being part of the planning process, the commitment to the goal increases dramatically.

Find Smart People to Surround You
Ineffective leaders sometimes have reputations for surrounding themselves with people who are less talented than them. Perhaps a leader lacks confidence or mistakenly assumes they need to know more than everyone else around them. In fact, nothing could be further from the truth. Ineffective leaders will likely stay that way if they follow this model because intentionally surrounding themselves with less-talented people will deny them opportunities for valuable insight. The very best leaders surround themselves with incredibly smart people. Ideally, they like to find people who are actually better than they are in areas where they are weak.

Coach Summitt took pride in surrounding herself with an extremely talented staff.

For example, if you are a leader in corporate America and have a blind spot when it comes to logistics, you might bring in a vice president with a truly world-class understanding of logistics. This would not be announcing your weakness, but rather announcing your ability to identify a need and recruit people who can meet that need. In an era where information is ever-expanding, it is frankly absurd to assume a leader can always know it all. The more information expands, the more we need expansive people willing to lead.

Based on what we've covered so far, which of these do you think is the most powerful way to get an organization to work both hard and smart?

Compromise values that get in the way of productivity.
Publish policies requiring employees to work both hard and smart.
Fill your team with people with less talent than you.
Influence a hard and smart working culture by being an example.

Incorrect. Correct answer: Influence a hard and smart working culture by being an example. Your answer: Compromise values that get in the way of productivity. Of these options, a leader can capitalize on influence and being an example of working both hard and smart.

Correct. Correct answer: Influence a hard and smart working culture by being an example. Your answer: Influence a hard and smart working culture by being an example. Of these options, a leader can capitalize on influence and being an example of working both hard and smart.

Influence and Example

An organization brings in a new leader who presents a highly polished and professional demeanor.
This new leader has a really positive attitude with everyone they meet. They remember details about people's personal lives. They're friendly and engaging, never missing an opportunity to make people feel good.
This individual is clearly a strong leader for the organization, not only showing both talent and hard work, but also a commitment to the entire team.

Chances are, that leader's positivity and engagement would literally influence the rest of the organization and serve as an example for others to follow.

A new leader comes into an organization. This person seems rather angry and is secretive about their work.
Employees begin to notice this leader has a political agenda to drive certain people out of the organization.
This leader has great talent for the work, but clearly brings some baggage and negativity with them.

That negativity is just as contagious as the positivity in the earlier example, isn't it? Perhaps it is even more contagious. Others will likely start operating this way and bring more of the same to the organization. Positively or negatively, no matter what a leader does, their leadership style, preferences, and habits will create influence and serve as examples. As such, leaders must be very thoughtful and self-aware of their actions and the messages they send to those around them.

How have you seen the power of influence and example play out in your team or organization, or in the world? What can you do to replicate that positivity or prevent that negativity in your own leadership practices?

video.transcript_text:
Don’t Just Work Hard, Work Smart: Wrap-Up, Featuring Marie Mouchet 
 
 
Marie Mouchet, VP & CIO Colonial Pipeline Company 
 
Pat Summitt was an expert strategist who knew how to chart the most intelligent path toward 
her goals. Pat said, “The blueprint is this: knowledge, confidence, relaxation, results. Knowledge 
builds confidence, which causes you to be relaxed, which gives you good results.”  
 
It is a simple, yet powerful approach, but only if the foundation is secure. Knowledge is the 
starting point and is crucial to effective leadership in professional settings. 
  
In this module, we learned that success requires strategy and clear communication. Establish 
concrete goals for your staff and focus team energy on fulfilling specific expectations. Healthy 
team culture shares the responsibility for ensuring expectations are met. 
  
Once the goals are clear, outline a coherent plan by prioritizing the order in which objectives 
are to be accomplished in order to pace your team’s preparation for success. To execute your 
strategy, you have to bring balance to your own strengths and weaknesses. Stay open to 
feedback, especially feedback from your peers. 
  
Next, apply the feedback by surrounding yourself with people who can complement your 
personality and offset your weaknesses. This frees you up to focus on your strengths and to 
lead through influence and example rather than fear and compliance. The more you know 
yourself, the better you’ll be at prioritizing between problems. Choose your battles wisely so 
you can maintain focus on progressing toward your goal.  
 
When you work smart, not only do you harness the power of your time and energy for 
maximum impact, you also help others find direction with their talents and abilities. Knowledge 
and understanding are the best tools for blending hard work with smart work so that you can 
get real results while staying focused, relaxed, and productive towards your goals.

Leadership Reflections: Open Your Eyes

In this module, we discussed that we all have weaknesses and blind spots and the importance of being able to identify them. Equally important, in turn, is identifying strategies to help prevent your weaknesses and blind spots from impeding your success. Put another way, your blind spots aren't going to harm you, as long as you acknowledge them and strategize accordingly.

Some examples include:

If... | Then you might consider...
you struggle with communicating in writing | consistently using an editor and planning accordingly
you consistently get anxious when speaking to large groups | allowing extra time to prepare
part of your job is evaluating marketing opportunities, and you don't have much experience or expertise in that area | identifying learning and professional development opportunities in the area of marketing and allowing extra time to develop

For this reflection exercise, spend some time honestly reflecting on your weaknesses and blind spots.

Identify several weak areas or blind spots. Be honest with yourself about things you just aren't very good at. Think about what each weakness might mean for you professionally.
For each weakness or blind spot, identify some simple habits or strategies you could employ that would allow you to live with this weakness and keep it from hindering your ability to perform. How might you adjust your strategies so that your blind spots don't keep you from being successful?

Reflect on this in your workbook.

This conversation needs to happen more than once a year, and it needs to be honest and strategic.

Teamwork is really a form of trust.
