Trust Falls Aren’t Enough

Some leaders, even with good intentions, may hold an annual meeting where certain activities are designed to build teamwork and improve the overall ethic of working together. These ceremonial activities or the equally popular enthusiasm of a motivational speaker won't be enough to truly build great teams. The construction of great teams comes from a strategic sense of purpose, the deliberate construction of teams, and the ongoing reinforcement of teams as family, every week and every day.

Let’s Get into the Details: What Does Our Team Do?

Getting into the details regularly is an important part of making sure teams have specific purposes and protocols. In business, for example, it's important to ensure teams are constructed in a way that every individual on the team has a purpose and a function, and that their purpose and function is demonstrated every time they get together.

What to Do with the Weakest Player? (aka, All of Us Could Be the Weakest Player)

It is said that any group is only as strong as its weakest link. While on the basketball court, that weak link may consistently be one person. In the world of business, it's often not that simple. In fact, when it comes to the weakest link, sometimes it can be entirely situational. There may be a season where a particular department within an organization simply has a difficult week or month. There could be a scenario where unique stress is placed on a department due to issues beyond their control. Suddenly, the organization is seen as weak in that particular area.

The adage that an organization is only as strong as its weakest link is certainly true, but there are two important things for leaders to keep in mind.

The weakest link, even if it's only situational, is only as painful and harmful to the organization as the team allows it to be. If a team works together consistently and effectively, those weak moments won't damage the overall progress of the group.
The weakest link could be any one of us at any given moment. Even the most consistent hero might need a great deal of support (and even saving) in an unforeseen circumstance. Furthermore, anyone within the organization is capable of stepping up and delivering in the face of certain moments of challenge. The best leaders create conditions where this is understood and consistently exemplified.

Put the Team Before Yourself: Pat in Her Own Words 
 
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
Every year, at the beginning of the year when we bring our team to the court, the first thing 
that we talk about is getting better as a team. We don’t talk about winning national 
championship. We talk about the details. We talk about being better ball handlers, being better 
shooters, being better screeners, learning how to play together. 
  
You know, it’s difficult sometimes for players to think about the team concept. But that’s what 
it’s all about. And the little things add up to the big things, to the great things. And so, as we are 
teaching, we’re teaching all the details, and we want them to embrace. 
  
We have a system. You know, if you’ve got a team, the team has to embrace the system. And 
here at the University of Tennessee, more times than not, the system works. Why? Because the 
players make it work. Why? Because they want to win. They want to find greatness together. 
And that’s what you do in corporate America. You bring a team together. And teamwork works. 
  
But everyone has to be on board. We’re only as good as our weakest player. We won’t want 
any weak players. We want great players, great competitors that will bring together a powerful 
team. It’s hard to get to the top. And when you get there, it’s even harder to stay there.  
 
As you think about your team, you look around the room and you ask each and every person, 
“Are you committed? Are you a great teammate? Are you going to help us have the most 
powerful team?” We do this together. Do it and do it now.

Put the Team Before Yourself: Introduction

Put the Team Before Yourself: Introduction, featuring Dr. Keith Gray

To me, teamwork is a lot like being part of a family. It comes with obligations, entanglements, headaches, and quarrels. But the rewards are worth the cost.
Pat Summitt

The Family You Choose
We are all born into a family. However, there's a second family in our lives. They are the people that we choose. Strong leaders understand that the instinct to build a family is very powerful, and taking advantage of it in terms of building strong teams can help lead to unprecedented success.

Your Family Has a Bond
With blood relatives, your bond is your genetic lineage and your family experiences. This can be the most powerful bond in your life. Your second family, which can be your team and/or your social circle, is likewise held together by a powerful bond. This bond is what makes all the difference in our lives. Chances are that bond has to do with some sort of collective experience that you shared together, a common moment or aspiration that you locked arms and worked together towards. Leaders need to remember that new families can be constructed when bonds are deliberately formed. This means that the best leaders bring groups together and give them those experiences that create the emotional bond.

Bonding Experiences
You and I have heard the term, "bonding experiences." You may have even been in a group activity involving some sort of bonding exercise designed to bring people together during the learning experience. When these are done well, they can work to bring a group together effectively. The best leaders and coaches understand that, when they bring a disparate group of people together with the collective aspiration of achieving a goal, a bonding experience or series of experiences is required to create the emotional tie that will hold them together. To that end, as a leader, you must remember that the degree to which your team will bond together and become a family will be driven directly by the quality, consistency, and sheer number of bonding experiences that pull them together and help them to perform as one. Without these collective experiences, the connectivity simply won't be as strong, and that family won't likely hold together during tough times. Build the bond, build the family, and enjoy the results.

Think about people in your life whom you consider family members by choice. What shared experiences led you to the emotional bond that holds you close to them? In your team, what experiences can you create to help the team develop emotional bond?

Families and Conflict

Now let's talk about conflicts happening in families and in teams. Which do you think is a sign of healthy team dynamics?

Team members never have conflicts.
Team members have occasional conflicts.
Team members always have conflicts.

Incorrect. Correct answer: Team members have occasional conflicts. Your answer: Team members never have conflicts.

Correct. Correct answer: Team members have occasional conflicts. Your answer: Team members have occasional conflicts.

Your chosen family will never be free of conflict. In fact, relationships that don't include conflict at all are not necessarily the healthiest ones. Without conflict, there's an implication that members of the family aren't close enough to be honest and get real with each other. As we all know, when you "get real," you run the risk of either offending or disrupting the status quo...and that disruption is where all the growth occurs. If you're not close enough to have a real conversation with someone, how close are you, really? Keeping everything polite and at a distance may be appropriate in certain social settings, but with teams that are trying to achieve at the highest level, that moment of raw honesty is essential. If you're truly going to take advantage of the team-building that's required to build a powerful family or team, you have to be willing to endure and embrace conflict.

High Regards and High Expectations
Your chosen family, when constructed in an optimal way, holds each member of the family or the team in high regard. First, team members know each other well enough to observe and appreciate the elements that make each person valuable to the team. They hold those assets or attributes close to their hearts, and they respect what they bring to the team. Second, the concept of high expectations is extremely important. When you care about somebody, you have high expectations for their future. The best leaders create conditions where the entire team or family pulls for each other after recognizing a skill or ability in an individual member. High regards and high expectations of each other within a team help it build that family bond and make it stronger.

Teamwork is really a form of trust. It's what happens when you realize that you wouldn't achieve your individual goals without the support of your colleagues.
Pat Summitt

Compromise and Collaboration
Compromise — A team member makes a sacrifice to support another team member at their own expense.
Collaboration — Team members successfully work together towards a common goal.

Shared Success

When teams learn to work together and operate like a family, their success becomes a shared success. The good thing about shared success isn't just that it creates a condition where celebrating good news is emotionally rewarded, it also creates a situation where team members get more actively involved in helping each other arrive at their destinations.

Checked vs. Unchecked Egos
Finally, one of the common denominators in making teams work within a family is observance of checked versus unchecked egos. An unchecked ego won't allow the appreciation of others to emerge for fear that they will somehow miss out on praise. The members of the team who have such fragile egos that they're unwilling to celebrate others see good news or compliments as limited commodities. An abundance of that commodity shining away from them creates nervousness and resentment.
Clearly, on effective teams, egos are checked at the door, and people are willing to set aside their own success for the success of the team. They don't worry about their personal praise as much as they worry about the collective success of the team, knowing that their moment will likely come, and to be patient until it does. Obviously, this isn't easily achieved. There are certain people who are so fragile from an ego standpoint that they will never allow their egos to go unchecked, and these individuals may never fit into a team or be part of a winning team culture.
However, there are others who simply have never been taught what it means to care for others and connect, and once they are given the opportunity to do so, they relish it. It forever changes their outlook and how they connect with people. Strong leaders help others learn to check their egos and appreciate other people...and everyone involved grows as a result.

Building a Great Team
Create regular opportunities for bringing the team together and giving team members quality experiences that create emotional bonds and a sense of unity.
Foster honesty and trust in team communication.
Do not leave team conflicts unresolved.
Teach team members to compromise and collaborate.
Create an environment where team members respect each other and recognize each other's skills and abilities.
Create an environment where team members help each other succeed and share each other's success.
Help team members learn to keep egos checked and to express appreciation for their teammates.

Put the Team Before Yourself: Introduction, Featuring Dr. Keith Gray 
 
 
Keith Gray, Senior Vice President & Chief Medical Officer, University Health Systems, Inc. 
 
The word “family” signifies a tight bond. In a literal sense, it applies to your relatives, but it can 
also speak to a deeper connection among friends and colleagues. You have your family of 
origin, and you have the family you choose. These are the people who form your support 
network, the ones you turn to when you want to share life’s joys and trials.  
 
While being in a family has its rewards, it also comes with conflict. The people you lean on the 
most are often the ones who hold your highest regard and your highest expectations. 
  
Pat Summitt considered teamwork to be a lot like being in a family. A team shares goals, 
responsibilities, arguments and heartbreak. It can be hard to stay in sync with the bigger picture 
while working through differences; but when a team is fully committed, greatness is possible. 
Working together, ordinary people can do extraordinary things. 
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
  
“Teamwork is really a form of trust. It’s what happens when you realize that you wouldn’t 
achieve your individual goals without the support of your colleagues.” 
 
Keith Gray, Senior Vice President & Chief Medical Officer, University Health Systems, Inc. 
  
So how do you get people to shift from thinking only about themselves to sacrificing for the 
greater good? How do you lead distinct personalities to practice compromise and 
collaboration? Pat cultivated a team-oriented mindset among her players every day because 
she knew that unchecked ego and jealousy could dismantle even the most talented collection 
of athletes. She was a master at harnessing the power of differing perspectives, backgrounds, 
and abilities into a shared and intensive focus directed toward excellence. 
  
In this module, you’ll hear from Virginia Means, the chief people officer of United Distributors, 
where she oversees all aspects of human capital strategy and operations, including talent 
acquisition and development.  
 
Virginia will teach you the basic principles and methods Pat used to help her players adopt a 
team mentality. After these modules, you will know what it takes to lead a group of highly 
talented individuals toward shared success.

6 of 15
4-Minute Mile Pacesetters

How do you create a successful team? How do you convince a group of highly talented individual performers to set aside their personal feelings, ambitions, and agendas in favor of a unified effort? It's no easy matter. As a coach, I have to be at my most inventive and articulate when I talk about teamwork. But basketball happens to be a wonderful tool with which to teach it. Pat Summitt

Put the Team Before Yourself: 4-Minute Mile Pacesetters, featuring Virginia Means

What are the ways to convince highly talented individual performers to "set aside their personal feelings, ambitions, and agendas in favor of a unified effort?"

Make it clear from the outset that no individual on the team is more important than the other.
Reinforce the notion that no individual is as good as the collective power and capacity of the team.
Let everyone enjoy the individual benefits of being part of a team, such as support and encouragement by the team members.

All three actions will help you cultivate a team-oriented mindset among the team members.

Teams Achieve More Than Individuals
Successful teams are made up of highly talented individuals. As we have suggested before, a championship team or industry-leading group doesn't achieve this status without assembling a collection of talented contributors. However, we have all seen talented individuals who make terrible team members. Leaders must understand that it isn't enough to simply group individuals together and call them a team. A team is something that has to be thoughtfully created, and its foundation needs to be nurtured, revisited, and reinforced.

Testing the Theory
Basketball coaches have often run famous drills with the fastest players dribbling the basketball and establishing a contest where blazing dribblers race down the court and try to beat the speed of teammates who passed the ball. Suffice it to say, even the fastest Division 1 athlete can't outrun the speed of a ball moving from one teammate to another, carefully placed with knowledge of where they want to go. The goal of an assignment like this is obviously to learn to pass. But it's more than that. It's also to learn that the most powerful individual isn't as powerful as a well-crafted, strategic team. Leaders must take the time to reinforce this notion and show members of the team that, by working together, there's nothing they can't achieve; and no matter how powerful one individual member of the team may be, no individual is as good as the collective work or capacity of the team.

You can train yourself to become a team player — by keeping a disciplined eye on the larger goal and realizing that when you help each other, you help yourselves.
Pat Summitt

There Are Individual Benefits to Team Membership
Even the most selfless team member becomes more dedicated to the team family when they begin to enjoy the individual benefits of being part of a team. Some of those benefits include extra levels of support, emotional engagement, and the closeness and positive stimulation that comes from having team members who are there to encourage them. The combination of social support and technical engagement makes team membership unbelievably valuable to individual team members. Leaders should support these benefits and illustrate them on a regular basis.

In your organization, how do the individuals benefit from team membership? As a leader, how would you make them aware of these benefits?

The only way for disparate talented singing voices to build a beautiful arc of music is to have a leader who brings them together and for the chorus to operate as a team.

video.transcript_text:
Put the Team Before Yourself: 4-Minute Mile Pacesetters, Featuring Virginia 
Means 
 
 
Virginia Means, Chief People Officer, United Distributors, Inc. 
 
Coach Summitt said, “How do you create a successful team? How do you convince a group of 
highly talented individual performers to set aside their personal feelings, ambitions, and 
agendas in favor of a unified effort? It’s no easy matter. As a coach, I have to be at my most 
inventive and articulate when I talk about teamwork. But basketball happens to be a wonderful 
tool with which to teach it.” 
 
Pat Summitt held an unfailing belief that her teams would always achieve more than any one 
individual superstar player. Pat also knew that it goes against human nature to put the team 
before yourself. Like all skills, you have to work at it.  
 
You may have heard of Roger Bannister. Roger was the first person to break the four-minute 
mile. So, what does a guy who ran a record breaking four-minute mile have to do with 
teamwork? On that cold day at Iffley Road Track in 1954 Roger Bannister had a plan. You see, 
when he walked up to that starting line, there were two other guys on his team, Chris Brasher 
and Chris Chataway. When the gun sounded, Brasher rushed into the lead, followed by 
Bannister and Chataway. And it stayed that way for half a mile. Bannister then gave the signal 
and Brasher fell back. Chataway went into the lead with Bannister right behind. It stayed that 
way until the final 200 yards of the race. When Bannister kicked it into top gear, passing 
Chataway and crossing the finish line in record time, 3 minutes and 59 and four tenths seconds. 
 
So, what role did Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway play? They were Bannister’s pacesetters. 
Bannister knew that his best chance to make history, especially on a day that had horrible 
conditions, was to have the help of others. His teammates, Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway, 
took on a specific role and quite frankly, humbled themselves for the greater good of the 
outcome. 
 
Working together as a team, even when you may not be the one to get the glory, can yield 
phenomenal results. Pat Summitt spent her career helping great athletes and role players work 
together to achieve greatness. In any team and in any enterprise, sometimes someone is the 
hero and sometimes someone is the pacesetter. But both are needed to achieve greatness.

8 of 15
Investing in Others

Teamwork is not a matter of persuading yourself and your colleagues to set aside personal ambitions for the greater good. It's a matter of recognizing that your personal ambitions and the ambitions of the team are one and the same. That's the incentive. Pat Summitt

Put the Team Before Yourself : Investing in Others, featuring Virginia Means

Every Family Needs Heroes
Heroes tend to get a lot of attention and, to some degree, they should. If your team doesn't have a few heroic figures who are willing to provide industry-leading performance and insights, it isn't likely that your business endeavor will be successful. Even with the numerous basketball examples provided, having a team full of unselfish players is wonderful, but if none of them can emerge as the hero, the chance of abiding success is weakened. Thus, leaders should understand that heroes are required. Indeed, every team who becomes a family needs to look for the heroes in their midst and work together to nurture those heroes so they are ready to perform when the moment arrives!

Some Days, Different Heroes Emerge
In the world of business, heroes can emerge at different times, from all directions. Approaching the end of the fiscal year, for example, the high-flying accounting department might wear the hero’s cape. During the middle of a logistics disaster, a dedicated set of administrative assistants may come through in the clutch and overcome what might have been a daunting technical issue. In healthy, well-led organizations, these heroes are always ready to emerge when needed. In other words, that heroic individual within the organization may play the role of bystander or support most of the time. However, they need to work in an organization that lets them know that when their time comes, it will be essential for them to perform. Time and again, the best leaders have found themselves in difficult situations, only to be bailed out by unexpected members of their team who showed up with heroic strength to remedy difficult situations.

Anytime Heroes
Without question, heroes can emerge anytime. In the best organizations, there is an understanding that heroism does not require permission. Someone can just step up and do their job in a way to deliver the desired outcome. Can people make mistakes? Of course. But which type of organization would you rather work in — one that consistently holds you back? Or, would you rather work in an organization where the leader sets the parameters and encourages everyone to own the journey and behave like heroes every day?

Every Family Needs Pacesetters
In this module, we discussed the emergence of Roger Bannister, breaking the previously unthinkable barrier of running a sub-four-minute mile. As the story goes, Bannister was able to set this pace throughout his record-breaking run by having dedicated pacesetters, running just ahead of him, creating a condition where he was more likely to push himself to keep up and ultimately break the record. The term pacesetter is important here. Leaders need to know that heroes can go farther and faster as long as those around them operate as pacesetters, helping them break records. The leader must once again be exceedingly clear with the team that, when the hero's time has arrived, it is important for everyone to not only graciously appreciate the effort, but do anything they can to accelerate the pace and maximize the possibility.

Roger Bannister reaches the finish line in a 1953 race. Source: Wikimedia.

So, how can you be a pacesetter? Simply support your heroes in their moment. For example, if some dedicated administrative assistants have rolled up their sleeves and are taping boxes and delivering packages due to the logistics nightmare, others in the organization may hear about their efforts and stop what they are doing, run down to the warehouse, and pitch in. The CEO and vice president may also contribute to the effort. Everyone can be a hero and everyone can be a pacesetter. Depending on the time of day and the challenge ahead, we all have to stand ready to deliver whatever is needed.

The Power of Caring
One of the amazing benefits of being a pacesetter for a hero is to demonstrate the power of caring. In the logistics example, above, imagine how the vice president of logistics felt when others jumped in to help? Imagine how administrative assistants felt when everyone stopped what they were doing, including the CEO, and helped deliver boxes so that everyone looked good in the process. This shows a genuine caring for one another and a willingness to do whatever it takes to get the job done. This is the stuff of high-performing groups and teams, and it builds family bonds that will last forever.

No one cares how much you know until they know how much you care.
Teddy Roosevelt

video.transcript_text:
Put the Team Before Yourself: Investing in Others, Featuring Virginia Means 
 
 
Virginia Means, Chief People Officer, United Distributors, Inc. 
 
Coach Summitt said, “Teamwork is not a matter of persuading yourself and your colleagues to 
set aside personal ambitions for the greater good. It’s a matter of recognizing that your 
personal ambitions and the ambitions of the team are one and the same. That’s the incentive.”  
 
Did you ever wonder what it would take to be one of the most respected leaders in your 
organization where people are energized by you and you are a pacesetter for team efficiency 
and success? Pat Summitt knew that every player on her team had a role to fill, a job to do. 
Without everyone’s full commitment, their team goals would never be accomplished.  
 
In 1984, Pat faced a unique situation as she coached the U.S. Olympic team in Los Angeles. At 
the end of the Olympic trials, the final roster had to be at 12 players, which meant six players 
had to be cut. Pat decided to let the team cast confidential ballots to vote on the 12 players 
that should represent the United States at the Olympics. Incredibly, the player votes matched 
identically to the roster the coaches had made.  
 
Even though this meant some players voted for others instead of themselves to have an 
Olympic opportunity, the final roster had a team full of superstars like Cheryl Miller, Anne 
Donovan, Lynette Woodard, and Denise Currie, none of whom were accustomed to sitting on 
the bench. 
  
Pat decided the best approach was to tackle the situation head on. At the first team meeting, 
she announced, “Seven of you will be sitting on the bench when the game starts and seven of 
you will be on the bench when the game ends.” 
  
Your team members work for your organization, but their satisfaction is tied directly to their 
relationship with you and with each other. Do you make investment in your people a priority? 
Do you show an interest in their interests? Do you embody putting the team before yourself?  
 
And here’s the bottom line. Do they know you care? “No one cares how much you know until 
they know how much you care.” Sometimes, putting the team first is as simple as putting the 
team first.

11 of 15
Carrots and Sticks

It's all about perception, and if teammates find you the least bit inconsistent, moody, unpredictable, indecisive, or emotionally unreliable, then they balk, and the whole team is destabilized. Pat Summitt

Put the Team Before Yourself: Carrots and Sticks, featuring Virginia Means

Carrots and Sticks
Longstanding managerial theory has reflected on the role of "carrots and sticks" in motivating people to perform at higher levels. It was understood under this theory that carrots served to lead and motivate people, and sticks were there to threaten, poke, and cajole others into behaving in a way that was expected or preferred.

When Carrots Work
Carrots tend to work in motivating people when the task is relatively simple, or when used as team-building motivation, as opposed to being the ultimate reward.

When Carrots Don't Work
Carrots have been seen as less effective over time because human beings tend to consume the carrot and then begin to be less motivated unless a bigger carrot is offered. When carrots are used to motivate people in their work, people may end up working for carrots rather than for each other. Ultimately, this keeps us from being as connected as possible to our purpose, and it doesn't lead to long-term growth that might otherwise be achieved.

When Sticks Work
Sticks, or the threat of punishment, exist in many forms in our lives. Does the fear of punishment keep us from driving too fast on the highway or in front of a school? Probably so. You might be genuinely concerned about the cost and the inconvenience of getting a ticket.

The Stick as Positional Power

In reflecting on this concept, think about the stick as positional power. If you are a leader in the organization, you likely have some positional authority over those you work with. You may have the right or authority to provide them with a raise or to even fire them from their position. You might control key elements of their working conditions that matter a lot to them. As a result, you have a "stick" to control them in terms of your positional power.

Because of this power, you could start making demands on those you work with by letting them know that by failing to comply with your expectations, they could run the risk of losing your favor and miss out on some of the opportunities that you hold over their heads. This is the very definition of getting your "power" from the position you hold, or using a "stick" to motivate others. So, is this effective? To some degree, the answer is "yes." Some individuals will respond to this.

When Sticks Don't Work
In terms of motivation, sticks don't work. Why? Because the person with the stick is generally the "enemy" and one's performance is driven by the desire to avoid pain rather than trying to ascend towards something positive or affirming.

Does having a stick over your head motivate you to work at your most connected, heartfelt, team-based best? The answer is no. Avoiding the slings and arrows of punishment isn't as powerful as locking arms with a teammate and racing toward a better outcome.

The Stick Comes From Behind
Lastly, in thinking about the stick, remember it tends to come from behind. This means the leader tends to watch the progress, and if progress isn't demonstrated to their liking, the stick is either used or threatened in order to create the conditions the leader wants. When the stick is delivered from behind it is entirely transactional and reactionary. Of course, the best leaders understand that planning for higher performance is much better than waiting for the exception and threatening or delivering a punishment.

Authority
When a leader has authority, they have the ability to inspire or move those whom they work with. For example, if a new leader comes into an organization and immediately demonstrates a high degree of knowledge and understanding, individuals may begin to defer to that leader and work diligently to operate in alignment with the goals of the new leader, out of respect and understanding that this leader can be trusted.

The stack of cards below contains indications of either a leader's authority or power. Sort the cards by dragging them into the appropriate category: Authority or Power.

Power: threatens punishment for non-compliance; is wielded; is reactionary, looking backwards to check the performance; relies on supervisory privileges; belongs to formal leaders; demands compliance; prescribes actions

Authority Is Earned, Power Is Wielded
As illustrated, authority is something that is earned within an organization. It can come to both formal and informal leaders. How many times have you worked in an organization where an individual without a formal title has a huge amount of authority simply because of how much others respect that individual's thoughts and opinions?

Power, however, isn't earned. It's wielded. In other words, an individual taking advantage of their power will demand compliance, or otherwise administer some sort of negative outcome, or a punishment delivered.

Authority is always better than power. This is not to say that there won't be times as a leader where you need to use your positional authority to make a decision or to move an individual. This can happen especially when the individual is working or behaving inconsistently with team or company standards. This can result in difficult confrontations, but indeed, there are circumstances where this degree of power is needed.

Authority Is Out Front
While the stick is reactionary and is delivered when the leader notices that performance isn't up to their prescribed standard, authority is more anticipatory. Authority is provided "out front," showing the pathway forward to better outcomes and achievements.

video.transcript_text:
Put the Team Before Yourself: Carrots and Sticks, Featuring Virginia Means 
 
 
Virginia Means, Chief People Officer, United Distributors, Inc. 
 
“It’s all about perception. And if teammates find you the least bit inconsistent, moody, 
unpredictable, indecisive, or emotionally unreliable, then they balk. And the whole team is 
destabilized.” 
  
This is a stick. It’s a fine stick. It’s a strong stick. And let’s say it’s your stick. But here’s the 
reality. Somebody will always have a bigger stick. And this stick is larger, more powerful. You 
can do more, both good and bad, with this stick. 
  
Usually, the person with this stick is the team leader or the departmental manager. And with 
this stick comes great power. Let’s face it, some people love to have the bigger stick and remind 
people of that power. 
  
So, here’s a question. Which is bigger? Power or authority? Power uses the big stick to compel a 
desired behavior but can damage relationships in the process. It’s using the big stick to poke, 
prod, scare the team members into shape. It’s using the power of intimidation. Hey, look, I’ve 
got this big stick to get people to do things. It’s leading from behind, like herding them. But 
here’s the reality. You cannot lead from behind.  
 
Authority is different. Authority is achieving a desired behavior through influence. It’s leading 
from the front. It’s having the bigger stick, but not having to use it. People are compelled, even 
inspired to follow you when you have the bigger stick because you’re helpful. You’re real. 
You’re approachable. You coach. You don’t intimidate. You put the needs of the team before 
yourself. 
  
If you know anything at all about Pat Summitt, you know she had authority and she was an 
expert on how to influence her team to work hard, play together, and commit to a larger goal. 
As Pat said, “Teamwork is taught. You don’t just lump a group of people together in a room and 
call them a team and expect them to behave like one.” 
  
Like Pat, there will be times in your career when you have the biggest stick in the room, and 
you’ll have to ask yourself, “Am I going to rely on the stick or am I going to rely on me and my 
character to lead this team?” Don’t let this get in the way of you leading from the correct 
position, from the front with authentic authority.

13 of 15
Wrap-Up

It needs to be 'our' team, not 'my' team. Pat Summitt

Put the Team Before Yourself: Wrap-Up, featuring Keith Gray

We vs. Me, or Selfless vs. Selfish
The best teams are made up of dedicated individuals who recognize that there is true power in "we." One of the first steps a team must take is to overcome selfishness.

The journey toward building a great team isn't easy. Every individual has needs, and the observance of those needs is important. However, the leader must look out for the team members who are only in it for themselves and do very little for the team. A leader can deal with this issue by being up front and honest about it.

Make Teaming an Integral Part of the Organization
Teaming is a strategic approach to running an organization that requires training, observance, evaluation, and the ability to overcome mistakes. Without a doubt, organizations that get serious about teaming often run into challenges. It takes time and effort to build successful teams.

Can you imagine what it would be like if you had a large family, always eating separately and never really communicating, suddenly being pulled together into family therapy? The results would be rather bumpy. However, most thoughtful leaders make a commitment to teaming and never look back. They make a commitment to building great teams and recognize that the process is never complete, and they can always do better at helping everyone in their organization be part of an amazing group that they call a "high-functioning team."

People will perform so much better if they understand their specific role and what is expected of them. It’s like the potluck dinner. It doesn’t work if it’s disorganized and unclear. If people don’t know what they are supposed to bring, you don’t get a good dinner. Some people bring too much, others bring nothing at all. Pat Summitt

Teams Have Roles
Team success is largely driven by the ability of the team members to embrace and execute various roles. For example, there should be opportunities for each person to lead the group. To have only one team member in charge all the time doesn't give everyone the opportunity to be fully engaged. During meetings, roles can be assigned, such as note taker, facilitator, time keeper, and even "innovator."

This notion of high-functioning teams, rotating roles, and collaborative engagement has been at the heart of much of the software development in Silicon Valley. The ability of these organizations' team members to consistently work together, share leadership, push themselves to innovate, and collectively resolve conflicts and challenges is at the heart of what it means to be a great team. It's working in all sorts of organizations today, and the best leaders are at the center of it.

Teamwork Is Taught and Modeled by Leaders
Hopefully, this unit has given you a leader's perspective on the importance of teamwork. Teams must be constructed and teamwork must be taught. This cannot be taken for granted or left to chance. Holding teams accountable for what they have been taught makes all the difference. If a leader values teams, they obviously value the collective voices of those they work with. In some cases, a leader will join a team and insist that their role is that of a pacesetter or support role. They may "join the team" to serve the organization as the leader, but they are there to serve and encourage. This sends an incredibly powerful message to everyone involved that teamwork, role consideration, and learning together is the work of everyone. It's not hierarchical. It is collaborative and done together.

Teamwork is not created by like-mindedness. As in a family, you have to be generous enough to take pleasure in someone else's success, not just your own. You have to have the smarts to realize that no one succeeds alone. Pat Summitt

Put the Team Before Yourself: Wrap-Up, Featuring Keith Gray 
 
 
Keith Gray, Senior Vice President & Chief Medical Officer, University Health Systems, Inc. 
 
When a team member fully understands and embraces the concept of We versus Me, great 
things happen. Pat Summitt often used the words “Selfless versus Selfish” to describe the 
desired attitude of her players. To Coach Summitt, the team was and always needed to be the 
center of the program. In business, the corporate team must also remain the core, the center 
and the essence of the enterprise.  
 
In this module, we learned that role players are essential to greatness. Effective team play will 
always be greater than one superstar. A well-organized team places equal value on heroes and 
pacesetters in order to achieve success. 
  
Second, we saw that investing in people and being honest about expectations clarifies roles and 
encourages the practice of putting team ambitions above individual interest.  
Relationships nurture commitment and commitment allow space for sacrifice when working 
toward a common goal. 
  
Finally, teamwork is taught and modeled by leaders. Strong relationships and a commitment to 
honesty are the foundational elements of influence. It’s influence that gives the leader the 
authority to blaze new trails while leading from the front.  
 
Your team members will be more likely to take risks for the collective good if they trust you. 
Trust is the product of authentic authority. Most great teams and organizations have a standout 
talent. But even superstars need a supporting cast. A healthy team structure recognizes each 
member as vital to achieving common goals. 
  
When the team wins, everyone wins. In the words of Pat Summitt ... 
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
“Teamwork is not created by like mindedness. As in a family, you have to be generous enough 
to take pleasure in someone else’s success, not just your own. And you have to have the smarts 
to realize that no one succeeds alone. As Alex Haley once said, ‘If you see a turtle sitting on a 
fence post, you know, he didn’t get there by himself.’”

Page 3 of 15
Make Winning an Attitude

Make Winning an Attitude: Introduction, featuring Sue Nokes

Winning Must Become an Attitude
Winning doesn't always look the same, right? Think about it. Sometimes a team may win even when members haven't had the best habits or put forth the best performance. On the other hand, sometimes a team can lose even when members have performed at their very best. Thus, it isn't enough to simply pay attention to the record of "wins and losses." The same is true in business with profit statements. Although profits and corporate financial success are very important to every business, they can't be the only measures of success.

Results are what you get at the end. They are summative. Your attitude, your practice habits, and your preparation all represent formative elements that get you ready for winning and losing. The formative nature of your attitude, then, means it can set you up for success or failure. Developing a winning attitude can have a long-term impact on success.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

What do you think could happen if a team is made up of members who have superior talent, but negative attitudes? Do any examples come to mind?

That team's negativity will likely result in the team being ill-prepared for tougher times.

Collective Attitudes That Can Make or Break the Team
The attitudes of the individuals who make up teams and organizations compound to form an overall attitude within the team or organization. That collective attitude might be:

positive; thankless; grateful; apathetic; urgent; losing; winning; negative

The attitude a group consistently maintains is arguably its most important predictor of success. Think about it. People with incredibly resilient attitudes usually find ways to make good fortune great and to get through bad fortune without completely derailing their progress. Therefore, leaders must keep in mind that attitude is everything. A negative attitude can consistently lead a team or organization to underperform more easily. A positive attitude will likely do the opposite. A leader must remember that the attitude or emotional state of the team will be a key driving factor of their success.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

What does it mean to have a winning attitude? How does it manifest itself within a team or organization?

Which of the following qualities and emotional attributes do you think reflect winning attitudes? Select all that apply.

waking up each day thinking about what you need in order to win
observing hindrances as temporary and resolvable
overcoming obstacles and finding new ways of winning
maximizing the moment and using time effectively
connecting with teammates with positivity and reassurance
viewing each day as an opportunity for potential winners to take steps required to claim what they want

Exactly! All of these attitudes and behaviors reflect a winning attitude!

Winning is a comprehensive attitude that a leader must first build for themselves, and then for everyone around them.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

Suppose your significant other or a close friend shares with you that they wake up each day, look in the mirror, and ask, "What is wrong with me?" What advice might you give that person and why?

It Takes Practice to Develop a Winning Attitude
You might try to help that person understand the very real impact their negative attitude has on their daily life, right? Maybe instead of focusing on what's wrong, you would hope to help this person start focusing on how they can do things right more often to lead to winning.

This same advice is important for yourself as well. If you find yourself frequently asking "What's wrong?" or "Why am I always losing?," your brain will get really good at constantly seeking answers to these questions in your life, in business, and otherwise. This is why winning people always seem to surround themselves with amazing outcomes. A simple shift can train your brain to consistently look for solutions, better opportunities, happier outcomes, and more relaxing points of view. This simple shift in context amounts to a huge shift in mental and emotional work.

Think, Feel, Say, Act!
We have to get ourselves into the right headspace to visualize winning. In other words, we need to consistently think and feel like winners. We also need to say it — that is, declare what winning looks like and declare that we plan to achieve it. No one ever broke an Olympic weight-lifting record by going to the gym and telling themselves they are weak, they are a loser, and they cannot break the world record. It simply will not happen with that kind of internal monologue.

But it's not enough to just think, feel, and say it. It also takes consistent action. Breaking that weight-lifting record takes more than talking a good talk and watching others put in the work at the gym. It takes getting in there, working hard, and giving it everything. Even then, success is no guarantee — but the only chance of becoming a champion is to live that winning attitude. As a leader, the closer you get to living out that winning attitude daily, the more successful you will be.

Your Outlook Is the Most Predictable Element of Your Potential Success
Your outlook and attitude are extremely strong predictors of your potential success. An individual of average intelligence, skill, and support can become an industry leader if they have an overwhelmingly positive, winning attitude driving them. Their energy and ambition — expressed in their daily outlook and evident to everyone around them — will create a positive climate that's impossible to deny. If you want to change your life and make a powerful impact on your team or organization, adopt a winning attitude that will shine on everyone around you.

video.transcript_text:
Make Winning an Attitude: Introduction, Featuring Sue Nokes 
 
 
Sue Nokes, Advisory Board Vice Chairman, Asurion; Former Chief Customer & Operations 
Officer, T-Mobile 
 
You don’t win on talent alone. You need to know how to handle adversity. You need the right 
attitude. It doesn’t matter how gifted you are. At some point, you’ll get knocked down. What 
do you do then? How do you turn trials into triumph? How do you make winning an attitude?  
 
Pat was no stranger to hardship. Her 1997 team lost 10 games on the way to their fifth national 
title. That sort of success doesn’t happen by accident. Pat daily encouraged her players to 
practice a positive outlook that steered every circumstance, good or bad, towards winning. She 
was able to get the most out of her teams because she knew how to apply pressure at just the 
right times in order to keep her players accountable to their vision.  
 
Pat’s mental game came from focus and hard work. She habitually focused on helping her team 
have a winning attitude. How did she do it? Pat said ... 
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
“With a combination of practice and belief, the most ordinary team is capable of extraordinary 
things.”  
 
Sue Nokes 
 
Pat believed attitude determines performance. When you prepare for victory, you visualize it. 
You train for it. You practice it in every area of your life. You make winning an attitude. With the 
right attitude, nothing can stop you from working setbacks into successes. 
 
In this inspirational session, you’ll hear from Timothy Alexander, who was a top-ranked high 
school football player headed for a division one career until a car accident paralyzed from the 
neck down. This didn’t stop Timothy from becoming the first paraplegic in D1 history to get a 
full-ride football scholarship with the University of Alabama, Birmingham. He later went on to 
graduate with a master’s degree and now he directs UAB’s Football Character Excellence 
Program, provides life coaching, and travels the country sharing his powerful story.  
 
As Timothy digs into the fundamentals of Pat’s Definite Dozen principle “making winning an 
attitude,” you will see how Pat cultivated a championship mindset in her players. In addition, 
you will learn foundational techniques for embodying a positive outlook that always wins, no 
matter the challenge. 
  
As Pat said, “You can’t determine the weather, luck, or other people’s opinion; but when things 
don’t go as planned, there is one thing you can count on: your own outlook.” That’s when 
attitude demonstrates the difference between winning and losing.

Leadership Reflections: Get an Attitude, Not an Outcome!

Winning doesn’t always feel good — for example, if the win is due to luck or other circumstances out of our control. While you may appreciate the victory, it doesn't feel as good as winning after working hard and paying the price. In this module, Coach Pat Summitt talks about leaders and peak performers who maintain a commitment to developing a winning attitude, rather than defining "winning" as only an outcome. A "winning attitude" means we expect to win and we will ourselves to win every moment of every day. This is quite advantageous because it helps us win more often and avoid allowing any losses to define us.

What are some specific things you can do to help make winning a daily attitude in your life?

Page 6 of 15
Practice Your Belief

Make Winning an Attitude: Practice Your Belief, featuring Timothy Alexander

I Believe. Therefore, I Am.
Everything you have achieved and become in your life is because, at some point, you believed it was possible. Let that sink in. If you graduated from college, at some point in high school (or even earlier), you decided to attend college, truly believing that if you attended and worked hard, you would graduate. If you are married and have a family, you believed at some point that someone would love you, share their life with you, and join you to form a family. That all happened first in your head and heart. Then your belief system allowed you to develop the courage to take action, which you knew would be worth it, because you truly believed it all could happen.

How to Create Belief in Self
Leaders of successful teams and high-performing organizations believe in themselves, and their teams are powered by high performers who likewise believe in their talents and skills. But an individual doesn't simply develop belief after, say, hearing a motivational speaker or reading an encouraging greeting card. Belief takes more than words. Belief requires action. Whether you are a team's leader or a peak performer, you are the first person you must teach the power of belief.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

If belief starts at the individual level, how do you think one might go from dreams or fanciful ideas to a heartfelt belief that leads to success?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

It Takes Consistent Action
We've established that the road to success starts with a dream at the individual level, followed by heart-felt belief that it can happen. Now, we add a third step to make the process look something like this:

Envision the dream of what you want to accomplish.
In your heart, believe you are capable of making that dream a reality.
Take action to make it happen.

Gina, an award-winning track star, thinks she might want to compete in the Olympics.
At first just a passing thought or fanciful idea, Gina recalls a coach or two mentioning they could see her as an Olympic competitor. The idea has sparked.
After some careful reflection, study, and analysis, Gina decides that, with the right work, she could see herself achieving what has become this dream of competing in the Olympics.
She knows the dream is nothing more than wishful thinking if she doesn't put in the work to make it happen. Her next step, obviously, is action.
She may have an enormous amount of work ahead of her to physically and mentally prepare for the rigors of an Olympic tryout.
Gina plans her fitness training. She decides to create a plan to gain sponsors to help pay for coaching to prepare her for this enormous challenge.
Clearly, Gina has a dream, believes she can achieve it, and now faces decisive, consistent, and intentional action to get there.

What About Groups or Teams?
The good news is, the formula is exactly the same for groups or teams:

Dream
Believe
Act

Being part of a team has the added advantage of teammates who can potentially push us to dream bigger and to work even harder than we perhaps would do alone.

Leadership within a major tech company believes they have a team capable of creating a game-changing sales app that could revolutionize their industry.
Leaders and team members chat about the idea and reflect on how it might look to compete with the most dominant apps in their space.
They talk about it enough and analyze the possibilities to the point they confidently believe they can do it.
The idea morphs from casual conversation to a group belief that they can achieve this major accomplishment.
Team members remind each other of their commitment and hold one another accountable for striving toward it.
They agree on the tasks needed to make it happen and they take action on those tasks, pursuing their dream with passion.

The formula of establishing the belief, making the belief a real pursuit, and then taking action will always lead to progress. It may not always lead to game-changing innovation or a guaranteed win, but it will always get the ball rolling in the right direction when pursued by leaders who care about their people and are faithful to the formula.

The Presence of Adversity
Adversity is inevitable, but it's also one of the most powerful forces capable of stimulating innovation. Adversity can come in the form of an unexpected loss or the emergence of a formidable competitor that begins to gobble up market share and challenge the organization's viability. Adversity can emerge after an unforeseen setback, putting the organization in a perilous position where the choice between winning and losing is hanging in the balance. The best companies led by the most forward-thinking leaders, however, understand that it is within these moments of adversity where some of the best outcomes can emerge.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

How can you handle adversity? As a leader, what approaches can you take to ensure your team overcomes adversity with the greatest chance of exceeding previous benchmarks?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Facing and Beating the Forces of Adversity
There are three steps you could take as a leader or individual performer when facing the negative forces of adversity. Remember, resiliency is the key, and the best leaders understand that learning is a continuous value proposition.

Make it personal.
See every setback as an opportunity to learn.
Expect the extraordinary.

Make it personal
Michael Jordan is one of the most celebrated winners of all time. He exemplifies nearly every concept covered in this leadership training program, but this idea of "making it personal" is perhaps one of his best-known attributes. As he has begun sharing more of his secrets to success, Jordan said that he consistently overcame adversity by making it personal and identifying adversaries he would devote to overcoming.

The two-time NBA champion Detroit Pistons team beat Jordan and his Chicago Bulls team numerous times, knocking Jordan around physically and sending him to the court repeatedly during games. Jordan says he took those behaviors personally and, in the off-season, he trained with renewed enthusiasm, refusing to allow those difficult moments to define him. He found the inspiration in his training to finally get past the Pistons on the way to winning multiple world championships.

As a leader, you can do this too. When the competition is fierce and your organization is losing ground while your competitors get all the positive publicity, these could be the battle cries that make it personal and lead to deeper commitment.

A word of warning, however: the idea is to make it personal, not to make it toxic. Remember, Michael Jordan had to face a lot of other teams besides the Detroit Pistons. If he spent all of his time hating the Pistons, he wouldn't have been able to focus. It's a fine balance. You can make it personal while keeping a broad perspective and avoiding toxicity.

See every setback as an opportunity to learn
While some high-profile winners have famously acted poorly when they lost, this is not necessarily a sign of strength. Disappointment is very real, and whenever you work at something and don't achieve it, a passionate person will feel deep pangs of disappointment. However, leaders and top performers who consistently stay in the winners' circle will often find themselves determined to use losses or setbacks as opportunities to grow.

Rather than being angry or pouting about the loss or setback, a smart leader might use these moments to self-scout—that is, take a look at what's being done well and what's being done poorly and evaluate what can be learned from these moments of truth:

- “What can we learn from coming away with less than we'd hoped?”
- “What did we fail to do? What did we lack?”

These may sound like negative questions. Rather, they can be formative and strategic questions that will allow the team members to gather themselves and better prepare to win the next time.

Expect the extraordinary
Those who expect the extraordinary are more likely to achieve it! This is not just hyperbole. If you have average expectations, you will achieve, at best, average results. Before he turned 40, professional football player Tom Brady planned to keep playing well into his 40s, an extraordinary goal. Many highly successful CEOs over the years famously made extraordinary demands and expected stellar results. They may have stretched the imagination for what's possible, but they likely broke records, even if they never reached the original goals. Even if you don't achieve the actual extraordinary outcome you expected, you will likely still be amazed at what you can accomplish along the journey. This is what leaders today need to think about as they reflect on just how aggressive their goals might be.

Again, these three steps can help you as a leader when you face the negative forces of adversity:
Make it personal.
See every setback as an opportunity to learn.
Expect the extraordinary.

body_blocks.text: Make Winning an Attitude: Practice Your Belief, featuring Timothy Alexander
I Believe. Therefore, I Am.

Everything you have achieved and become in your life is because, at some point, you believed it was possible. Let that sink in. If you graduated from college, at some point in high school (or even earlier), you decided to attend college, truly believing that if you attended and worked hard, you would graduate. If you are married and have a family, you believed at some point that someone would love you, share their life with you, and join you to form a family. That all happened first in your head and heart. Then your belief system allowed you to develop the courage to take action, which you knew would be worth it, because you truly believed it all could happen.
How to Create Belief in Self

Leaders of successful teams and high-performing organizations believe in themselves, and their teams are powered by high performers who likewise believe in their talents and skills. But an individual doesn't simply develop belief after, say, hearing a motivational speaker or reading an encouraging greeting card. Belief takes more than words. Belief requires action. Whether you are a team's leader or a peak performer, you are the first person you must teach the power of belief.
If belief starts at the individual level, how do you think one might go from dreams or fanciful ideas to a heartfelt belief that leads to success?
It Takes Consistent Action

We've established that the road to success starts with a dream at the individual level, followed by heart-felt belief that it can happen. Now, we add a third step to make the process look something like this:

items: Envision the dream of what you want to accomplish.
In your heart, believe you are capable of making that dream a reality.
Take action to make it happen.

body_blocks.text: Gina Olympic example
items: Gina, an award-winning track star, thinks she might want to compete in the Olympics.
At first just a passing thought or fanciful idea, Gina recalls a coach or two mentioning they could see her as an Olympic competitor. The idea has sparked.
After some careful reflection, study, and analysis, Gina decides that, with the right work, she could see herself achieving what has become this dream of competing in the Olympics.
She knows the dream is nothing more than wishful thinking if she doesn't put in the work to make it happen. Her next step, obviously, is action.
She may have an enormous amount of work ahead of her to physically and mentally prepare for the rigors of an Olympic tryout.
Gina plans her fitness training. She decides to create a plan to gain sponsors to help pay for coaching to prepare her for this enormous challenge.
Clearly, Gina has a dream, believes she can achieve it, and now faces decisive, consistent, and intentional action to get there.

body_blocks.text: What About Groups or Teams?
The good news is, the formula is exactly the same for groups or teams:

items: Dream
Believe
Act

body_blocks.text: Being part of a team has the added advantage of teammates who can potentially push us to dream bigger and to work even harder than we perhaps would do alone.
Tech-company sales-app example
items: Leadership within a major tech company believes they have a team capable of creating a game-changing sales app that could revolutionize their industry.
Leaders and team members chat about the idea and reflect on how it might look to compete with the most dominant apps in their space.
They talk about it enough and analyze the possibilities to the point they confidently believe they can do it.
The idea morphs from casual conversation to a group belief that they can achieve this major accomplishment.
Team members remind each other of their commitment and hold one another accountable for striving toward it.
They agree on the tasks needed to make it happen and they take action on those tasks, pursuing their dream with passion.

body_blocks.text: The formula of establishing the belief, making the belief a real pursuit, and then taking action will always lead to progress. It may not always lead to game-changing innovation or a guaranteed win, but it will always get the ball rolling in the right direction when pursued by leaders who care about their people and are faithful to the formula.
The Presence of Adversity

Adversity is inevitable, but it's also one of the most powerful forces capable of stimulating innovation. Adversity can come in the form of an unexpected loss or the emergence of a formidable competitor that begins to gobble up market share and challenge the organization's viability. Adversity can emerge after an unforeseen setback, putting the organization in a perilous position where the choice between winning and losing is hanging in the balance. The best companies led by the most forward-thinking leaders, however, understand that it is within these moments of adversity where some of the best outcomes can emerge.
How can you handle adversity? As a leader, what approaches can you take to ensure your team overcomes adversity with the greatest chance of exceeding previous benchmarks?
Facing and Beating the Forces of Adversity

There are three steps you could take as a leader or individual performer when facing the negative forces of adversity. Remember, resiliency is the key, and the best leaders understand that learning is a continuous value proposition.
Make it personal
items:
Michael Jordan is one of the most celebrated winners of all time. He exemplifies nearly every concept covered in this leadership training program, but this idea of "making it personal" is perhaps one of his best-known attributes. As he has begun sharing more of his secrets to success, Jordan said that he consistently overcame adversity by making it personal and identifying adversaries he would devote to overcoming.

The two-time NBA champion Detroit Pistons team beat Jordan and his Chicago Bulls team numerous times, knocking Jordan around physically and sending him to the court repeatedly during games. Jordan says he took those behaviors personally and, in the off-season, he trained with renewed enthusiasm, refusing to allow those difficult moments to define him. He found the inspiration in his training to finally get past the Pistons on the way to winning multiple world championships.

As a leader, you can do this too. When the competition is fierce and your organization is losing ground while your competitors get all the positive publicity, these could be the battle cries that make it personal and lead to deeper commitment.

A word of warning, however: the idea is to make it personal, not to make it toxic. Remember, Michael Jordan had to face a lot of other teams besides the Detroit Pistons. If he spent all of his time hating the Pistons, he wouldn't have been able to focus. It's a fine balance. You can make it personal while keeping a broad perspective and avoiding toxicity.

video.transcript_text:
Make Winning an Attitude: Practice Your Belief, Featuring Timothy Alexander 
 
 
Timothy Alexander, Director of UAB Football Character Excellence Program & Life Coach 
 
As Pat said, “Belief is actually a fairly practical matter. Most people think of it as something 
mystical, or at least highly conceptual. I don’t. To me, the strongest kind of belief is grounded in 
reality. Like anything else, it’s largely a result of focus, hard work, and other verifiable things.” 
  
I’m Timothy Alexander. I was on my way to a Division I college football career until a car 
accident left me paralyzed from the neck down. The doctor told me I had a 5% chance of ever 
being able to walk, talk, or do anything on my own. I thought to myself, “If I believe what the 
doctor is saying, then my story ends right here. But if I keep on pushing, then my story begins 
right here.” 
  
When adversity comes, how do you respond? Every comeback starts with belief. You have to 
remember everything you’ve practiced up to the present and believe it’s enough to carry you 
forward. Winning is a habit that starts with your mind. Pat Summitt coached 12 seasons and 
went to the Final Four seven times before winning her first national title in 1987. Pat’s mental 
focus helped her hold the course and find success.  
 
Here are three ways to practice believing in yourself when you encounter adversity. 
  
Number one, make it personal. When life hands you a loss, don’t let it be the end of your story. 
Make it the beginning. Begin with saying, “Yes, I can.” And then live that belief out day by day. 
  
Number two, see every setback as an opportunity to learn. With this perspective, the weakest 
moments of your life are positioned to become the strongest parts of your testimony. You have 
to take everything you’ve learned and apply it in adversity. Belief is not just for the sunshine. 
It’s for the rain. When you make failure your teacher, you learn to never give up, even through 
the storms. 
  
Number three, let your attitude drive what you do. What you believe about yourself in any 
situation will inform how you apply yourself to that situation. So, believe you can win. Then, 
form your work ethic around that core belief.  
 
Don’t give up when something goes wrong. Don’t just sit back when the excitement fades. 
Continue moving forward. If you think you can, you will. If you think you can’t, you won’t.  
 
Are you ready to practice your positivity? Start with believing in yourself today. Win with your 
mind and train yourself to expect the extraordinary.

Attitude & Positivity

Make Winning an Attitude: Embody Your Positivity, featuring Timothy Alexander

Attitude Can Determine Performance

Don’t ever settle for being on "autopilot." Even if you are executing a task you have done several times, the attitude you bring to any moment of the day can influence your performance. For example, if you are exercising and lifting a weight you are accustomed to lifting, your experience can vary dramatically depending on your attitude. If you are optimistic, excited, and somewhat fired up, you might push that weight and make it feel light. If you are exhausted or distracted, the weight might feel heavy.

The same is true with nearly everything in your work. If a customer service agent comes to work after struggling with a child or a difficult marriage counseling session, these events will impact that employee's attitude. To this point, the most successful leaders understand that setting the emotional tenor of an organization can make a huge difference in the attitude team members bring to their work. Strong leaders work hard to build a specific cultural tone within their organizations to help create a winning "attitude" or environment through the system.

For example, creative companies that specialize in art and design often create beautiful, interesting, and stimulating workspaces to help inspire creativity among team members. As a leader, you must identify and employ mechanisms for creating an outstanding attitude for yourself and your team. Investing in culture makes all the difference.

When Positive People Enter a Room, Everything Changes

Numerous studies show that our body temperature, heart rate, and emotions can change when different people enter a room. Happy and engaging people, unsurprisingly, bring happy and engaging vibrations. Angry and toxic people bring negative feelings. Perplexingly, there's almost nothing you can do to avoid at least feeling the vibrations of these people when you're near them. No matter how positive you may be, your psychology will be affected if you are consistently shoulder-to-shoulder with negativity. It can take a lot of energy to fight that off, and it's something to consider when reflecting on those with whom you regularly surround yourself.

As a leader, think about the energy that you bring to every team meeting. Whether it's a video meeting or face-to-face, evaluate your energy by asking yourself things like:

Do I tend to give or take more energy?
Do my colleagues and team members feel inspired and excited to engage with me? Or are they fearful they may get scolded?
Do my team members feel the need to pursue growth? Or do they feel they need to avoid me because I might call them out on things they aren't prepared to discuss yet?

The way you make people feel when you enter the room is really important, and you need to think about the vibrations you hope to put out. Input from trusted colleagues and 360 evaluations (discussed earlier in the course) can give valuable insights into this.

It's really helpful to try to unpack exactly what people think when they see you or the energy you give off. You may imagine yourself as a powerful, positive energy-giver. Is that what others are feeling? It may or may not be, so consider asking to see if people's perceptions align with your intentions. Similarly, hire the right people who are giving out the right kind of energy to positively impact your organization.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

Think about your team right now. What kind of energy is present and what kind of energy is needed? What might you do to help maintain or improve that energy? What might you look for in any future hires in terms of energy?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

If your team is collectively quiet and withdrawn, perhaps your next hire could be someone with contagious energy. If you have a very energetic group that is extremely talkative, maybe your next hire could be someone quiet and reflective to help establish a nice balance and help the entire team achieve even more.

There are no right or wrong answers. Finding the right energy balance is part of the art of effective leadership. It's all about discovering yourself and figuring out what kind of energy is needed to make the most out of the people you work with daily.

Attitude is a choice. What do you think of that statement? What comes to mind?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Attitude Is a Choice, Followed by Action

It may seem cliché, but attitude is a choice. If you're not feeling optimistic and your friend says, "You can feel better if you just decide to," you may not necessarily feel that advice is very helpful. The simple truth is, however, attitude does revolve around the concept of feelings or emotion. If your attitude is positive and affirming, it's because you feel that way. If you're feeling grateful and happy, chances are you will carry that into all you do. Yes, attitude is a choice, but it requires at least some action.

As part of the drug rehabilitation process, a counselor might ask a struggling addict to foster dogs and cats. At face value, it may seem odd to ask someone who is already overwhelmed with repercussions of their addiction to take on responsibilities of caring for animals. However, when the addict takes the actions of consistently caring for something other than themself, it also establishes that same condition or attitude of consistency and caring for themselves. Consistently being there and caring for the animals requires a change in attitude, which can then translate to a change in attitude and behavior for themselves as well.

The message here is simple. Actions matter. If someone with an ungrateful attitude is placed in a position to give things up for people who are less fortunate, it can completely change their perspective and open up their hearts and minds in appreciation of what they have.

As a leader, think about the kind of attitude you want your team to consistently demonstrate.

What attitude do you expect throughout your organization? Do you see it portrayed consistently? If not, what actions might you take to create a condition where that attitude might emerge?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

video.transcript_text:
Make Winning an Attitude: Embody Your Positivity, Featuring Timothy 
Alexander 
 
 
Timothy Alexander, Director of UAB Football Character Excellence Program & Life Coach 
 
As Pat said, “With attitude, you can determine your own performance. But more than that, you 
can help determine the performance of others. A single individual with a strong, positive 
attitude can lift those around her. She can change the course of events. Sometimes a positive 
person can walk into a room and immediately the air feels different. It’s as though her presence 
literally converts ions from negative to positive.” 
  
When you encounter doubt in yourself or negativity from others, that’s when choosing to have 
a positive attitude sustains your performance.  
 
Here are three ways to embody your positivity when life throws you a curveball.  
 
Number one: resist negativity with resiliency. Resiliency is the capacity to respond to adversity 
quickly. Don’t avoid your problems by playing hide and seek with them. Problems are 
challenges that give you the opportunity to renew your mind and be transformed. Embrace 
your problems and make the most of them.  
 
Number two: do your doubt. The only way to handle doubt in a positive way is to simply do 
what your doubt is keeping you from doing. With so much going on in the world, information 
overload is just a click away and it can be easy to feel overwhelmed. Lean into your doubts 
because you’ll never know what’s possible until you try. If you quit, you’ll never win.  
 
Number three: be accountable in a positive way. A winning attitude has to face reality and take 
responsibility. Good leaders make space for acknowledging challenges. Once you see the 
challenge, ask yourself, “What do I do with this challenge?” Ask, “What needs to change?” 
Then, go be that change and embody your positivity for others.  
 
When someone under your leadership is struggling, remind them why they started this journey 
in the first place. Sometimes, it means being direct about why you’re applying pressure: 
because you know they can do better and them doing better is beneficial for both of you. 
  
As Pat said, “Attitude is a choice. What you think you can do, whether positive or negative, 
confident or scared, will most likely happen. When you doubt, you create a negative. It will 
affect your performance and probably drag others down, too.”  
 
Are you willing to be the difference for your team? Choose to operate in gratitude every day. Be 
thankful for your challenges. When you make winning an attitude, adversity helps you find out 
who you’re truly meant to be.
