Page 11 of 15
Visualize Your Victory

Make Winning an Attitude: Visualize Your Victory, featuring Timothy Alexander

Do You See What I See?
Probably not — at least not at first. Elon Musk had a vision for a company and a myriad of innovations he wanted to bring to fruition. He imagined things that did not yet exist, but he believed they were possible long before Tesla and all its innovations emerged. Before any investor would give him a dollar, he believed it was possible. He had visions of what he hoped to create and went about the work of putting it together. Strong leaders have a unique ability to see what's possible before anyone else and then spend their days bringing that vision to fruition.

The Specificity of the Dream
Most people allow themselves to dream on some level. The difference between casual dreamers and dreamers like Elon Musk is the specificity of the dream, the belief in its possibility, and the relentless pursuit of the end goals.

When certified financial planners sit down and talk to people about their future and ask them what they are saving for, a common answer is, “I want to be rich.” Unfortunately, richness isn't very specific. When a dream or vision isn't very specific, it's hard to get real about its pursuit. If a leader in an organization says, "I want my team or my group to be successful," can that leader define what success actually means? Do they know what specific outputs would represent an amazing effort in the business? If you want to be a leader who helps move an organization to a new level of success, you must be very clear about what "success" actually means.

Believing in the Possibility
At some point, every astronaut who ever went into space or walked on the moon had to decide they were going to become an astronaut. Many would find that to be fantastical. Others might have the same dream. However, the select few who actually make it happen adopt a belief system within themselves that moves them into action. They go from a casual imagination of what something might be like to believing that, with effort, energy, and dedication, this dream could become reality. It takes a bit of boldness, creativity, and a whole lot of heart.

The Relentless Pursuit
From the perspective of having a winning attitude, we can break down success into a formula. Which of these components do you think are key factors in that formula? Select all that apply.

having the dream
believing the possibility
taking intentional action to make it happen

That is correct! It takes all three of these and many people never seem to get there. That third step — taking action — is much more than just a checklist of To Do items or a fleeting resolution. It involves early mornings and late nights, tirelessly pursuing the lofty goal.

Successful leaders demonstrate a localized relentlessness that can't be denied. They go after their dreams and goals with unrelenting energy and aspiration, and they achieve their desired outcomes. If you want to be a successful leader, dream that dream, and then commit to its relentless pursuit, doing whatever it takes to make it happen.

Simulations Help
A winning attitude can be a rather cerebral experience. This can be reinforced through simulations. When a leader simulates "winning," they become increasingly acquainted with what it will take to compete. The most successful stock traders who have made their investors millions likely took time beforehand to simulate stock trades on software designed for that purpose. The game of Monopoly simulates what it takes to earn a salary and make a living with residential or commercial real estate. With every simulation, our brains get to experience the feeling of actually competing to be in the winner’s circle.

Simulations not only help prepare for the real thing, but they provide insights into the kinds of activities that will be required to win. In a stock trading simulation, the junior trader may discover some technical deficits that could be remedied with study. Ultimately, putting yourself in a position where you practice what you hope to win will lead to greater degrees of confidence, experience, and preparation. How many simulations do you suppose those astronauts experienced before they actually went into space?

What are some ways you might simulate winning as a leader? How might you help your team simulate winning?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

A Winning Attitude Has No Finish Line
By adopting, maintaining, and consistently nurturing and improving upon a winning attitude, a leader will come to realize that a winning attitude has no finish line. It doesn't allow for complacency or a sense that the winner has "arrived." Interestingly, some of the most competitive athletes in history have not only dominated their chosen field, but stayed in the winning circle for a really long time.

Think about a competitor like Tom Brady. As an athlete, he reached an unprecedented level of success in every individual and team category in professional sports. He simply reached a point where there were no other peers. Why not just quit after reaching that benchmark? Why keep striving for more? The answer is pretty simple:

A daily winning attitude is the reason champions become champions, and it has no finish line.

In order to stay in the winner's circle, even winners who don't have any competitors in their space look for ways of making it better. Immediately after one of his team's national championship wins, college football coach Nick Saban was spotted pulling a notepad out of his pocket and writing himself a note. His team had just won the championship. Players were jumping into the air and celebrating all around him. When a reporter asked what he wrote, he said it was a note about a recruit he hoped to sign, and he didn't want to forget about it. Here he was, in the moments of celebrating a national championship, working on the steps he needed to take to get back to the championship game again. While he most certainly had a great celebration, in that moment, his drive towards the next championship had no finish line, even with the championship in his hand.

video.transcript_text:
Make Winning an Attitude: Visualize Your Victory, Featuring Timothy Alexander 
 
 
Timothy Alexander, Director of UAB Football Character Excellence Program & Life Coach 
 
As Pat said, “We simulate and prepare. We expect to win because we rehearse it. I believe you 
get what you deserve.” When you’re already working hard and making progress towards your 
goal, it can be tempting to get caught up in wins along the way. Don’t let someone pass you 
because you were celebrating on the way to the finish line. 
  
A winning attitude maintains focus on victory and prepares for it. As Pat said, “There are some 
concrete ways to create a winning attitude. But nothing beats practicing it. When you prepare 
to win, belief comes easily.” 
  
A winning attitude visualizes and practices every path to victory. This works in multiple 
professional settings. In sales, for example, if you have a big presentation, it’s better if you 
rehearse your talking points and delivery repeatedly until everything feels natural. By the time 
the meeting arrives, you are prepared to handle multiple outcomes. You are ready to execute 
the presentation with poise and confidence because you’ve already visualized your victory. 
  
Coach Summitt regularly forced her players to make game-time decisions in practice. She put a 
time and a score on the clock and simulated end-of-game pressure by giving her players the ball 
and asking them to make the calls. No matter the opponent, her players believe they could 
outplay any competition in high-pressure situations because they’d done it all year in practice. 
They were prepared for victory.  
 
To claim victory, you have to see it before anyone else sees it. You have to be present to your 
vision, so immersed in your dream, that you recognize opportunities right away. A winning 
attitude doesn’t wait to be in the right place at the right time. A winning attitude looks ahead to 
victory and gets there first. When you focus on your dreams, you have clear, established goals.  
 
Not only do you see what needs to happen in everyday life to meet your goals, you visualize 
what victory looks like beyond your goals. A winning attitude has no finish line. Every 
experience is an opportunity to get better and go farther. A winning attitude always leads to 
more opportunity. If you’re not dedicated to your dream, then you’re just a dreamer.  
 
Choose to be a winner by pursuing your dream every single day, in every area of your life. 
Visualize your success and make victory an instinct.

Wrap-Up

Make Winning an Attitude: Wrap-Up, featuring Sue Nokes

Expecting Loss
Individual and team losses are a natural part of any organization. The best leaders understand that even in championship seasons, losses will come in one form or another. How we respond to losses will have a significant impact on our overall success.

A team can have an undefeated season, yet individuals on the team can find themselves experiencing loss. They can lose a starting position, get injured, or lose focus and be unable to perform as well even in the face of continued winning within the program.

Benchmarking Losses
Obviously, it's easier to quantify success or failure in sports than in business, where benchmarking "wins or losses" isn't as straightforward. Consider these examples:

A company posts robust profits one quarter. Further examination reveals this "win" was due to selling off income-generating assets that could cost profitability in coming quarters.
A company has a less-productive quarter due to internal investments in preparation for gigantic steps forward.
A company launches a new product or service after months of market research, but the new offering doesn't resonate with customers.

Clearly, in business, wins and losses don't always tell the whole story. When it comes to losses, the key is to make sure teams or businesses take time to reflect on them. Losing is hard enough on its own — but then also missing out on the opportunity to grow is almost like losing twice.

What Is Your Story?
Stories are very powerful. Consider an example:

A team wins the national championship.
The very next season, the same team struggles just to get a regular season win.
A newspaper runs the story: "The championship must have been a fluke. The team had one really strong player and once that player graduated from the program, the magic was gone."
Another source says the team has lost its hunger and no longer has it in them to compete on this level.

Stories are also psychological. Everyone you know is living the story of their life. One individual's story might be that they are going to leave their home country, start a new business in a new land, and be wildly successful. Another person's story might be that they and their children are doomed to repeat the fate of their alcoholic parents. Some are living stories that suggest their best days are behind them. For others, their best days are still ahead.

Our stories are powerful because they set our expectations and put us on a pathway that's hard to deny. Remember, a story isn't a dream. A story is something that you live. While a dream might have gotten you to start living your story, a "story" is more linear.

Each of us lives the story we have established for ourselves. If you're looking to change your fortune as a leader, thinking deeply and honestly about the story you have told yourself about your life is perhaps one of the most powerful things you can do. If you've told yourself you lead a division within a company that won't let you be as effective as possible, you will likely continue with that exact path. Or, if you told yourself a very different story, you're likely to pursue that as well. The first step is acknowledging that your story has authentic elements that can drive your ultimate success. And if you want to change your life... change your story.

Are You Living Your Comeback Story?
Everyone loves the story of a comeback, rising from defeat or from the ashes of obscurity and achieving victory. The Rocky film franchise is based on the story of an athlete who rises up in the face of unlikely odds. Rocky lives a story on his own terms and doesn't allow the story others would write for him to manifest. He takes action and generates a different future for himself. As a leader, recognize that your business and every team member is living out their story. Their stories, at least partly crafted by your strong leadership, have a huge impact on how the story ends.

What story are you living? What about your story are you happy about? What would you like to change?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Convincing Others That They Are Writing This Story, Not Somebody Else
To help a team lead its comeback story, a strong leader must first convince team members that they are in charge of their own stories. This is harder than it sounds. In many cases, individuals tell themselves a story that someone else is in charge of the story of their lives — perhaps they would be more successful if somebody wasn't writing their story for them.

Once a leader convinces their followers that they are in charge of their story, and that by rewriting the story of their lives, they can have virtually any destiny, their results can be amazing. Small victories and achievable elements of their story will begin to convince them that, indeed, they are in charge. When you can empower them with this truth, as a leader, you will be giving them the "keys to the kingdom" to control their own destinies.

A newspaper runs the story: "The championship must have been a fluke. The team had one really strong player and once that player graduated from the program, the magic was gone."
Another source says the team has lost its hunger and no longer has it in them to compete on this level.

body_blocks.text: stock-image.jpg

Stories are also psychological. Everyone you know is living the story of their life. One individual's story might be that they are going to leave their home country, start a new business in a new land, and be wildly successful. Another person's story might be that they and their children are doomed to repeat the fate of their alcoholic parents. Some are living stories that suggest their best days are behind them. For others, their best days are still ahead.

Our stories are powerful because they set our expectations and put us on a pathway that's hard to deny. Remember, a story isn't a dream. A story is something that you live. While a dream might have gotten you to start living your story, a "story" is more linear.

Each of us lives the story we have established for ourselves. If you're looking to change your fortune as a leader, thinking deeply and honestly about the story you have told yourself about your life is perhaps one of the most powerful things you can do. If you've told yourself you lead a division within a company that won't let you be as effective as possible, you will likely continue with that exact path. Or, if you told yourself a very different story, you're likely to pursue that as well. The first step is acknowledging that your story has authentic elements that can drive your ultimate success. And if you want to change your life... change your story.
Are You Living Your Comeback Story?

Everyone loves the story of a comeback, rising from defeat or from the ashes of obscurity and achieving victory. The Rocky film franchise is based on the story of an athlete who rises up in the face of unlikely odds. Rocky lives a story on his own terms and doesn't allow the story others would write for him to manifest. He takes action and generates a different future for himself. As a leader, recognize that your business and every team member is living out their story. Their stories, at least partly crafted by your strong leadership, have a huge impact on how the story ends.
stock-image.jpg
What story are you living? What about your story are you happy about? What would you like to change?
Convincing Others That They Are Writing This Story, Not Somebody Else

To help a team lead its comeback story, a strong leader must first convince team members that they are in charge of their own stories. This is harder than it sounds. In many cases, individuals tell themselves a story that someone else is in charge of the story of their lives — perhaps they would be more successful if somebody wasn't writing their story for them.

Once a leader convinces their followers that they are in charge of their story, and that by rewriting the story of their lives, they can have virtually any destiny, their results can be amazing. Small victories and achievable elements of their story will begin to convince them that, indeed, they are in charge. When you can empower them with this truth, as a leader, you will be giving them the "keys to the kingdom" to control their own destinies.

video.transcript_text:
Make Winning an Attitude: Wrap-Up, Featuring Sue Nokes 
 
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
I’ve said that success in my business is about putting the right people in the right place at the 
right time. But all too often, it doesn’t work out that way. Times like that, you’d better have a 
winning attitude. Many times, you have to hand off an important job to someone who isn’t 
necessarily your first choice. Maybe the person you wanted to take the shot is on the bench in 
foul trouble or is denied the ball. In any business, you’re going to have people in roles where 
they’re not always 100 percent comfortable. 
  
Sue Nokes, Advisory Board Vice Chairman, Asurion; Former Chief Customer & Operations 
Officer, T-Mobile 
 
Pat said, “It is extremely important to make sure that your leaders have that crucial blend of 
emotion and logic because their attitude will infuse your entire organization.” You have the 
ability to create a winning culture by the very power of your own positive outlook. As others 
follow your example, they will be emboldened to meet hardship with preparation and focus. 
  
In this module, we learned that winning starts in the mind by combining practice and belief, 
even in adversity. The extraordinary is always within your reach when you believe in yourself 
enough to position every loss as a beginning of your comeback story. You must see every 
setback as an opportunity to learn and let your attitude drive what you do. A winning mindset 
says, “Yes, I can” and claims victory day by day. 
  
Second, a winning attitude embodies positivity when it responds to pressure with action. The 
best way to handle negativity is continually do your doubts and hold yourself and others 
accountable to shared goals. When you do this, you sustain growth through the grind. 
  
Finally, we learned the importance of visualizing your victory. When you are present to your 
vision, you are 100 percent truthful with yourself and never cut corners in your preparation. 
You follow through. A positive outlook anticipates the outcome and trains every habit, routine, 
and thought to go beyond the finish line towards continued success.  
 
Pat said, “With the right attitude and mindset, huge obstacles are suddenly surmountable. 
When you make winning your attitude, you are unstoppable.”

Leadership Reflections: What Do You Do with Your Losses?

Losses happen. You can lose out on an opportunity to sell a client your product. You can pursue a new job promotion and fail to achieve your objective. In this module, we learned that high-achieving leaders treat losses differently. They see them as setbacks that opened the door for new levels of growth. Put another way, they see a loss as only temporary and the pathway towards victory is just ahead.

Most of us don't handle losses perfectly in our personal and/or professional lives. For this reflection, think back on a time when you were unsuccessful. How did you process that loss and what could you have done differently based on what you know now? How might this impact future losses that might come your way?

Pat in Her Own Words

Trust me, you have more within you than you realize. Competition is one of the great tools for exploring yourself and surprising yourself.
Pat Summitt

Be a Competitor: Pat in Her Own Words

Are You Ready to Compete? Do You Believe Your Own Answer?
In the video, Coach Summitt talked about a rather famous moment with a team of her All-American players where she challenged them to communicate their readiness to compete.

There is a great exercise that you can do, too, to achieve more, develop a stronger mindset, stay focused on your goals, believe in your abilities, and improve mental readiness and determination to compete as a leader or as an individual performer.

Competitiveness Affirmation Mirror Technique

Set the Competition Goal
Express your competition goal as an affirmative, declarative statement. For example, "I will lead my state in life insurance policy sales next year."
Say Your Goal Out Loud in Front of the Mirror
Stand in front of a mirror and make the statement out loud as if you were greeting yourself and sharing the news.
Repeat the Affirmation Until You Firmly Believe It
As you state your goal you want to achieve, look into your own eyes and see the expression on your face. Do you believe your own answer? Do you believe that the person in the mirror is capable of what you are saying you're going to achieve? Continue to double down on the certainty of that statement. Apply this technique to many things you are trying to achieve.

What emotions, thoughts, or discoveries did you experience while doing this exercise? Did you feel more powerful, more assertive and energized?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Be a Competitor: Introduction

You can't always be the most talented person in the room. But you can be the most competitive.
Pat Summitt

Be a Competitor: Introduction, featuring Roberto Fernandez

Competition Is Coming
Competition is one of the key elements in outstanding work. No one stays on top forever, and opportunities are always up for grabs. Your competitor is always either rising or will be rising soon. It comes down to how much you are willing to embrace competition to reach the most exalted level of performance.

While sports may only crown one winner a year, in business and other elements of our lives, we often have more than one winner. A burning sense of "competition" encourages organizations to create outstanding products and services. The message here is clear. Striving to be the best is important. And the best way to ignite that pursuit is to ignite the sense of competition.

How Competitive Are You and Your Team?
This is where leadership truly matters. When a coach inspires a team at halftime, challenging them to ignite their energies and actions, they are pressing the buttons of competition. When a longstanding champion sees a rival rising up and feels threatened, that sense of competition comes alive. The question is, how competitive are you as a leader? Do you feel that same sense of competitive juice when you observe a competitor gaining on you? Do you feel yourself wanting to overtake the champion? These are honest questions that you must reflect upon.

Part of what can help you learn to compete more often and with enthusiasm is to recognize that competition is an important part of what it means to lead. If you read these words and feel like you "don't like to compete," you may want to ask yourself, how bad do you want to win?

Wanting to win, and wanting to beat the competition, is at the heart of what it takes to improve your performance. If you want to nurture your sense of competition, the best thing to do is to treat it like a muscle and use it. This is why so many coaches are so good at creating competitions in practice. They want to ignite that spirit and get their team members to think consistently about the presence of competition in their practices, and then in games.

In your team or organization, how can the leader ignite a sense of competitiveness?
Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

You have to love your adversaries. They make you better. They force you to improve, to stretch your capacities.
Pat Summitt

Harnessing the Power of Competitiveness
Don't Seek Out Weak Competition. Compete Against the Best
Coach Pat Summitt said, "If you want to be the best, you have to compete against the best, even if it means risking a loss. Why seek out weak competition?" Rigorous competition makes competitors stronger and brings the winners more valuable rewards. Hoping for the competitors' failure or weakness is a sign of weakness. Rather than praying for weakness within a competitor, develop your own strength and skill that is capable of beating even the most formidable competition.
Identify the Rival
The rival, or the competition, is absolutely key in this formula. Can you identify a rival in your business? We all have rivals in our lives. Maybe you are in line for a promotion at work. Is there a rival for that position? Maybe you and your team are trying to break a sales record, and the rival company just opened a new office in your area. Recognizing the presence of a rival — small or large — is key to igniting that sense of competition.
Keep Your Rival in Sight to Motivate You
One of the most motivating things you can do to help maintain your discipline and focus is to picture your rival and imagine that they are one step ahead of you. When businesses are run poorly or teams are poorly led, there is a habit of forgetting about the rival. For example, if you own a restaurant and your staff members are embroiled in a number of internal battles, those problems could negatively impact the service to your diners. In this context, instead of focusing on your business and staying ahead of your rival, you might forget about your rival, allowing it to go after your most important asset...your diners. If you're a competitive person, what are you going to do? Keep your rival in sight.
Appreciate Your Rival
Our rivals make us better. The most competitive leaders and peak performers have come to realize that appreciating your rival is one of the healthiest, most forward-thinking, competitive things you can do. Rather than being driven crazy by the achievements of your rival, appreciate their grace and strength, admire what they are doing to stay competitive, and then recognize that they are there in your life to, indeed, make you better. The presence of your rival will force you to raise your standard and improve your game.

Let's Summarize
Don't seek out weak competition. Compete against the best.
Identify the rival.
Keep your rival in sight to motivate you.
Appreciate your rival.

In this context, instead of focusing on your business and staying ahead of your rival, you might forget about your rival, allowing it to go after your most important asset...your diners. If you're a competitive person, what are you going to do? Keep your rival in sight.

Appreciate Your Rival: Our rivals make us better. The most competitive leaders and peak performers have come to realize that appreciating your rival is one of the healthiest, most forward-thinking, competitive things you can do. Rather than being driven crazy by the achievements of your rival, appreciate their grace and strength, admire what they are doing to stay competitive, and then recognize that they are there in your life to, indeed, make you better. The presence of your rival will force you to raise your standard and improve your game.
Don't seek out weak competition. Compete against the best.; Identify the rival.; Keep your rival in sight to motivate you.; Appreciate your rival.

Be a Competitor: Introduction, Featuring Roberto Fernandez 
 
 
Roberto Fernandez, Medical Director, The Pat Summitt Clinic at The University of Tennessee 
Medical Center 
 
“How badly do you want to succeed? Bad enough to push through any obstacle, to push 
beyond the perception of your limits?” Pat (Summitt) shared these thoughts on being a 
competitor. “What are competitive instincts good for? Why were we given them? I believe that 
they are meant to help us battle adversity, to help us endure difficult situations, to help us get 
up when we’ve been knocked down, and to help us prevail over the blows that life deals us. 
Really. When I teach basketball, I am trying to teach our players about life.”  
 
Pat Summitt was a competitor in the truest sense of the word, from growing up playing Halo 
basketball with her three older brothers to fighting for and earning respect as a champion 
collegiate coach, all while stretching the public perception of what women can do in sports; Pat 
never backed down from a challenge. She rose to every occasion and redefined her limits by 
expanding her expectations for herself and for others. Pat Summitt understood the power that 
competition had to bring out one’s best. 
  
In this module, you will hear from Phillip Fulmer. You will hear from this NCAA championship 
football coach that being a competitor is not just about ability, but about aspiration. It’s about 
the heart and the impenetrable grit that grounds you in the face of extreme challenges. You will 
learn how to use the power of a competitive spirit as leverage for success in your own battles. 
  
Pat Summitt said that “competitiveness is what separates achievers from the average. Only by 
learning to compete can you discover just how much you are capable of achieving.” So once 
again, the question is, “How badly do you want to succeed?” Don’t settle for anything less than 
your best. Journey with us and discover how to unlock the full expanse of your own potential.

6 of 15
Set High Goals

You have to set high goals in order to achieve. That's why we routinely require overachievement at Tennessee. We don't always get it. But my experience is that when you ask for a lot, you just might get some of it.
Pat Summitt

Be a Competitor: Set High Goals, featuring Phillip Fulmer

At Tennessee, we expect to go to the Final Four. ... The reason we get there so often is because we demand it, and we say it out loud.
Pat Summitt

Winners and high achievers often publicly declare their goal and commitment to win. It helps them to _____. Select all that applies.
increase their drive to succeed
discover their full potential
persevere in reaching the goal
build a stronger version of themselves
In fact, all of these factors contribute to the peak performer's success, through an enhanced commitment to reaching a winning goal.

Don't Be Afraid to Say You Want to Win
When you declare that you want to win, you put yourself in a position of either winning or publicly failing to do so. It is, however, that public declaration that often drives peak athletic performers to practice and compete at a higher level. The same is true in business. Some of the best business leaders are famous for making extraordinarily intense promises that require a significant commitment in order to achieve. This public declaration drives unusual levels of success through an enhanced commitment to rising up and meeting the publicly declared standard.

The reason so many people underachieve, instead of overachieve, is simply because they are afraid to make a mistake, or to fail, or to be wrong. They are afraid to find out what's inside of them. Competitiveness is the opposite of complacency. It's disquieting and uncomfortable. It requires commitment, and risk, and soul-searching. When you choose to compete, you take a huge gamble.
Pat Summitt

You Find Out What's Inside
Another reason that public declaration of a goal is so terrifying is that it reveals an opportunity to expose what's inside. In other words, if on the inside beats "the heart of a champion," capable of rising up and delivering, even if winning eludes the competitor, we find out that the potential to win is there. Or you may find out on the inside that the person can't compete at all. After all, failure happens every day, and true competition will reveal it. Peak performers and the very best leaders are always on a relentless search for what's inside. They have an optimistic view of who they are and what they can become under the weight of competition. They believe that the best version of themselves will emerge under the scrutiny of the opportunity to compete and win.

Timidity or Tenacity?
In the roar of the fight, there will always be those who retreat for the quiet shade. They will let somebody else fight the fight and claim the ring. The best leaders understand that they must commit to remaining enormously tenacious in the face of competition to advance their skills.

Unfortunately, you can't always tell immediately whether a person is going to step up in the face of competition. How would you find out a new employee's capability to be tenacious under the weight of competition?

video.transcript_text:
Be a Competitor: Set High Goals, eaturing Phillip Fulmer 
 
 
Coach Phillip Fulmer 
 
My good friend, Pat Summitt, had a favorite quote ...  
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
“Competitiveness is not the most sociable quality you can possess, but competitiveness is what 
separates achievers from the average. Only by learning to compete can you discover just how 
much you are capable of achieving. Too many people elect to be average out of timidity. As I 
look around, I see scores of underachievers. The world is full of them.”  
 
Coach Phillip Fulmer 
 
A competitive spirit won’t always win friends, but it will earn respect. People limit themselves 
when they choose being timid over tenacity. While it’s natural to hold a desire for acceptance, 
if you let that desire dictate everything you do, you may find yourself compromising your own 
ambitions for approval. The ultimate goal of competition is not popularity, it’s winning. 
  
When you apply yourself fully toward the accomplishment of your goals, you orient yourself 
toward success no matter what the cost. Success generates credibility, and if people see results, 
they will be more likely to respect and trust you in your leadership. Pat Summitt was as tough 
as they came, and she expected the same toughness from her players. Her 1987 team drove her 
crazy with how polite they were to each other on the court. Pat needed them to stop playing 
nice. The 1987 team got the message. Their toughness earned the Lady Vols their first NCAA 
championship. 
  
Winners aim high and true. Competitors never settle. They don’t wait for success to just 
manifest. They push themselves to go after their goals. The way Pat thought about it was, 
“People rise to the level of their own expectations and of the competition they seek out.” You 
put your toughness to the test when you continually set new goals that push your limits and 
raise the bar of expectation. 
  
Pat was intense with the physical demands she required from her players because she believed 
it was crucial for them to learn how to dig deeper.  
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
“People are afraid to make a mistake or to fail or to be wrong. They’re afraid to find out what’s 
inside of them. Competitiveness is the opposite of complacency. It’s uncomfortable. It requires 
commitment and risk and soul-searching. When you choose to compete, you take a huge 
gamble. You might just lose. You might just have to admit, ‘That’s the best I can do.’” 
  
Coach Phillip Fulmer 
 
Oftentimes, what you perceive to be a limit of your own grit and endurance is really just a self-
imposed ceiling. When you push yourself to exceed your perceived limits, you develop mental 
fortitude and inner strength. Both are fundamental to being a competitor.

8 of 15
Influence Your Opponent

There are bound to be days when you run into someone who is better than you. What can you do about it? You can compete, that's what. You can put forth so much effort that you cut your opponent down to size and force him to play below his own abilities. Competitiveness allows you to influence your opponent.
Pat Summitt

Be a Competitor: Influence Your Opponent, featuring Phillip Fulmer

How Do You Influence Your Opponent?
You influence your opponent by studying them, and then playing to your strengths and against their weaknesses. As a player, Pat Summitt fought for a seat in the Olympic squad against a superior player. She won the contest by forcing her opponent — a strong offensive player — to play a defensive game. In the world of business, a new competitor can apply similar tactics of influencing their opponents.

Getting More Competitive by Competing More Often
Once again, the key to getting better in this space is to compete more often. None of us are born in a perfect, competitive condition until we learn how to compete and get used to it. This is why participating in sports at a young age plays such an important role in the lives of youth. They learn what it's like to face competition at an early age and what to do in those high-pressure situations. The opportunity to grow never ends, and the best leaders understand that the best way to get their team to be more competitive is to compete, adjust, reflect, and compete again.

Two Strategies for a Call to Compete
To be competitive, leaders and peak performers must get good at answering a call to compete. Here are two strategies to consider.
Posting the Bulletin-Board Material
One strategy is the presence of "bulletin-board" material. You don't have to wait for a competitor to say something negative about you or your work to create that material. If you are a software designer trying to compete with another designer, and you post articles in your workspace reminding you of their latest innovation, it may motivate you to rise up, compete, and win. Seeing an accolade your competitor won within view of your workspace may inspire you to keep working when fatigue sets in.
Identifying a Rival
In some cases, a rival may not be as easy to identify. For example, if you work in a large corporation doing quality control, you may not have the day-to-day "wins and losses vs. the competitor" that other departments may experience. On this note, leaders may need to get creative and find existing metrics that would allow for competition. In some cases, companies are big enough for internal departments to compete with each other for some level of excellence. Who is your rival? Identify it and keep it in front of you.

What Does Competition Do to Us?
There is an old adage that competition doesn't build character, it reveals it. It's likely that competition does both. By consistently competing, you learn what it means to compete and how to improve your readiness to match wits and energy with whomever you're up against. On the other hand, competition indeed reveals our character. As we continue to face competition, we ultimately unlock an ancient potential within us. The reason you are here reading these words at this moment is because countless ancestors who came before you had the agility to survive. Human beings have been very successful at meeting challenges, rising to the competition, and evolving. Our bodies have literally learned to grow and change in order to compete.

In your life and career, who are you competing with? How do you identify your rivals? And how can you influence them?
Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

video.transcript_text:
Be a Competitor: Influence Your Opponent, Featuring Phillip Fulmer 
 
 
Coach Phillip Fulmer 
 
Influencing your opponent is a critical strategy to utilize as a leader. My good friend Pat 
Summitt said, “You can put forth so much effort that you cut your opponent down to size and 
force them to play below his or her own abilities. Competitiveness allows you to influence your 
opponent.” 
  
In order for Pat Summitt to accomplish her goal of making the 1976 Olympic team, she knew 
she had to perform well against players who were younger and better than her. What Pat had 
on her side, however, was her sheer competitive spirit. She refused to back away from a 
challenge and resolved to outwork and outsmart anyone who got in the way of her dream. 
  
Competitors find a way to gain the advantage by forcing their opponents to take unexpected 
detours. Pat said, “Influencing your opponent is a matter of forcing them to do something 
they’d rather not, of making them go around instead of taking the easy path.” Strong leadership 
requires being prepared for tough opponents. The more knowledgeable you are about your 
situation, the better equipped you’ll be to guide your team through adversity.  
 
This means you have to be willing to do your homework. How well do you know the 
competitors in your field? Do you know their strengths? How might you be able to expose their 
weaknesses? If you find yourself in situations where you’re outmatched, use insight, 
awareness, and effort to force your competitor to engage with you on your terms. 
  
True competitors practice good defense. This goes for anything in life, not just basketball. Pat 
said, “Defense is purely a matter of attitude. It’s within your control. When two teams are 
evenly matched, the hustle plays can win it.” To be a competitor, you have to be willing to 
hustle. Learn how to influence your opponents, study your competition, expose their 
weaknesses, and play to your strengths by spending the effort it takes to succeed. As Pat said, 
“The team that makes the first effort and the extra effort will win.”

Leadership Reflections: Winning as a Declaration

Everyone wants to win. But interestingly, people who don't win very often become hesitant to declare that winning is the objective. Perhaps, psychologically, it's easier to refrain from making that declaration as protection against disappointment. However, we learned in this module that successful leaders are unafraid of declaring winning the goal and benchmarks of success as the clear objective of their efforts. They are willing to boldly declare that they intend to win and how winning will be defined.

What could you identify in your work as a declaration of winning?

What specifically could you identify, and how can you bring that "declaration" to the forefront?
Could your team openly declare a challenging production goal for next quarter?
Could you identify some other metric of success and clearly state what winning would mean?

If you or your team did this, how would it make you feel?
What do you think the impact would be on others in the organization?
Reflect on these questions in your workbook.

steps.exact_visible_copy:
11 of 15
Love Your Adversaries

Your competitors make you better. Having worthy adversaries stimulates your work ethic, and brings out qualities you may not have known you had. So don't resent them. You should love your competitors. And you should thank them.
Pat Summitt

Be a Competitor: Love Your Adversaries, featuring Phillip Fulmer

Your Rivals Force You to Stretch and Grow
More than simply getting your attention or keeping you hustling, the presence of a great rival stretches you to achieve more. How many times have great rivals credited each other for some of their best work? In professional men's basketball, the rivalry between Larry Bird and Magic Johnson is one of the best examples of a fierce rivalry spanning more than a decade. They competed with each other in college and in the pros and gave each other credit for pushing one another to develop parts of their game that wouldn't have emerged otherwise.

Each of us needs to identify our rival. Furthermore, we need to be grateful for their presence and recognize their abilities. Then, commit to stretch and grow in a way that will allow you to meet and exceed whatever challenges your competition will bring.

When rivalries are appreciated and embraced, they can be leveraged to encourage breakthroughs. Breakthroughs represent unprecedented leaps forward.

What's Your Bulletin-Board Material?
Bulletin Board Material
In sports, a rival's comment or detail that is used by the opposite team for motivation

An up-and-coming rival may say that the champion is "getting old," "slowing down," or no longer able to compete for whatever reason. That declaration, to the champion, may be "bulletin-board material" that they communicate to the rest of the team as motivation. Before the era of social media, coaches might take a disparaging quote and post it in the locker room to remind the team of how they had been disparaged by the rival.

Sometimes these reminders can be useful in getting ready for a competition, inspiring days, weeks, and even years of work in developing the skills necessary to compete with the offending party. This can obviously work in business as well. This only works if there is a deep and abiding competitive spirit. Michael Jordan was known to push himself into a competitive frenzy over even the slightest disrespect from his competition.

Do you think the Bulletin Board Material approach would fire up competitiveness in your organization? Why or why not?
Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Do Some Self-Scouting: How Is Your Rival Planning to Overtake You?
In creating an environment that's more competitive, one of the smart things a leader can do is to get team members to thoughtfully reflect on how the competition is likely observing their performance. For example, if your team owned a number of fast food restaurants and your speed ratings by the consumers had suffered, you might observe that the competition may very well take advantage of this weakness. Only through self-scouting can you get a good look at yourself and recognize how the competition may try to take advantage.

video.transcript_text:
Be a Competitor: Love Your Adversaries, Featuring Phillip Fulmer 
 
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
You have to love your adversaries. They make you better. They force you to improve, to stretch 
your capacities. Competitors respond to a challenge from their opponents and to negative 
motivation, as well as to positive. Competitors seek revenge for losses. They crave a 
compliment if they haven’t had one. They are constantly asking, “Did I do the right thing? Was I 
good enough?” 
  
Competitors want to prove everyone else wrong. They want to show skeptics, “I am better than 
this. I am a winner.”  
 
Coach Phillip Fulmer 
 
It can be a hard thing to have love and gratefulness for your opponents. After all, they’re the 
ones standing in the way of your success. 
  
But as the saying goes, “If you want to be the best, you have to beat the best.” True 
competitors never stop challenging themselves, and they don’t play it safe. You have to be 
willing to dream big, work hard, and take risks. Otherwise, you’ll never grow. Your competition 
will work just as hard as you at gaining an advantage. They’ll expose your weaknesses and try to 
capitalize on them. 
  
Great adversaries force you to improve. In leadership, you have to constantly be finding ways to 
grow so that you can be ready to handle those tough situations that come along right before a 
major breakthrough. How do you seek out being challenged so you can grow in your field? Who 
are the competitors that push you to be greater? These rivals are crucial to the development of 
your talent and stamina for success, even if you fall short and take losses en route to meeting 
your ultimate goals. 
  
Good competition will keep you focused. There was no other competitor the 1997 Lady Vols 
team respected more than Connecticut. Tennessee had suffered a humiliating loss to them 
during the regular season. When the team found out that Tennessee and Connecticut would be 
in the same bracket for the tournament, the players were excited. Not only did Tennessee beat 
Connecticut 91 to 81, the team’s competitive drive gave them the motivation and hunger they 
needed to go on and win the NCAA championship for the second year in a row. 
  
Be grateful for your opponents. It’s a sign of respect to take your rival seriously. Doing so will 
allow you to discover new areas for improvement and take the team that you lead to another 
level.  
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
Your competitors make you better. Having a worthy adversary stimulates your work ethic and 
brings out qualities you may not have known you had. So, don’t resent them. You should love 
your competitors and you should thank them.

13 of 15
Wrap-Up

When you choose to compete, you make the conscious decision to find out what your real limits are, not just what you think they are. Competition trains you to accept risk and to endure setbacks. By embracing it, you can enhance your life. But it will also pull you through those painful, frightening, everyday battles we all have to face at one time or another.
Pat Summitt

Be a Competitor: Wrap-Up, featuring Roberto Fernandez

Competition Can Create a “Whatever It Takes” Mentality
Have you ever noticed how hard it is to beat a sitting champion? They already know how to win, and they have at their disposal a number of tools to hold off the competition. While this is probably more easily visualized in sports, it's true of virtually any type of challenge. When a team has worked hard to reach a goal and understands the challenges of success, team members are far more likely to commit to whatever it takes to win! As a leader, this "whatever it takes mentality" will show up more often when competition becomes a regular element of practice and preparation, and resilient leaders within the organization are consistently encouraged and supported.

The Urgency of Failure
Failure, or the threat thereof, can create a great deal of urgency. Teams who have been working a long time to accomplish a goal will feel the emergency of impending failure, perhaps brought on by the emergence of competition, and will use that fuel to redouble their efforts. Leaders need to be aware that the urgency of failure can show up at every turn.

Raising the Standards in the Face of Urgency
Urgency brings out our very best at a cellular level. Athletes have actually reported that at times they have performed at peak performance while on the verge of getting sick, likely because their brains and bodies felt a sense of urgency due to the impending illness, causing an even greater level of focus. Wilt Chamberlain was reportedly sick the night before he scored 100 points in a single NBA game. The key takeaway for leaders is this: make sure you respond to a sense of urgency by raising standards, not inducing panic. Some groups don't respond as well in cases of urgency or emergency. They may collapse under stress and refrain from doing their very best. This panic can come due to a lack of experience on how to perform under a sense of urgency. Coach Summitt famously had her team practice for hours with simulated end-of-game situations, forcing players to take the last shot or to make split-second decisions under a variety of circumstances. By helping the players get used to a sense of urgency and training them to raise their standards when it happened, there was a much greater chance that game-winning performance was going to happen.

Bringing the Battle, or Waiting for War
We’ve learned in this unit that competition is going to emerge no matter what we do. To this end, leaders have two choices. They can respond to the competition by simply waiting for it to show up, or preemptively bring the best of themselves to battle, anticipating competition. A seasoned, peak-performing athlete may know that a competitor is likely to emerge at any time and attempt to dethrone them in new ways. By preemptively being ready for battle, it's far more likely that the competition will be a fierce one when it arrives.

Raising the Standard, and Leaving Others Behind
Don’t be surprised if the act of raising the standard makes others feel uncomfortable. If your peer group tends to be out of shape, and you decide to commit to a rigorous workout routine, your new standard may not necessarily be met with open arms. While it may not be your intention, the very act of raising the standard for yourself or for your team may send a message that they are being "left behind." The desire to raise your standard and do whatever it takes to remain competitive will attract others who are hungry for competition, but you will face opposition from those who are uncomfortable with the same. The harder you push to be competitive, the more the divide will increase. Don't be surprised if you leave behind some folks who just weren't ready for the challenge.

Competition Ignites Both Success and Failure. Leadership Matters!
Throughout this module, you've been exposed to the many merits of competition. However, jumping into a competition doesn't mean that you or your team will automatically achieve or experience all the amazing benefits. One of the best things that a leader can do, however, is to test the mettle and see where they stand. A coach may look at their team and think they know who the real competitors are, only to discover that, when tested, different leaders and intense competitors rise and fall. Competition ignites both success and failure, and to be an outstanding leader, the presence of competition must ignite in you a sense of innovation, and the willingness to raise your own standards. Without question, competition and the ability to manage this dynamic is an absolute must for high-performing leaders and individual performers to achieve the highest results.

Let's Summarize
Make competition a regular element in your practice.
Be prepared to face the urgency of failure at any time.
Respond to a sense of urgency by raising standards.
Anticipate and prepare to compete at any time.
Accept that not everyone will accept raised standards.
Accept the risk of failures.
Be willing to innovate and raise your own standards.

video.transcript_text:
Be a Competitor: Wrap-Up, Featuring Roberto Fernandez 
 
 
Roberto Fernandez, Medical Director, The Pat Summitt Clinic at The University of Tennessee 
Medical Center 
 
Coach Summitt believed being a competitor meant that you were willing to do whatever it took 
to get things done. No job was too big or too little. You were either all in, or you’d be left out. 
For Pat, the payoff was worth it. She said, “Competitiveness is not meant for peacetime, but it 
is an invaluable quality in coping with misfortune. Channeled correctly, you can use it to battle 
all sorts of hardship in your life, not just the athletic kind, or the corporate kind, or the 
managerial kind.” 
  
In this module, you learned what it takes to be a competitor and how to use competitiveness as 
your advantage in difficult situations. First, you saw that true competitors are tough and set 
high goals. Pleasing others shouldn’t be the primary motivation. Competitors need to be 
assertive and proactive in their pursuit of success. They must be willing to embrace new 
challenges and stretch their limits. This is the only way to avoid the seductive comforts of being 
average or an underachiever. 
  
Next, competitors win battles by influencing their opponents. Force opponents to take 
unexpected detours from their strengths by knowing their tendencies and using that knowledge 
to make them rely on their weaknesses. Devote yourself to the hustle as you study your 
competitors and expose their deficiencies. When you influence your opponents, you rely on 
effort to outwork the opposing talent. 
  
Finally, competitors love their adversaries. They are not frightened by intense opposition. 
Instead, they embrace the challenge and use it as an opportunity for improvement. Strong 
competition demands your best and helps you achieve your best. Be grateful for opponents and 
take them seriously. This is how competitors stay hungry for success. 
  
Pat Summitt used competitiveness to get through adversity and achieve the extraordinary. 
When you choose to be a competitor, you unlock the potential for success, and you train your 
mind to persevere through every challenge. Pat said, “Competition trains you to accept risk and 
to endure setbacks. By embracing it, you can enhance your life; but it will also pull you through 
those painful, frightening, everyday battles we all have to face at one time or another.” 
 
Are you pushing yourself to be all that you can be? Don’t settle for average. Be a competitor 
and reach for greatness.

Page 1 of 15
Pat in Her Own Words

I'm constantly trying to look for ways to improve in the off-season. I promised our team, 'I will be better next year. Will you be better?' — because everyone should want to continue to improve and everyone should realize that you may have to change to get better.
Pat Summitt

Page 3 of 15
Change Is a Must

Change Is a Must: Introduction, featuring Karen Hilton

Peak Performers Seek Change Constantly
Top leaders and peak performers realize that getting to the top and staying on top both require continuous pursuit of change. Growth cannot happen without change. The pursuit of change sounds really good...until we are challenged with actually thinking, feeling, and acting differently. Without question, humans instinctively tend to resist unfamiliar patterns. In a world where we seek excellence or exceptional results, however, it's important to go against our natural instinct of avoiding change. Rather, we must continuously, relentlessly, and passionately pursue it. The willingness and ability to pursue change is part of the definition of success for high-performing leaders.

Familiarity Breeds Laziness
Peak performers learn to loathe familiarity. If something becomes too familiar or easy, it's important for them to shake it up and make it harder. Peak performers and members of teams that become dynasties will win a championship only to return the next year with a new strategy, improvement, or approach designed to improve on previous performance. As a leader, be on the lookout for familiarity. If team members become too familiar and too comfortable, they won't perform at their very best.

Flexibility Wins, Stubbornness Loses
Often, being a novice at an endeavor brings flexibility to the work. A rising performer with great potential but limited experience may be willing to try a greater variety of techniques to take on the champ. Meanwhile, the champion may be less likely to try something new because, after all, they have already won the gold and know what it's like to stand in the winner's circle. This is why experience alone isn't enough. Experience with flexibility is a wonderfully powerful combination. That champion could potentially climb to even greater heights if they embrace flexibility to go along with all that experience.

If You Don’t Like It, Change It — The Mantra of the Most Successful
In teams and in life, stubbornness results in being stuck — a terrible place to be both personally and professionally. If you're stuck in a job you don't like or a situation that makes you uncomfortable, it can feel suffocating. High-performing leaders understand the need to embrace the mantra of change and to be willing to change virtually everything. If your job isn't what you would like, you can change it. If there are things about yourself that you don't like, take steps to change your life so you reach your personal goals. The willingness to change and the desire to improve are at the heart of what it means to be successful.

Take Action!
When people or teams fail to change, it's often due to "analysis paralysis." A team's members may have studied many different ways to address a problem and begin to feel overwhelmed. When there are too many choices, people tend to refrain from taking action. This is why salespeople commonly limit choices so a buyer can feel less overwhelmed and make a buying decision. An effective leader can make sure team members have choices, while keeping those choices simple. Team members must then be expected to commit to take action. Growth, change, and improvement can't happen without action. Even if team members take action and make the wrong decision, they can adjust — but those discoveries don't happen unless they take action in the first place.

What Are Your Limits? Change Will Tell You
The biographies of peak performers and strong leaders often reveal these individuals weren't entirely sure of their own performance limits. However, committing to change and growth often helps people solve that mystery and find out just how high is "high," or what sort of capabilities lie within. You'll never know if you could have been a great coach, CEO, or renowned performer in whatever venue you seek if you don't pursue a plan for improvement and chase it with relentless grit.

Change Requires Internal Shift First
Thinking of change from Gandhi's perspective makes it quite practical and applicable. In order to inspire change in others, you have to be able to conceive of change within yourself. In other words, from within your heart and mind, do you have the ability to conceptualize change and make the shifts necessary to make it happen? Incredible entrepreneurs who want to reshape the world must first overcome their own doubts and surround themselves with people who believe their work can change the world. Companies made up of leaders and top performers who have this ability to shift and believe in themselves usually have a much better chance of getting the market to believe in them.

Think about the concept of familiarity. Which of these statements do you think apply to familiarity? Select all that apply.
Familiarity drives ongoing achievement and success.
Familiarity can lead to laziness.
We can continually improve when we stick to the familiar.
Growth and achievement require stretching beyond the familiar.
Correct
Exactly! When we stick to only what's familiar, we can get lazy. And we can only grow and achieve more when we're willing to stretch beyond what's familiar.

What tells you that you need to make a change? In other words, how do you test your own limits and know when change might be warranted?
Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

The willingness to experiment with change may be the most essential ingredient to success at anything.
Pat Summitt

You must be the change you want to see in the world.
Mahatma Gandhi

Change Is a Must: Introduction, Featuring Karen Hilton 
 
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
“If I don’t seek change constantly in my profession, I get left behind. Familiarity is not a good 
thing on the basketball court. It’s a game of constant shifts and adjustments, but it applies to 
any field. If you aren’t flexible, if you don’t change your mindset to meet the circumstances and 
your personnel, you will lose. If you grant yourself the freedom to change, it will open worlds to 
you. Don’t like your job? Change it. Don’t like your attitude? Change it. You can change the way 
you think. You can change your game plan and you can change your life. Don’t just sit there in 
your comfortable chair. Do something.” 
  
Karen Hilton, Founder & President, Executive Coaching 
 
Hi, I’m Karen Hilton. This module introduces one of my favorite Definite Dozen principles: 
change is a must. Peyton Manning, one of the NFL’s greatest players, and the league’s only 
five-time MVP award winner, was Pat Summitt’s friend and probably one of her biggest fans. 
Peyton’s favorite Pat Summitt quote is, “When you choose to be a competitor, you choose to 
be a survivor. When you choose to compete, you must make the conscious decision to find out 
what your real limits are, not just what you think they are.” 
  
Leadership and change management experts from all over the world agree with Pat. Just like 
Pat, the experts have discovered that before we can inspire others to change, we need to 
change. We need to find out what our real limits are, not just what we think they are. We need 
to understand that it’s the inner change that makes the outer change possible.  
 
And I think you’re in for a big treat because we’ve asked Professor Steve Olson, an award-
winning teacher and a leadership expert, to help us better understand why change starts from 
within. Steve is a distinguished lecturer at the University of Tennessee, Chattanooga. He’s been 
a pioneering leader in executive development for more than 25 years. He’s coached more than 
2,000 executives as they have strived to reach their full potential as leaders, innovators, and 
change makers. 
  
Professor Olson, through his engaging stories and unique teaching style, will show us how Pat 
came to embrace change, inspire change, and lead change; and then do it all over again and 
again, year after year. Are you ready to change? Let’s get started.

steps.source_title: From Shy Tomboy to Coaching Legend
steps.exact_visible_copy:
Page 6 of 15
From Shy Tomboy to Coaching Legend

Change Is a Must: From Shy Tomboy to Coaching Legend, featuring Steve Olson

Leaders who are committed to taking their teams to the next level must be willing to publicly declare they will take whatever action is required to grow and make necessary improvements. Without question, there is something very powerful to a public declaration. Often, someone needs to make a public declaration to make a significant change in their lives. They say it aloud and to enough people that they feel a sense of accountability to make good on their commitment.

You’ve Changed! Why, Thank You!
In this module, we've made it clear that it's a huge compliment if someone says that you've changed (assuming it's a positive change). If people around you notice that you're always changing, it's likely a sign of continuous growth and improvement.

Remember, Change Does Not Always Mean Improvement
This is not to suggest that all change relates to improvement. Have you ever known someone who changed in a negative way? Maybe they developed some poor habits or allowed some influencer to negatively change how they live or how they treat other people. Maybe it's an organizational leader who made ineffective changes just for the sake of change. Perhaps a family member fell victim to some sort of addiction that changed their behavior or lifestyle. Maybe a friend or loved one has changed in a way that causes friction or distance in your relationship. Not all change is improvement. When we use the term "change" here, we mean continuous, positive change that helps you become a better person. Your willingness to create positive change is what ultimately leads to success.

Aspire to Become Something New, and Love the New You
The solution here is to continuously aspire to become a better version of who you are. Visualize that better version of you on the horizon and take whatever action you need to make sure you embody all of those wonderful attributes. Fall in love with the "new version of you" that you were trying to create, and then your ongoing pursuit will become a labor of love.

Commit to Growing Professionally, Forever
When it comes to change, you won't always make the right decisions. You may choose to change something that should have been left alone, and you may have to change back. You may change too quickly and not embrace it for the long haul. Perhaps the most empowering thing you can do is to commit to growing, both personally and professionally, for the rest of your life. If you can always commit to learning and becoming more, there's nothing that you can't achieve. There is no shelf life on learning either. We all know there is no profession today that will allow anyone to sit idly for long without being left behind. Commit to lifelong growth and love the journey.

If someone comes to you and says you have changed, how would you accept it? Would you take it as a compliment?
Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

How do you decide what change is important for yourself? How do you make sense of what to change and what to keep the same?
Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

It's what you learn after you know it all that counts the most.
Coach John Wooden

Change Is a Must: From Shy Tomboy to Coaching Legend, Featuring Steve Olson 
 
 
Steve Olson, Distinguished Lecturer, UT Chattanooga 
 
“As badly as I wanted to become someone new, I resisted saying it aloud. I viewed it as a sign of 
weakness if I had changed. Today, if someone tells me that I’ve changed, I take it as a 
compliment.” 
  
Pat Summitt’s teams won because Pat Summitt changed. Pat Summitt’s teams won so much 
because Pat Summitt changed so much. Pat knew that it was impossible to win the national 
championship if she didn’t change. Change is a must. But it wasn’t going to do any good if only 
she changed. She had to inspire, motivate, and teach her players and assistants to change. And 
she knew that in order to repeat as national champions, she would have to change again and 
again and again. 
  
Pat’s eight national championship teams and her lifetime winning percentage bear testimony to 
the timeless wisdom of her Definite Dozen principles, but none more so than Change is a must. 
Pat’s story is so simple and surprising and its implications so profound, it bears retelling. Pat 
was a farm girl. When she arrived at college, she was so shy and modest that she dressed 
herself in her closet. But she finally decided she was tired of being known as the “5-foot-11 
tomboy.” 
  
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
You probably won’t believe this, but I was incredibly shy. I was shy with my peers. And actually, 
I joined a sorority, which no one would ever think that I would be the sorority girl type. I think 
that is one of the best things that happened to me. My sorority sisters made fun of my clothes. I 
didn’t wear makeup, and they were going to give me a makeover and change my wardrobe. 
And, you know, it was tough for me because, you know, I just basically surrendered to a group 
of people and said, “Okay, here I am.” That really had a big influence on my life and just kind of 
taught me the ropes because I’d pretty much been on the on the dairy farm all my life.

In fact, she changed so much that her friends back home commented on it. She’d react 
defensively and deny it, of course; but deep down, she knew that they were right. She had 
changed. And what’s more, she liked who she was becoming. So, she determined that while she 
would stay true to who she was and where she came from, she would also commit to growing 
professionally for the rest of her life; and that’s just what Pat Summitt did.

Page 8 of 15
Interpersonal Expectancy

Change Is a Must: Interpersonal Expectancy, featuring Steve Olson

How High Is High? You’ll Never Know Until You Change
Could you be a CEO? If you're working in the mailroom and you don't apply for the "next job," challenging your comfort level, you'll never know. Change is the key to finding out every team member's capabilities and potential for growth. If a leader realizes the team hasn't reached its potential, they can make a change and evaluate the results. Still not there? Make a change. Getting close but not quite there? Make a change. Arrive at the top and want to stay in the winner's circle? Continue to change.

Leaders Who Challenge You Know Your Potential
Some of the best leaders can be extremely demanding, asking a lot of everyone. It's true of coaches, CEOs, and bosses at every level. In many cases, a strong leader will see more in their team member or player than anyone else does. They may see more than the individual sees within themselves. The leader is there to help the individual find the champion within.

Interpersonal Expectancy Effect
In psychology, the tendency for a person to behave toward another person according to their expected behavior is known as the interpersonal expectancy effect. With this phenomenon, an individual or group's expectations for others may, perhaps unintentionally, bring about those expected behaviors, positive or negative. For example, a negative, toxic teacher may expect her students to behave badly and to be disruptive — and this interpersonal expectancy may well bring that to reality. Conversely, leaders who see outstanding things in others will remind those individuals of the emerging champions within. Simply believing in a higher level of performance in someone can help them find the next level of performance. This is an incredibly powerful element of what it means to embrace change, and leaders must keep this in mind. If you want to be a highly successful leader, think about how you see those around you and what you expect. If you are the type of leader that manages by exception, is quick to punish, and is consistently negative, you are far more likely to get those behaviors out of others. On the other hand, if you are a leader who knows how to see unexpected abilities in others and encourage them to be their best, it's far more likely that amazing people will emerge from within your organization. Have you ever noticed that some of the top leaders seem to have an amazing group around them almost everywhere they go? Sometimes this is because "great people follow great people," but other times it's because great people harvest the amazing strengths of others by the power of interpersonal expectancy.

How might you use the interpersonal expectancy effect to inspire others to reach new heights? How might you position yourself to be the recipient of the interpersonal expectancy effect when trying to make your own personal or professional changes?
Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

This concept of interpersonal expectancy is also powerful from an individual performance standpoint. Keep in mind that if you are a top performer, this notion of expectancy will matter. If a Division I athlete is trying to figure out which college to attend, she might surround herself with coaches or teammates with high expectations. They might want that degree of positivity around if they expect to grow. The same is true with work. This is why organizational culture is so important. When it comes to hiring, the organizational climate is one of the most important factors individuals consider when making a decision. Climates that encourage harvesting the very best from within us are far more likely to attract and keep the best people.

Interpersonal Expectancy and Self-Efficacy
As a leader reflecting on the merits of interpersonal expectancy, it may be tempting to assume the very best leaders have the ability to make virtually anyone into a better version of themselves. Unfortunately, this simply isn't enough. If a leader and team members recognize incredible talent within another team member, they may encourage, cajole, and push that individual, but change will only come when that person builds the self-efficacy within and believes that improvement is possible. This is inspiring, yet perhaps a bit maddening to leaders, because they can do everything right, do everything possible for the individual to find the greatness within them, and it still may not happen. Likewise, you will never achieve your highest level of performance as an individual or as a leader without a deep sense of belief in yourself. This is indeed the divining rod. The best leaders help team members find that self-efficacy within. Imagine the power of combining both interpersonal expectancy and self-efficacy!

video.transcript_text:
Change Is a Must: Interpersonal Expectancy, Featuring Steve Olson 
 
 
Steve Olson, Distinguished Lecturer, UT Chattanooga 
 
“To outsiders, I’m that mean lady on the sidelines yelling at my players, but I’m determined to 
get the maximum potential out of them. I don’t care if I have to coax, pull, push, or haul it out 
of them. When I challenge them, what I’m really saying is, ‘You’re better than this and you 
don’t even know it.’” 
  
Pat always considered herself to be a teacher, and she realized that driving people to change, 
challenging them to improve, was at the heart of being a good teacher. 
  
Coach Pat Summitt 
 
Are you going to come along and run this basketball team or are you going to play like you’re 
scared out of your mind? You start the game with a turnover. It’s time for you to grow up right 
here and everybody else follows your lead and plays nervous.  
 
Steve Olson, Distinguished Lecturer, UT Chattanooga 
 
So, what made Pat Summitt more successful? It’s quite simple, really, but it’s also quite rare. 
Pat really believed that her players, all of them, could meet her high standards for excellence. 
Scientists call this high expectation the interpersonal expectancy effect, and it is one of the 
most powerful drivers of high performance. If this sounds a bit like Pat Summitt and the effect 
that her sorority sisters had on her, it should. It’s the same principle. In fact, the belief and 
expectation that someone can do something if they’re just willing to stay at it long enough to 
learn it is so powerful that armies around the world have tried to harness the effect. 
  
Sadly, scientists discovered that you can’t teach the effect. It has to be believed. You have to 
really believe that others can meet your highest standards. So, where does the belief that 
others can meet the highest standards come from? It comes from ourselves. We have to really 
believe that we can do it. Researchers call this belief self-efficacy, and it’s the single most 
important factor in an individual’s success. You won’t be surprised, then, to learn that Pat 
Summitt had the highest self-efficacy you can imagine, and she held the same belief about her 
players.

We learned in these sections that interpersonal expectancy has a huge impact on the actions we take and our ability to achieve a goal. We've all met people who seemed to expect failure or disappointment and, not surprisingly, those expectations were consistently achieved. Remember, it's not enough to simply cross your arms and expect great things to happen just because you dream them. But having expectancy around positive outcomes should change both your actions and your attitudes.

As you think about this concept, what could you do to create a set of expectations for yourself that would be inspiring and maybe even breathtaking?

Reflect on this question in your workbook.

Think about some expectations for your career and your current working situation and reflect on how often those expectations manifest themselves daily. For example, do you spend more time worrying about a burdensome weekly meeting or a blue-sky opportunity that's available if you simply focus on that outcome? Be specific with your reflections.
