Page 11 of 15
The Physics for Positive Change

Change Is a Must: The Physics for Positive Change, featuring Steve Olson

m11v5_transcript.pdf
147.2 KB

Change Requires Reaching Beyond the Comfort Zone

Suppose you are attempting to build muscle, but you only lift light, easy-to-move weights. Your body most likely will not respond to this comfortable — if not boring — workout routine. Instead, most trainers will suggest that you push yourself by getting out of your comfort zone, lifting heavier weights and following the routines required to take your body to a new level of fitness and strength. The same is true in virtually any other type of change. Reaching a higher level requires some straining and struggling to climb. In most cases, the higher the destination, the greater the sacrifice. To win a gold medal, Olympians must compete against the best athletes in the world who are all pushing themselves out of their comfort zones every day. The athlete who's able to push themselves the farthest will be more likely to win the gold. Similarly, a team competing in business will never grow to a new level if members don't get out of their comfort zones.

Why We Seek to Avoid Disequilibrium

Equilibrium is the status quo. It's what we are used to — normal habits and patterns that allow us to pretty much keep things the same. When we challenge ourselves and add new levels of intensity to what we do, it creates a sense of disequilibrium. Although it isn't necessarily described this way in personal training, your muscles go through a state of disequilibrium when you push them with heavy weights. Once your body recovers and you have a new level of strength, equilibrium is restored. When you've reached this new level of equilibrium and you challenge yourself with even heavier weights, the disequilibrium emerges again.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

Given how good disequilibrium is for our growth, why do you think we tend to avoid it?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Disequilibrium takes a lot of energy and is exhausting. From a survival standpoint, our brains and bodies don't want to be in a state of permanent disequilibrium. If we were living in the woods, it would be counterproductive to continually have to work extremely hard at everything from getting water, to finding food, to building shelter, and so on. At some point, there are advantages to making things a little easier on ourselves.

We tend to try to avoid challenging what we already know how to do when it might permanently disrupt our equilibrium. Much like rigorous exercise can be uncomfortable (but still good for us), we might avoid studying something we know will only make us smarter. Our brains and bodies tend to avoid the hard work. However, our ability to overcome this tendency is at the heart of continually improving as leaders and peak performers.

video.transcript_text:
Change Is a Must: The Physics for Positive Change, Featuring Steve Olson 
 
 
Steve Olson, Distinguished Lecturer, UT Chattanooga 
 
We’ve already learned that Pat Summitt insisted on respect – respect for oneself and for others 
– all others, including your opponents. That was Pat’s first principle. And it has to be ours, too. 
So, what does respect have to do with change? In short, everything. Here’s why. Teams and 
groups, like whole organizations and whole societies, don’t really change until they are taken 
out of their comfort zone long enough to begin discarding the beliefs, attitudes, and habits that 
no longer work. 
  
The technical term for being out of our comfort zones is disequilibrium. As the stress of being 
pushed out of our comfort zones goes up, so does our performance, but only to a point. Too 
much disequilibrium and our learning and performance starts to degrade. So, changing requires 
that we modulate the stress of being pushed to become better, slowly raising our performance 
over time. 
  
A leader is someone who uses the forces of disequilibrium to get people to change for the 
better. Pat Summitt was the master of managing disequilibrium. She was forever forcing her 
players out of their comfort zones in order to spur them to become better. That’s because, just 
like you and me, even great players naturally want to return to low levels of disequilibrium. But 
Pat wouldn’t let them. She’d make them play other positions. She’d make them run and run 
and run again until they thought they couldn’t run anymore. And then she’d run them some 
more. She’d make them practice and practice, staying all over her players until they got it right. 
Only then were her players ready to replace their old beliefs about what they were capable of 
and their old habits with better beliefs and better attitudes and better habits. 
  
In other words, Pat knew that none of us will change until we really feel and really believe that 
the status quo won’t work anymore. We know we are going to have to learn. We know we are 
going to have to change. But the reason that Pat Summitt could do this was because she knew 
that, as a leader, her job was not to be liked by her players. She knew that her job was to be 
disliked by them at a rate that they could tolerate. Pat’s job was to keep her players in what 
leadership scholars call the productive zone of disequilibrium long enough to change their 
game.

m11v6_transcript.pdf
114.6 KB

Continue to Visualize Who You Want to Become

One of the most famous movie lines of all time is from the Kevin Costner film, "Field of Dreams."

"If you build it, he will come."

From the film, Field of Dreams
Photo Credit: H. Michael Miley, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

In the movie, the narrator whispers the line, "If you build it, he will come" to the main character about taking what appeared to be an absurd risk. A voice in his head told him to build a baseball field on his farm, and it made no sense to anyone except him. Costner's character had a vision for what he wanted to build and, even though there was resistance all around him, he had to commit to that vision to persist. As a leader, if you dream and visualize what you want for yourself, you position yourself to achieve the unachievable or become what you have not yet become. See it first in your mind and heart, and then chase it with your hands, feet, and energy. That is the formula for outstanding success.

Change Makes Us All Uncomfortable — Get Comfortable with Discomfort

Your success as a leader or peak performer may come down to the degree to which you consistently get comfortable with discomfort. Returning to the example of exercise, if someone wants to remain extraordinarily fit for the rest of their life, they must consistently take actions that would be uncomfortable to some people. They may have to make uncomfortable food choices and do uncomfortable physical activities. Getting comfortable with these consistent, yet uncomfortable habits will very likely determine success.

It's also easy for a strong leader or peak performer to get overly comfortable with their own approaches. After all, they've already won and can reference the steps they took to get there. It's uncomfortable to make a winning coach, CEO, or peak performer change their practices to achieve the next level. How many times have championship athletes won the crown, lost a crown, and somewhat reinvented themselves to get the crown back again? Change, then, is at the heart of what it means to be a champion.

video.transcript_text:
Change Is a Must: Wrap-Up, Featuring Karen Hilton 
 
 
Karen Hilton, Founder & President, Executive Coaching 
 
Congratulations you have completed Change is a must. I don’t know about you, but I really 
enjoyed Steve Olson’s insights and stories about how Pat Summitt overcame her fears to not 
only embrace change, but to find innovative ways to inspire others to change, too. 
  
As a senior executive, I agree with Steve that we began the process of change when we decide 
that we’re tired of being “that person,” whoever that person might be. And just like Pat 
Summitt, we’ve got to really, really like the person we’re trying to become. 
  
Some of my key takeaways from Steve’s videos are, first, nobody likes change, at least not at 
first. That’s because change is, indeed, scary and uncomfortable. But we can’t improve if we 
don’t change. And change that’s truly worthy of the effort will help us dramatically improve 
ourselves again and again and again. To inspire others to change, we must change first. We 
need to model the way.  
 
Second, as Steve recommends, we have to work like crazy to make sure that the lessons we 
learn become our new habit and the new habit of everyone on our team and in our company. 
  
Third, change is a force of nature. To change, we must be humble. We have to be humble 
enough to admit to others and to ourselves that we don’t know it all and that we can get 
better. Pat Summitt never lost that humility. She changed constantly, experimenting with 
anything and everything that would help her and her teams improve. As Pat’s dear friend Coach 
John Wooden said, “It’s what you learn after you know it all that really counts.”  
 
As Professor Olson taught us, scientists and change experts know that Pat Summitt was right: 
change is, indeed, a force of nature. We know now scientifically that people are wired for 
excellence, and by creating positive relationships and carefully cultivating each person’s 
growth, every organization is capable of achieving excellence. 
  
So, what are you going to change about yourself? Who can help you along the way? Who can 
you benchmark yourself against in a way that will help you achieve leadership excellence?

Leadership Reflections: Are You Willing to Get Uncomfortable?

Learning yoga requires many hours of "discomfort," trying to achieve proper form and struggling to keep balance. Learning to play an instrument requires many hours of discomfort in the struggle to play fundamental scales and chords. When it comes to trying something new, many of us talk a good game but are rarely willing to actually break through that comfort zone and have a growth opportunity.

Practice breaking out of your comfort zone and identify some areas of growth. What do you need to learn that might require you to start from the very beginning to reach a working level of competence? For example, maybe you could use more proficiency with technology, and it will require asking a lot of questions. Are you too afraid to look like you don't know what you're doing? Think of some areas you'd like to grow and improve.

Reflect on this question in your workbook.

Now that you have identified these areas of weakness, zone in on specifically what you could do to build up your proficiency. Address what it would feel like to grow in these areas. What would you get from this commitment to growth in an area that may be difficult for you currently?

Reflect on this topic in your workbook.

Congratulations! That concludes this lesson. Please remember to close it before opening another lesson. You can revisit the completed course material at any time.

Page 1 of 15
Pat in Her Own Words

Notice something about all the various forms of success. They are open-ended. They aren't tasks that you finish. Success is a project that's always under construction.
Pat Summitt

Handle Success Like You Handle Failure: Pat in Her Own Words

m12v1_transcript.pdf
111.4 KB

On the Road to Success, You Never Arrive

It’s bittersweet to realize that on the road to success, you never reach your destination. But if a leader doesn't appreciate their progress or a benchmark that they've reached, those alongside them may begin to feel burned out. Reaching a winning milestone needs to be warmly celebrated and embraced. By never truly "arriving," you position yourself for continuous growth.

Failure and Success Can Bring Out the Best and Worst

Legendary UCLA basketball coach John Wooden famously said, “Sports don't build character; they reveal it.” This is very true. Have you ever heard of an athlete or elite leader who achieves success, only to burn out soon after because their character couldn't handle it? Enduring champions reveal something different about themselves in pinnacle moments, namely working just as hard to defend their crown as they did to earn it. All matters of success tend to follow this trend.

How do you evaluate your team members' abilities to handle success and failure? By being a careful observer. As a leader, create conditions where you can observe individuals on your team and see how they respond to reaching success or experiencing failure. For example:

- How does a high-potential employee respond when they don't get the promotion they want?
- How does a team member respond when suddenly given the opportunity to supervise a group or own a major project?

You can harvest these revealing behaviors when the time is right.

video.transcript_text:
Handle Success Like You Handle Failure: Pat in Her Own Words 
 
Coach Path Summitt 
The point that I'll make on teambuilding and things I've learned is how to handle success and failure. 
Sometimes as coaches, because maybe we feel more pressure or we think it means more to us than it 
means to kids, we don't handle failure. And I want to remind you to really check after a game on how 
you're going to handle it. I know, for me, a lot depends on the effort that was put right here on the floor. 
I don't want to teach effort, do you? I don't want to teach it. I don't want to have to try and coach it 
every day. There are things you can do to instill, through your competitive drills or whatever, better 
effort – a reward system, whatever. But you just hope that you’ve got kids that just absolutely love the 
game. But you're going to have some that just want to be on the team, without paying a big old price.  
You're going to have to handle things when they don't go well. Somebody asked me how I handled our 
loss to Connecticut. And I told those kids it was a lot different from how we lost a year ago, because a 
year ago, we didn't have a team ego. We had a lot of selfish players. But this year, we had a group that 
really committed to playing together, and they just played a team that was better, and we didn't play 
well. The wheels fell off, and against a great team like that, it can get really ugly. You can sit there as a 
coach and it seemed like an 80-minute game, but it was just a 40-minute game. And I reminded them 
that the one thing that I would remember was what kind of kids they'd been every day and what kind of 
competitors and what kind of season we'd had. 
I said, “I don't want you to think about that game unless you're thinking about whether or not you're 
going to work out in the off-season, and then you think about it. Then, you need to go the gym and take 
that with you and say, ‘Here's how we'll get better.’ Failure can bring out the absolute best in people or 
the worst. Success is the same way, and I addressed that earlier. But you have to look at this game and 
say, ‘You never arrive. You never arrive. You're always striving to get better.’”

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Page 3 of 15
Handle Success Like You Handle Failure: Introduction

You can't always control what happens, but you can control how you handle it.
Pat Summitt

Handle Success Like You Handle Failure: Introduction, featuring Doug Buce

m12v2_transcript.pdf
118.1 KB

Learn to Welcome Both Success and Failure

Learning, growth, and evolution are always at the heart of great success. Next-level success happens when dedication and intelligence meet learning, followed by adjustment, and adjustment again. This lesson is all about taking advantage of salient learning moments — in this case, both successes and failures. For athletics, competition presents the opportunity to measure progress. Wins and losses represent key benchmarks. The very best leaders put both winning and losing moments under a microscope and use both outcomes as chances to reflect, grow, and ultimately evolve.

Losses: Tantrums for Testimony

No one with even the slightest competitive spirit likes to lose. In fact, if losing doesn't impact you emotionally, how invested are you in winning? The lack of emotional engagement will keep you from the training and preparation needed to bring the best of yourself to competition.

That being said, we've all seen examples, particularly in sports, of leaders who don't respond well to losing. The moments where temper tantrums are caught on video certainly help illustrate what happens when a passionate leader gets caught up in the moment and frustration takes over their bodies. It isn't pretty, and sometimes it can cost a career.

On a more positive note, a loss can give you the opportunity for reflections and heartfelt gut-checks, leading to improvement. If you study their biographies, you'll find that many of the most successful winners had to experience more than a little losing to better understand what it takes to grow. There are few champions in any walk of life who are able to get to the winners' circle unscathed, undefeated, and without a few painful scars. The trick, obviously, is to prepare to win, and win often, however you define "winning." Then, when you don't win, respond thoughtfully, gracefully, and redouble your efforts in getting where you need to go.

When you fail, you have a natural tendency to examine it more closely. You analyze it. You critique it. You look at every second of your performance, every possession, and every turnover. I'll tell you straight out, I've learned more from losing than from winning.
Pat Summitt

In this lesson, we will talk about the importance of reflecting on "what's next" after you win. What are the most successful practices that top performers and forward-thinking leaders embrace? They learn the process of continuously evaluating the merits of their winning ways, reflecting on what got them to the winners' circle.

video.transcript_text:
Handle Success Like You Handle Failure: Introduction, featuring Doug Buce 
 
Doug Buce, President & CLO, Boing Dynamics, Inc. 
At first glance, you might assume that, for all her records, accolades and accomplishments, Pat Summitt 
was a winner at every turn. Well, in many regards, she was. But as you're about to find out, Pat learned 
more from her losses than any of her wins. These difficult and often heartbreaking lessons helped her 
become the person and championship coach that she was. Without losing, Pat Summitt may never have 
achieved the level of greatness that she did. And that's a great lesson for all of us in sport and in 
business. Learn from your losses and failures.  
As Pat said, “I've learned more from losing than from winning. If you win, you're not nearly as concerned 
with your mistakes. I've learned to welcome loss and failure and adversity. Why? Because they erase 
success. Success lulls you. It makes the most ambitious of us complacent and sloppy. Failure is simple. It 
gives you a distinct blueprint of where you've gone wrong.” 
At some point, every great leader must come to understand why failure does not mean disaster and why 
success does not mean you have ‘arrived.’ Failure and success have so many lessons to teach us if we 
are willing to listen and do the hard work of analyzing what made it successful and where we need to 
improve. No one was more committed to this process of discovery than Pat Summitt. Coach Summitt 
summarized this Definite Dozen principle by saying, “You can't always control what happens, but you 
can control how you handle it.” So, let's get started on our journey of discovering how to handle success 
like you handle failure.

Leadership Reflections: What to Do When You Lose

Strong leaders and peak performers respond to failure by treating it as a learning moment. Clearly, some responses may be more impactful and useful than others.

Learning from Success and Failure

It's much harder to handle success than it is to handle failure. You have to learn to handle them alike. Only by placing success and failure in their proper perspectives can you maintain the principles and priorities you arrived with.
Pat Summitt

Handle Success Like You Handle Failure: Learning from Success and Failure, featuring Greg Hiebert

122.5 KB

Unfortunately, we don't automatically learn from winning, and it can actually be harder to learn from winning than from losing. When winning, we tend to take a breath and feel like simply repeating the steps, even if they aren't quite as intense as the previous time, will be enough. Furthermore, a bit of ego can also begin to emerge. Team members may have been laser-focused on the process of winning, but then the win itself made them become ego-driven or credit-seeking.

Leadership Challenges

Let's review three concepts that may present common leadership challenges and examine how leaders can address them. For each card below, think what the term might mean and then select the card to reveal the definition.

Fundamental attribution error
Here, attributing a person's success or failure to their personal traits, rather than to the situational factors.

Overconfidence bias
Here, belief that a moment of success will automatically lead to more success.

Failure to ask "Why" questions
Here, the tendency not to investigate the causes of good performance systematically.

Fundamental Attribution Error

When it comes to team or organizational success, it's important to avoid a fundamental attribution error — a human tendency to attribute our own and others' behaviors to personality traits and abilities while underestimating the role of situational factors. Let's take a basketball game win as an example.

Basketball Win: Let's Unpack the Process

If a player makes a game-winning shot, it's easy to get lost in the glorification of that shot and the shooter as the buzzer sounds. It's fun to put an almost mystical quality on the shooter, adding them to legend. In reality, in order for that shooter to hit that shot, a lot of things had to happen in the process.

- The shooter would have to work unusually hard to develop a shot that goes into the basket consistently. Additionally, that shot has to be released quickly so that defenders can't consistently knock it down. Then, the shooter has to have the ability to shake a defender, get open, and handle pressure, understanding that even if they are a great shooter, it's likely that four times out of 10, the shot is not going to go in.
- The shot isn't possible without the team running a play, setting screens, and expertly getting the shooter the ball at the right time to make the game-winning point. If it's at the college level, recruiters would have had to bring in the right people and the coach would have had to run the right play to get them all pulling together.
- The strength and conditioning coach would have to make sure that they weren't so tired at the end of the game that they couldn't hit the shot.
- The nutritionists would need to make sure that the pre-game meal was enough to power them through the game without bogging them down or making them sleepy or slow.

There are, of course, a myriad of other things that have to happen in order for that winning shot to drop. A successful coach would recognize all the things that went into hitting that shot and would do everything necessary to make sure that all those moving parts are either as good or better the next time around.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

What are some ways you might avoid fundamental attribution errors?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

How to Avoid Fundamental Attribution Errors

Winning teams consistently observe the process it took to make a victory and study the process for the next time around. The same is true in business. Studying all the moving parts and focusing on the process makes the outcome more likely to become predictable and consistent. The way to avoid fundamental attribution errors lies in a deeper analysis of the formula for success. This requires honesty and research. There may have been a certain amount of luck or coincidence that created a unique moment in time for the victory. You can avoid fundamental attribution errors by truly studying the variables that led to your success.

Overconfidence Bias

Overconfidence bias emerges when an individual or a group experiences some form of victory, and that leads them to believe that they can maintain the same level of success in the future, without any extra effort. Winning at any level can be deceiving. We all have experienced some overconfidence bias somewhere along the way. We get a taste of success and assume it gets easy...and then we are corrected. This is human nature and happens to all of us. It's important to be aware of the overconfidence bias effect and be ready to respond to it.

I want our team to experience victory, and to develop some confidence. And yet, right about the time that they have the world by the tail, just when they have it all figured out, I don't mind if they get knocked down. It's the best lesson they can learn.
Pat Summitt

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

As a leader, how might you help your team eliminate overconfidence bias?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

How to Address Overconfidence Bias

Strong leaders unpack these situations and can remedy them sooner. The quickest way to resolve an overconfidence bias is for that person to experience a little bit of a loss and then pull themselves together, build up their confidence, and get to the next level. Convince them that, as a result of this setback, they may need to reinforce the processes it took to get to that level before and to assume that it is reachable again.

Asking "Why Did We Win?" Questions

The best leaders and peak performers don't fall into the trap of taking their successes for granted. Instead, they take time to understand why they found success. Without answers to why, it is very difficult to repeat success or take it to the next level. Coach Summitt explains it like this:

A lot of people succeed once, but never understand why. They don't examine what they did right or wrong. It's important to define your method and know what you did right, so you can reemphasize it. It's amazing how much intensity comes from what you emphasize. If you pay fierce attention to a few important fundamentals, you can fight complacency. The most successful organizations tend to have a signature. They do two or three things extremely well. They don't try to be all things to all people. You can try to do fifty things not very well. Or you can emphasize a few things to perfection.
Pat Summitt

video.transcript_text:
Handle Success Like You Handle Failure: Learning from Success and Failure, 
featuring Greg Hiebert 
 
Greg Hiebert, Leadership Coach & Managing Partner 
We know the importance of learning from failure, as Pat so eloquently pointed out. Yet surprisingly, 
learning from success can present even greater challenges. Pat also said, “It's much harder to handle 
success than it is to handle failure. You have to learn to handle them alike. Only by placing success and 
failure in their proper perspectives can you maintain the principles and priorities you arrived with.” 
That's why I want to examine a commonly made leadership mistake. Too often people get blinded by 
their success and start believing they are infallible due to their brilliance and overconfidence. 
The first challenge is what psychologists call fundamental attribution errors. When we succeed, we're 
likely to conclude that our talents and our current strategy are the reasons for our success. However, we 
tend to underestimate the role that external factors, situational influences, and random events may 
have played. 
The second challenge is overconfidence bias. Success increases our self-assurance and, while confidence 
in ourselves is a great thing, too much can make us believe we don't need to change. 
The third challenge is the Failure to Ask Why syndrome, the tendency not to investigate the causes of 
good performance systematically. When leaders suffer from this syndrome, they fail to ask the tough 
questions that would help them alter their assumptions and even worse, create the conditions where 
dissention is not allowed.  
Pat Summitt outright refused to engage in the Failure to Ask Why syndrome. In fact, not only did Pat ask, 
"Why did we lose” – she just as regularly asked, “Why did we win?” In an effort to understand the 
team's performance, Pat was known to relentlessly review film after both wins and losses to determine 
the source of the team's success or failure.  
There's nothing wrong with celebrating your success, but if you only revel in your wins, you've missed a 
huge opportunity to investigate what led to success with the same scrutiny, the same rigor you might 
apply to understand the causes of failure. As Coach Summitt said, “The reason success is so hard to 
duplicate is because we tend to stop doing the disciplined things that made us successful in the first 
place.”

Overcoming the Fear of Failure

We keep score in life because it matters. It counts. Too many people opt out and never discover their own abilities because they fear failure. They don't understand commitment. When you learn to keep fighting in the face of potential failure, it gives you a larger skill set to do what you want to do.
Pat Summitt

Handle Success Like You Handle Failure: Overcoming the Fear of Failure, featuring Greg Hiebert

m12v4_transcript.pdf
119.7 KB

Fear of Failure Is Logical and Real

Picture an actor, athlete, or business leader who has fought the good fight and is on the verge of a major win. Just at the last moment, they struggle and fail to claim the prize! We've all seen it happen. The person's hesitation or perhaps private self-sabotage can come out of an abiding fear of failure.

We can't always predict how an individual will respond as they near a victory. Consider a couple of examples:

- A peak performer stands in the face of a seemingly impossible, pressure-filled situation. They respond with smiling grace, deliver stellar performance, and win without reservation.
- A team plays in the championship and the star player stands with the ball on the line. Victory comes down to one shot. The player, who has easily and routinely made the same shot before, misses and the team loses the championship.

The truth is, this fear is real. Fear is a psychological dynamic that’s present in everyone to some degree.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

Do you have any goals or dreams from which fear of failure is holding you back? Identify the specific fears and then try to think of some ways you might seek to overcome them.

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Overcoming the Fear

There are many ways to overcome psychological fears. Arguably, the most often-applied method is familiarity. As our familiarity with what we fear increases, our fear likely decreases.

Think of a child with her family at the pool. She wants to have fun with her family and friends, but she has a problem: she's afraid of the water. If someone teaches her to swim, she will face her fears and the familiarity will relieve her uncertainties. Imagine all the fun she'll have, splashing and playing in the water. Her family may have to make this child, who was previously held back by fear, leave the pool to go do other activities.

The same is true in other life situations. Imagine it's the first day of your new job. You know you can do the work and you are excited to start this new adventure. At the same time, though, now that your first day is here, deep down, you are a bit fearful something may go wrong today. As you perform the expected job functions, though, you become more and more confident and your fear of failure is relieved.

How do we breed familiarity? Practice! When we practice, we develop the skills needed to respond in any related situation.

Suppose Charles works for a brokerage firm that sells exchange securities. He enjoys his job and is relatively successful, but every time he faces a customer, he feels anxious that they may ask him a question that is he unable to answer. How does he resolve that fear? Preparation and hard work. He might:

- meet with his manager or a trusted colleague for some tips and pointers;
- study documentation available on the company's internal information hub to be sure he's ready for most anything customers may ask; or
- watch some online videos or take some refresher courses on relevant topics in his industry.

Coaches often help their players overcome fear of taking the last shot in a game by having them practice that scenario beforehand. The coach sets up a buzzer and creates the conditions of an all-on-the-line, game-defining moment, giving players the opportunity to simulate that kind of pressure.

Fear of Success

Psychologists have found that the fear of success is more common than many of us may realize. Outwardly, we may declare that we want to succeed at something, yet subconsciously, we may be a bit nervous about what will happen if we do succeed. We might have thoughts like:

- If I succeed, I might get asked to do it again. What if I can't?
- What if I succeed and I'm suddenly thrown into a leadership role? What if I can't continue holding up to those standards or consistently succeed at this enormous goal? Will I end up looking foolish?
- What if I achieve my goals and people start feeling uncomfortable around me or even reject me?

Fear of success can be difficult to understand because most of us tell ourselves we want success. We may not even be aware that, deep down, we would rather not achieve that big goal because we're afraid of what might happen if we do. Strong leaders get themselves ready to respond to both victories and failures. The more they openly discuss it with team members, the better prepared they will be for both wins and losses.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

If we were to suggest to you that failure can be your friend, what do you think we might mean by that? How can failure possibly be a friend if success is your goal?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Failure Is a Friend That Teaches

Have you ever had a particularly communicative friend? You likely valued your personal connection with them and learned from their trusted wisdom. Great leaders and peak performers understand that failure can actually be that kind of friend. It's not that you'll want to welcome failure, but when it arrives, treat it like a friend. Renew your acquaintance and learn whatever you can from the situation.

There's no advantage to beating yourself up after a failure. Instead, you'll end up psychologically exhausted and less energized to meet future challenges. Your effort is better spent on allowing that failure to be a communicative friend, ready to inform and teach you. Maybe you gave it your all, but you focused on the wrong things. Maybe you had excellent intensity, but a poor strategy that just didn't work. Let that failure be your friend to help discover what to do better next time.

The key to doing this effectively is to minimize the emotional tumult you bring to the analysis. Even if you discover you poorly executed some things that were in your control, acknowledge it and analyze what you can do differently next time. Let the failure motivate and energize you. Unfortunately, good leaders have been known to give up their sport or career out of the pain of having failed in a season. Had they listened to their failure as a friend, they may have discovered they were only a slight adjustment away from a complete reversal of fortunes.

Take Some Risks and Plan to Hit the Floor

You never would have learned to walk if, as a baby, you hadn't stood up and risked falling. You might have fallen and cried, but you gathered yourself and tried again. One of the great merits of youth is that we know we might get knocked down, but we'll hopefully have the energy to get back up. Unfortunately, as time marches on, we see "falling" as beneath us. We expect that we know enough by now and shouldn't have to put ourselves out there anymore. In reality, though, we will only see better outcomes once we are willing to "wobble before we walk" and gather ourselves when we fall (because we will, at times).

Excelling as a leader in any profession requires taking some risks:

- Are there some things that you're doing even now that make you a bit nervous?
- Are you asking yourself, "Am I crazy for trying this? Is this out of line?" If you don't feel a little bit of that along the way, you're probably not risking enough.

Successful people are willing to take some risks. In fact, the most successful people on the planet are willing to do things every day that might make those around them nervous. If you are brave enough to try new things, you undoubtedly will hit the floor more than someone who doesn't. But you're also likely to get over the wobbling, start walking, and maybe even run — all while the competition is still crawling and unwilling to risk failure.

items: meet with his manager or a trusted colleague for some tips and pointers;
study documentation available on the company's internal information hub to be sure he's ready for most anything customers may ask; or
watch some online videos or take some refresher courses on relevant topics in his industry.

body_blocks.text: Coaches often help their players overcome fear of taking the last shot in a game by having them practice that scenario beforehand. The coach sets up a buzzer and creates the conditions of an all-on-the-line, game-defining moment, giving players the opportunity to simulate that kind of pressure.
Fear of Success

Psychologists have found that the fear of success is more common than many of us may realize. Outwardly, we may declare that we want to succeed at something, yet subconsciously, we may be a bit nervous about what will happen if we do succeed. We might have thoughts like:

items: If I succeed, I might get asked to do it again. What if I can't?
What if I succeed and I'm suddenly thrown into a leadership role? What if I can't continue holding up to those standards or consistently succeed at this enormous goal? Will I end up looking foolish?
What if I achieve my goals and people start feeling uncomfortable around me or even reject me?

body_blocks.text: Fear of success can be difficult to understand because most of us tell ourselves we want success. We may not even be aware that, deep down, we would rather not achieve that big goal because we're afraid of what might happen if we do. Strong leaders get themselves ready to respond to both victories and failures. The more they openly discuss it with team members, the better prepared they will be for both wins and losses.
Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.
If we were to suggest to you that failure can be your friend, what do you think we might mean by that? How can failure possibly be a friend if success is your goal?
Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.
Failure Is a Friend That Teaches

Have you ever had a particularly communicative friend? You likely valued your personal connection with them and learned from their trusted wisdom. Great leaders and peak performers understand that failure can actually be that kind of friend. It's not that you'll want to welcome failure, but when it arrives, treat it like a friend. Renew your acquaintance and learn whatever you can from the situation.

There's no advantage to beating yourself up after a failure. Instead, you'll end up psychologically exhausted and less energized to meet future challenges. Your effort is better spent on allowing that failure to be a communicative friend, ready to inform and teach you. Maybe you gave it your all, but you focused on the wrong things. Maybe you had excellent intensity, but a poor strategy that just didn't work. Let that failure be your friend to help discover what to do better next time.

The key to doing this effectively is to minimize the emotional tumult you bring to the analysis. Even if you discover you poorly executed some things that were in your control, acknowledge it and analyze what you can do differently next time. Let the failure motivate and energize you. Unfortunately, good leaders have been known to give up their sport or career out of the pain of having failed in a season. Had they listened to their failure as a friend, they may have discovered they were only a slight adjustment away from a complete reversal of fortunes.
stock-image.jpg
Take Some Risks and Plan to Hit the Floor

You never would have learned to walk if, as a baby, you hadn't stood up and risked falling. You might have fallen and cried, but you gathered yourself and tried again. One of the great merits of youth is that we know we might get knocked down, but we'll hopefully have the energy to get back up. Unfortunately, as time marches on, we see "falling" as beneath us. We expect that we know enough by now and shouldn't have to put ourselves out there anymore. In reality, though, we will only see better outcomes once we are willing to "wobble before we walk" and gather ourselves when we fall (because we will, at times).
Excelling as a leader in any profession requires taking some risks:

items: Are there some things that you're doing even now that make you a bit nervous?
Are you asking yourself, "Am I crazy for trying this? Is this out of line?" If you don't feel a little bit of that along the way, you're probably not risking enough.

body_blocks.text: Successful people are willing to take some risks. In fact, the most successful people on the planet are willing to do things every day that might make those around them nervous. If you are brave enough to try new things, you undoubtedly will hit the floor more than someone who doesn't. But you're also likely to get over the wobbling, start walking, and maybe even run — all while the competition is still crawling and unwilling to risk failure.

video.transcript_text:
Handle Success Like You Handle Failure: Overcoming the Fear of Failure, 
featuring Greg Hiebert 
 
Greg Hiebert, Leadership Coach & Managing Partner 
Pat Summitt spoke these words about the fear of failure: “Too many people opt out and never discover 
their own abilities because they fear failure. They don't understand commitment. When you learn to 
keep fighting in the face of potential failure, it gives you a larger skillset to do what you want to do.”  
A necessary part of reframing failure is to recognize that we have to make failure our friend. And it's 
been put in our path to help us grow and learn. Pat Summitt said, “You can't have continued success 
without experiencing failure.” 
Consider this: as an inventor, Thomas Edison made 9000 unsuccessful attempts at inventing the light 
bulb. And when a reporter asked, “How did it feel to fail 9000 times,” Edison replied, “Why would I feel 
like a failure? And why would I ever give up? I now know definitely over 9000 ways an electric light bulb 
will not work. Success is almost in my grasp.” 
Certainly, failure is painful and causes emotional turmoil, as well as inflicts agonizing pains of guilt, 
remorse, and regret. However, for those who have known true failure and have bounced back from it, 
they understand that failure in life is necessary for success. In fact, if we studied highly successful 
people, we would learn that most of them failed numerous times before understanding the right 
patterns and formulas for success. 
Conrad Hilton, the historical and famous hotel magnate, went bankrupt numerous times before 
succeeding. Walt Disney did the same. It's no surprise that Pat had an excellent analogy about failure 
and winning basketball games. Pat said, “You don't win basketball games on first shots. You win them on 
second and third and fourth shots, and you can't achieve multiple success on first shots either. Follow-
up is the secret to continued success in anything.”  
If you try to go through life without failing at anything, then you're not really living a life at all. Taking 
risks and falling down flat on our faces is part of life. It makes us into who we are. Pat Summitt 
understood the value of failure. How can you use failure to improve your game?

steps.exact_visible_copy:
Page 10 of 15
Leadership Reflections: Learning from Success Isn’t the Same as Celebrating Success

Celebrating success is powerful. Giving your heart and mind a chance to experience the good feelings around winning actually makes it easier to do it again because your brain begins to associate the discipline and potential with those good feelings.

However, learning from success is different than celebrating it. It's important to take time to reflect on your success and learn the lessons associated with it. You may discover you need to work even harder next time to continue high performance. Even successful leaders and peak performers have failed to follow again the pathway that brought them their success because they didn't reflect on the precise steps it took and, unfortunately, they missed the mark next time around.

Think back on a relatively recent achievement or success.

- Beyond the celebration, what can you learn about yourself and your approach from this victory?
- What key takeaways should you reflect upon as you think about this victory?

Reflect on these questions in your workbook.

Treating Success with the Same Respect as Failure

Most of us overreact when we lose and over-celebrate when we win. I used to have a hard time letting go of a defeat. Finally, I had to force myself and our team to move on. We have a rule: We got twenty-four hours to enjoy a win or recover from a loss.
Pat Summitt

Handle Success Like You Handle Failure: Treating Success with the Same Respect as Failure, featuring Greg Hiebert

161.1 KB

Has Success Gone to Your Head? Let’s Hope So

Have you ever received the advice, "Don't let success go to your head?" Typically, someone saying this is suggesting not to take success for granted, become conceited, look down on others, or act superior or unbecoming. From that regard, it's good advice. But we're going to challenge it just for a moment and suggest that success does need to go to your head in one particular way: when you succeed, think about how you got there.

- How did you arrive at success?
- What created the conditions that led to success?

The point here is that success is the reward for hard work, discipline, and focus. Following success, the best leaders stop to consider what it took to get there and what needs to be done to ensure it wasn't luck or coincidence.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

What are some strategies you might use to distinguish between success you and your team genuinely earned and success that primarily came about due to luck or coincidence?

Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

Pinpoint the Sources of Success

While reflecting on a success, it's critical to identify what factors enabled that success.

- Was it your effort?
- Was it the effort of your team members?
- Were there environmental factors or other variables that created the conditions for success?
- If so, are those variables likely to still be at play and is success replicable?

Consider an example:

Suppose you are the head of a department in a company that just experienced an unbelievably fortuitous windfall.

This resulted in a large influx of cash and greatly improved the bottom line for the quarter.

The board of directors reviews the results and congratulates you on a fantastic quarter.

You take a step back and think about what brought about such amazing results.

What if the success came as a result of market conditions or environmental variables outside your control and you just happened to be the one in charge?

That kind of success may or may not be sustainable or replicable.

Gratitude in Success

Earlier, we challenged the adage of not letting success go to one's head solely in the sense that we should reflect deeply upon our success. However, we would be amiss to ignore the face value of the saying as well: there's a certain humility in a leader who looks at success with gratitude.

Have you ever known of someone who entered the winner's circle and failed to give credit to the biggest contributors to that success? They have forgotten, ignored, or taken for granted the myriad of other people and factors that led to their success. When a leader takes all the credit in this way, it brings about two obvious problems:

- The success is less likely to be repeated.
- The people and mechanisms that supported the success may be weakened or even absent next time.

Instead, if a championship coach or successful leader wins big and credits, by name, those who were instrumental to their success, it is deeply motivating, rewarding, and forever memorable to those individuals. This can have a powerful and lasting impact on the organization.

Individual success is a myth. No one succeeds all by themselves.
Pat Summitt

Moments of Reflection: Was It Luck?

It’s a fair question. Granted, the best teams or most successful organizations who work hard find themselves in lucky positions more often than their less successful counterparts. They are usually the ones who stumble upon an innovation because they are awake and active. In other words, luck is out there, but finding it requires kicking over a few stones and trying a few things. However, it's important to ask:

- Is the win due to luck? Is it replicable?
- If the win came down to luck, what can be done to make sure that lucky break happens again?
- How might we move beyond luck and make our success a strategic imperative?

Wow! That Worked Better Than We Thought!

Sometimes success can bring about unexpectedly great results. A logistics company once produced a television ad illustrating a startup company launching their website. Leaders and team members watched their first order come in — followed by 10 more, followed by 100 more, and then followed by 10,000 orders. The mood in the room went from excited to suddenly overwhelmed. Their innovation had worked much better than they thought, and now they had to figure out how to fulfill all those orders with thousands more on the way!

Indeed, sometimes our plans for success work even better than we expect. It would behoove the leaders of the company that launched the successful website to study their win to identify what worked. Identifying the tactical elements of any success helps build exponential success that could be game-changing. This is critical because, unlike the actors in the TV commercial, we want to avoid being ill-prepared for potential success. Plan for success carefully to avoid a future scenario where success ends up overwhelming you. Some companies have ended up bankrupt when their leaders became so overwhelmed with initial success that they were unable to scale and fulfill orders.

When the celebrations end, bring the leaders and team members together to carefully study their success with just as much scrutiny as if it had been a loss. This helps determine the essential moving parts and the replicable elements to inform future planning so that victory is much more than a lucky, episodical, or random event.

video.transcript_text:
Handle Success Like You Handle Failure: Treating Success with the Same Respect 
as Failure, featuring Greg Hiebert 
 
Greg Hiebert, Leadership Coach & Managing Partner 
In 1996, the Lady Vols won the national championship, and, by all outward appearances, they were 
poised to do the same in the 1997 season. But nothing came easy for the Lady Vols that year, and many 
wondered not only if they would not make it to the Final Four, but whether they would make the 
tournament at all. After a soul-crushing loss to UConn in the regular season, Pat addressed the team and 
reminded them they must handle the loss.  
Coach Pat Summitt 
All right, everybody, get your heads up. We’ve got to handle this. We talked about handling success and 
now we're in a position we don't want to be in. We're having to handle failure. 
Greg Hiebert, Leadership Coach & Managing Partner 
While everyone would rather handle success, you must be equally prepared to handle failure – and not 
only handle it but come back from it. 
Of course, the Tennessee Lady Vols are not the only team, organization, or collection of individuals 
who've had to come back from failure. Probably the greatest example of how failure has facilitated great 
success was in the life of Abraham Lincoln, certainly one of our most respected leaders in American 
history. Born into poverty, Lincoln was faced with multiple failures throughout his life. He lost eight 
elections, twice failed in business, endured the loss of loved ones, and led America through its darkest 
time as a nation. Many believe that it was Lincoln's ability to learn from failure that enabled him to be 
the leader America needed at such a difficult time in our history. 
Jamie Holmes, the author of Nonsense: The Power of Not Knowing, suggests that you look at any success 
you encounter in the same way you look at failure. Otherwise, you might miss out on taking new risks 
that could lead to even greater success. Consider Steve Jobs’ decision to launch what would become the 
iPad. Jobs and others at Apple were undoubtedly concerned about plunging ahead with the iPad 
because of the failure of Apple's Newton tablet in the 1990s. In a brilliant move, they recognized that, 
given the existing smartphone market, a touch phone would be more strategic to launch first. This 
would be the perfect vehicle for Apple to learn about and perfect touch devices. So, you guessed it. 
Apple went on to market the iPhone first, and after learning all the lessons that came with developing 
the iPhone, Apple was poised to then release the iPad.  
This example points to a better model for learning, one in which failure and success are on equal footing 
and both trigger further investigation that help us revise our assumptions, models, and theories. I'd ask 
you to consider, to look back on your journey, and to see and reflect on how failure has shaped who you 
are today.

Somehow, we have to make a commitment to get better every day, no matter how successful you were the day before. At Tennessee, our system and our philosophy are designed to narrow our focus. Winning, Losing, and Always Growing

This learning experience has provided you a myriad of Coach Pat Summitt's secrets for leading her teams to uncommon success. That kind of success requires more than any single attribute or variable, but rather a variety of factors working together to make a winning program that stands the test of time.

In this final lesson, we've looked at why and how to Handle Success Like You Handle Failure. This principle says you should:

- Appreciate what brought you success; and
- Anticipate what it will take to maintain that level of success.

Winning and losing tells us a lot, but as we've discussed, they don't tell the complete story. We might reach our potential and still lose. We might fail greatly at being what we want to be and still find a way to win. We might win for a season and quickly fall from the pedestal. Or, we might maintain the status quo in the "muddling middle," refraining from growth.

You can't always control what happens, but you can control how you handle it.
Pat Summitt

Based on what we've covered about handling success like we handle failure, which of the following would you say are critical behaviors if we want to reach the highest levels of success and peak performance? Select all that apply.

- Study our results and evaluate how we're doing.
- Examine our losses to identify what it will take to get to the winner's circle.
- Determine the variables that empower our wins.
- Identify the steps that will help us keep growing and returning to the winner circle again and again, with grace.

Correct
Yes, exactly! These are all important behaviors for the best leaders and peak performers.

video.transcript_text:
Handle Success Like You Handle Failure: Wrap-Up, featuring Doug Buce 
 
Doug Buce, President & CLO, Boing Dynamics, Inc. 
One hallmark of a great leader is their ability to learn from both success and failure. Pat Summitt was 
equally dedicated to analyzing her team's wins, as well as their losses.  
In this module, we have learned three key takeaways about handling success like you handle failure. 
First, we examined why learning from success is often more difficult than learning from failure. Second, 
we learned how extraordinary leaders and innovators like Thomas Edison were able to overcome the 
fear of failure. And finally, in the last segment, we explored how to treat success with the same respect 
as failure. 
Coach Pat Summitt 
I don't handle losing very well at all. I get physically ill when I lose. Losing is not a good thing for me at 
the moment, but it is a great thing for me long-range because it gives me a blueprint for what we need 
to do and do better. 
Doug Buce, President & CLO, Boing Dynamics, Inc. 
You may recall that, in 1996, the Lady Vols won the national championship and by all outward 
appearances, they were poised to do the same in the ‘97 season. But the 1997 season, in many respects, 
was one of Coach Summitt's worst seasons ever. Not only did the Lady Vols lose ten games, but they lost 
to perennial powerhouse programs like Stanford, Old Dominion, UConn and Louisiana Tech. In fact, 
some pundits weren't sure if Tennessee would make the postseason tournament at all. But, in a 
stunning display of grit, determination, and togetherness, the Lady Vols danced through the tournament 
and defeated UConn in the NCAA regionals and went on to defeat Old Dominion for the national 
championship.  
Pat and her Lady Vols learned how to turn failure and losses into wins. Coach Summitt said, “You don't 
win basketball games on the first shots. You win them on second and third and fourth shots. Follow-up 
is the secret to continued success in anything.” Are you giving your all on your second, third and fourth 
shots? As Pat reminds us, you can't have continued success without experiencing failure.

Leadership Reflections: Being Grateful

As you’ve learned throughout this training, there are many differentiators within your control that can make you an effective leader or a high achiever. However, to a great extent, success also requires a little bit of grace. In most cases, our victories come as a result of our hard work; but also due to things in our lives for which we owe some gratitude. Perhaps it is a supportive partner or friend. Maybe it's an investment that someone made in us years ago that continues to pay off. Maybe it's a generous supervisor who overlooked some weaknesses, focused on our strengths, and helped us to grow.

The very best leaders and peak performers practice deep levels of gratitude on the way to high levels of achievement. Take some time to think about the things that you are grateful for that have a significant impact on your ability to achieve today and tomorrow.

• If you won an award for an achievement or leadership and had to give a speech to express gratitude for your success, what would you say?
• What or who would you thank?

As always, reflect from the heart! Reflect on these questions in your workbook.

Congratulations! That concludes this lesson. Please remember to close it before opening another lesson. You can revisit the completed course material at any time.

EXIT LESSON

mini_programs.source_overview: Even the best leaders and peak performers will face some failures along the way. We tend to examine and seek to learn from our failures, but we don't always do the same with our wins. In this module, we consider what might happen if we handle our successes much like our failures so that we can understand and appreciate the people, processes, and factors that contributed to those successes.
